Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 1:

Surat ash-Shu'ara' (The Poets)

In the tafsir of Imam Malik, it is named Surat al-Jami'a (the Comprehensive Surah).

It is narrated in the transmission of Ibn Mardawayh, from Ibn Abbas and Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it is unqualifiedly Meccan. Al-Nahhas narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that it was revealed in Mecca except for five verses at its end, which were revealed in Medina, namely ﴿And the poets—the erring follow them﴾ to its end. This is also related from Ata' and Qatada. Muqatil said: ﴿Is it not a sign for them﴾ and the verse following it is also Medinan. Al-Tabrisi said: the number of its verses is two hundred and twenty-seven according to the Kufan, Syrian and First Medinan counts, and two hundred and twenty-six according to the rest.

The connection of this surah with what precedes it lies in its containing an expansion and elaboration of some of what was mentioned earlier. It also contains consolation for the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in what it includes. Both surahs open with that which indicates the praise of the Noble Qur'an and close with the threat to those who deny it, as is evident.

(In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)

﴿Ta Sin Mim﴾ The discussion of similar letters has preceded, both grammatically and otherwise, and the discussion here is like the discussion there, except that Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b that he said regarding this: the Ta is from Dhu al-Tawl (the Bountiful), the Sin is from al-Quddus (the Holy), and the Mim is from al-Rahman (the Merciful). Hamza, al-Kisai and Abu Bakr inclined the fatha of the Ta. Nafi', as Abu Ali al-Farisi narrated from him in al-Hujja, read it between between (bayn bayn). He did not incline it purely, because the alif is converted from a ya', so if it were inclined toward it, the purpose of the conversion, which is lightening, would be defeated.

Some narrators related from him that he read like the rest of the Seven without any inclination at all, considering that the Ta is a letter of elevation (isti'la') which prevents inclination. Hamza read the nun of Sin with idhhar (clear pronunciation), because it is originally, being one of the names of the disjointed letters, separate from what follows it. The others assimilated it (idgham), since they saw them as connected and in the ruling of a single word, especially according to the view that it is a proper name. Isa read the Mim of "Ta Sin Mim" with a kasra here and in al-Qasas, and this was also reported from Nafi'. In the Mushaf of Abdullah it is written (T S M) without connection, and this is the reading of Abu Ja'far.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 2:

﴿These are the verses of the Clear Book.﴾ "These" is a demonstrative referring to the surah, and the sense of distance in it serves to draw attention to the high rank of what is pointed to in grandeur. By "the Book" is meant the Qur'an, and by "the Clear" (al-mubin) is meant the one whose inimitability is manifest, on the basis that it derives from abana in the sense of baana (to be manifest). The statement is either according to an elided genitive (taqdir mudaf) or on the basis that the attribution in it is metaphorical (majaz 'aqli). It has also been permitted that al-mubin derives from abana in its transitive sense, with its object omitted, i.e., "the rulings of the Sharia" or "the truth." The first is more fitting to the context. The meaning: these are particular verses of the Qur'an, distinguished by a separate name. By explaining that they are a part of it, what is meant is describing them by the sublime qualities for which the whole is renowned. It has been said: the demonstrative refers to the Qur'an, and the feminine form is for agreement with the predicate. By "the Book" is meant the surah, and the meaning is: these are the verses of this Qur'an, composed of the ordinary letters, like the verses of this surah with which challenge was issued. You were unable to produce the like of this surah, so the ruling on those verses is likewise, and this is, as you see, far-fetched.

Among the people is one who interpreted "the Clear Book" as the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), and its description as "clear" is because it makes manifest the states of things to the angels, peace be upon them. But the preferable view is what you have heard first.

[Page 59]

﴿Perhaps you will destroy yourself﴾: that is, killing it out of intense grief, as al-Layth said. He quoted the verse of al-Farazdaq:

Surely the grief that destroys its own soul is for a thing whose decree has taken it out of his hands.

Al-Akhfash and al-Farra' said: It is said, "bakha'a yabkhau bakhan and bukhuwwan," meaning he was destroyed by intense grief. Its root meaning is exertion (al-juhd). From this is the saying of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with both of them, about Umar: "He exhausted the land," meaning he exerted it until he took what was in it of the wealth of kings. Al-Kisa'i said: "He exhausted the land through cultivation," meaning he made it weak by repeatedly ploughing it. Al-Zamakhshari, and al-Mutarrizi following him, said: The origin of bakh' (destroying, slaughtering to the limit) is to cut through the slaughter until one reaches the bikha' (with a kasra on the ba'), which is a vein running along the spine, and that is the furthest limit of slaughter. Ibn al-Athir did not notice this, despite his great research, and there is no harm in that.

Zayd ibn Ali and Qatadah, may Allah have mercy on them, read "bakhi'u nafsika" with the construct form (idafah), contrary to the original rule. The original rule for the active participle (ism al-fa'il) when it fulfils the conditions for governing (al-'amal, i.e. grammatical government over its object) is that it governs, as Sibawayh indicated in al-Kitab. Al-Kisa'i said: governing and the construct form are equal. Abu Hayyan held that the construct form is better than governing. Perhaps in a place like this the word "la'alla" (perhaps) expresses the speaker's concern. Since this is impossible with regard to Allah, Glorified is He, they made it refer to the addressee. And since it also did not occur from him, they said: the intended meaning is a command to him, due to the denial implied by the context of the speech. So it is as if it were said: "Be concerned for yourself lest you kill it through grief and regret over what has escaped you of your people's acceptance of Islam."

Al-Askari said: In a place like this, it is placed in the position of a prohibition (nahy), and the meaning is: "Do not destroy yourself." It was also said: it is placed in the position of an interrogative (istifham), and the implied meaning is: "Are you destroying yourself?" Something similar is reported from Ibn Atiyyah, except that he said: the intended meaning is denial, i.e., "Do not be one who destroys himself."

﴿That they will not become believers﴾: this is the reason for the destroying. Since it cannot be that their not becoming believers in the future, as the apparent meaning of the speech indicates, is the cause of it, because there is no simultaneity (al-muqaranah), and the cause should be simultaneous with the effect, they estimated "khifata" (for fear that), and said: for fear that they will not believe in this Clear Book. Some of the eminent scholars did not make that estimate, on the basis that what is intended is their continuance in not accepting faith in this Book, because the word "kana" (was/is) indicates continuance, and the future form is for its emphasis, and the continuation of the negation is intended. It is also permitted that "kana" means "to be valid/correct," and the meaning is: because their faith is impossible. The view that the verb "kana" was brought for the sake of the rhyme (al-fasilah) is nothing.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 4:

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿If We will﴾ and so on, is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) giving the reason for the command or prohibition concerning his solicitude for himself (ﷺ), or the prohibition against al-bakh' (excessive grief that destroys oneself). The object of the will is omitted; according to the well-known view it is what the meaning of the conditional clause indicates. It is also permitted that it be indicated by what precedes, i.e., "If We will their faith, ﴿We would send down upon them from the heaven a sign﴾" compelling them to faith and forcing them to it, as He uprooted the mountain over the Children of Israel. The fronting of the two adverbial phrases before the direct object, as has been mentioned many times, serves to give importance to what is fronted and to build suspense toward what is delayed.

Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of Harun from him, read «if He wills, He sends down» in the third person, the pronoun referring to Him, Exalted is He. In some of the codices there is: "If We willed, We would have sent down..." ﴿So their necks would remain humbly submissive to it﴾, i.e., compliant. It is a predicate concerning "the necks." The necks acquired the masculine gender and the attributes of rational beings from the genitive noun attached to them, so the predicate concerning them was given in the plural form for those who reason, as Abu Hayyan transmitted from some of the leading scholars of Arabic. The restriction of permissibility of such usage to poetry, as al-Sirafi related from the grammarians, is something the verifiers did not accept, among them Abu al-'Abbas, and he is among those who explained the verse according to that.

It is also permitted that this is because they were described with an action that can only be intended by a rational being, namely submission, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾. It is also permitted that the speech contains an omitted modifier, and it was observed after its omission, i.e., "the owners of their necks." It is not hidden that this estimate is weak with the attachment to their pronoun.

Al-Zamakhshari said:
The original wording is: "their necks would remain humbly submissive to it," so "the necks" was inserted to specify the locus of submission, because before reflection it appears, from the manifestation of submission in the neck through bowing and the like, that it is the one submitting, not its owner. The plural was left after the insertion as it was before. Al-Kisa'i said: "Submissive" (khadi'in) is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the pronoun in the genitive, not to "the necks."

Abu al-Baqa' criticized him, saying: "This is far-fetched in verification, because 'submissive' would then be going as a modifier of other than the subject of 'remained' (zallat), so it would require an explicit pronoun for the subject, so it should have been: 'submissive, they' (khadi'in hum). Understand this."

Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and al-Akhfash said: "al-a'naq" means groups; it is said: "He came in a neck (una'q) of the people," i.e., a group. The meaning is: "their groups remained," i.e., their totality.

It was said: what is meant by them is the leaders and foremost ones, figuratively, just as they are called "heads" and "chests," so the ruling applies to others by a stronger reasoning. The apparent sense of their words is that applying "neck" to a group absolutely, whether leaders or not, is literal. Al-Tibi mentioned from al-Asas that among metaphorical usages is: "A neck of the people came to me," for a preceding group, and "They came as envoys, envoy after envoy, and in necks, neck after neck, the speech taking some of it by the necks of others." Then he said: It is understood from the contrast of "envoy after envoy" with "neck after neck" that in applying "necks" to groups there is consideration of the gathered form, so the meaning is: "they remained submissive, gathered in submission, agreed upon it, none of them departing from it."

Isa and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read «submissive» (khadi'a) in the feminine singular, and it is apparent under all the views concerning the necks; however, when what is meant by them is the plural of "neck" in the sense of the bodily part, the attribution to it is figurative. The clause "zallat" in both readings has it as a relative or descriptive element, and the fronting is for the sake of the rhyme-final (fasila), or something similar, not for restriction. "Zallat" is conjoined to "nunazzil." One of the two verbs must be interpreted as being of the same type as the other, because although it is valid to conjoin a past verb to a present one, here it is not appropriate: the past cannot be consequent upon the future with the consequential or causal fa', and that is not conceivable, while the reverse is conceivable. By interpreting one of the two verbs this objection is removed. However, some scholars chose to interpret "zallat" as "tazull" (present), and the departure from it seems intended to indicate, through the past tense, the swiftness of the effect, and that the sending down of the verse, given the strength of its authority and the speed with which what was mentioned follows from it, is as though it had already occurred. Others interpreted "nunazzil" as "anzalna" (past), and perhaps its placement there is to evoke the image of the sending down of that great sign that compels faith, and the submission of their necks at that moment in the mind of the hearer, so that he may marvel at it. So reflect.

Talha read «fa-tazulla» with the disjunction of the assimilation (fakk al-idgham) and the jazm. Al-Hariri, in Durrat al-Ghawwas, deemed disjunction of assimilation in such a case weak, while the author of al-Kashf preferred the reading on the ground that it is more eloquent in conveying the past meaning you have just heard.

Furthermore, the apparent view is that the sending down of this sign did not in fact take place, because the sunnah of God Exalted is to impose belief upon people without compulsion. Yes, if it is said that what is meant is "a sign that humiliates them," as was related from Qatada, it is permissible to say that this did occur. Perhaps what was related from Ibn 'Abbas, as in al-Bahr and al-Kashshaf, namely his saying: "This verse was revealed concerning us and the Banu Umayya: we shall have dominion over them, and their necks will be humbled after hardship, and abasement will befall them after honor," refers to this. And from Abu Hamza al-Thumali: that the verse is a voice heard from the sky in the middle of Ramadan, and unmarried women are brought out of their houses for it. This is a view that the sending down takes place later, and it seems that this was in the time of the Mahdi, may Allah be pleased with him. And there is something in the soundness of the traditions mentioned concerning the heart. And Allah Exalted knows best.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 5:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there does not come to them any reminder from the Most Merciful, newly revealed, except that they turn away from it﴾, is an explanation of the severity of their obstinacy and their failure to desist from their disbelief and denial, apart from the compelling sign that was mentioned; it is an emphasis on diverting the Messenger of Allah, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, from being eager for their Islam.

The first "min" (from) is extra (zaʼida), to emphasize generality. It is also permissible for it to be partitive (tabʻidiyya). The prepositional phrase and its object are connected to a omitted element, which is an attribute of an implied noun, as we will indicate, God willing. The second "min" is for the beginning of the limit (ibtida' al-ghaya), used figuratively, and it is connected to (yatihim) or to an omitted element which is an attribute of (dhikr). In either case, there is in it an indication of its excellence and nobility, and of the abomination of what they did to it.

The mention of the title "Mercy" is to intensify their wickedness and to magnify their crime, for turning away from what comes to them from His presence, exalted and high, absolutely, is hideous and ugly; and turning away from what comes to them by the requirement of His mercy, exalted is He, for the pure benefit of them, is even more abominable and uglier. That is: no reminder or admonition, or portion of the Qur'an, comes to them from Him, mighty and majestic, by the requirement of His vast mercy, renewing its revelation as wisdom and benefit require, except that they renew their turning away from it and persist in what they were upon. The exception is a truncated exception from the most general of states; its place is the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object of (yatihim), with or without the implied "qad", according to the well-known difference of opinion. That is: no reminder comes to them in any state except in the state of their turning away from it.

"Then they have indeed denied": that is, they denied the Reminder (al-dhikr) that comes to them with an explicit denial, accompanied by mockery of it. They did not content themselves with turning away from it, for they variously called it sorcery (sihr), at other times "the fables of the ancients" (asatir al-awwalin), and at still other times poetry (shi'r).

Some of the virtuosos (al-fudala') said: That is, they completed their denial, and their denial, together with the arrival of what necessitates ceasing from the repeated coming of the Reminder, was like their denial the first time. To draw attention to this, it is expressed by a form that denotes an occurrence that has happened (al-hadith) and indicates the consideration of mockery accompanying it, as is alluded to by the words of the Exalted: ﴿So there will certainly come to them the news of that which they used to mock﴾, because it requires the prior occurrence of mockery. It has also been said that this (the expression) points to the denial and turning away indicating mockery. The meaning of "news" (anba') of that is what will befall them of punishments, both hastened and deferred, and everything that is to come is near. It has been said: it is the punishment of the Day of Badr or the Day of Resurrection, and the first is preferable. It is expressed as "news" because it is among what the Mighty Qur'an has informed of, or because by witnessing it they will come to know the true state of the Qur'an, just as they come to know the hidden conditions by hearing reports. In this there is an amplification of it, for the word naba' is applied to a weighty report that has a great impact. That is: there will certainly come to them, without doubt, the fulfilment of what they used to mock before, without having reflected upon its circumstances and considered it.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 26, verse 7:**

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Have they not looked at the earth?﴾ are an explanation of their turning away from the cosmic signs (*al-ayat al-takwiniyya*), following the explanation of their turning away from the revealed signs (*al-ayat al-tanziliyya*). The *hamza* (ء) here is for rebuking denial (*al-inkar al-tawbikhi*), and the *waw* (و) is for coordination (*al-ʿatf*) with an implied element required by the context. The meaning is: "Do they persist in what they are upon of disbelief in Allah the Exalted and denial of what calls them to believe in Him, Mighty and Majestic, and have they not looked at the wonders of the earth, which restrain them from that and call them to belief in Him, Exalted?"

Abu al-Su'ud, after making the *hamza* a denial and the *waw* a coordination with an implied element required by the context, said: "That is: Have they done what they did of turning away from the signs, denying them and mocking them, and have they not looked at the wonders of the earth, which restrain them from what they did and call them to turn toward what they turned away from?" End of quotation.

This clearly indicates that the verse is connected to what precedes it, from the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And there does not come to them﴾ etc. This is close in terms of wording. However, it has the issue that looking at the wonders of the earth does not clearly appear to restrain them from denying that the Qur'an was sent down from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, nor to call them to turn toward Him. Ibn Kamal said: "The implied meaning is: Did they not reflect upon the wonders of His power, Exalted, and not look?" End of quotation.

Apparently, according to this view, the verse begins a new statement, so understand this. It has been said that it is an explanation of their denial of the Return (*al-maʿad*), following the explanation of their denial of the Origin (*al-mabda'*) and their disbelief in Him, Mighty and Majestic. The coordination here is also with an implied element, and the implied meaning is: "Did they deny the Resurrection, and not look at the wonders of the earth, which restrain them from denying that?" The first view is preferable and more evident. In any case, the statement involves an omitted noun (*hadhf mudaf*), as was indicated, and it was permitted that by "the earth" is meant its wonders, metaphorically (*majaz*).

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿How many of every noble pair have We caused to grow therein?﴾ are a resumptive statement (*istinaf*) explaining the signs in the earth that restrain from disbelief and call to belief.

**كَمْ** (*kam*) here is informative (*khabariyya*), in a position of accusative object governed by what follows it, and it indicates abundance. **كُلٍّ** (*kull*) was brought with it to indicate comprehensiveness and totality. So it indicates that the abundance of individuals of each kind is a kind (of wonder). The meaning then is: We caused to grow therein a great quantity of every kind, with **مِن** (*min*) being partitive (*tabʿidiyya*); or the abundance of kinds, and the meaning is: We caused to grow therein a great quantity which is every kind, with **مِن** being explicative (*bayaniyya*). In either case there is no repetition between the two. It may be said that the meaning is: Did they not look at the earth itself, which is one nature, how We made it a place of growth for many plants of differing natures? In that case there is no omitted noun and no metaphor, and the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿How many We caused to grow therein﴾ etc. are a substitution of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*) in meaning. This is a good view, so understand it, so that you do not think it refers back to what came before and needs the omission or metaphor it required.

The **زَوْج** (*zawj*, pair) is the kind, as we have indicated. Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) mentioned that everything in the world is a pair in that it has some opposite, or some like, or some composition; indeed it does not separate from some composition in some respect. The **كَرِيم** (*karim*, noble) of anything is that which is pleasing and praiseworthy in it. From this is the saying:

*"Until he cleaves the ranks by his nobility"*

for he meant by his nobility that he was pleasing in his courage.

The word **كَرِيم** is an attribute of **زَوْج** (pair), meaning: of every pair of abundant benefits. It admits of being restrictive (*takhsis*) or clarifying (*tawdih*). The aspect of the first is that it indicates what other things indicate concerning the Necessary Being, Exalted, and additionally that it indicates a blessing which also restrains them from what they are upon. The aspect of the second is an alert that He, Exalted, did not cause anything to grow except that there is a benefit in it, as His words indicate: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is in the earth﴾. In any case, the apparent view is that animals are not included in the generality of "that which grows." Some have held that they are included, on the basis that their creation from the earth is a causing-to-grow for them, as His words indicate: ﴿And Allah caused you to grow from the earth as a growth﴾.

From al-Sha'bi there is an explicit statement that humans are included in it. It is narrated from him that he said: "People are from the growth of the earth. Whoever goes to Paradise is noble, and whoever goes to the Fire is the opposite of that."

[p. 62]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 8:

﴿Indeed, in that﴾ — that is, the growing (al-inbat) or the place where things grow (al-manbat) — ﴿is surely a sign﴾, a great sign indicating the matters of His — exalted and majestic is He — in which it is obligatory for them to believe. How elegant is what has been said about the narcissus:

Reflect upon the gardens of roses, and look at the traces of what the Sovereign has made.

Eyes of silver, gazing, ∗∗∗ upon whose lids is refined gold,

Upon stems of chrysolite, bearing witness ∗∗∗ that God has no partner.

﴿And most of them were not believers﴾. It has been said: that is, this was in the knowledge of God, exalted is He. This was objected to on the basis that causation is understood from the context, so that His knowledge, exalted is He, is not the cause of their non-belief, since knowledge follows the known and not the reverse. It was answered that the meaning of His knowledge, exalted is He, following the known is that His knowledge, glorified is He, in eternity, of a specific known object, is contingent and follows its quiddity (mahiyya). The meaning is that the particularity of the knowledge and its distinction from the other knowledges is only by virtue of its being knowledge of this quiddity. As for the existence of the quiddity in what is still to come, it follows His eternal knowledge, which follows its quiddity. The meaning is that, since He, exalted is He, knew it in eternity with this particularity, it necessarily follows that it be realized and exist in what is still to come in the same way. Thus their very dying in disbelief and their not believing is something followed by His eternal knowledge, and its occurrence follows it.

It is related from Sibawayh that (kana) is a connective particle (silah), and the meaning is: ﴿and most of them are believers﴾. So the intent is a report about their state in reality, not in God's eternal knowledge. Shaykh al-Islam approved this and said: it is the most fitting for the context of explaining their obstinacy and their extremity in stubbornness and rebellion, along with the binding of the grounds for belief from His side, exalted and majestic is He. As for attributing their disbelief to His knowledge, exalted is He, it may give rise to the impression that they are excused in it outwardly, and then it would be necessary to establish the absence of excuse by what is hidden from the discerning scholars. The meaning according to the additional sense: ﴿and most of them were not believers﴾ despite the magnitude of the sign that necessitates belief, due to the extent of their persistence in disbelief and error and their immersion in deviation and ignorance.

And it is permissible — according to the analogy of what has passed from some of the eminent scholars — regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they not become believers?﴾ to say: if (kana) is for continuity and is taken after negation, then the intent is the continuity of the negation of belief in most of them despite the magnitude of the sign that necessitates their belief, and in this there is what there is of condemnation of their state.

And this meaning — although it is achieved on the assumption of dropping (kana), by considering the continuity which the nominal sentence conveys after negation as well — nevertheless distinguishes between the two continuities after taking kana into account in terms of strength and weakness, so reflect. And the attribution of non-belief to most of them is because among them are some who were not like that.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 9:

﴿And indeed your Lord is the Almighty﴾ i.e., the Overpowering over everything He wills among matters, among which is taking vengeance upon these disbelievers, ﴿the Most Merciful﴾ i.e., the one who is most profound in mercy. For this reason He gives them respite and does not seize them suddenly for what they have dared to do of great offenses that necessitate various kinds of punishment. Or: ﴿the Almighty﴾ in His vengeance upon those who disbelieve, ﴿the Most Merciful﴾ toward those who repent and believe. Or: ﴿the Almighty﴾ in His vengeance upon the disbelievers, ﴿the Most Merciful﴾ toward you, by decreeing that whoever believes in you will be (granted success) if these people do not believe. And the mention of the attribute of lordship (rubbubiyyah) together with its addition to his pronoun ﷺ carries, of honoring him (peace be upon him) and the hidden promise to him (may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace), what is not hidden. And the precedence of ﴿al-'Aziz﴾ is because what precedes it is more evident in showing power, or because it is more indicative of warding off harms, which is more important than bringing about benefits.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 10:

﴿And when your Lord called out to Moses﴾ is a resumptive statement (kalam mustaʾnaf) that establishes the wretched state of those people, and also consoles the Prophet (ﷺ), but with another kind of consolation, according to what has been said. "Idh" (when) is in the accusative as an object of an implied verb addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), coordinated with what precedes it as the coordination of one narrative with another. The implied verb, according to some, is: "Remember, within yourself, the time of His, the Exalted's, calling out to your brother Moses (peace be upon him), and what befell him with his people of denial despite the manifest signs and the shining miracles; so that you may know that the denial of nations toward their prophets is not the first bottle broken, nor the first scroll unfolded, so that the matter becomes easier for you and your soul finds rest from the anxiety you are in."

According to Shaykh al-Islam: "Remember to your people the time of His, the Exalted's, calling out to Moses (peace be upon him), and admonish them with what befell the people of Pharaoh because of their denial of him (peace be upon him), as a deterrent for them from the denial they are upon, and a warning lest there befall them the like of what befell them, until it becomes clear to you that they are in the utmost obstinacy and persistence; the seizing of their likes among the wicked deniers does not deter them, and admonition and warning do not affect them." This implied verb suits the opening of the following narrative, namely His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And recite to them the report of Abraham﴾. The first suits the narratives introduced by "kadhdhabat" (they denied), according to what has been said.

The more evident view to me is to imply "Remember" to your people, because of the clear requirement of "And recite to them" for it. We do not accept that those narratives introduced by "kadhdhabat" require the implied "remember" within yourself. The matter of suitability is shared; and even if its exclusivity to that is granted, it does not withstand the stated requirement.

Yes, the more evident view is that the aspect of consolation through what was mentioned is that he (peace be upon him) is not an innovation among the messengers, nor is his people an innovation among peoples in denial despite the manifest signs and shining miracles. The command to mention that to them has included the command to console oneself with it in the most complete manner, so reflect.

In any case, the aspect of directing the command to remember toward the time, although the intent is the matter within it, has been discussed repeatedly. It has been said that this implied verb is coordinated with another implied verb, i.e., "Take the signs," or "Await the arrival of the reports, and remember." This is an artificiality for which there is no need.

It has been said: "Idh" is an adverb governing "qala" (said) afterward, but this is not so. The meaning of "nada" (called out) is "da'a" (called), and it has been said: "amara" (commanded). ﴿That come﴾, i.e., with "an" (that) — "an" being verbal (masdariyyah) with the preposition dropped from it — or, meaning: "come," with "an" being explanatory (mufassirah).

﴿the wicked people﴾ by disbelief and sins, and the enslavement of the Children of Israel, and the slaughter of their sons. This is not the beginning of what is recorded within the scope of the calling out; rather, it is what is detailed in Surah Ta-Ha in His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Indeed, I am your Lord﴾ up to His, the Glorified's, saying: ﴿That We may show you of Our greater signs﴾. The Noble Qur'an's practice is to present what occurred in a single narrative through various statements in diverse expressions and styles, as the context requires which expressions are used therein, as has been verified in its proper place.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 11:

﴿The people of Pharaoh﴾ is an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan) to "the wrongdoing people" (al-qawm al-zalimin). It is brought for the purpose of indicating that they are a paradigm (ʿalam) in wrongdoing, as if the meaning of "the wrongdoing people" and its explanation is "the people of Pharaoh." Abu al-Baqa' said: it is a substitute (badal) from it. Abu Hayyan preferred the first view, on the grounds that it better fulfils the demands of eloquence (haqq al-balagha), because of its indication of what you have heard. Perhaps the limitation to "the people" is because it is known that Pharaoh is more deserving of what has been mentioned, and he has been singled out in some passages to indicate this. It has also been permitted to say: "the people of Pharaoh" is inclusive of him in the way that "the children of Adam" includes Adam, peace be upon him. ﴿Will they not fear (Allah)?﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) with an implied "saying" (taqdir al-qawl), i.e.: go to them saying to them, "Will they not fear (Allah)?"

Abdullah ibn Muslim ibn Yasar, Shaqiq ibn Salama, Hammad ibn Salama, and Abu Qilaba read it with the second-person ta' (taʾ al-khitab), i.e. ﴿tattaqun﴾. In such cases both direct address (khitab) and third-person address (ghayba) are permissible, so one says: "Say to Zayd: 'You give ʿAmr such-and-such'" and "He gives ʿAmr such-and-such." It has also been read with a kasra on the nun, both with direct address and third-person address. The original form is "yattaqunani," then one of the two nuns was deleted because of the convergence of two identical letters, and the ya' of the first person was deleted, being sufficed by the kasra.

Moses' saying that, peace be upon him, is by way of speaking on behalf of Him, exalted and majestic, and is similar to what is in the saying of the Most High: ﴿And when My servants ask you about Me, indeed I am near﴾ (Q 2:186). It is as if it were said: go to them saying My word to them: "Will you not fear Me?" Al-Zamakhshari said: it is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf), which Allah, exalted and majestic, followed by sending him to them for warning and for condemning them with wrongdoing, in amazement at Moses, peace be upon him, at their condition, which was shocking in its wrongdoing and oppression, and at their security regarding consequences and their lack of fear and caution regarding the days of Allah, exalted and majestic. The reading in direct address is according to the manner of iltifat toward them, confronting them and striking their faces with denial and anger against them. Carrying this in speaking to the one sent to them has the sense of conducting it in their presence and casting it into their ears, because he is its conveyer, reporter, and spreader among the people, so it does not matter that they are literally absent at the time of the address. In it there is further exhortation to piety for whoever reflects and contemplates. End of quote.

As for the resumption (istiʾnaf) in it, it has been said to be explanatory (bayani) with the implied question: "Why this command?" It has also been said to be grammatical (nahwi), since there is no need for this question after mentioning them under the title of wrongdoing. This was answered by the consideration (ʿinaya). Perhaps what we have mentioned is quicker in coming to understanding.

He also said: It is possible that ﴿Will they not fear (Allah)?﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (al-zalimin), i.e.: they wrong while not being mindful of Allah, the Most High, and His punishment, exalted and majestic. So the interrogative hamza of denial was placed before the circumstance, indicating denial of the absence of piety and rebuke for it, so as to convey the denial of wrongdoing by way of priority, for the benefit of bringing this circumstance is to signal that the absence of piety is what emboldened them to wrongdoing.

Abu Hayyan criticized this, saying it is a gross error, because it involves, together with separating the governing element from the governed by a foreign element, the necessity of the preceding of the hamza governing what follows it. It was answered by denying that the intervening element is foreign, and that the hamza is given latitude, and this is as you see. It was also permitted for ﴿Will they not fear Me?﴾ with the yaʾ of the third person and kasra on the nun to mean "Will you not, O people, fear Me," like His saying, the Most High: ﴿Will they not prostrate?﴾ (Q 27:25). Then "alla" is a single word of exhortation, and "ya" of calling whose alif fell away because of the meeting of two unvoweled letters, the addressee and what follows it being a verb in the imperative. The dropping of the two alifs would be contrary to analogy. It is not hidden that this is a distant interpretation, and that the apparent meaning is that "alla" is for an exhortation implying urging toward piety in all the readings.

﴿He said﴾ is a clarifying resumptive clause (istiʾnaf bayani), as if it had been asked: "Then what did Musa, peace be upon him, say?" So it was answered: "He said, humbly beseeching Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

Page 65

﴿My Lord, indeed I fear that they will deny me﴾ from the very beginning of the matter.

﴿And my chest tightens, and my tongue does not speak freely﴾ are conjoined to the predicate of (inna) (indeed). This indicates that he, peace be upon him, had three impediments: fear of being denied, tightness of chest, and the inability of his tongue to speak freely. The apparent meaning is that the last two were established in themselves and were not consequences of the denial, so that they would fall under the fear. However, al-A'raj, Talhah, Isa, Zayd ibn Ali, Abu Haywa, and Za'idah from al-A'mash, and Ya'qub read both verbs in the accusative (naşb), conjoined to (they deny me). This indicates that both fall under the fear. Also, since the basic principle is the agreement of the two qira'at (recitations), it has been said that they are derived from that, as if it were said: "My Lord, I fear their denying me, and my chest tightens from being affected by it, and my tongue does not speak freely from the prison of the impediment and the fetter of inability, through the contraction of the animal spirit by which the muscles move, which occurs when the chest is tight and the heart is distressed." The meaning is that a stammering of the tongue occurs to him, peace be upon him, because of this, just as is observed in many eloquent people when their grief becomes intense and their hearts constrict, so that their tongues falter and they can barely express their intended meaning. This holds if we say that this statement was after his supplication, peace be upon him, for the untying of the knot and God Most High's answering him by removing it entirely. Or the meaning is an increase in what he, peace be upon him, already had, if we say that it was before the supplication or after it, but the knot was not removed entirely; rather, only that part of it which prevented his speech from being understood was loosened, so his speech became understandable while a slight impediment remained.

Some have said: there is no need for the discussion of derivation; rather, both fall under the fear through conjunction with (they deny me), as in the accusative reading. This is based on what al-Biqa'i permitted, that (akhafu, I fear) may mean (a'lamu, I know, or azunnu, I think), so that (an) is a lightened form of the heavy (anna), because it occurs after a word indicating knowledge or supposition. On this view, (akhafu) in the accusative reading must be kept in its apparent meaning, so that it is not contradicted and the unity of outcome is maintained. Abu Amr al-Dani relayed from al-A'raj that he read (yadiqu) with the accusative and (yanṭaliqu) with the nominative. The discussion of this can be understood from what has been mentioned. In any case, what is meant by tightness of chest is tightness of heart, and it was expressed in this way for emphasis; what is intended is distress.

Then this statement from him, peace be upon him, is not a clinging to the skirts of excuses, nor an evasion of carrying out the command of His Majesty, the Mighty and Glorious, and receiving it with hearing and obedience. Rather, it is a preparation of an excuse in requesting help for him in carrying out the command and establishing the call in the most complete manner, for what he mentioned may perhaps cause the disruption of the call and the dispersal of the proof. This request includes His Exalted saying: ﴿So send [word] to Harun﴾. It is as if he said: "Send Gabriel, peace be upon him, to Harun, and make him a prophet, support me through him, and strengthen my arm with him," because in sending to him, peace be upon him, all these purposes are achieved. But this has been elaborated in Surat al-Qasas, and here it has been suffice with the principle regarding what is contained within it.

Among the evidence that the meaning is as stated, and that the phrase (So send [word]) is not an intervening parenthetical between the first and the fourth (what is meant is (and they have a charge against me) and so on), is that it is connected to them, and if it were a parenthetical it would have been postponed. Commanding him to go does not necessarily entail what he, peace be upon him, requested. The estimate of the object of (send) as we have indicated has been held by more than one scholar, and some estimated it as an angel, since there is no certainty that he, peace be upon him, at that time knew that Gabriel, peace be upon him, was the messenger of God, the Mighty and Glorious, to whomever He, glorified be He, would make a prophet from among mankind.

In a report, God Most High sent Musa to Harun, and Harun was in Egypt when God Most High sent Musa as a prophet in al-Sham.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi, who said: Musa, peace be upon him, set out toward his family and traveled with them toward Egypt until he arrived there at night. He became a guest of his mother, without her knowing who they were, on a night when they were eating al-Tafayshal (a kind of plant), so he was lodged at the side of the house. Harun, peace be upon him, came, and when he saw his guest he asked his mother about him, and she informed him that he was a guest. He invited him, and he ate with him. When they sat, they talked, and Harun asked him: "Who are you?" He said: "I am Musa." Each of them rose toward the other and embraced him. When they recognized each other, Musa said to him: "O Harun, go with me to Pharaoh, for God Most High has sent us to him." Harun said: "I hear and obey." Their mother then rose, cried out, and said: "I beseech you by God Most High not to go to Pharaoh, lest he kill you." But they both refused, and they set out toward him at night. The report continues, and God Most High knows best its authenticity.

[66]

That is, the consequence (tabi'ah) of a sin, so the modifier (mudaf) was omitted and the modified noun (mudaf ilayh) was put in its place. Alternatively, the word "sin" was used to name the consequence figuratively (majaz), by a causal relation (ʿalaqah al-sababiyyah). What is meant is the killing of the Copt, the baker of Pharaoh, with the blow he struck him. The story is related at length in more than one place. Calling it a sin is according to their assumption, and this is indicated by the words of Allah the Exalted to them: ﴿so I fear﴾ that if I come to them alone, ﴿they will kill me﴾ because of that. His purpose, peace be upon him, in this was to ward off the calamity, out of fear that the interest of the message would be lost and its affair would not spread, as is fitting for the station of the Ulu al-ʿAzm (the Messengers of firm resolve). They guard against such things, just as the Prophet (ﷺ) used to do, until there was revealed to him: ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾. Perhaps the truth is that the intention to preserve one's own life does not contradict their station.

In al-Kashshaf, it is said that he, peace be upon him, feared being killed before conveying the message. Its apparent meaning is that he, even though he was a prophet, did not know that he would remain alive until he conveyed the message. Some scholars held this view, since it is possible that he was only commanded to do so on condition of empowerment (tamkin, being enabled by Allah), and since Allah may abrogate (naskh) that ruling before it takes effect.

Al-Tibi said: The more correct view is that the prophets, peace be upon them, when Allah charges them with conveying the message, know that He will empower them and that they will remain alive until that time. But this is clearly open to objection. In al-Kashf, it is said that according to both views, the words of al-Zamakhshari "he feared... etc." are valid, because that occurred before the prophetic commission (istinba', being entrusted with prophethood), since the call was its preliminary stage. I do not think you would say this.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 15:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He said, "No! So go, both of you, with Our signs"﴾ is a response by him (peace be upon him) to the two requests, since He, Mighty and Majestic, promised him the removal of the enemies' harm by restraining him from fear. He joined his brother to him by saying "go" (idhhaba, in the dual). It is as if He had said to him, Mighty and Majestic: "Be restrained from fear of being killed, for you are under Our eyes. So go, you and your brother Aaron, whom you requested." The arrangement (al-nashr, the order in which items are mentioned after a previous list) came in reverse order of the folding (al-laff, the earlier mention of two items) for the sake of singling out what was mentioned first, namely Moses (peace be upon him). The apparent context requires that Aaron was not present, so in the address there is a case of prevalence (taghlib, giving precedence to one of two related parties in a grammatical form). The verb is coordinated with the verb implied by "No!" (kalla), as we have indicated. It has been said that the fa' is an explanatory fa' (fa-fasiha), and by "the signs" is meant the miracles with which God Exalted sent them both, and in this is a hint that they repel what he fears.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, We are with you, listening﴾ is a justification for the restraint from fear, and an added consolation to them both by guaranteeing complete protection and support, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I am with you both; I hear and I see﴾. The address is to Moses and Aaron and those who follow them from the Children of Israel, so the statement includes good news by alluding to the elevation of their affair and the people's following of them. Sibawayh (d. c. 180 AH) held that it is addressed to the two of them (peace be upon them), and that because of their nobility and greatness before God Exalted they were treated in the address as a plural. This was objected to on the grounds that what comes after and before it contains the dual pronoun.

It has also been said that it is addressed to the two of them (peace be upon them) and to Pharaoh, and this is considered because the one promised was in his presence. If you wish, add to that the people of Pharaoh as well. It was objected that general accompaniment, meaning the accompaniment of knowledge, is not specific to anyone, based on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nor is there less than that or more except that He is with them﴾. Special accompaniment, which is the accompaniment of compassion and support, does not befit a disbeliever even by way of prevalence. It was answered that the particularity of the accompaniment does not necessarily have to be by what was mentioned, but rather by another aspect, namely the rescue of one of two disputants from the other by supporting the one in the right and avenging the one in the wrong. In any case, the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is in the position of the predicate, because ﴿listening﴾ is a second predicate, or the predicate is ﴿listening﴾ and the adverbial phrase is connected to it, or it is connected to an omitted element that occurred as a circumstantial clause (hal) from its pronoun. Its fronting is for emphasis, or for the sake of the closing rhyme (al-fasila), or for specification, based on the view that by accompaniment is meant listening on His part, Mighty and Majestic. This is a metaphor for hearing, chosen for emphasis, because it implies the reception of perception, and this is something from which God Exalted is exempt, whether by a sense organ or not. So what has been said falls away, namely that hearing in reality is perception through a sense organ. If by it is meant the absolute perception, then listening is like it, so there is no need for a figurative usage in it. Several scholars went to this figurative usage.

Some of them said: ﴿Indeed, We are with you, listening﴾ is a sentence in the form of an allegorical metaphor (al-isti'arah al-tamthiliyyah, a metaphor presented as an extended image). He, Glorified is He, depicted His state, Mighty and Majestic, by the state of a powerful person who has attended the dispute of a people and listens to what passes between them, in order to aid his allies and make them victorious over their enemies, as an exaggeration in the promise of help. In this case, none of its individual words is used figuratively, and ﴿listening﴾ is not used absolutely of Him, Exalted is He, so there is no need to make it mean "hearing." Except that it may be said that in the borrowed source it is likewise, because the intended meaning is hearing, not listening, which may not reach him. But this is as you see.

It was permitted that ﴿Indeed, We are with you﴾ alone be an allegorical depiction of His state, Mighty and Majestic, in His support and aid by the state of the one mentioned, and that listening be a figurative usage for hearing. Its apparent meaning, because it was not applied to Him, Glorified, in the way hearing was, is like a clue, though it is a figurative usage. The clue in reality is rational, namely the impossibility of His presence, exalted is His majesty, in a place. Based on this, it must be said that the listening mentioned in the framing of the allegory is not the same as what occurs in the noble text, but rather it is one of the necessary implications of the presence of the judgment in the dispute. This is far-fetched.

Furthermore, what they mentioned, although it is based on making the address to Moses, Aaron and Pharaoh, can be applied to making it to the two of them (peace be upon them) and those who follow them, or to the two of them alone too, with little effort. So understand, and do not be heedless.

Some of them claimed that accompaniment and listening are in their literal senses and there is no allegory, and the meaning is that Our angels are with you, listening. This is something that should not be listened to. On this interpretation, there must be an intention of aid and support in the speech; otherwise, the mere accompaniment and listening of the angels (peace be upon them) would not comfort the heart of Moses (peace be upon him).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 16:

The fa' (the particle of consequence) in His words, exalted is He, ﴿So come to Pharaoh and say: Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds﴾ serves to order what follows it upon what precedes it, namely the generous promise. This is not merely an emphasis on the command to go, because its meaning is arriving at the destination (al-ma'ti), not merely heading toward the destination the way going (al-dhahab) does.

The word rasul (messenger) is used here in the singular because it is originally a verbal noun (masdar) that was used as a description, as other masdars are used as descriptions for emphasis, as in "a just man" (rajul 'adl). Therefore it may be treated in the same ways as other such cases, and the most preferred of these possibilities is not hidden. In the sense of masdar, the apparent meaning is the verse of Kuthayyir 'Azza:

Surely the slanderers have lied, I have not divulged a secret to them, nor have I sent them as a messenger (bi-rasul).

And more apparent than this is the verse of al-'Abbas ibn Mirdas:

Is there no one to convey from me to Khafaf a message (rasulan), from the House of Ahlik, its furthest point?

Or it is singular because the two are united in brotherhood, or because the sender or the one sent with is one, or because His words, exalted is He, "Indeed we" (inna), are understood as meaning "indeed each one of us," so that the singular predicate is permissible just as it is permissible in that case. Its benefit is to indicate that each of them is commanded to convey this even when alone. In the phrase "Lord of the worlds" there is a refutation of the accursed one and a nullification of his claim to divinity which he had established, and a gentle guidance leading him to obey the command.

That is, "an arsil ma'anā Banī Isrā'īl" (﴿Send with us the Children of Israel﴾) is an explanatory clause (mufassirah), because the sending (irsal) understood from "rasul" (messenger) carries the sense of saying. Abu Hayyan permitted that it be a verbal (masdariyyah) clause, with the meaning: "We are His messengers – exalted and majestic is He – [commanding] the sending," and this means releasing and letting go, as in your saying: "I sent the stone from my hand" and "the falcon was sent," and the intended meaning is: let them go with us to Palestine. That was their dwelling place – peace be upon them both –
