and the Children of Israel had been enslaved for four hundred years. Their number at the time Musa – peace be upon him – was sent was six hundred and thirty thousand, as mentioned by al-Baghawi.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 18:**

﴿He said﴾: that is, Pharaoh said to Musa (upon him be peace), after the two of them had come to him and said to him what they had been commanded to say. It is related that they went to the gate of Pharaoh, but they were not admitted for a year, until the doorkeeper said: "Here is a man who claims that he is the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds!" Pharaoh said: "Admit him, so that we may laugh at him." He was admitted, and the two of them delivered the message to him. Musa (upon him be peace) was recognised, and at that point he said: ﴿Did we not raise you among us as a child?﴾

In another report, they came at night and knocked on the gate, and Pharaoh was startled and said: "Who is this who strikes my gate at this hour?" The doorkeeper looked down on them and spoke with them, and Musa said to him: "I am the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds." So he went to Pharaoh and said: "Here is a madman who claims that he is the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds!" Pharaoh said: "Bring him in." He entered and said what God the Exalted has recounted.

The accursed one intended by his words ﴿Did we not raise you﴾ ... and so on, a reminder of favour. "Among us" (*fīnā*) is to be understood with an omitted noun (*mudaf*, a noun governed in a construct phrase whose first term is dropped), meaning "among our households." *Al-walīd* is on the pattern *faʿīl* in the sense of *mafʿūl* (passive), said of one whose birth is recent. Al-Raghib said that in its original usage it may be applied to one whose birth is recent or distant, just as a fruit recently picked is called *janiyy*, but when it grows older this name is dropped. Some have said that its indication of recency derives from the form of intensification (*mubālagha*), and from the fact that birth itself admits of no difference in itself.

﴿And you remained among us for a number of years of your life.﴾ It is said: he remained among them for thirty years, then he went out to Madyan (Midian), and stayed there ten years, then he returned to them calling them to God the Exalted for thirty years, then he remained after the drowning for fifty. It is also said: he remained among them twelve years, then fled after he struck the Coptic man to Madyan, and stayed there ten years tending the sheep of Shu'ayb (upon him be peace), then eighteen years after his marriage to Shu'ayb's daughter, so that he completed forty years. Then God sent him, and he returned to them calling them to Him, Mighty and Majestic. And God knows best.

Abu 'Amr recited in one transmission ﴿min ʿumrika﴾ with the *mīm* sukūn (*min ʿumrika*). The prepositional phrase (*al-jārr wa-l-majrūr*) is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*) of *sinīn*, as is well known in the case of an indefinite noun (*nakira*) qualified when it is placed first (*idhā quddima*).

[Page 69 of the source edition appears mid-passage.]

﴿And you did your deed which you did﴾. He means the killing of the Copt. He rebuked him for it after having reminded him of the favour and magnified it to him through the vagueness of the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*). In this he intended to disparage the prophethood of Moses (peace be upon him). Al-Sha'bi read «fi'latak» with a kasra on the fa', meaning the manner (*hay'ah*). It was a killing by striking with the fist (*al-waks*). The reading of the majority, with a fatha on the fa', denotes a single occurrence. ﴿And you were among the disbelievers﴾, that is: ungrateful for My blessing, in that you deliberately killed a man from among my intimates, as reported from Ibn Zayd. Or: at that time you were among the group of people whose disbelief you now claim, as related from al-Suddi. This judgement by Pharaoh was based on what he knew of the outward condition of Moses (peace be upon him) at that time, owing to Moses' mingling with them and his dissimulation (*taqiyyah*) with them by not denouncing them. Otherwise, the prophets (peace be upon them) are infallible (*ma'sum*) from disbelief both before and after prophethood. It has also been said that this was a fabrication (*iftira'*) by him against Moses (peace be upon him). This was deemed unlikely, on the grounds that had he known of Moses' faith earlier, he would have imprisoned or killed him. According to both possibilities, the clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to one of the two "ta'"s in the two preceding verbs.

It is also permissible that this be an independent judgement against him (peace be upon him), that he is among the disbelievers in His divinity, as related from al-Hasan. Or that he is among those who disbelieve in their religion, since they had gods they worshipped. Or among the disbelievers in blessings, habitually given to denying them. One who is habituated to that would not consider such a crime unusual from himself. Thus the clause is then a new sentence or conjoined to what precedes it. However, in my view the preferable reading is what was previously mentioned, namely making the clause a circumstantial clause, so that it is of one pattern with its counterpart in the reply, since the circumstantial sense is determined there. Also, the words of the accursed one contain two matters, which he (peace be upon him) undertook to refute in the manner of *laff wa nashr* (folding and unfolding, a rhetorical arrangement) in disordered fashion. First he refuted what he had been rebuked for, which was a disparagement of his prophethood, namely his saying: ﴿And you did your deed which you did﴾ and so on, giving it attention and concern. This is by what He, glorified and exalted, related of his statement, saying:

﴿He said, "I did it"﴾. That is: that deed. ﴿Then﴾ (إذًا): that is, at that time, according to what some of the verifiers (al-Muhaqqiqin), may God Almighty water his grave, preferred, that (إذًا) is an adverb of time cut off from being followed by a genitive, with the fatha preferred over the kasra because it is lighter and occurs more often. He, peace be upon him, acknowledged the killing because he trusted in God Almighty's protection of him. He qualified the act with something that removes any suggestion that it discredits his prophethood, namely the clause ﴿and I am among the misguided﴾, that is, among the ignorant. This reading also appears in the recitation (qira'a) of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, as Abu Hayyan reported in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit), but he said: "It appears that this is an explanation (tafsir) of ﴿misguided﴾, not a recitation transmitted from the Messenger (ﷺ)." He, peace be upon him, meant by this, according to what is related from Qatadah, that he did it in ignorance of the matter, not intending it deliberately, for he, peace be upon him, only intended to strike with his fist to discipline him, and it led to what it led to. In the same sense is what is related from Ibn Zayd, that the meaning is: "and I am among those ignorant that my blow would reach his soul." It was also said: the meaning is: "I did it, proceeding to it without concern for its consequences," with the understanding that jahl (ignorance) here means proceeding without concern, just as it was explained in this sense in the verse of the poet:

"Let no one act with ignorance toward us, lest we act with more ignorance than the ignorant ones."

This is one of the things that is fitting, on some of the aspects of the answer mentioned. It was said: the "misguidance" here is love, as it was explained in this sense in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you are in your old misguidance﴾. He, peace be upon him, meant that he killed the Copt out of zeal for God, exalted and majestic is He, since he, peace be upon him, was among those who love Him. But this, as you see, is weak. Similar to it is what was said: he meant "among those ignorant of the sharia (laws)," and misguidance was explained in this sense in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "among the forgetful," and misguidance was explained as forgetting in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿lest one of them err and the other remind her﴾. Accordingly it was said: the meaning is "I did it forgetting its prohibition," and it was said: "forgetting that my striking him was of a kind that usually leads to killing." Of these opinions, the one I incline to is what is related from Qatadah. Later, if God Almighty wills, in Surat al-Qasas, there will be what relates to this point.

Abu 'Ubayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Jurayj related from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited: "I did it, when I was among the misguided."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 21:

﴿So I fled from you when I feared you﴾ That is, I went out fleeing ﴿from you when I feared you﴾, meaning: when I anticipated harm from you. This was when he was told: "Indeed, the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you." From here the reason for the plural form of the address pronoun becomes clear. Hamza, in one narration, read (limā) with a kasra on the lām and a light mīm, taking the lām as a preposition (ḥarf jarr) and mā as a verbal-source particle (maṣdariyyah), meaning: "because of my fear of you." ﴿Then my Lord bestowed upon me judgment﴾, that is, prophethood, or knowledge and understanding of things as they truly are. The first meaning is related from al-Suddi. Some scholars interpreted it as meaning knowledge that is among the special attributes of prophethood, so that "judgment" in this sense is more specific than in the second sense. ʿIsā read "ḥukuman" with a ḍammah on the kāf. ﴿And made me among the messengers﴾ indicates, according to the apparent first of the two interpretations of "judgment", His favour upon him with a rank above the rank of prophethood, namely the rank of messengership. He did not say "then my Lord bestowed upon me judgment and messengership" or "and made me a messenger", in order to magnify the matter of messengership and to alert Pharaoh that his own messengership, upon him be peace, is not an innovated matter, but is among what has been the practice of God, exalted is His majesty. The summary of the rebuttal is that what you mentioned regarding the attribution of killing to me is accepted, but it is not something for which I am rebuked, nor does it discredit my prophethood; for it happened before prophethood and without intent, since the striking was for discipline and that outcome followed from it.

He then rebutted secondly the favour he reminded of, contained in his saying: ﴿Did We not raise you among us as a child?﴾ and so on, saying:

[Page 70]

﴿And this﴾, i.e., the upbringing understood from His saying ﴿Did We not raise you among us﴾ and so on, ﴿is a favour you reckon upon me﴾, i.e., you confer it upon me. This is from the category of ellipsis and transitivity (al-hadhf wal-iisal, the omission of a preposition so that the verb takes a direct object), and tamunnuha (you reckon) is from al-imnah, meaning conferring a benefit. The present tense is used to bring the scene to mind. It is also permissible that it derives from al-mann (reproach), and the meaning would be: this is a favour you count against me, so there is no ellipsis and transitivity here. It has been said that the present tense is on its literal sense of the future, and this is clearly problematic.

﴿That you have enslaved the Children of Israel﴾, i.e., you subjugated them and made them slaves. It is said: ʿabbadtu al-rajul and aʿbadtuhu, when you take a man as a slave. The poet said:

*"Why does my people enslave me, when among them there are abundant camels, whatever they wish, and servants?"*

The clause introduced by an (that) and what follows it is in the sense of a nominal verbal noun in the nominative, being the predicate of an omitted subject. The clause is either circumstantial or explanatory. Alternatively, it is a substitute for (this) or (a favour), or a conjunctive apposition, or in the accusative as a substitute for the pronoun in (you reckon it), or in the genitive by the implied causal preposition bi- or li-, according to one of two opinions regarding its position after the removal of the preposition. The other opinion is that its position is accusative.

The essence of the rebuttal is that what you mention is apparently a favour, but in reality it is a calamity, since it came about through the humiliation of my people and your intention to them by slaughtering their sons. Had it not been for that, I would not have come into being before you, nor would I have been in the cradle of your upbringing. It has also been said: (this) points to an ugly, vague matter whose nature is not known except through its explanation, and that you have enslaved is an explicative apposition to it. The meaning is: your enslaving the Children of Israel is a favour you reckon upon me. The essence of the rebuttal is then the denial of what he cited as a favour as well. The intent is to read the statement as a refutation that this is a favour in reality. The reading of al-Dahhak is: ﴿And this is a favour; what right have you to reckon it upon me?﴾ Qatadah took this view, as did al-Akhfash and al-Farra', except that they said the interrogative hamzah for denial is to be understood after the waw, and the original is: ﴿And is this a favour...﴾. Some grammarians refused to omit the interrogative particle in such a position.

Abu Hayyan said: The apparent meaning is that this statement is an acknowledgement by him, peace be upon him, of Pharaoh's favour, as if he were saying: your upbringing of me is a favour upon me, inasmuch as you enslaved others, left me, and took me as a son. But this does not negate my prophethood. This interpretation was adopted by al-Suddi and al-Tabari, but it is not the right one.

Whatever the case, the verse clearly shows that the disbelief of a disbeliever does not nullify his favour. Some have held that disbelief nullifies favour, so that the deserving of praise and the deserving of blame would not coincide. But there is no harm in this, since the two aspects of desert are different.

Furthermore, al-Zamakhshari held that (then) in His saying ﴿I did it then﴾ is a response and a recompense. He explained the way in which the statement is a recompense by his saying: The phrase "and you did your deed" implies that you repaid my favour with what you did. Then Moses, peace be upon him, said to him: Yes, I did it, repaying you, in acceptance of your saying, as if his favour in his view deserved to be repaid with a similar recompense.

It has been objected that this does not fit His saying ﴿and I was of the erring﴾, because it indicates that he acknowledged doing that in ignorance or forgetfulness. In al-Kashf there is a verification of what al-Zamakhshari stated: the sequence which is the meaning of the conditional and its response is present. Since both verbs are in the past, this is hypothetical, as if he said: if that was ingratitude for your favour, then I did it as a recompense. But the description, namely that it was ingratitude, is not granted. He supported this with His saying ﴿And this is a favour you reckon upon me﴾, and in it is also the argument by what is entailed (al-qawl bil-mujib).

His saying ﴿and I was of the erring﴾ according to this is like a second excuse, meaning: you deserved that from me; and also I was among those who deviated from the path of rightness, not believing that your kindness deserved repayment with the like of it, but in proceeding before the permission of the King, the All-Knowing.

The summary is that he attributed to him the repayment of kindness with evil and established it by his being a disbeliever. Moses, peace be upon him, answered that the repayment did occur, but where is the kindness? I was not a disbeliever in you, for that is the very essence of guidance, but I was astray in proceeding to the act. I was not a disbeliever in the favour of a benefactor at all, but I was doing that in error. From this it is clear that His saying ﴿and I was of the erring﴾ does not contradict al-Zamakhshari's exposition, but rather supports it. End of quotation.

[Page 71]

It is not hidden that what better suits the matter of recompense is that the intended meaning of His saying ﴿I did it and I was of the erring﴾ is: I did it, proceeding with it without concern. The erring here means ignorance, explained as proceeding without concern. But insisting that (then) here is for response and recompense is insisting on something not required, for the correct view held by most is that it may be purely for response. In al-Bahr it is said that they interpreted what is in this verse in that way. Explaining its being for recompense in this verse by what was mentioned involves some artificiality. In my view, the more evident meaning is what one of the distinguished verifiers preferred: that it is an adverb cut off from annexation (to a following clause). I see nothing to object to in it except that it is a meaning which most scholars of Arabic did not mention, and they did not encompass all knowledge. If you reject this, then it is for response only. It is strange that Ibn Atiyyah said that it is here a filler word in the speech, and then said: it is as if it means "then," and if he had confined himself to this as an explanation of meaning, it would have had some validity. So reflect. And God Most High knows best.

[Fir'awn] said, asking [in disbelief] about the Sender, glory be to Him: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾

The explanation of this, as stated by the scholar al-Tibi (al-Tayyibi), is that when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded the two of them with His words, glory be to Him: ﴿So go to Pharaoh and say, "Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds," [saying], "Send with us the Children of Israel"﴾, it was necessary that they be obedient and deliver that very message before the accursed one. When it had been delivered to him, he first objected with his words: ﴿Did we not raise you among us as a child?﴾ to the end, and second with his words: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ For this reason the conjunction "wa" (and) was used, and "qala" (he said) was repeated because of the length [of the speech]. It is as if he said: "Are you the messenger, and what is the Lord of the worlds?"

al-Zamakhshari said: when his gatekeeper told him, "Here is someone who claims that he is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds!", he said to him upon [Musa's] entrance: "And what is the Lord of the worlds?" This was objected to on the grounds that it is a disordered arrangement, since the exchange between them had already preceded, as he himself indicated in his earlier words. The author of al-Kashf defended it, saying: [Zamakhshari] meant that Allah, exalted is He, mentioned once: (So say, "Indeed, we are messengers of your Lord, so send with us") and another time: (So say, "Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds"). The story is one and the assembly is one. So he interpreted the second as what the gatekeeper conveyed from the tongue of [Musa], peace be upon him, and the first as what Musa, peace be upon him, addressed to him directly. And the accursed one first began to attack him, [saying] that one like him, who is stained with vile character traits, is not qualified for a lofty position, let alone for what he claims. Second, he asked about the status of the one who claimed prophethood, mockingly. From this it becomes clear that the preceding exchange does not indicate a disorder in the arrangement that he pointed to. End of quotation.

Some scholars allowed that the command occurred twice, and that Pharaoh asked first with his words: ﴿Who, then, is the Lord of you two, O Musa?﴾ and asked a second time with his words: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾ Allah, exalted is He, related the first in what He revealed first, which is Surah Ta-Ha, and the second in what He revealed second, which is Surah al-Shu'ara'. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that Surah Ta-Ha was revealed, then al-Waqi'a, then Ta-Sin-Mim al-Shu'ara'.

Another said: it is possible that they only said: ﴿Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds﴾, and the limitation in Surah Ta-Ha to mentioning His lordship over Pharaoh was because it was sufficient for what was intended. And on the view that the command occurred twice, it has been said: Pharaoh asked the first time with his words: ﴿Who is your Lord?﴾, seeking a descriptive identification as the apparent answer requires, unlike al-Sakkaki's claim that it was a question about the genus, as if he said: "Is he a human, an angel, or a jinn?" The answer is from the wise approach (al-uslub al-hakim, an indirect manner of response that addresses the questioner's real concern). The second time he asked with: ﴿And what is the Lord of the worlds?﴾, seeking the quiddity and reality, moving to what is more difficult, so that through this he might reach some of his corrupt aims, as Allah, exalted is He, related afterward.

And (ma) is used to ask about a reality in general, whether the one asked about its reality is among those possessing knowledge or not. So it should not be imagined that the proper wording here would be: "Who is the Lord of the worlds?" so as to be objected to on the grounds that, because the accursed one denied Him, Mighty and Majestic, [the verse] used (ma). And since asking about the reality [of Allah] is something unbefitting His majesty, Exalted is He, [this is the reason].

[Page 72]

Said [Moses] - upon him be peace - turning away from answering [Pharaoh's question] to the mention of His attributes - Exalted and Majestic is He - in the manner of wise discourse, as an indication of the impossibility of explaining the reality: ﴿The Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them﴾. The discussion on the impossibility of knowing the reality and its absence has passed before you, so recall it. The raising of (rabb) is on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., He is the Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them of elements and elementals. ﴿If you are certain﴾, i.e., if you are certain of things, verifying them, you would know that. Or, if you are certain of any of things, then this is more deserving of certainty, due to its manifestness and the illumination of its proof. For these sensible bodies are contingent, because of their composition, their multiplicity, and the change of their states. Therefore they have a principle that is necessary in itself. Then that principle must be the principle of all other contingent beings, whether they can be sensed or not; otherwise it would entail either a plurality of necessary beings or the independence of some contingent beings from it, and both are impossible. The answer to (in, "if") is omitted, as we have indicated.

﴿Said﴾ Pharaoh, upon hearing his reply, peace be upon him, fearing that something from it would take root in the hearts of his people, ﴿to those around him﴾ among the nobles of his people. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: They were five hundred men, wearing bracelets, which were reserved for kings alone. ﴿"Do you not listen?"﴾ to his answer, intending to express astonishment at it and to belittle the one who said it. This was because the answer did not correspond to the question, since it did not clarify the reality that was asked about. Pharaoh, in his own view, regarded it, given the ignorance in which his people were, as unclear in itself, because knowledge of the possibility of what was mentioned, or of its coming into being, which is the cause of the need for the Necessary Existent in Himself (al-mabda' al-wajib li-dhatihi) over them, was obscure. The accursed one went to great lengths in indicating that the answer mentioned should not be taken into account, for he implied that merely hearing it was sufficient to reject it and not accept it. It is as if Musa, peace be upon him, when he sensed this from the accursed one,

ِ﴿Qāla﴾ (He said): turning to what is clearer and closer, giving the office of guidance its due as far as possible, since reaching the Reality itself is impossible, as you have heard: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest ones﴾. For the createdness (ḥudūth) of those addressed and their forefathers, who have passed away and ceased to exist, and their need of a Necessary Being, Fashioner and Wise, is more evident; and reflection upon the self is closer and clearer than reflection upon the horizons. When the accursed one (al-La'īn) saw this, and his fear of the strife (fitnah) of his people grew strong within him,

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 26, verse 27:**

﴿قالَ﴾ (He said), emphatically rejecting his claim and indicating that it is not to be taken into account. He openly states what would repel their hearts from its speaker and from accepting what he brings: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is mad!﴾ In that he is asked about one thing and answers about another, and is alerted to what his answer contains but does not notice it. He called him "messenger" sarcastically, and attributed him to those addressed, to show disdain that he should be sent to himself. He confirmed this with the description. In this there is an incitement of their anger and a provocation to deny his prophethood after hearing the report, out of pride in themselves, that they should not be deemed fit to have a madman sent to them.

Mujahid, Humayd, and al-A'raj read «أرْسَلَ» (ursila, "was sent") in the active form (bina' al-fa'il), meaning: "the one whom his Lord sent to you." It is as though he (peace be upon him), when he saw harshness in the reply of the accursed one, and an allusion from him, did not notice the concealment in his first answer among his people. Rather, his turning away from it to the second answer was because of what the accursed one (upon him be the curse) had hurled at him.

﴿He said﴾, peace be upon him, explaining his first answer and removing its obscurity, so that it would be known that the shift [in the discourse] was only to make manifest what he shifted to, and to clarify it and bring it close to the one who looks, and not because of what he was accused of, and far be it from him. Along with this is an indication that the reality cannot be explained, also, by insisting on the answer through attributes: ﴿Lord of the East and the West and whatever is between them﴾. This is because in the first answer there was no explicit statement that the movements of the heavens and what is in them, and the changes of their states and conditions, and the earth's being at times dark and at other times illuminated, are attributed to God Most High. This verse points to that. The mention of the East and the West indicates the rising and setting of the sun, which depend on the movements of the heavens and what is in them, in a wondrous pattern from which these sound conditions result. All of these are created things, and there is no doubt that they need a Creator who is powerful, knowing, and wise. He, peace be upon him, employed harshness, just as [his interlocutor] had employed it with him, by saying: ﴿If you are people who use reason﴾. That is: if you understand anything at all, or if you are among the people of reason, you would know that the matter is as I have said and pointed to. This contains an allusion that they are far outside the circle of reason, and that they are the most deserving of the accusation of madness that they leveled at him, peace be upon him.

Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud] and his companions and al-A'mash read «Lord of the easts and the wests» in the plural in both places. When the accursed one heard from him, peace be upon him, those statements, founded on profound wisdom, and witnessed the firmness of his resolve and the strength of his determination to carry out his mission, and that he was one who could not be matched in the arena of debate,

Page 73

He said, turning away from argument to threat, as is the habit of the stubborn disputant: ﴿If you take a god other than me, I will surely place you among the imprisoned.﴾ In this there is an exaggeration in rejecting him from the claim to prophethood. He wanted from him what he wanted, and he was not satisfied with Moses (ﷺ) merely abandoning the claim and not confronting him. In it there is also another act of arrogance, for he implied that Moses (ﷺ) was taking him as a god at that time, and that Moses's taking another god after him was doubtful. He also went to extremes in the distance, on the supposition that it would happen, by emphasizing the verb with what he emphasized it with, and he departed from "la-asjununnaka" (I will surely imprison you), the shorter form, for this reason too. The definite article in "al-masjunin" (the imprisoned) is for prior acquaintance, so it is as if he said: "I will surely make you one of those whose conditions you know in my prisons." The accursed one used to throw them into a deep pit, said to be five hundred cubits deep, containing snakes and scorpions, until they died.

Now, some of them said: the question here and in Surat Ta-Ha concerns the description (of the Lord), the story is one and the session is one, and the difference in expressions is due to the demands of each situation, so that what is expressed in each place is what is meant. It must be affirmed that what actually occurred is the common element among all those expressions. By this the problem of the difference in expressions, despite the claim that the story and the session are one, is resolved. However, determining the common element that can be expressed by each of those expressions requires careful consideration, together with much grace and divine success.

Then the scholars differed over whether the accursed one knew first that the world has a Lord, namely Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Some of them said: he knew it, based on ﴿Certainly you know that none has sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾. Others argued from his request for an explanation of the essence, supposing that it contains an acknowledgment of the basic existence (of God). They mentioned that his claim to divinity and his saying ﴿I am your most high lord﴾ were only a means of terrorizing his people, whom he had deceived, and were not based on belief. And how could he believe that he is the Lord of the world while he knows necessarily that he came into existence after not having existed? Thousands of years passed over the world while he was not in it, and he had no dominion except Egypt. Hence Shu'ayb said to Moses, peace be upon them both, when he came to him in Madyan: ﴿Do not fear, you have escaped from the wrongdoing people.﴾

Others said: he was ignorant of Allah, the Exalted, and yet did not believe himself to be the creator of the heavens and the earth and what is between them. Rather, he was a dahri (a materialist who denies a Creator), denying the Maker, glorified is He, believing that the spheres necessarily exist by themselves and that their movements are causes for the occurrence of events. He believed that whoever possesses a region and manages its affairs, by the strength of his fortune, deserves worship from its people and becomes their lord. For this reason he restricted his divinity and lordship and did not generalize them, when he said: ﴿I do not know for you any god other than me﴾ and ﴿I am your most high lord﴾.

It is also permitted that he was one of the ḥulūliyya (those who believe in the indwelling of the Lord, glorified and exalted, in some beings), and that he believed in the indwelling of the Lord, Mighty and Majestic, in himself, which is why he named himself a god. It was also said that he claimed divinity for himself and for others, namely those he worshipped besides Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as the apparent meaning of the Exalted's saying indicates: ﴿and forsake you and your gods﴾. But this, and likewise what precedes it, is far-fetched.

What prevails in opinion and what the majority of the apparent indications require is that the accursed one knew Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and that He, glorified is He, is the Creator of the world. However, his wretchedness overcame him, and his dominion deceived him, so he showed his people the opposite of what he knew. Thus among them those whose ignorance was great and whose intellect was small submitted to him. It is not unlikely that there are people who accept such fables and do not realize that they contradict what is self-evident. A trustworthy person related to me that two men from Najd, before the emergence of the affair of the Wahhabi among them, were once in a field of theirs when a bird with very long legs, of a kind they had never seen in that land, passed by them and landed near them. One of them said to the other: "What is this?" The other replied: "Do not raise your voice, this is our lord." The first said to him, believing the truth of that delirium: "Glory be to Him! How long are his shanks and how great are his wings!"

As for those among them who have intellect and for whom the falsity of such things is not hidden, it is possible that he agreed outwardly out of excessive fear of Pharaoh, or out of excessive desire for what he had of worldly life, as we observe many intellectuals and corrupt scholars agreeing with the tyrant kings in their false scholarly and practical doctrines, out of love for the base world, or out of fear of the calamity they imagine. It is also possible that he truly believed that, by some kind of interpretation, though it was corrupt, such as the claim of indwelling and the like. The one who denies the saying of the one who says "I am the Truth" and the one who says "there is nothing in the cloak but Allah" claims that his belief in the truth of these is like his belief in the truth of Pharaoh's saying: ﴿I am your most high lord﴾.

As for the accursed one's question to Moses, peace be upon him, which recounts what occurred in his words with "what is the Lord of the worlds," it was due to his denial of the apparent possibility that there could be a lord of the worlds other than himself. Moses's answer to him was only to nullify what he apparently claimed and to guide his people to what is the truth worthy of acceptance. For this reason he did not restrict the address in the answers to him. The amazement understood from the saying ﴿Do you not listen?﴾ is because he apparently claimed that Moses, peace be upon him, asserted the opposite of a established matter, namely his own lordship. When there entered him the fear that his people would submit to what Moses, peace be upon him, had said, he was extreme in turning them away from accepting the truth by saying: ﴿Indeed your messenger who has been sent to you is surely a madman.﴾ When he saw that this did not avail in preventing Moses, peace be upon him, from manifesting the truth and nullifying what he had been showing of falsehood, he defended his false claim with threats and severe warnings, saying: ﴿If you take a god other than me, I will surely place you among the imprisoned.﴾ Perhaps Moses's answers, peace be upon him, point to the refutation of the belief in such things as indwelling, since it involves preference without a preferrer, and since it entails being a created, lordly being because of the change it involves.

After this statement, in my view, is the statement of some of them that he, may the curse of Allah be upon him, was a dahri, and so on to the end of what you have just heard. The amazement, according to his claim, is at the reality that Moses, peace be upon him, asserted the opposite of an established matter, namely his own lordship, may the curse of Allah be upon him. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

When Moses, peace be upon him, saw the harshness of Pharaoh

"He said" — in a tone of gentle address to him, hoping for his faith: "Even if I bring you something clear?" That is, would you do that even if I bring you something clear, i.e., manifest, evidencing the truth of my claim? He means by it the miracle (mu'jizah), for it combines the indication of the existence of the Creator and His wisdom with the indication of the truth of the claim of the one through whose hand it appears. The expression "something" (shay') is used to magnify it. The waw is for conjunction, coordinating with a sentence opposite to the sentence mentioned, and the two conjoined sentences together are in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). The "law" (law) here is for explanation, verifying what the preceding speech implies of the judgment concerning every supposed circumstance accompanying it in general, by introducing these circumstances upon the most remote of them and the most contrary to it, so that its realization with what is other than it of circumstances becomes evident by way of priority. That is: would you do that to me in the state of my not bringing something clear, and in the state of my bringing it? The introduction of the coming with "law" rather than "in" (in) is not to indicate its improbability in itself, but in relation to Pharaoh.

Some of them made the waw for the circumstantial (hal), meaning that the sentence following it is a circumstantial clause, i.e., "Would you do that to me while coming with something clear?" This is the apparent meaning of the words of al-Kashshaf here. The apparent meaning of the words of al-Kashf is that the interrogation is for denial, meaning: you are not able to do that, although I am a prophet by the miracle. The apparent connection of this speech is with the threat issued by the accursed one, so that in its interpretation it is an allusion to his (peace be upon him) being made one of the imprisoned. It is as if he said: "Will you make me one of the imprisoned if I take a god other than you, even if I bring you something clear?!"

On this basis al-Tibi interpreted the words of al-Kashshaf, then said: It may be said that the waw is conjunctive, and it requires a conjoined element, which is what preceded at the beginning of the conversation between the prophet of God, exalted is He, and his enemy. The hamzah is inserted between the conjoined and the conjoined-to for affirmation, and the meaning: Will you acknowledge the Oneness and my messengership if I come to you after the argument with the overpowering proofs and the dazzling, manifest miracles?

("Law" in the sense of "in", as in "whoever is mighty plunders".) This interpretation is supported by what is in al-A'raf: "Indeed I have come to you with a clear sign from your Lord, so send with me the Children of Israel." "He said: If you have come with a sign, then bring it, if you are of the truthful." End quote. And it is as you see. In it, "mubin" is taken from abana, intransitive, in the sense of "baana"; and taking it from abana, transitive, with the object omitted, as we have indicated, is more suitable to the context. When Pharaoh heard this speech from Musa, peace be upon him,

﴿قالَ﴾ [He said], when he (Pharaoh) hoped to find a point of counter-argument. ﴿فَأْتِ بِهِ﴾ [then bring it], that is, bring something clear. ﴿إنْ كُنْتَ مِنَ الصّادِقِينَ﴾ [if you are among the truthful]: that is, in what your speech indicates, that you will bring something that makes the truth of your claim clear; or, among those truthful in the claim to be a messenger from the Lord of the worlds. The answer to the conditional (*jawab al-sharṭ*) is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it. That is: "if you are among the truthful, then bring it." Al-Zamakhshari (*al-Zamakhsharī*) estimated it as: "you have brought it." The well-known view is to estimate it as being of the kind of proof.

Al-Hawfi (*al-Ḥawfī*) said: It is possible that what preceded is the answer, and it is permissible to place the answer first, because the deletion of the conditional did not affect the wording with anything. Al-Zamakhshari, may God treat him with His justice, slandered the people of the Sunna (*Ahl al-Sunna*, the adherents of the prophetic tradition) with what they are free of, as the author of *al-Kashf* and others have explained. So refer to it if you wish.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 32:

﴿So he cast down﴾ Musa, after Pharaoh had said that to him, ﴿his staff, and behold, it was a manifest serpent﴾, its serpent-nature being evident, meaning it was not by deception and illusion as the sorcerers do. The thu'ban (serpent) is the largest of snakes. Its derivation is from tha'iba al-ma'u, meaning the water flowed in a widespread flow, and it is named so because of its swift movement without feet, as if it were flowing water. The apparent view is that the staff itself was transformed into a serpent. This is not impossible, if it occurs by stripping away the attribute by which it was a staff and creating in it the attribute of that which becomes a serpent, according to the opinion of some theologians regarding the homogeneity of substances and their equal capacity to receive attributes. What is impossible is its transformation into a serpent while it remains a staff, because it is impossible for one thing to be a staff and a serpent at the same time. It has been said that this occurred by creating a serpent in place of the staff, but the apparent meanings of the verses make this unlikely. Reports have come that indicate the great size of this serpent. Nothing can overcome Allah the Exalted, and the explanation of the manner of the matter has already passed.

ِAnd he drew out his hand from his bosom, and behold, it was white to the onlookers. That is: its whiteness drew the spectators to gaze at him, because it departed from the usual, and it was a luminous whiteness.

It is narrated that when he saw the matter of the staff, he said: "Do you have anything other than it?" So he (peace be upon him) brought out his hand, and he said: "What is this?" He said: "My hand." Then he put it into his armpit, then drew it out, and it had a ray that nearly overwhelms the sights and fills the horizon.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 34–35:

﴿Said to the chiefs﴾ (al-mala', the nobles) of his people ﴿around him﴾: "around him" is grammatically in the accusative (manṣūb) as a locative adverb (ẓarf). It is a stationary adverbial phrase (ẓarf mustaqirr) placed in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), meaning: those stationed around him. It is also permitted that it occupies the position of an attribute (ṣifah) of al-mala', on the pattern of the line of verse:

"And I pass by the base man who abuses me..."

The first view is easier and more appropriate.

Page 76

It is among the surprising things that Abu Hayyan transmitted from the Kufans that they treat al-mala' as a relative noun (ism mawsul), and "around him" as attached to a deleted element that serves as its relative clause, as if it were said: He said to those who were stationed around him: ﴿Indeed, this is a sorcerer, knowledgeable﴾, outstanding in the knowledge of magic, ﴿who wants to expel you﴾ by force ﴿from your land﴾ in which you grew up and settled ﴿with his magic﴾. In this is the utmost incitement against him, peace be upon him, and seeking harm against him, since among the hardest things for souls is leaving one's homeland, especially when it is by force. This is the secret in attributing the expulsion and the land to them.

﴿So what do you advise?﴾ That is: what command you command. Thus the place of "mādhā" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah). "Ta'murūn" (you command) is from command, the opposite of prohibition, and its object is deleted, i.e., "you command me." In making his servants, by his own claim, commanders over him, despite what he used to show them of claiming divinity and lordship, there is an indication that the power of the miracle overwhelmed him and bewildered him so that he did not know which of the two ends was longer. He slipped at the mention of the claim of divinity, lowered from his shoulders the grandeur of lordship, and fell from the peak of tyranny down to the depths of humble poverty. For this reason he displayed a sense of fear of being overcome by him, peace be upon him, in his kingdom.

It is also permitted that "mādhā" be in the accusative as an object (maf'ūliyyah), and that "ta'murūn" be from consultation (mu'āmarah), meaning consultation so that each one gives the command that his opinion requires. But what preceded is more preferable.

They said: ﴿Put him off, and his brother﴾, meaning: defer their matter until the sorcerers come to you. It is from *arja'tuhu*, "I delayed him," when you postpone him. From the same root comes the *Murji'ah* (a sect whose name means "those who postpone," holding that deeds are deferred and not part of faith), who are the people who postpone action and never perform it, and who say: sin does not harm alongside faith, just as obedience does not benefit alongside disbelief.

The people of Medina, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read «أرْجِهِ» (*arjihi*) with a kasra on the ha'. Asim and Hamza read «أرْجِهْ» (*arjih*) without a hamza and with the ha' sukun. The rest read «أرْجِئْهُ» (*arji'hu*) with a hamza and a damma on the ha'. Abu Ali said: the damma on the ha' with the hamza is necessary and nothing else is permissible, and it is best that the damma not be extended to become a waw. As for the one who reads with a kasra on the ha', «أرْجِهِ» in his reading comes from *arjaytuhu* with a ya' and without a hamza. According to what al-Tibi transmitted, the hamza is more eloquent. The ha' mentioned may also be joined to a ya', so one says «أرْجِهِي», just as one says «مَرَرْتُ بِهِي». Al-Zajjaj mentioned that some of the skilled grammarians do not permit the sukun of a pronoun ha' such as the ha' of «أرْجِهْ», meaning the pronominal ha'. Some grammarians claimed that it is permitted, and cited as evidence an anonymous line of poetry mentioned by al-Tabarsi, and said: it is a verse whose composer is unknown, and a poet may make a mistake.

Some eminent scholars said: the sukun is weak, because this ha' only becomes silent in pause, but the reader has treated connection as if it were pause. It was said: the meaning is "detain him." Perhaps they said this out of extreme bewilderment, or out of feigned firmness and flattery toward Pharaoh; otherwise, how could he detain him, given the signs he had witnessed from him? ﴿And send into the cities gatherers﴾, meaning police who will gather the sorcerers and bring them together before you.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 37–38:

﴿Ya'tuka﴾ is in the jussive mood as an answer to the imperative, meaning: if you send them, they will come to you ﴿with every skilled sorcerer﴾ (sahhar), one who works much in magic, ﴿knowing﴾ (alim), excelling in his knowledge. Because the important matter here is the practice (al-'amal), they came with what indicates superiority in it. Al-A'mash and 'Asim, in one narration, read "bi-kulli sahirin 'alim" (with every sorcerer, knowing).

﴿So the sorcerers were assembled﴾ (fa-jumi'a al-saharah), i.e., those who were known (al-ma'hudun), on the basis that the definite article here, as in al-Miftah (al-Miftah fi 'Ulum al-Balaghah by al-Sakkaki), is "ahdi" (referring to something previously known). The eminent verifier (al-Fadil al-Muhaqqiq) said: the known may be general and all-encompassing, as here, and there is no contradiction between the two as is imagined. There is a discussion in this, so reflect.

﴿For the appointment of a known day﴾ (li-miqati yawmin ma'lum): for what was fixed for it of the hours of a specific day, which was the time of mid-morning (waqt al-duha) on the day of the adornment (yawm al-zinah), on the basis that "miqat" is an attribute of time. In al-Kashshaf: it is that which is set for it, i.e., determined of time or place, and from it come the miqat (fixed points) of ihram.

﴿And it was said to the people﴾
Page 77
This is said to urge them to hasten to gather and to show impatience at their delay in assembling. ﴿Are you assembling?﴾ at that appointed time. The interrogative here is metaphorical, meaning urging and hurrying, as in the verse of Ta'abbaṭa Sharran:

Are you sending a dinar for our need, or a slave of the Lord, the brother of ʿAwn ibn Mikhraq?

He means: send one of them to us quickly, and do not delay with him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 40:

﴿Perhaps we will follow the magicians﴾, that is: in their religion, ﴿if they are the victors﴾, not Musa (peace be upon him). Their intention by this was nothing more than that they should not follow Musa (peace be upon him) in his religion, but they phrased their speech in the manner of a metaphor (kinayah), so as to convey to the magicians the seriousness and earnestness in the contest. It is also permitted that their intention was to follow the magicians, i.e., to remain steadfast upon the religion they were upon, and it is claimed that they were upon what Pharaoh wanted of religion.

It is apparent that Pharaoh is not among the speakers. And on the assumption that he is included, some did not permit that the literal meaning of this statement be intended, because it is impossible for one who claims divinity to follow magicians. Others permitted it, on the possibility that he said this because of the astonishment that overcame him regarding the matter of Musa (peace be upon him), just as he sought the matter from those around him for this purpose. Perhaps their use of ﴿if﴾ (in) was for stirring up (the audience), since otherwise the more fitting expression for their situation would be: "since they are the victors."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 41:

﴿So when the magicians came, they said to Pharaoh: "Will there indeed be a reward for us," i.e., a great reward, ﴿if we are the victors?﴾ Not Musa, peace be upon him. Perhaps they expressed the condition in the style of what was said by the speakers, in agreement with them; otherwise, their situation does not suit showing doubt about their victory.

"Fir'awn said to them, "Yes" (to that for you), "and indeed you will, in addition to that, be among those brought near" (to me).

It was said: he said to them, "You will be the first to enter upon me and the last to leave me."

(Idhan) with a group (of grammarians) is, according to what is commonly held of its function as an answer and a consequence. Al-Zarkashi, in al-Burhan, related from some of the later scholars that here it is composed of (idha), which is a temporal adverb of past time, and the tanwin that serves as a substitute for a deleted clause following it, and it is not the one that puts the verb in the subjunctive (nasiba li-l-mudari').

Al-Kafiyaji and the judge Taqi al-Din ibn Razin went this way regarding the like of this verse, and I am among those who affirm this meaning for it. The meaning according to it is: "And indeed you, if we overcome, or if you are the victors, will be among those brought near."

It was also read "Ni'im" with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the ayn, and that is a dialectal form of (na'am, "yes").

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 43:

﴿Musa said to them﴾, that is, after the magicians had said to him: ﴿Either you throw, or we will be the first to throw﴾, [he said:] ﴿Throw what you are going to throw﴾. Musa, peace be upon him, did not literally command them to perform magic and deception, for magic is forbidden, and it may amount to disbelief (kufr), so it is not befitting for one who is protected from error (al-ma'sum) to command it. Rather, [the permission he gave was] to let them go ahead with what was known, through inspiration (ilham), or true insight (firasa), or the circumstances (qara'in al-hal), to be something they would certainly do. For this reason he said: ﴿what you are going to throw﴾, so that through it he could reach its refutation.

This is like the case of the heretic (zindiq) being ordered to state his argument so that it may be refuted. There is nothing in that of the prohibited consent (al-rida al-mumtani'), for that is consent in the sense of approval (al-rida 'ala tariq al-istihsan), and there is nothing of it in the permission mentioned. Consent in its general sense is not prohibited. As for the widely repeated saying, "Consent to disbelief is disbelief," it is not to be taken in its absolute sense, as the verifying (muhaqqiqun) jurists and usulis hold.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 44:

﴿So they cast down their ropes and their staffs and said﴾ i.e., they said this at the time of casting, ﴿by the might of Pharaoh﴾ i.e., by his strength by which one is protected from humiliation, from their saying "arḍun ʿizāz" (a hard land), meaning firm and solid, ﴿Indeed, it is we who will be the victors﴾, not Moses, peace be upon him. The apparent meaning is that this is an oath on their part by his might - may the curse of God be upon him - that they would prevail, and they singled out the oath here because it suits the context of victory.

Their swearing to this was due to their excessive confidence in themselves and their bringing the utmost that could be brought of magic. In this, according to their assumption, there is an intimidation of Moses, peace be upon him. They turned from address to the third person in their saying ﴿by the might of Pharaoh﴾, out of glorifying him. This kind of oath is of the type of the oaths of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance). Many Muslims have adopted in their oaths something more reprehensible than their oath: they are not content to swear by God Most High and His attributes - Mighty and Majestic is He - and they do not consider it binding until one of them swears by the blessing of the sultan, or by his head, or by the head of the one who makes him swear, or by his beard, or by the dust of his father's grave; then he is considered bound. They have other things which they venerate and swear by besides these. It is not far-fetched that swearing by God Most High falsely is less sinful than swearing by these truthfully. This is something widespread, and there is no power and no might except by God, the Exalted, the Mighty.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said, after mentioning that it is an oath: "The more fitting is that it be by way of glorification and seeking blessing through His name, if they were worshipping Him, as you say when you begin something: 'In the name of God Most High,' and 'by the blessing of the Messenger of God' (ﷺ), and the like."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 45–46:

﴿Then Moses threw down his staff, and behold, it swallowed up﴾, meaning it swallows quickly. The root meaning of talaqquf (quickly seizing) is taking hold of something swiftly. Most of the seven readers recited ﴿تَلَقَّفُ﴾ (talaqqafu) with a fatha on the lam and a shadda, the original form being ﴿تَتَلَقَّفُ﴾ (tatalaqqafu), with one of the two taʾs deleted. The use of the present tense conveys the vividness of the scene and the sense of continuity. ﴿what they falsely fabricate﴾, meaning what they turn from its original state and form by their deception and forgery, so that they make their ropes and staffs appear to be snakes moving about. Here ﴿ما﴾ (ma) is a relative pronoun whose returning pronoun has been omitted for the sake of the verse-ending (fāṣila). It is also permitted for ﴿ما﴾ to be a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya), meaning "it swallows their falsehood", with the thing falsely fabricated being named metonymically for emphasis. ﴿So the magicians were cast down prostrate﴾, meaning they fell prostrate immediately upon witnessing that, without hesitation or wavering, because they knew that such a thing lies beyond the limits of magic, and that it was a divine matter that had appeared at the hand of Moses, peace be upon him, as confirmation of his prophethood. The falling down is expressed by the verb "cast" (ilqāʾ) because it was mentioned alongside the other instances of "casting" (ilqāʾāt), so the expression follows the device of mushākala (rhetorical correspondence between words). There is also in it, together with observing this correspondence, the idea that when they saw what they saw, they could not restrain themselves from throwing themselves to the ground in prostration, as though they had been seized and flung down. Thus there is a metaphor in the verb (istiʿāra tabaʿiyya, a verbal metaphor), whose beauty is enhanced by the mushākala. Some scholars have discussed this by saying that according to the People of Truth, God Most High creates their falling down, and His creating it is the "casting", so there is no need for a figurative usage.

You know that the bringing into being of their falling down and its creation in them is not called "casting" in the literal or linguistic sense. Moreover, the apparent sense of their statement, were the agent of the casting to be stated, is that the agent is God, Mighty and Majestic, by the success He granted them. Al-Zamakhshari permitted that the agent might be their faith, or the dazzling miracle they witnessed. Then he said: "You may also not posit an agent, because (ulqiya) means (they fell down and dropped)."

Abu Hayyan criticised this, saying it is not a valid view, since a verb cannot be put in the passive form with an unnamed subject unless the agent has been omitted and that omission has been compensated for by the passive construction. As for the claim that no agent is to be posited, this is a view far from the correct position. Sahib al-Kashf (al-Kashf, the commentary of al-Tibi) explained this by saying that he meant there is no need to posit a different agent besides the one to whom the passive verb is attributed, since he is the agent of the casting. Do you not see that if you were to interpret (sagata, fell) as (alqā nafsahu, cast himself), it would be correct?

Al-Tibi (said) that he meant there is no need to specify an agent, because the intended meaning is the one cast down, not the identity of the one who cast him, just as you say: "The Kharijite was killed."

You know that the explanation al-Zamakhshari gave is closer to what Sahib al-Kashf preferred. In general, one must interpret the words of Sahib al-Kashf (al-Zamakhshari), for he is too great to have intended their apparent meaning, which would be refuted by what Abu Hayyan raised.

In the prostration of the magicians and their submission there is evidence that the ultimate end of magic is deception and embellishment, which makes one imagine something that has no reality, because magic was at its strongest in the time of Moses, peace be upon him, and the one who brought it, Pharaoh, was the most knowledgeable person of his age in it. They had exerted their utmost effort and displayed the greatest of what they had, [p. 79] and they brought nothing but deception and embellishment, so it is said. The verified view is that this is the predominant character of magic, not that every magic is like this.

As for al-Qazwini's statement that the claim that magic involves a real transformation of form is one of the superstitions of common people and the tales of women, since that is impossible for any magic ever, it is not free from rashness. It has also been argued from this that immersion in every branch of knowledge is beneficial, for those magicians, through their deep immersion in the science of magic, came to know the truth of what Moses, peace be upon him, had brought, and that it was a miracle, and so they benefited from the increase in their knowledge, because it led them to acknowledge the truth and to faith, by distinguishing between miracle and magic.

It has been objected that this establishes only a particular judgment, as is not hidden. Some eminent scholars mentioned that they only came to know the truth of this after Moses, peace be upon him, took the staff and it returned to what it had been, for they had not yet seen any trace of their ropes and staffs. They said: "If this were magic, our ropes and staffs would have remained." Perhaps on this view they became scattered particles of dust, or they ceased to exist because the will's connection to their existence had been severed.

The Greatest Shaykh (Ibn al-ʿArabi), may God sanctify his secret, said in the sixteenth chapter and the fortieth chapter of the Futuhat: the staff only swallowed the forms of the snakes from the ropes and staffs. As for itself, it remained and was not annihilated, as some commentators supposed. This is indicated by God Most High's words: ﴿it will swallow what they have made﴾, while they had made only the forms. Otherwise, doubt would have fallen upon the magicians regarding the staff of Moses, peace be upon him, and they would not have believed. End of the summary, so reflect.

You know that the explanation al-Zamakhshari gave is closer to what Sahib al-Kashf preferred. In general, one must interpret the words of Sahib al-Kashf (al-Zamakhshari), for he is too great to have intended their apparent meaning, which would be refuted by what Abu Hayyan raised.

In the prostration of the magicians and their submission there is evidence that the ultimate end of magic is deception and embellishment, which makes one imagine something that has no reality, because magic was at its strongest in the time of Moses, peace be upon him, and the one who brought it, Pharaoh, was the most knowledgeable person of his age in it. They had exerted their utmost effort and displayed the greatest of what they had, [p. 79] and they brought nothing but deception and embellishment, so it is said. The verified view is that this is the predominant character of magic, not that every magic is like this.

As for al-Qazwini's statement that the claim that magic involves a real transformation of form is one of the superstitions of common people and the tales of women, since that is impossible for any magic ever, it is not free from rashness. It has also been argued from this that immersion in every branch of knowledge is beneficial, for those magicians, through their deep immersion in the science of magic, came to know the truth of what Moses, peace be upon him, had brought, and that it was a miracle, and so they benefited from the increase in their knowledge, because it led them to acknowledge the truth and to faith, by distinguishing between miracle and magic.

It has been objected that this establishes only a particular judgment, as is not hidden. Some eminent scholars mentioned that they only came to know the truth of this after Moses, peace be upon him, took the staff and it returned to what it had been, for they had not yet seen any trace of their ropes and staffs. They said: "If this were magic, our ropes and staffs would have remained." Perhaps on this view they became scattered particles of dust, or they ceased to exist because the will's connection to their existence had been severed.

The Greatest Shaykh (Ibn al-ʿArabi), may God sanctify his secret, said in the sixteenth chapter and the fortieth chapter of the Futuhat: the staff only swallowed the forms of the snakes from the ropes and staffs. As for itself, it remained and was not annihilated, as some commentators supposed. This is indicated by God Most High's words: ﴿it will swallow what they have made﴾, while they had made only the forms. Otherwise, doubt would have fallen upon the magicians regarding the staff of Moses, peace be upon him, and they would not have believed. End of the summary, so reflect.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 47–48:**

﴿They said: "We believe in the Lord of the worlds"﴾ is a *badal ishtimal* (an inclusive apposition, a second term that includes the first) to "(was thrown)", because of the connection between the throwing mentioned and this statement. Alternatively, it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), with *qad* (قَدْ) implied or omitted. It is also possible that it is an explanatory resumption (*istiʾnaf bayani*), as if it were said: "What did they say?" and the answer was: ﴿They said: "We believe in the Lord of the worlds"﴾, ﴿the Lord of Moses and Aaron﴾. This is an explicative apposition (*ʿatf bayan*) to "the Lord of the worlds", or a substitution (*badal*) from it. It was brought in to remove the suspicion that Pharaoh was meant, since his ignorant people used to call him by that title. It also indicates that what made them believe in Him, exalted be He, was the overwhelming miracle that He, glory be to Him, brought about through the two of them. The meaning of His being their Lord, exalted be He, is that He is their Creator and the Owner of their affairs.

It is also permissible that the attribution of "the Lord" to the two of them is based on their description of Him, glory be to Him, by what preceded in the words of Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿the Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾, and his words: ﴿your Lord and the Lord of your earliest ancestors﴾, and his words: ﴿the Lord of the east and the west and what is between them﴾. So it is as if they said: "We believe in the Lord of the worlds whom Moses and Aaron described." The flaw in this is not hidden, even if it is granted that they heard the aforementioned description after they had been gathered from the cities.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 49:

﴿Said﴾ Pharaoh to the magicians, ﴿"Have you believed in him before I give you permission?"﴾ That is, without my giving you permission to believe in him, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿before the words of my Lord are exhausted﴾ — except that permission from him is possible or expected. ﴿Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic.﴾ So you colluded over what you did, and this is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is a plot you have plotted﴾, etc. Or [it means] he taught you one thing and not another, and therefore he overcame you, as has been said. And it is not objected to this that the two statements are then incompatible, since it is possible that Pharaoh said each of them — even though they are not mentioned together here — and the accursed one intended by that to confuse his people, so that they would not believe that they had believed with insight and the manifestation of truth.

Al-Kisa'i, Hamzah, Abu Bakr and Rawh read ﴿"Have you believed?"﴾ with two hamzahs (ءأمنتم), ﴿so you will soon know﴾ the consequence of what you have done.

The lam (in fa-la-sawfa) is said to be the lam of initiation (lam al-ibtida'), which enters the predicate to emphasize the content of the sentence, and the subject is omitted, i.e. "fa-la-antum sawfa ta'lamun" (so indeed you will know). It is not the lam of oath, because that does not enter the imperfect tense except with the emphatic nun, and its combination with sawfa indicates that the knowing is certain to occur, even if it is delayed for a reason. It is also said to be the lam of oath, and the rule of the necessary association between it and the nun applies except in the case of separation between it and the verb by the particle of future (sawfa), and the case of separation between them by a complement of the verb, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, to Allah you will be gathered﴾.

Abu 'Ali said: it is the lam found in (la-aqumanna), and sawfa has replaced one of the two emphatic nuns, so it is as if it were said: (fa-latalamunna). His saying, Exalted is He, quoting him: ﴿I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, and I will surely crucify you all﴾ is an explanation of the omitted object of (ta'lamun) to which we have alluded, and a detailing of what was summarized; and for this reason it was detailed and joined with fa' in another place. The meaning of (min khilaf) has already passed.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 50:

﴿They said﴾, that is, the magicians: ﴿No harm﴾, that is, there is no harm upon us in what you have mentioned of cutting off the hands and what accompanies it. Al-ḍayr is a verbal noun of ḍārra (to harm), and its verbal noun also came as ḍawr. It is the ism of lā (the noun governed by the negative particle lā), and its predicate (khabar) is omitted, and omitting it in such a context is common. His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, to our Lord﴾, that is, the One in whom we believed, ﴿we will return﴾, are a reason (ta'līl) for negating harm. That is, there is no harm in that; rather, for us in it there is great benefit, due to what we gain from patience upon it for the sake of God, exalted is He, of great reward. Or: there is no harm upon us in what you do, because death by some cause is inevitable, and the return is to God, mighty and majestic is He.

Whoever does not die by the sword dies by other means;
the causes are many, but death is one.

The sum of this is the negation of concern about being killed, with the reason being that death is inevitable. A parallel to this is the saying of ʿAlī, may God ennoble his face: "I do not care whether I fall upon death or death falls upon me." Or: there is no harm upon us in that, because our destiny and your destiny are to a Lord who will judge between us, and He will take vengeance on us from you. And in the meaning of this is his saying:

To the Judge of the Day of Religion we proceed,
and before God the adversaries will gather.

Some of them did not approve of this, because it involves a disruption of the pronouns, since they refer to the magicians both before and after it. And it was prevented by their inclusion in the plural pronoun, so reflect. And his saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 51:

﴿Indeed, we hope that our Lord will forgive us our sins, because we were the first of the believers.﴾ That is, "because we were the first of the believers." This is a second causal justification (ta'lil, giving the reason) for the negation of harm, and it is not joined by a conjunction (ʿaṭf), to signal that it is something that independently serves as the cause. It has been said that the absence of the conjunction is because the causal clause is connected to the first thing being justified together with its own justification. It has also been permitted that it be a justification of the cause. The first view is more evident. That is: there is no harm upon us in this, "indeed, we hope that our Lord will forgive us our sins, because we were the first of the believers." The hope (ṭamaʿ) may be in its literal sense, as Abu Hayyan preferred, since forgiveness is not obligatory upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Or it may mean certainty, as has been said regarding the words of Ibrahim, upon him be peace: ﴿And the One from whom I hope that He will forgive me my sin on the Day of Judgment﴾.

As for their words ﴿the first of the believers﴾, it is possible that they meant the first of the believers among the followers of Pharaoh, or the first of the believers among those present at the gathering, or the first of the believers among the people of their time. Perhaps the statement that they were such was made because they did not know of any believer who had preceded them in faith, so it is a report based on the strongest assumption, and there is no objection to it. So it has been said.

It has also been said: they meant the first to openly manifest faith in Allah the Exalted and His Messenger before Pharaoh, face to face, after the call and the appearance of the sign. Thus the believer of Pharaoh's household and Asiya are not an objection to this. Likewise the Children of Israel are not an objection, because they, as in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit), were believers before them, either because the sorcerers did not know of this, or because each of those mentioned did not openly manifest faith in Allah the Exalted and His Messenger before Pharaoh, face to face, after the call and the appearance of the sign. So reflect.

Aban ibn Taghlib and Abu Muʿadh read ﴿in kunnā﴾ with a kasra on the hamza of ﴿in﴾. It has been construed that ﴿in﴾ is conditional (sharṭiyya), and the apodosis (jawab) is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, that is: "If we were the first of the believers, then we hope." The author of al-Lawami' made the apodosis the earlier ﴿we hope﴾, and said: the deletion of the fa' (of the apodosis) from it is permitted because it precedes. This is based on the view of the Kufans, Abu Zayd and al-Mubarrad, who permit placing the apodosis of the conditional before it. On this basis, the apparent meaning is that they were not certain that they were the first of the believers. It has been said that they were certain of this, but they expressed it in the form of doubt, to present a matter of established certainty as if it were other than it, out of delicacy and humble supplication to Allah the Exalted. In this there is self-abasement and exaggeration in seeking truthfulness. The correspondence (mushakala) with ﴿we hope﴾ is in accordance with what is apparent in it. Abu Hayyan permitted that ﴿in﴾ be the lightened form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy (thaqila), and that the distinguishing lam (lam al-fariqa) is not needed, since the context indicates that they are believers, so there is no possibility of negation. Similar usage occurs in eloquent speech. In a hadith: "If the Messenger of Allah ﷺ liked honey..." And a poet said:

"We are the refusers of oppression from the family of Malik, and [even] if Malik's people were noble in origin."

On this view, they would be firmly certain that they were the first of the believers with the utmost certainty. It has been disputed whether Pharaoh did to them what he had sworn to do or not. Most scholars hold that he did not, based on the apparent words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿You and whoever follows you will be the victors﴾. Some of these claimed that when they prostrated, they saw the Gardens and the Fires and the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and their souls were taken while they were prostrating. The apparent meanings of the verses refute the matter of death during prostration. As for seeing what was mentioned, I am not certain of its truth. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

[Page 81]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 52:

﴿And We revealed to Moses: "Travel by night with My servants."﴾ This was after years in which he had remained among them, calling them to the truth and showing them the signs, but they only increased in arrogance (utuww) and obstinacy (inad), as has been detailed in Surat al-A'raf in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We had seized the people of Pharaoh with years [of drought]...﴾ and so on.

It has been read as "ani isri" with a kasra on the nun and a waslah on the alif, from sara (to travel by night, sarā). Al-Yamani read it as "an sir," an imperative from sara yasiru (to journey). ﴿Indeed, you are being pursued.﴾ This is the reason (ta'lil) for the command to travel by night, meaning: Pharaoh and his army will follow you at dawn. So travel by night with those who are with you, so that they do not overtake you before you reach the sea, but rather they will be at your heels when you enter the sea, and they will enter your passages, and then I will close it over them and drown them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 53–54:

﴿Then Pharaoh sent﴾. The *fa'* here is *fa'* of explanation (al-fa' al-fasiha, the *fa'* that signals an unstated step). That is, [Moses] set out by night with them, Pharaoh was informed of this, and so he sent ﴿into the cities﴾, meaning the cities of Egypt, ﴿gatherers﴾, meaning those who gather the armies so that they may pursue them. ﴿Indeed these﴾ refers to the Children of Israel. The speech is taken as implying an act of saying, and the apparent reading is that the phrase is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: saying, "Indeed these ﴿are a small band﴾", that is, a group of people. It was said that it refers to the lowest of them, and it was said that it means the remnant of anything base. From this comes the phrase *thawb shirdhām* and *shirdhāma*, meaning a torn, cut-up garment. The poet said:

*The winter has come, and my shirt is in tatters, laughed at by the one who longs for me.*

It was read as *la-sharru dhimmatin* (لَشَرِّ ذِمَّةٍ), with *sharr* (evil, the opposite of good) annexed to *dhimma*. Abu Hatim said: this is the reading of someone whose reading is not taken, and no one has transmitted it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). ﴿Few﴾ (*qalīlūn*) is an adjective of (*shirdhima*). The apparent form would have been *qalīla*, but it was made plural in consideration of the fact that the *shirdhima* comprises the tribes, each tribe of whom is few. The accursed one (Pharaoh) exaggerated their fewness, since he first described them with a noun that indicates fewness, which is *shirdhima*, then described them as few, then made the word *qalīl* plural to indicate the fewness of each division among them. He used the sound plural, which has been said to indicate fewness, and he regarded them as insignificant in comparison with his soldiers.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from al-Suddi that Musa (peace be upon him) went out with six hundred thousand and twenty thousand, among whom were not counted anyone under twenty because of his youth, nor anyone over sixty because of his age. Pharaoh followed them, with Haman at the head of his vanguard, with one million and seven hundred thousand horses.
[Page 82]
It was also said: Pharaoh sent after them one million five hundred thousand crowned kings, with each king having a thousand [men]. He himself went out in a great host, and his vanguard was seven hundred thousand men, each man on a horse, and on his head a helmet. It is related from Ibn Abbas that they numbered six hundred and seventy thousand. I say: they were fewer than Pharaoh's armies, though I do not assert a number for either of the two groups. The reports on this matter barely can be authenticated, and they contain exaggerations beyond what is customary. The well-known view among the Jews is that the Children of Israel, when they left Egypt, were six hundred thousand men apart from the children, and this is the clear statement of the Torah that is in their hands.

It is also permissible that by *qilla* (fewness) is meant humiliation rather than fewness of number. Rather, it is derived from (*shirdhima*), meaning that because of their fewness they are humbled and not regarded, and their victory is not expected. It was also said that humiliation is understood from (*shirdhima*), on the basis that what is meant by it is the remnant of anything base, or the lowest of people. And *qalīlūn* is either an adjective for it, or a second predicate of *inna* (إنَّ). The apparent reading is what was mentioned earlier.
