Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 55–56:

﴿And indeed they are enraging us,﴾ meaning: they are doing what enrages us, by opposing our command and going out without our permission, while they have with them our borrowed property.

It is related that God Most High commanded them to borrow the ornaments from the Copts, so they borrowed them and went out with them. The placing of (lana, "to us") first serves to restrict (hasr) and for the sake of the rhyme (fasila, the verse-ending); the lam is for emphasis (taqwiya), or it is a case of treating a transitive verb as intransitive (tanzil al-muta'addi manzilat al-lazim). ﴿And indeed we are a multitude taking precautions﴾, that is: we are a company whose habit is caution (hadhar) and guarding oneself, and the exercise of resolve in affairs. He first pointed out the absence of anything that would prevent their pursuit by their might, then to the confirmation of what calls him to it of their extreme enmity, and the necessity of vigilance regarding their affair, either to urge him toward it or as an excuse to the people of the cities, so that he (upon him be the curse) would not be suspected of what would break his authority.

Several of the Seven Readers and others read «ḥadhirūna» without an alif. A distinction was made between (ḥādhir) with the alif and (ḥadhir) without it: the first is an active participle (ism fa'il) indicating renewal and occurrence, while the second is an adjective of quality (sifa mushabbaha) indicating permanence. Close to this is what is related from al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i, that the ḥadhir is one in whose very nature caution exists, so he is watchful and alert. Abu 'Ubayda said: they both have one meaning. Sibawayh held that ḥadhir may be for intensification (mubalagha) and that it operates as ḥādhir operates, governing an object in the accusative. He recited:

*ḥadhirun umūran lā taḍīru wa āminun*
*mā laysa munjīhi min al-aqdār*

This has been disputed, by what is mentioned in the books of grammar.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and others that the ḥādhir is one fully equipped with weapons, and they explained the verse by this meaning. It seems to be in the sense of one possessing ḥadhar, and the word for instrument of war is so named metaphorically. Upon this is understood the words of the Most High: ﴿Take your precautions (khudhū ḥidhrakum)﴾.

Samit ibn 'Ajlan, Ibn Abi 'Ammar and Ibn al-Sumayqa read «ḥādirūna» with the alif and the unpointed dal, from their saying: "a ḥadrah eye," i.e., large, and "Fulan ḥādir," i.e., swollen. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the meaning is filled with rage and disdain. Ibn Khalawayh said: the ḥādir is the fat, strong, vigorous one; the meaning is: strong and fierce. From it is the saying of the poet:

*aḥabba al-ṣabiyyu al-sū'a min ajli ummihi*
*wa abghaḍahu man baghaḍahā wa huwa ḥādiru*

It was also said: the meaning, on this reading too, is "fully equipped with weapons," taken from ḥadara meaning bulk and strength, for one fully equipped with weapons is strengthened by them as he is strengthened by his limbs. And (jami') in all the readings and meanings is in the sense of "a multitude," and it is not the (jami') by which emphasis is made, as we indicated; had it been that emphatic one, it would have been put in the accusative.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: the meaning is filled with rage and disdain. Ibn Khalawayh said: the ḥādir is the fat, strong, vigorous one; the meaning is: strong and fierce. From it is the saying of the poet:

*aḥabba al-ṣabiyyu al-sū'a min ajli ummihi*
*wa abghaḍahu man baghaḍahā wa huwa ḥādiru*

It was also said: the meaning, on this reading too, is "fully equipped with weapons," taken from ḥadara meaning bulk and strength, for one fully equipped with weapons is strengthened by them as he is strengthened by his limbs. And (jami') in all the readings and meanings is in the sense of "a multitude," and it is not the (jami') by which emphasis is made, as we indicated; had it been that emphatic one, it would have been put in the accusative.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 57–58:

﴿So We expelled them﴾ i.e., Pharaoh and his host. That is, We created in them the impulse to leave by this cause which the three verses contain, and so they were driven to it. Or, We created their departure ﴿from gardens and springs﴾ which they had along the banks of the Nile, as narrated from Ibn 'Umar and others, ﴿and treasures﴾ i.e., wealth they had hoarded and stored beneath the earth. It was singled out for mention because apparent wealth is something that necessarily belonged to them, since it is among the necessities of their livelihood; so their being expelled from it is known by necessity. It has also been said that it is because their apparent wealth had been obliterated by the destruction.

It has been objected that the expulsion took place before the obliteration, since among apparent wealth are the gardens, and the report about them that they were expelled from them is under the description of their being gardens, and the original meaning of such a report is literal.

And even if we grant that it came afterward, it may be objected that what was destroyed was what Pharaoh and his people made and what they built up (the verse refers to), which is explained as palaces, buildings and gardens; so whatever is other than that remains not judged as destroyed among the apparent wealth, although they were expelled from it too. Thus justifying the non-mention of it requires a reason other than what has been stated.

It has also been said: the intended meaning of "treasures" is their wealth, both hidden and apparent, and the term was applied to it because none of it was spent in obedience to God Most High. This is reported from Mujahid. The first view, however, is more in accord with the language.

Most of the ignorant people of Egypt claim that these treasures are in al-Muqattam in the land of Egypt, and that they still exist to this day. They have spent large sums seeking to extract them, paying the devils of the Maghrebis and others, but they gained nothing except dust or kadhdhan stone. Ibn Jubayr said: the intended meaning of "springs" is springs of gold, which is contrary to what is immediately understood. Similar to this is what al-Dahhak said, that the intended meaning of "treasures" is rivers. ﴿And a noble station﴾ means fine dwellings, as al-Naqqash said. From Ibn Lahi'a it is reported that they were in al-Fayyum in the land of Egypt. It has been said: they are the assemblies of the princes, the nobles and the rulers, surrounded by their followers. It has been said: they are couches in canopies. Al-Mawardi related that they are tethering-places for horses. From Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak it is reported that they are the pulpits for preachers. Qatada and al-A'raj read "wa-muqamin" with a damma on the mim, from aqama.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 59–60:

﴿Thus﴾ may be in the accusative position, as an adjective (sifah) of an implied verbal noun (masdar), meaning: "We brought them out with a bringing out like that bringing out," the demonstrative referring to the verbal noun of the verb. Or it may be in the genitive position, as an adjective of "maqam" (station), meaning: "a noble station like that station which they had." On both readings, there is no objection that it entails likening a thing to itself, as Abu Hayyan claimed, for the reason whose verification has already passed. Or it may be in the nominative position, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "The matter is thus," and the intent is to affirm and establish the matter. Al-Tibi chose this, saying: "It is the strongest of the views, so that the words of His, exalted is He, ﴿And We caused the Children of Israel to inherit it﴾ — that is, We made it their possession by way of inheritance — may be a conjunction (atf) upon it, and the two clauses are parenthetical between the conjoined element, which is ﴿So We expelled them﴾, and the conjunct, which is His, exalted is He, saying ﴿so they pursued them﴾, because the pursuit came after the expulsion, not the inheritance."

Al-Wahidi said: God, exalted is He, returned the Children of Israel to Egypt after He had drowned Pharaoh and his people, and He gave them all that had belonged to Pharaoh's people of wealth, property, and dwellings. In other than this reading, "awrathna" would be a conjunction upon "akhrajna," and an implied element must be supplied, such as: "So We willed to expel them and to cause the Children of Israel to inherit their dwellings, and they went out and they pursued them," end of quote.

It is understood from the words of some that the clause "awrathnaha" etc. is parenthetical between the conjunct and the conjoined element in all the readings. What al-Wahidi mentioned, that God, exalted is He, returned the Children of Israel to Egypt after He had drowned Pharaoh and his people, apparently means that this occurred immediately after the drowning without any lapse of time.

More evident than this is what is reported from al-Hasan, who said: "As they crossed the sea and returned, and they inherited their dwellings and their wealth." I have seen in some books that they returned with Moses, peace be upon him, and remained with him in Egypt for ten years. It is also said that some of them returned after the drowning of Pharaoh, and they are the ones who were given the wealth of the Copts as inheritance, while the rest went with Moses, peace be upon him, to the land of Syria.

It is also said that after they crossed the sea they went to Syria and did not enter Egypt during the lifetime of Moses, peace be upon him, and they ruled it in the time of Solomon, peace be upon him. The text in the Torah that is in the hands of the Jews today clearly states that after they crossed the sea they headed to the land of Syria, and the story of their going there is detailed, and most histories agree with this. The apparent meanings of many verses require what al-Wahidi mentioned. And God, exalted is He, knows best.

The meaning of ﴿they pursued them﴾ (atba'uhum) is "they overtook them." It is said: "I followed the people and I pursued them," meaning: I came after them and I overtook them. It is as if the meaning is: "I made them followers of me after they had been followers of me," emphasizing the reaching. The subject pronoun refers to the people of Pharaoh, and the object pronoun to the Children of Israel.

Al-Hasan recited (fa-ittaba'uhum) with a connecting hamzah and a doubled ta'. ﴿at sunrise﴾ (mushriqin) means: entering the time of the sunrise, that is, its rising, from (ashraqa Zayd), he entered the time of shuruq (sunrise), just as (asbaha) means he entered the time of morning, and (amsa) means he entered the time of evening. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is from (ashraqa), meaning "he headed toward the east," just as (anjada) means "he headed toward Najd" and (a'raqa) means "he headed toward Iraq." That is: they pursued them heading toward the east. The majority hold the first meaning.

It is reported from al-Suddi that God, exalted is He, cast death upon the Copts on the night Moses, peace be upon him, went out with his people, so every firstborn male among them died, and they were occupied with burying them and were distracted from pursuing them until the sun rose. Something similar is in the Torah, with the addition that the firstborn of their livestock also died. The descriptive phrase is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject. It is also said that it is a circumstantial clause from the object.

The meaning of ﴿mushriqin﴾ is "in light," based on what is reported: that the Children of Israel were in light, while Pharaoh and his people were in haze and darkness, in which they were bewildered until the Children of Israel crossed the sea. This hardly holds, given His, exalted is He, saying:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 61:

﴿Then when the two hosts saw each other﴾, i.e., they drew so near that each of them saw the other.

Yes, it is mentioned in the Torah, in substance, that when the Children of Israel set out, there went before them by day a pillar of cloud and by night a pillar of fire, to guide them on the way. When Pharaoh pursued them and they saw his armies, they were greatly afraid and blamed Moses (peace be upon him) for the departure, and said to him: "Did you bring us out from a lack of graves in Egypt, so that we would die in the wilderness? Did we not tell you: Leave us to serve the Egyptians, for that is better for us than dying in the wilderness?" Moses said to them: "Do not fear; stand firm and see the help of God Most High for you." Then God Most High inspired Moses to strike the sea with his staff, and the pillar of cloud moved behind them and came between them and Pharaoh and his armies. Night fell, and none of Pharaoh's armies advanced throughout the night, and the sea was split, and then the Children of Israel entered. There is nothing in this that confirms the aforementioned state of affairs, so consider it.

Al-A'mash and Ibn Wththab recited «tara» without a hamza, according to the方式 of easing (takhfif) by the intermediate pronunciation (bayn bayn). Its full realization by substitution (qalb) is not valid, because it would require three consecutive alifs, and that never occurs, so said Abu al-Fadl al-Razi. Ibn Atiyyah said: Hamzah recited «tarīʾī» with a kasra on the ra', then a long vowel, then a hamza, and the like was narrated from ʿAsim. It was also narrated from him «tarāʾā» with a fatha and a long vowel. Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Ali al-Ansari said in his book al-Iqna': ﴿tarāʾā al-jamʿān﴾ in al-Shu'ara', when Hamzah and al-Kisa'i paused upon it, they inclined the alif that has turned from the lam of the verb, and Hamzah inclines the alif of tafā'ala both in continuity and in pause, like the inclination of the alif that has turned; and it was also read «falammā tarāʾati al-fiʾatān» (when the two groups saw each other).

﴿The companions of Moses said: Indeed, we are overtaken﴾, i.e., we are about to be caught up with. They used the nominal sentence emphasized by two particles of emphasis, to indicate the certainty of the overtaking and the attainment and their immediacy, and by this they intended grief and the manifestation of complaint, seeking a remedy.

Al-A'raj and Ubayd ibn Umayr read (lamudarrikūna) with a fatha on the dal, shadda, and a kasra on the ra', from al-idrāk in the sense of perishing and dwindling away, it is said: adraka al-shay' when it perished successively, and its root meaning is succession, which is one going after the trace of another; then in the common usage of the language it came to mean destruction, namely that something gradually perishes until all of it is gone. Succession has come in this sense in the verse of the poet of the Hamasa:

Is it after the sons of my paternal uncle, those who succeeded one another, that I hope for a longer life, or do I fear death more?

The meaning is: "Indeed, we are destroyed at their hands little by little."

Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, commentary on Surah 26, verse 62:

﴿He said﴾: Musa, peace be upon him, said this to rebuke them for that (fear) and to guide them to the understanding that the planning of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, suffices in place of their own planning. ﴿No!﴾ They will not overtake you. ﴿Indeed, my Lord is with me﴾ in protection and support. ﴿He will guide me﴾ soon to what contains your deliverance from them and your victory over them. He did not include them, peace be upon him, in the companionship and the guidance, in order to make the statement fit what they had pointed to in their words: ﴿Indeed, we are overtaken!﴾, which was a request for a plan from him, peace be upon him. It has also been said: since he, peace be upon him, was the origin, and others were followers of him, protected and supported through his mediation, his nobility and his honour, he said "with me" (ma'iya) rather than "with us" (ma'ana), and likewise he said "He will guide me" rather than "He will guide us." It has also been said: he said this as a punishment for them for their heedlessness of the words of Allah, the Exalted, to him, peace be upon him: ﴿You two and whoever follows you will be the victors﴾ (28:35), so that they became frightened and said what they said. For the apparent meaning is that they heard that from Musa, peace be upon him, during the period they remained with him in Egypt, or (it was due to) their heedlessness of Allah's care for them when they were among the Qibt (Copts) in Egypt, where they were not struck by what befell the Copts of the plagues such as blood and the like, which required, through good assumption, their deliverance from them when they were commanded to leave, but the Copts followed them. His rebuke of them for this was by merely their not being included in what was mentioned, not that he negated it from them, as may be imagined from the fronting of the predicate. The fronting was for the sake of emphasis on the matter of companionship, which is the basis of the sought-after deliverance. It has also been said that it is for restriction, but relative to Pharaoh and his assembly. It has also been said, on the second opinion regarding the reason for not including them, that it is for restriction relative to them as well, in the sense: indeed, with me first and essentially is my Lord, not with you in the same way. It has also been said: companionship was fronted here and postponed in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed Allah is with us﴾ (9:40), because the addressees here are the Children of Israel, who were dull and recognised Allah, Mighty and Majestic, only after reflection and hearing from Musa, peace be upon him, whereas the addressee there is al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr), may Allah be pleased with him, who sees Allah, the Exalted, before everything else. Because the situations differ, our Prophet ﷺ coupled his companion with himself in companionship and did not put him first as a rebuke or reprimand, and he addressed him in a manner like the address of Allah, the Exalted, to him, peace be upon him, in consoling him with what amounts to a prohibition of grief. He used the comprehensive name, which is the word Allah, rather than a name suggesting a single attribute, for example. The speech of Musa, peace be upon him, and his address to his people, did not follow this pattern. Glory be to Him who favoured some of the worlds over others.

Some have claimed that there is an ellipsis in the statement, and the estimate is: "Indeed, with me is the promise of my Lord," and for this reason he said "with me" rather than "with us." But there is what there is in this.

[p. 86]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 63 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿So We revealed to Moses: "Strike the sea with your staff."﴾ It is the Qulzum (the Red Sea) according to the sound view. It was said: it is a sea behind Egypt called Asaf. It was also said: it is the Nile. The apparent meaning is that this revelation came after the aforementioned statement, and he had not been commanded to strike on the day of the command to travel by night.

Ibn Abd al-Hakam related, from Mujahid, that when Moses (peace be upon him) and the Children of Israel reached the sea, the believer from the family of Pharaoh said: "O Prophet of Allah, where were you commanded to go? The sea is in front of you, and the people of Pharaoh have overtaken us!" Moses said: "I was commanded to go to the sea." The believer from the family of Pharaoh then plunged his horse into it, but the current turned it back. Moses (peace be upon him) did not know what to do. Allah the Exalted had revealed to the sea: "Obey Moses, and the sign of that is when he strikes you with his staff." So Allah the Exalted revealed to Moses: "Strike the sea with your staff."

He also related, through the chain of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, that when Moses reached the sea, Yusha' ibn Nun came forward on his horse and walked upon the water, while others plunged their horses in and were drowned. The companions of Moses said: "Indeed, we are overtaken!" Moses supplicated to his Lord, and a mist covered them and came between them and him. It was said to him: "Strike the sea with your staff."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related, from Ibn Abbas, that Allah the Exalted revealed to Moses: "Strike the sea with your staff," and revealed to the sea: "Listen to Moses and obey him when he strikes you." So the sea was seized with a tremor (afkal), meaning trembling, not knowing from which of its sides he would strike it.

Ibn Abi Hatim related, from Muhammad ibn Hamzah ibn Yusuf ibn Abd Allah ibn Salam, that when Moses (peace be upon him) reached the sea, he said: "O You who existed before everything, who brought everything into being, and who exists after everything, make for us a way out!" Then Allah the Exalted revealed to him: "Strike the sea with your staff."

It is also narrated that he (peace be upon him) said: "O Allah, to You belongs all praise, to You is the complaint, from You is the help sought, and You are the One sought for aid; there is no power and no strength except through Allah, the Most High, the Mighty."

In al-Durr al-Manthur (al-Suyuti's tafsir), on the authority of Ibn Mardawayh, from Ibn Mas'ud in a marfu' report (traced back to the Prophet), there is what indicates that he (peace be upon him) said this at the moment of the splitting. ﴿Then it split﴾, that is: he struck it and it split. The fa' here is fasihah (an elliptical fa' indicating an implied clause). Ibn Usfur claimed that in this type of construction the omitted element is "he struck" (daraba), and the fa' that is present is the fa' of "he struck," and the verb "it split" (infalaqa) is the consequence. This is most like the chirping of sparrows, and it seems he was drunk when he said it. In this ellipsis there is an indication of the swiftness of his (peace be upon him) obedience. He (peace be upon him) was commanded to strike and he struck, and the splitting was made to follow upon it, to exalt Moses (peace be upon him) by making this great sign follow upon his action. Had He, Exalted and Majestic, willed, He could have split it without his striking it with the staff.

It is also related that it did not split until he addressed it with the kunyah (teknonym) "Abu Khalid," saying: "Split, Abu Khalid!" and this was by the command of Allah the Exalted to him.

From Qays ibn Abbad: when Moses (peace be upon him) came to it, he said to it: "Split, Abu Khalid!" It replied: "I will never split for you, O Moses! I am older than you and greater in creation!" At that moment it was called out to: "Strike the sea with your staff," so he struck it and it split.

In another report from Ibn Mas'ud: when he (peace be upon him) reached it, he said: "Split apart!" It said to him: "You have grown arrogant, O Moses! Have I ever split for any of the children of Adam?!" So Allah the Exalted revealed to him: "Strike the sea with your staff," and he struck it and it split.

In a hadith that al-Khatib (al-Baghdadi) recorded in al-Muttafiq wa al-Muftariq, from Abu al-Darda', in a marfu' report: "He (peace be upon him) struck it, and it shook as the Throne shakes. Then he struck it a second time, and similarly. Then he struck it a third time and it split apart." This is explicit that the striking was three times. It was also said: he struck it only once and it split. It was also said: he struck it twelve times, and it split at each strike into a path for one tribe.

Ibn Abi Hatim related, from Ibn Jubayr, that he said: "The sea had been still and not moving. When the night came, Moses struck it with the staff, and it began to rise and recede." But I do not think this has any authenticity. The apparent meaning is that the rising and receding were already present before Allah the Exalted created Moses (peace be upon him), and no intelligent person should believe otherwise. Many of the earlier reports are similar to this in my view. The safest course is to limit oneself to what Allah the Exalted has related: that He, glorified is He, revealed to Moses: "Strike the sea with your staff," so he struck it and it split.

﴿So every part became like a great mountain﴾, that is: like a lofty mountain firmly fixed in its place. The apparent meaning of the verse is that al-tawd (the mountain) refers to any mountain. In al-Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari), it says: al-tawd is a great mountain.

What is meant by al-firq (part) is a piece of water that rose up, so that what lay beneath it became like a sirdab (an underground chamber), according to what some of the eminent scholars have mentioned. In that case, there is no difficulty in the view of those who say that the parts were twelve and the paths likewise, corresponding to the number of the tribes of the Children of Israel, each tribe having traveled through one of them. The well-known view is that the parts are sections separated from the water from what lies opposite them. In that case, that view cannot stand, but rather, according to what has been said, there must be thirteen parts so that twelve paths arise between them, corresponding to the number of the tribes. It was also said: if the parts are twelve, the paths must be thirteen, because the first and the twelfth part must each be separated from what lies opposite them of the sea, so there is a path between each of them and the water opposite it, even if it is not like the other paths between two parts; for if they were joined they would not be distinguished from it, and then there would not truly be twelve parts but fewer. There is no remoteness in choosing that the parts are twelve and the paths thirteen, by making the first and twelfth parts separated from what lies opposite them of the sea, with a path between each of them and it. It is said that each of the twelve tribes traveled in one path, and in the thirteenth path traveled those of the Copts who believed in Moses (peace be upon him). End of quotation.

It has been objected that it is not mentioned in the reports that the paths were thirteen; rather, what is mentioned is that they were twelve. Whoever claims otherwise must provide proof. The one further from idle talk and dispute is what was mentioned earlier from some of the eminent scholars. The sign of Allah's power in it is greater, and the creation of the motive to travel that path in the hearts of those who entered, especially the people of Pharaoh, is more remarkable. Likewise, the need for openings (kuwa, windows or apertures) is more evident.

It has been related that the Children of Israel said: "We fear that some of us will drown without our knowing." So Allah the Exalted made openings between them so that some could see others.

Yes, it was said in objection: some of the reports contradict this. Abu al-Abbas Muhammad ibn Ishaq al-Sarraj related in his History, and Ibn Abd al-Barr in al-Tamhid, through the chain of Yusuf ibn Mihran, from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), that the ruler of the barrier (sahib al-radm) wrote to Mu'awiyah asking him about several matters, among them: "A place where the sun rose which it had not risen over before or after?" Mu'awiyah did not know the answer to this, so he wrote asking Ibn Abbas, who answered each question, until he said: "As for the place where the sun rose which it had not risen over before or after, it is the place where the sea split for the Children of Israel. The part being vaulted like a sirdab prevents the sun from rising and shining onto the earth without an intermediary, as is apparent from the question."

It was answered: even after accepting the soundness of the report, there is no contradiction, because the sun could rise onto the land of the vaulted part without an intermediary from the direction of the entrance and exit, or the sun could rise onto the land of the sea before it was vaulted. The commentators here, as far as I have found, did not address the manner of the passage. I have seen in what is attributed to al-Kulliyyat of Abu al-Baqa' that it is reported that when the Children of Israel entered the sea, they came out from the side from which they had entered. In that case, this would not be possible if the splitting was linear; it is only possible if the splitting was curved (qawsiyyah, arc-shaped). Then he mentioned, regarding the number of parts and paths, a statement whose apparent meaning is confused, and some scholars have undertaken to explain and interpret it in a way that is not free from strained reasoning. The essence of what that scholar said, with some addition, is that it is possible, if the splitting of the sea was into twelve parts, that the first and twelfth parts were connected to the shore on the land side, in that the water opposite each of them from the direction of the land rose up and was joined to each and counted among its parts, such that the raised, joined water and the original part to which it is joined become one part, its edge connected to the land with no separation between them by anything.

It was objected to this that it would follow that the paths would be eleven, so two tribes would need to travel together, or successively in one path wider than the rest, or equal to it. There is no doubt that this contradicts the apparent meaning and what is transmitted. Also, it would follow that each of the first and twelfth parts would be thicker than each of the others, because of the joining you have heard of, whereas the apparent meaning is that they are equal in that respect. Also, it would follow that the water adjacent to the land would leave its original state without any reason for that. It is possible that the water opposite each of the first and twelfth parts, from the direction of the land, rose up in the sense of departing, and the two mentioned parts are connected to the land by virtue of being connected to the two apparent paths beneath the departing water that are connected to the land. This is subject to some of the objections that applied to the previous view, and to the remaining of one tribe or two tribes without a barrier of water between them and Pharaoh and his armies.

It is also possible that these two parts are separated from the land, in that the water connected to it remains as it was, a sea, without rising. In that case, it is possible that the paths were thirteen, by considering that the land was uncovered between the first part and the sea that remains in its state connected to the land, so this path lies outside the first mountain. And the land was uncovered between the twelfth part and the sea that remains in its state connected to the land on the other side, so this path lies outside the twelfth part. According to this possibility, it would follow that one of the paths was rendered useless, or that only those of the Copts who believed would be committed to traveling in it. It is also possible that the paths were twelve like the parts, in that the uncovering was between the first part and the sea that remains in its state connected to the land from the direction of Pharaoh and his armies only, or the uncovering was between the twelfth part and the sea that remains in its state from the other side only. This is remote, due to the great size of this uncovered arc and the long time it would take to cross. So the apparent case is the possibility that the uncovering was between the first part and the sea that remains in its state from the direction of Pharaoh. In sum, the possibility that the first and last parts are separated, and that the uncovering was between the first and the sea on the side facing Pharaoh but not between the last and the sea on the side facing the other shore, and the agreement of the paths and the parts in being twelve each, is the most likely to have occurred. (End of quotation.)

It should not be missed that this implies that not all of the paths lay within the gaps between the divisions. If it is not necessarily asserted that all of them were within it (since the reports do not say more than that the paths were twelve), then there is no harm in it. And if you find what was mentioned earlier from some of the eminent scholars about the meaning of "firq" (division) appealing, then consider it on the assumption that the splitting was also arc-shaped (qawsi). Next, what was mentioned, that the exit was from the same direction as the entry, I have not seen except in what is attributed to the Kulliyyat of Abu al-Baqa'. This is more consistent with the view that Musa (peace be upon him) and his people returned to Egypt after coming out of the sea and the drowning of Pharaoh and his soldiers in it. This depends on the splitting being arc-shaped (qawsi), because if it were linear (khatti), it would follow that the return would be along the path of entry, which is clearly false, since the enemies were behind them.

As for the possibility that the linear paths were thirteen, that the Children of Israel traversed twelve of them, that Pharaoh and his soldiers followed them along those paths, and that they (the Israelites) came out before reaching them, and that they all entered the thirteenth path from the side opposite to their entry, heading in it toward the side of their entry, so they did not come out until all their enemies were in those twelve paths that they had followed them along, and then they came out and the sea covered their enemies with what covered them: what this involves is not hidden.

The view that they returned to Egypt together with the view that the splitting was linear depends on this, or on another splitting, or on crossing by ships, or on taking a route to Egypt other than the one they took leaving it for the sea.

The apparent position is that none of that happened. There is no harm, as has been said, in holding that the splitting was arc-shaped, whether we say they returned to Egypt or not. What may be objected to it, that it would then follow that the entrances to those paths and their exits would be on the side of Pharaoh and his soldiers, which would cause the Children of Israel to fear entering, since their enemies might come upon them from the other side, which is the place of exit, and meet them on the path at the edge of al-Thumam (a plant), as is not hidden from people of understanding.

It has also been permitted, on the view that the splitting was arc-shaped, that the entry of Musa (peace be upon him) and his people was from one end of the arc, and the entry of Pharaoh and his soldiers from the other end, so that they would meet Musa (peace be upon him) and his people. When the two groups had fully entered, Musa (peace be upon him) and his people retreated backwards (qahqara) until they had all come out, and then God Most High drowned Pharaoh and his soldiers. Or (it is permitted) that when the group of Musa (peace be upon him) had fully entered and the first of those entering to meet them became visible, they retreated backwards, until they had all come out while the group of Pharaoh had fully entered, and then God Most High destroyed their enemy, and the sea covered him with what covered him. This, as you see, is far-fetched.

What the People of the Book hold is that the splitting was linear, that the paths were twelve paths, one for each tribe, with no arc-shaped curvature there. They also hold that openings (kuwan) were made for them so that a near one could see his near one, and a man from one tribe could see his wife from another tribe; that they came out from the direction opposite to their entry and headed toward the land of Syria. There is nothing in our Book that explicitly denies this, and indeed in the reports there is what testifies to the soundness of part of it. The equality of the divisions and the paths in number needs a sound transmission to establish it. The verse here does not indicate more than a multiplicity of divisions. And God Most High knows best.

Ya'qub reported from some reciters that he recited "kullu filqin" (every cleft) with a lam in place of the ra. Al-Raghib said: "firq" is close to "filq", but "filq" is used with regard to the aspect of splitting apart, while "firq" is used with regard to the aspect of separation, and from it comes "firqah", meaning a group separated from the people.

[p. 89]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 64:

﴿And We brought near﴾ is coordinated with (awhayna, "We revealed"). It has also been said that it is coordinated with an omitted element required by the context, and the implied meaning is: So We made the children of Israel enter what was split of the sea, and We brought near ﴿there﴾, i.e., at that place, ﴿the others﴾, i.e., Pharaoh and his soldiers. That is, We drew them close to the people of Musa (peace be upon him), until they entered their places following in their footsteps. It is also permissible to take it to mean: We drew some of them near to others and gathered them so that none of them would escape.

Ibn Abd al-Hakam narrated from Mujahid, who said: Jibril (peace be upon him) was among the people, between the children of Israel and the family of Pharaoh. He would say to the children of Israel: "Let your last join your first," and he would face the family of Pharaoh and say: "Slow down, so that your last may catch up with you." The children of Israel said: "We have not seen a driver whose driving is better than this." The family of Pharaoh said: "We have not seen a restrainer whose restraining is better than this."

Al-Hasan and Abu Haywa read "wa-zallafna" (﴿وزَلَّفْنا﴾) without a hamza. Ubayy, Ibn Abbas and Abdullah ibn al-Harith read "wa-azlaqna" (﴿وأزْلَقْنا﴾) with a qaf in place of the fa, meaning: We made their feet slip, and the meaning is: We removed their dignity, as in the verse:

"You two overtook Absa when its throne was shaken, and Dhubyan when the sandal slipped under its feet."

It is also possible that God, exalted is He, made their path in the sea, contrary to what He made for the children of Israel (dry ground), so that He caused them to slip into it.

Moreover, the author of al-Lawami said: It has been said that whoever reads with the qaf intends by "the others" Pharaoh and his people, and whoever reads with the fa intends by them Musa (peace be upon him) and his companions, meaning: We gathered their scattered company and brought them near to salvation. It is not hidden that it is far-fetched to intend Musa (peace be upon him) and his companions by "the others."

And We delivered Moses and those with him, all of them. That is, We delivered them from destruction at the hands of their enemies, and from drowning in the sea, by preserving them in that condition until they came out onto dry land. It has also been said that "and those with him" points to the fact that their deliverance came through the blessing of accompanying Moses, peace be upon him, and following him. It has also been said that it is so as to include those Copts who believed in him, peace be upon him, for if it had been said "and his people," the Children of Israel would have been understood from it. And in it

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 66:

﴿Then We drowned the others﴾, Pharaoh and his soldiers, by closing the sea over them after the departure of Musa (peace be upon him) and those with him, and it was a loud roar.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that when the Children of Israel departed, they heard the roar of the sea, and they said: "What is this?" Musa (peace be upon him) said: "Pharaoh and his companions have drowned." So they turned back to look, and the sea cast them up onto the shore.

The expression of Pharaoh and his soldiers as "the others" is for belittlement. The apparent meaning is that "thumma" (then) indicates temporal sequence (al-tarakhi al-zamani), but it is likely better to interpret it as indicating a sequence of meaning (al-tarakhi al-ma'nawi) due to the notional distance between the two conjoined clauses.

[Page 90]

﴿Indeed, in that﴾ is a reference to the story that has been mentioned, and the sense of distance in it serves to magnify the one being referred to. It has also been said that the distance is because of the span of the story from its beginning. ﴿is a sign﴾, meaning a great sign that necessitates belief in Musa (peace be upon him) and affirmation of what he brought. It is said that what is meant by the sign is the transformation of the staff into a serpent, the emergence of his hand white to onlookers, and the splitting of the sea. The word is given in the singular because the referent is one.

﴿But most of them were not believers﴾, meaning: most of the people of Pharaoh to whom Musa (peace be upon him) was commanded to go, namely the Copts, according to what Abu Hayyan favoured, since none of them believed except the believer of Pharaoh's family, Asiya the wife of Pharaoh, and some of the magicians, on the view that some of them were Copts and not all of them, as the People of the Book hold and as the apparent meaning of some of our scholars' words suggests. Also included is the old woman who showed Musa the grave of Yusuf (peace be upon them both) on the night of the departure from Egypt so that he could carry his bones with him.

It has also been said that what is meant by the sign is what occurred in the sea: the deliverance of Musa and those with him and the drowning of the others. The pronoun in ﴿most of them﴾ refers to the people who existed after the drowning and the deliverance, from among the people of Pharaoh who had not come out with him for some excuse, and from among the Children of Israel. The belief that is negated of them is certain, firm assent that does not admit of any removal at all. That is: most of the people who existed after the realisation and manifestation of this great sign were not believers with certain, firm assent that does not admit of removal. The remaining Copts in Egypt did not have a single believer among them at all, and most of the Children of Israel were not certain, which is why they asked for a cow to worship and worshipped the calf. So they cannot be called believers in the sense mentioned. The belief of a portion, which is indicated by the implication, is sufficient, namely that some of the believing portion were from the Children of Israel. Since the intended meaning is: most of them were not believers after the realisation and manifestation of the two signs of the drowning and the deliverance, it is not valid to make the pronoun refer to the Copts unless one specifies a minority who believed and a majority who disbelieved among them after the realisation of the two signs. What was mentioned about the believing minority among them is not like this, since the belief of those mentioned was at the beginning of the mission.

Moreover, the old woman was from the Children of Israel, as is reported in a hadith transmitted by al-Firyabi, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, from Abu Musa, raised to the Prophet. Indeed, Ibn Abd al-Hakam transmitted through al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that she was Sharah, daughter of Ashir ibn Yaqub (peace be upon him). Thus she was the daughter of the brother of Yusuf (peace be upon him), and so she was closer to Musa (peace be upon him) in lineage to Israel.

It has been answered that whoever makes the pronoun refer to the Copts is not obliged to interpret the sign as the drowning and the deliverance. Rather, he may say: what is meant by it is the miracles, namely the staff, the hand, and the splitting of the sea. He may also say that the belief of the minority after the realisation of some of them is sufficient for the unity of their signification in the realisation of the implication. As for making the pronoun refer to the people who existed after the drowning and the deliverance from among the Children of Israel and the people of Pharaoh who had not come out with him, that is contrary to the apparent meaning. Likewise, taking belief in the sense mentioned and making most of the Children of Israel who were singled out for deliverance non-believers, even though some of them did things at the occurrence of some signs that should not proceed from believers, is also problematic, since they did not persist in it.

Al-Khatib reported in al-Muttafiq wal-Muftariq, from Abu al-Darda': "The Prophet (ﷺ) began clapping his hands and marvelling at the Children of Israel and their obstinacy when they reached the sea and their enemy arrived. They came to Musa and said: 'The enemy has arrived; what have you been commanded?' He said: 'To descend here. Either my Lord will open for me and defeat them, or He will split this sea for me.' A group of them set off until they fell into the sea. Then Allah the Exalted revealed to Musa: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff﴾. He struck it and it rose up as a mountain rises. Then he struck it a second time and it did the same. Then he struck it a third time and it split. They said: 'This is not because of the authority of Musa.' So they crossed the sea, and no people were ever heard of who had a greater sin or were quicker to repent than they."

When belief is understood in the sense mentioned, and it is valid to negate belief from those who did things that indicate its lack of firm establishment, it is permissible to make the pronoun refer [Page 91] to the Children of Israel specifically, since most of them were not firmly established in it. The apparent wording of some of them suggests that it refers to them, but that is not sound.

Shaykh al-Islam has taken a path in interpreting the verse that, as far as I think, he alone pursued. He said: ﴿Indeed, in that﴾, that is, in all that has been detailed of what proceeded from Musa (peace be upon him) and appeared at his hands of compelling miracles, and of what Pharaoh and his people did of sayings and deeds, and what was done to them of punishment and retribution, ﴿is a sign﴾, what a sign, a sign upon sign, a great sign that cannot be described, necessitating that those who take heed take heed from it, and compare the affair of the Prophet (ﷺ) with the affair of Musa (peace be upon him), and their own condition with the condition of those destroyed, and avoid engaging in what they used to engage in of disbelief, sins and opposing the Messenger, and believe in Allah the Exalted and obey His Messenger (ﷺ), lest what befell those befall them.

Or: indeed, in what has been detailed in the story, from the viewpoint of his (peace be upon him) relating it as it is, without having heard it from anyone, is a great sign indicating that this is by way of true revelation, necessitating belief in Allah the Exalted alone and obedience to His Messenger (ﷺ). ﴿And most of them were not﴾, that is, most of those who heard their story from him (peace be upon him) were not believers, not by comparing his affair (ﷺ) with the affair of Musa (peace be upon him) and their own condition with the condition of those deniers who were destroyed, nor by reflecting on his (peace be upon him) relating their story without having heard it from anyone, even though each of these two ways leads to belief with certainty. The meaning of ﴿most of them were not believers﴾ is "how many of them were believers!", on the basis that kāna is superfluous, as is the view of Sibawayh (the classical grammarian). This would be like the Exalted's saying: ﴿And most of mankind, even if you were eager, would not be believers﴾. It is a statement from Him, Exalted, about what will happen from the polytheists after hearing the verses that narrate the story, confirming what has passed of His saying: ﴿And there does not come to them any reminder from the Most Merciful, newly revealed, except that they turn away from it﴾, ﴿so they have certainly denied﴾, etc. The choice of the nominal sentence indicates their steadfastness in not believing and their persistence in it.

It is also possible to make kāna mean "became", as in the Exalted's saying: ﴿and he became of the disbelievers﴾. The meaning then is: "and most of them did not become believers, despite hearing the great sign that necessitates belief by the two ways mentioned." The statement is then about not becoming before the occurrence, to indicate the full realisation and establishment of it, like the Exalted's saying: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾.

He claimed that this interpretation is what the eloquence of the noble arrangement demands, from the beginning of the noble surah to the end of the seven stories, and indeed to the end of the noble surah, demanding it clearly. Then he said: As for what has been said, that the pronoun in ﴿most of them﴾ refers to the people of the age of Pharaoh, among the Copts and others, and that the meaning is: "most of the people of Egypt were not believers, since none of them believed except Asiya, the believer of Pharaoh's family, and the old woman who showed the grave of Yusuf (peace be upon him); and the Children of Israel, after they were saved, asked for a cow to worship and took the calf, and said: ﴿We will never believe you until we see Allah openly﴾" — this is far from verification. How could it not be, when the thrust of every story in the surah, except the story of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), is only to explain the condition of a specific group who had rebelled against the command of their Lord and disobeyed His messengers, as is made clear by the opening of the stories with their denial of the messengers after they had witnessed the great signs before them, which should have obliged them to believe and restrained them from disbelief and disobedience, yet they persisted in what they were upon of denial. So Allah the Exalted punished them for that with worldly punishment and cut off their remnant entirely. How then is it possible to report about them that most of them did not believe, especially after reporting their destruction?!

To count the believers among them at first, and then to exclude them at the end, even though they did not share with them in anything of the crimes related about them at all, is something the revelation must be exalted above.

Nor is it possible at all to make the pronoun in ﴿most of them﴾ in the story of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) refer to his people, for it is clear that they increased in nothing from what they heard from him except transgression and disbelief, until they dared to commit that great crime they committed against him. How then can they be described as most of them not believing, when only Lut believed in him, and Allah the Exalted delivered the two of them to the Levant?! So reflect.

It has been objected to this that it contains a problem from several aspects:

Firstly, taking kāna as a superfluous particle, despite the sound correct meaning being clear, is not valid. Here, after this, it leads to taking the nominal sentence as indicating continuity, so that they would not be believers after the revelation of this verse. If it is taken to mean "became", it would require making it a present-tense verb. But this was avoided to indicate full realisation. This too, even with the possibility of a meaning free of the need for that, is not appropriate.

Secondly, making the pronoun in ﴿most of them﴾ refer to the people of our Prophet (ﷺ) is a diversion from its previously mentioned referent in wording, especially in the stories that follow, which are introduced with ﴿Denied﴾.

Thirdly, his saying: "not by comparing his affair (peace be upon him) with the affair of Musa (peace be upon him)," and so on, is not free from difficulty. The shared matter between them both (peace be upon them) is only that each is a prophet supported by miracles absolutely. As for the particulars of the miracles, it is clear that there is no sharing between them. Likewise, comparing their condition to the condition of Pharaoh and his people is not free from this on this kind of analogy.

Fourthly, the Exalted's saying ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign﴾ and so on has been stated in this pattern in seven places, and it is necessary to arrange its interpretation in one system in all of them as far as possible. Among that is what is in the story of the prophet of Allah Lut (peace be upon him), in which is mentioned the detestable known deed of his people, and then the destruction of all of them. And what is in the story of the prophet of Allah Shu'ayb (peace be upon him), in which is mentioned the deed of the People of the Thicket concerning measure and weight, and then the destruction of all of them without explicitly stating the reason for each people's disbelief. So it is not fitting in these two to say: "Indeed, in that is a sign necessitating the belief of the Quraysh," by comparing their own condition to the condition of those destroyed and avoiding engaging in the sins they used to engage in. This is according to the first way. As for the second way, it also has several problems.

Firstly and secondly, for the reasons mentioned first and second. Thirdly, both of these two stories are mentioned here in summary and are mentioned in detail in another surah, and each of them is a newly revealed reminder according to its descent. So there is no soundness in saying: "and most of them were not believers in you, by reflecting on your relating their story without having heard it from anyone," on the basis that they had heard it from him (peace be upon him) in detail before the revelation of this verse. Moreover, that his (peace be upon him) relating this without having heard it from anyone, in a way that leads to their belief with certainty, is open to doubt.

Fourthly, the end of this story is His saying, exalted is He: (And We delivered), (then We drowned the rest). Likewise, the end of the story of Lot, peace be upon him, is His saying: (So We delivered him), (then We destroyed the others), (and We rained down upon them). The obvious reading is that the reference is to the narrated matter itself, which contains the wondrous divine acts, and not to the narration of it.

As for what he said in refuting what was said, it is also nothing, because attributing denial to each of the peoples to whom it is attributed is only in terms of the majority, as is indicated by His saying, exalted is He, in the story of the people of Noah, peace be upon him, quoting them after He had said, glorified is He: ﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾: ﴿They said, "Shall we believe you, when the lowest of people follow you?"﴾ And His saying, mighty and majestic is He, after that, quoting Noah, peace be upon him, what he said in reply to them: ﴿I am not one to drive away the believers﴾. So the pronoun in (most of them) refers to the people, without that being intended as applying to all of them.

A great deal of this occurs in speech, and by "the majority" in the seven places is meant a plural described as having an excess of multitude, whether the believing portion is one person or more. Therefore it is not objected that how can the people of Abraham, peace be upon him, be described as mostly not believing, when only Lot, peace be upon him, believed. So reflect. End of quotation. And what is in it of the worthless and the valuable is not hidden.

I choose, as Shaykh al-Islam chose, that the pronoun refers to the people of our Prophet, prayers and peace be upon him, since the beginning and end of the noble surah concern discourse about them, and his consolation ﷺ regarding what they said about his noble Book, and his prohibition, explicitly and allusively, against letting his noble self go to waste in grief over them. All of this requires, beyond any doubt, that the pronoun refer to his people, peace be upon him, and the matter of its not referring to the nearer antecedent in wording is made light of. On this reading the connection between the verses is stronger.

I choose that the reference is to what this story contains, and that the meaning is: in what this story contains there is a great sign indicating what your people must believe concerning His affairs, exalted and mighty is He, and that most of them were not believers in that. The same is said of everything that comes after, God willing, and all of it follows the pattern of what came before. Likewise the discussion applies to "kana" (was) and what relates to the sentence.

The discussion of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed your Lord, He is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾, is like the discussion of what came before it as well. Perhaps the explanation of what has been mentioned in this way is better than the explanation of Shaykh al-Islam, so reflect carefully. And God, exalted is He, knows best the realities of what He has sent down of speech.

Translation:

﴿And recite to them﴾ is a conjunction with the pronoun that governs "when he called" (idh nada), and so on. That is: mention this to your people. ﴿And recite to them the story (naba') of Abraham﴾, that is, his great and momentous account, just as it was revealed to you; so that it may be firmly established for you, since they are not affected by what it contains, which indicates the intensity of their obstinacy. The change of style is for greater emphasis on the matter of this story, because the failure to believe after they have become acquainted with what it contains is the strongest proof of the firmness of their stubbornness, given that Abraham (peace be upon him) is their forefather, the one they take pride in being descended from and in emulating (ta'assi, following his example), (peace be upon him).

﴿Idh qala﴾ (when he said) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarfiyya) governed by (nabaʾ) (the news), according to the view of Abu al-Baqa'. The meaning is: the news of him at the time he said to his father and his people. Alternatively, it is in the accusative as an object (mafʿūliyya) governed by (utlu) (recite), being an apposition (badal) to (nabaʾ), as the statement of al-Hawfi implies. The meaning is: recite to them at the time he said to them ﴿What do you worship?﴾, with what is recited being what he, peace be upon him, said to them at that time.

The pronoun in (qawmihi) (his people) refers to Ibrahim. It has also been said that it refers to his father, so that it agrees with God's words ﴿Indeed, I see you and your people in manifest error﴾. On this view, there would be what is called tafkīk (disjunction of pronouns), which is a consequence.

He, peace be upon him, asked them what they worship in order to build upon their answer that what they worship is wholly without any claim to be worshipped. It was not for the sake of seeking information, since that was already known and evident to him, peace be upon him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 71:

﴿They said: "We worship idols, and we remain devoted to them."﴾ They did not confine themselves to a sufficient answer by saying merely "Idols" (aṣnāman), as in His saying, ﴿"What has your Lord sent down?" They say, "Good."﴾ and ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say, "The surplus."﴾, and so on. Rather, they elaborated on it by stating the verb and adding the continuation of their devotion to their idols, although he had not asked about that, intending to display what was in their wicked souls of delight and pride in that. This, according to what is in al-Kashshaf, is a foolish style. The meaning of ẓall (remain) is continuance, as in their saying: "If injustice persisted (law ẓalla al-ẓulm), people would perish." In this sense ẓalla is a complete verb (tammah), and Ibn Malik affirmed that it comes thus, while some grammarians denied it. It was also said: he did the thing by day (ẓalla al-shay' nahāran), for they used to worship them by day and not by night; in this sense ẓalla is a defective verb (nāqiṣah), indicating the establishment of its predicate for its subject during the day.

Some eminent scholars preferred the first view, because continuance is what comes to mind and it is more eloquent and suited to the context of delight and pride. Al-Zamakhshari preferred the second, because it is the original meaning, and it is also suited to the context, since it indicates their public display of the act for the sake of their pride in it. ʿĀkifīn (devoted) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) according to the first view, and a predicate (khabar) according to the second, with the prepositional phrase attached to it.

The use of the lām rather than ʿalā conveys an additional meaning, as if they said: "We remain for their sake," i.e., "turning toward their worship" or "circling around them." This also, according to what has been said, is part of their elaboration.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 72–73:

﴿Qala﴾ (He said) is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) built upon a question arising from the detail of their answer. ﴿Hal yasma'unakum﴾ (Do they hear you?): the verb of hearing (fi'l al-sama') has entered upon a non-heard object. According to al-Farisi's view, it then transitively takes two objects, and the second must be something that indicates a sound. So the kaf here, in his view, is the first object, and the second object is omitted. The estimate is: "Do they hear you calling (tad'una)?" It was omitted because of the indication of His saying, ﴿idh tad'un﴾ (when you called), upon it. According to others' view, it is then transitive to one object. If a clause, whether spoken or implied, follows it, then it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from it if it is definite, and in the position of a qualifying clause (sifah) for it if it is indefinite.

It is also permitted that the clause is in the position of a substitute (badal). When it enters upon something heard, it transitively takes one object by consensus. It is permissible that what is here, entering upon that, is with the estimate: "Do they hear your supplication (du'a'akum)?", so the modified noun (al-mudaf) was omitted, because of the indication of "idh tad'un" upon it as well. It was also said: hearing here means answering, as in his saying ﷺ: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from a supplication that is not heard." And from it is His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿innaka sami' al-du'a'﴾ (Indeed You are the Hearer of supplication), meaning: "Do they answer you?" In that case there is no dispute that it is transitive to one object, and it does not need an estimated modified noun.

The better course is to keep it on the apparent meaning, for it is more fitting to the context. Yes, it may be said that what was said is more in accord with the reading of Qatadah and Yahya ibn Ya'mur: "yusmi'unakum" with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the mim, from (asma'a), and the second object is omitted, its estimate being "the answer." ﴿Idh﴾ (when) is an adverbial of time for what has passed, and the present tense was used to summon the past state and narrate it.

As for the fact that (hal) makes the present tense specific to the future, this does no harm here, because what is considered is the time of the judgment, not the time of speaking, and it is so here, because the hearing is after the supplication. Abu Hayyan said: there must be a figurative usage in (idh), by making it mean (idha), or a figurative usage in the present tense, by making it mean the past. Considering the summoning of the state is more eloquent in rebuke. It was also read with the assimilation of the dhal of (idh) into the ta' of (tad'un), by changing it into a ta' and assimilating it into the ta'.

﴿Aw yanfa'unakum﴾ (or benefit you) by reason of your worshipping them. ﴿Aw yadurrun﴾ (or harm you): that is, they harm you by your abandoning their worship; since worship—especially when it is of the degree of intensity you have described—necessarily brings either the acquisition of a benefit or the averting of a harm. The object was omitted for the sake of the fasilah (verse-ending), and what precedes it indicates it. It was also said: the intended meaning is: "or they harm those who turn away from their worship, whoever he may be," but this contradicts the apparent meaning that the conjunction requires.
