They said, "Rather, we found our fathers doing thus."

Here, they turned away from [the claim] that these idols have hearing, benefit, or harm, in acknowledgment of what they had no way to deny, and they were compelled to show that they had no support other than imitation (taqlid). It is as though they said: "They do not hear, nor do they benefit us, nor do they harm us; we only found our fathers doing the same as what we do, and worshipping them the same as we worship them, so we followed them." And the placing of the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq) first is for the sake of the fasilah (the rhyming pause at the end of the verse).

He said: "Have you considered what you have been worshipping, you and your forefathers of old?" That is: have you looked and seen, or have you reflected and known, what you have persisted in worshipping, or: what it is that you have been worshipping? The phrase is one of rebuke and reproach, and it implies the falsity of their gods and of their worship, and that worshipping them is an ancient error whose antiquity serves no purpose except to make its falsehood manifest, as the description of their forefathers as "the most ancient" indicates.

He said: "Have you considered what you have been worshipping, you and your forefathers of old?" That is: have you looked and seen, or have you reflected and known, what you have persisted in worshipping, or: what it is that you have been worshipping? The phrase is one of rebuke and reproach, and it implies the falsity of their gods and of their worship, and that worshipping them is an ancient error whose antiquity serves no purpose except to make its falsehood manifest, as the description of their forefathers as "the most ancient" indicates.

The commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 26, verse 77:

It is said of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, they are enemies to me﴾. It is said that this is a justification for what is understood from that, namely, "I do not worship them," or "their worship is not valid." It is also said that it is a predicate (khabar) for (ma kuntum), since the meaning is: "Shall I inform you and teach you the content of this?" Some of the eminent scholars chose that it is an explanation and elaboration of the state of what they worship, which, if they comprehended it with knowledge, they would not have worshipped. That is: "Know that they are enemies to their worshippers, who love them as they love Allah, Exalted is He, because they are harmed by them in the way a man is harmed by his enemy." Thus, applying the term "enemy" to them is a case of eloquent metaphorical comparison (al-tashbih al-baligh).

Page 95

It is permitted that it be a case of rational metaphor (al-majaz al-'aqli, a figure in which an attribute is ascribed to something other than its true agent) by applying the description of the cause to the effect, in that the one who incites and drives them to worship them is Satan, who is "a manifest enemy to humankind." The first (interpretation) is more apparent. The reason for needing an interpretation is that idols, being inanimate objects, are not fit to be enemies. As for the claim that the speech is inverted (al-qalb), and the original is "Indeed I am an enemy to them," it is worthless.

Al-Nasafi said: "The word 'enemy' is a term for both the one who is hostile and the one who is hated (al-mu'ada) together, so it needs no interpretation. It is like His words: ﴿And by Allah, I will surely plot against your idols﴾. The matter is presented in its own essence as an allusion to them, as in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And why should I not worship the One who created me, and to whom you will be returned?﴾, so that it is more eloquent in advice and more likely to be accepted. From this, the eminent scholars employed allusion (al-ta'rid) in giving counsel."

Among such examples is what is related from al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, that a man confronted him with something, and he said: "If I were in the position you are in, I would need discipline."

A man heard some people speaking about al-Hijr, and he said: "It is neither my house nor your house."

The pronoun in (innahum) refers back to (ma), and it was made plural in consideration of its meaning. The use of the singular "enemy," despite it being a predicate of a plural subject, is either because it is originally a verbal noun (masdar), which is applied to a single masculine (referent) and others, or because all of them are unified in the meaning of enmity, or because the speech is in the sense of (fa-inna kullan minhum, "for each one of them"), or because it carries the meaning of a relation, i.e., "possessing such-and-such," in which case the singular and others are equal, as has been said.

His words, glorified is He: ﴿except the Lord of the worlds﴾ are, according to a group, among whom is al-Farra', a disjunctive exception (istithna' munqati', an exception not belonging to the same category as what precedes it) from the pronoun of "innahum." Al-Zamakhshari chose this, meaning: "But the Lord of the worlds is not like that, for He, Majestic and Exalted, is the protector of whoever worships Him in this world and the Hereafter, never ceasing to bestow favours upon him."

Al-Zajjaj said: "It is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil, an exception belonging to the same category as what precedes it) from that pronoun which refers back to (ma ta'buduna, "what you worship"). It is to be considered that it includes Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and among their ancient forefathers were those who worshipped Allah, Exalted is He, without doubt. Or it may be said that the addressees were polytheists who worshipped both Allah, Exalted is He, and the idols." The specification of the idols here by mention is for the purpose of refutation, and not because their worship was restricted to them. Even if it is granted that it was for this purpose, it is in consideration of the continuity of devotion, and that does not contradict their worship of Him, Mighty and Majestic, at times.

Al-Jurjani said: "The exception is from (ma kuntum ta'buduna, "what you used to worship"), and (illa) has the meaning of (dun, "other than") and (siwa, "besides"). In the verse there is an inversion of order, and the original is: 'Have you considered what you and your ancient forefathers used to worship, other than the Lord of the worlds? For they are enemies to me.'" The problems with this are not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 78:

﴿Who created me﴾ is an attribute (sifah) of (Lord of the worlds). His describing Himself, the Exalted, with this and with what is conjoined to it, although all of creation falls under His lordship over the worlds, is an increase in clarification in the context of guidance. It has also been said that it is an explicit mention of the blessings specific to him, peace be upon him, and a detailing of them, because they are more apt to require that worship be restricted to Him, the Exalted, and that reliance be confined to Him in attracting religious and worldly benefits and in averting immediate and deferred harms.

﴿And He guides me﴾ is conjoined to the relative clause (al-silah), meaning: He alone, exalted is His majesty, guides me to everything that concerns me and sets right my affairs in matters of this life and the Hereafter, a guidance connected to the moment of creation and the breathing of the spirit, continuously renewed over time, as indicated by the fa' (fa, "so") and the form of the present tense. For He, the Exalted, guides everything He has created to that for which it was created, a gradual guidance from the beginning of its bringing into existence to the end of its term, by which it is enabled to attract its benefits and avert its harms, either by nature or by choice. Its beginning, with respect to the human being, is the guidance of the fetus to suck the blood of menstruation, according to the well-known view, and its end is the guidance to the path of Paradise and enjoyment of its everlasting bounty.

Al-Hawfi and others permitted that the relative pronoun be the subject (mubtada'), with the sentence (huwa yahdini, "He guides me") as its predicate (khabar), and the fa' entered the predicate because it implies the meaning of a condition (shart), as in: (alladhi ya'tini fa-lahu dirham, "whoever comes to me, for him is a dirham").

Abu Hayyan objected to this: the fa' is only brought into the predicate of a relative pronoun because it implies the meaning of a condition when the relative is general (amm), and here no generality can be imagined, so what we are dealing with is not analogous to the example. Also, the verb (khalaqa, "created") is one in which renewal cannot occur with respect to Ibrahim, peace be upon him. So perhaps this is according to the view of al-Akhfash that the fa' may be added to the predicate absolutely, as in: (Zayd fa-idribhu, "Zayd, so strike him").

It was answered that the stipulation of generality is not accepted, as al-Radi detailed, and it is only a general tendency (aghlabi). And that the absolute act of creating is among things in which renewal can occur, and it is possible to intend it, even if it appears in the form of a specific case, and creation causes guidance in accordance with wisdom. It has been said that it is a cause for informing about it because it is realized, but this is not correct. And it follows from the aforementioned grammatical analysis that the relative pronoun in His words, glorified is He:

The one who gives me food and drink ﴿والَّذِي هو يُطْعِمُنِي ويَسْقِينِ﴾ is a subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence) whose predicate (khabar) is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it. The same applies to the two relative clauses that follow. The implications of this, both in wording and in meaning, are not hidden. The reading most fitting to the eloquence (jazalah) of the revelation is the first i'rab (grammatical analysis). On this reading, the relative pronoun is coordinated (ma'tuf) with the first relative pronoun. The relative pronoun is repeated in the three places, even though coordinating what falls within the relative clause (silah), namely the six sentences, with the silah of the first relative pronoun would have sufficed, in order to indicate that each of those relative clauses is a sublime attribute of Him, the Exalted, that independently merits the judgment, and that it is right for each to be ascribed to Him, Glorious and Majestic, on its own, and not treated as a mere accessory of another. The apparent meaning is that what is intended is feeding with the well-known food and giving drink with the familiar drink. The pronoun هُوَ (huwa) is used here rather than "the Creator" because the attribution of feeding and giving drink to others besides Him, Glorious and Majestic, is widespread, unlike the attribution of creation. The same reasoning applies to the places where هُوَ is used and where it is omitted, of what comes later, God willing.

It is also narrated from Abu Bakr al-Warraq that the meaning is: He feeds me without food and gives me drink without drink, as in the saying: «Indeed I spend the night, my Lord feeding me and giving me drink». This is a Sufi interpretation.

These two attributes are mentioned after what preceded them, because the continuance of life and the preservation of the order of human creation depend upon food and drink, and in these two matters the path of moderation (al-'adl) has been followed. Man is more in need of them than of anything else. Do you not see that the people of the Fire, while they are in the Fire, were not distracted by the torment they are in from asking for them? They said: ﴿أَفِيضُوا عَلَيْنَا مِنَ الْمَاءِ أَوْ مِمَّا رَزَقَكُمُ اللَّهُ﴾?!

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 80–81:

﴿And when I am ill, it is He who cures me.﴾ This is coordinated (ʿatf) with "who feeds me and gives me drink" (yut'imuni wa yasqini). It is arranged along with them in the same chain of the relative clause (silah) of one relative pronoun, because health and sickness are, for the most part, branches of eating and drinking:

"Indeed, the disease is most often what you find to come from food or drink."
The wise have said: "If most of the dead were asked, 'What is the cause of your deaths?', they would say: 'Overeating (takhamm).'"

The attribution of sickness, which is a punishment (niqmah), to himself, and of healing, which is a blessing (ni'mah), to God, may He be exalted, is for the sake of observing good manners (husn al-adab), just as al-Khidr, peace be upon him, said: ﴿So I wished to damage it﴾ and said: ﴿So your Lord intended that they should reach their maturity﴾. His attribution of death to God, may He be mighty and majestic, in His words ﴿And who causes me to die, then brings me to life﴾ is not objectionable, though death is more severe than sickness, because a distinction can be made: death is known and widely recognized as a decree binding upon all of mankind from God, may He be mighty and majestic, and a general ruling that does not single out anyone. Sickness is not like this, for many are spared from it until death suddenly seizes them. So the consolation of the universality of death removes the effect of its being a punishment, and good manners permit attributing it to God, exalted is He. As for sickness, since it befalls some people and not others, it is a definite punishment; so the height of good manners requires that a person attribute it to himself, in terms of the cause that he cannot be free from.

This is supported by the fact that everything mentioned alongside sickness was reported as occurring definitively and with certainty, because it is something unavoidable. As for sickness, since it may or may not happen, he introduced it tied to the condition "idha" (when), saying: ﴿And when I am ill﴾. He could have said: "And He who makes me ill, then He cures me," as He said elsewhere, but he did not depart from the transmitted correspondence and parallelism except for this reason. So said Ibn al-Munir.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "He said 'I am ill' rather than 'He made me ill' only because many causes of sickness arise from a person's negligence regarding his food, drink and other things." It seems that in this explanation he departed from good manners, because he saw that [Abraham], peace be upon him, attributed death to God, may He be mighty and majestic, and death is more severe than sickness, and the distinction explained above, or something like it, did not occur to him. He overlooked that the meaning he gave for sickness is also broken by death, for just as sickness may come about through a person's negligence in eating and other matters, so too death arises from a cause of this sickness, which comes about through a person's negligence. Yet he, peace be upon him, attributed death absolutely to Him, exalted is His majesty.

Some eminent scholars said, after explaining the attribution of death to God by good manners: since it is the greatest of His distinctive attributes, like giving life at the beginning and in return, and all the affairs of the Hereafter are attached to it and to what follows it of resurrection, He joined the two in one string in His words ﴿And who causes me to die, then brings me to life﴾. Moreover, death, being a means to attaining, peace be upon him, eternal life, is far from being something he did not relish. He said: "Ended." Better than this addition is what has been said: death is, for people of perfection, a link to attaining the eternal beloved things, before which worldly life is held in contempt. In it is the rescue of the sinner from acquiring sins. Then, taking sickness and healing in their apparent sense is what the exegetes have followed.

It is reported from Ja'far al-Sadiq, may God be pleased with him, that the meaning is: "And when I am ill through sins, it is He who cures me through repentance." Perhaps this does not hold; and if it is sound, it belongs to the domain of allusion (ishara), not expression (ibara). The "thumma" (then) in His words ﴿then brings me to life﴾ denotes temporal sequence, because what is meant by bringing to life is reviving for the resurrection, which in reality is separated in time from causing death, though every coming thing is near. Ibn Abi Ishaq read the first-person ya' (yaʾ al-mutakallim) in "yahdiyani" and what follows, and this is a transmission from Nafi'.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 82:

﴿And the One from Whom I hope He will forgive me my sin on the Day of Recompense﴾. He (peace be upon him) magnified whatever slight deviation from the better course might have come from him, to the point that he called it a sin. It has also been said that by it he meant his saying: ﴿Indeed, I am ill﴾, and his saying: ﴿Rather, this one among them did it﴾, and his saying to Sarah: "She is my sister." That he (peace be upon him) counted these among the sins is indicated by what is reported in the hadith of intercession, concerning his refraining from interceding out of shame before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, because these had proceeded from him.

In this there is the point that, even if counting them as sins is correct with regard to his station (peace be upon him), since they say: "The good deeds of the righteous are the bad deeds of those brought near," it is still not correct to intend them here, because they proceeded from him (peace be upon him) only after this exchange that took place between him and his people. As for the third, it is clear, since it occurred after his migration (peace be upon him) to al-Sham. As for the first two, they occurred surrounded by the breaking of the idols. And it is evident that the taking place of these exchanges among them was at the beginning of the matter. This is preferable to what has been said, that they were among the ma'arid (indirect statements), which, because they are in the form of a lie, prevent the one from whom they proceed from intercession, and because they are not literally lies, do not require seeking forgiveness. So it is not correct to intend them here, since that refraining is only due to counting them among the sins, and whenever they are counted among them, they require seeking forgiveness.

It has also been said: he meant by it what proceeded from him at the sight of the star, the moon and the sun, his saying: (This is my lord). That was before this exchange, as is not hidden, and it has already been mentioned that this is not a sin in any way. It has been said: he meant by it the minor sins that might slip from him, and this is close to what preceded. It has been said: he meant by it the sin of those who believe in him (peace be upon him), as something similar has been said about His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That Allah may forgive you your earlier and later sins﴾, and this is as you see. The hope (ṭama') is on its apparent meaning, and he (peace be upon him) did not affirm it with certainty, since he knew that there is no obligation upon Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It is reported from al-Hasan that the intended meaning is certainty (yaqin), but this is not so.

The two adverbial phrases are connected to (yaghfira, "forgive").

The use of the first (the first phrase, "a sin") is to indicate that the benefit of Allah's forgiveness returns only to him (peace be upon him). The linking of forgiveness to the Day of Recompense, although sins are forgiven in this world, is because their effect becomes manifest on that day; and because in that there is an awe-inspiring depiction of that day, and an indication that recompense will occur in it if it is not forgiven. In this sentence there is also what there is of gentleness toward his father and his people in calling them to faith. Al-Hasan read ﴿خَطايايَ﴾ ("khatāyāya", "my sins") in the plural.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 83:

﴿My Lord, grant me wisdom﴾ When He mentioned to them some of His attributes, glorified and exalted is He, which indicate the perfection of His gentle kindness toward him, mentioned by Him, this led him to address his Lord, exalted is He, and to supplicate Him, in order to bind what is ready (al-'atid) and to attract what is more (al-mazid).

By "wisdom" (al-hukm) is meant, according to what the Imam (al-Razi) chose, the wisdom (al-hikmah) which is the perfection of the theoretical faculty (al-quwwah al-'ilmiyyah), namely that one be knowing of the good for the sake of acting upon it. It has been said: the preferable interpretation is that it be explained as the perfection of knowledge concerning the Essence, the Attributes, and all of His affairs, glorified and exalted is He, and His rulings by which He is worshipped. It has been said: it is prophethood. This was refuted on the grounds that it was already present in him, peace be upon him. So what is sought is either the very thing already present, which is impossible, since it is necessarily impossible to obtain what is already obtained, or something other than it, which is also impossible, because one single person cannot be a prophet twice.

It has been answered: by denying that it was present at the time of the supplication, and granting that it was, there is still no objection, since it is permissible that what is meant is seeking the perfection of it, through greater nearness and comprehension of the divine secrets, and the prophets, peace be upon them, differ in this. It has also been permitted that what is meant is seeking steadfastness, and nothing is obligatory upon God, exalted is He.

By His saying: ﴿And join me with the righteous﴾ is meant seeking the perfection of the practical faculty (al-quwwah al-'amaliyyah), namely that he be enabled to deeds which qualify him to be included in the company of the perfected, those firmly established in righteousness, free from the major and minor sins. He placed the first supplication before the second, because the theoretical faculty precedes the practical faculty: it is possible to know the truth even if one does not act upon it, while the reverse is not possible. Also, because knowledge is an attribute of the soul and action is an attribute of the body, so just as the soul is more noble than the body, knowledge is more noble than action. It has been said: by "wisdom" is meant the wisdom which is perfection in knowledge and action.

By His saying: ﴿And join me﴾ etc., is meant seeking perfection in action, and mentioning it after that is specification after generalization, out of concern for action insofar as it is the result and fruit of knowledge. It has been said: by the first is meant what relates to livelihood, and by the second what relates to the hereafter. It has been said: by "wisdom" is meant leadership over creation, and by "joining with the righteous" is meant enabling him to justice among them while maintaining the rights of God, exalted is He. It has been said: by this is meant his being joined with the righteous in Paradise. And you know that after this supplication it is not fitting to ask that he be among the heirs of the Garden of Bliss. In my view, the preferable interpretation is that "wisdom" be explained as wisdom in the sense of perfection in knowledge and action, and "joining with the righteous" as making his station like their station in the sight of God, exalted is He. The meaning of seeking this is that his knowledge and his action be accepted, for if they are not accepted, their possessor is not joined with the righteous, nor is his station made like theirs. And perhaps it is for this reason that he turned away from saying "My Lord, grant me wisdom and righteousness," or "My Lord, grant me wisdom and make me among the righteous," to what is in the noble wording. So reflect, and do not be heedless.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 84:

﴿And make for me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations﴾. That is: make for my praise a truthful remembrance in all matters until the Day of Resurrection. Its essence is the perpetuation of my renown and my good mention in this world, and that is by Your granting me success in good deeds and praiseworthy ways that are pleasing and approved in Your sight, which the later generations follow, and by means of which they mention him with goodness, and they are truthful in doing so.

So "tongue" is a metaphor for remembrance, by the relation of causation, and the lam is for benefit, and from it is derived the description with what is beautiful. The definite article in "al-akhirin" (the later ones) is for comprehensiveness (istighraq). The statement necessarily implies a request for success in the good deeds to which we have alluded, and it seems that this is the intended object of the request in the most eloquent manner. There is no harm in his wishing for the perpetuation of his good remembrance and praise for what he was upon in his time (peace be upon him), and because good praise is among the things that indicate the love of God Most High and His good pleasure, as is reported in the hadith, it is fitting to request it from the great ones from this aspect; and the purpose, entirely, is good pleasure.

It is possible that by "the later ones" is meant the last nation in which a prophet is sent, and that he (peace be upon him) sought a good reputation and a beautiful remembrance among them through the sending of a prophet among them who renews the foundation of his religion and calls people to what he called them to of monotheism, teaching them that this is the creed (millah) of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). Thus it is as if he requested the sending of a prophet like that at the end of time, whose law would not be abrogated until the Day of Resurrection; and that is none other than our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. He requested his sending, peace and blessings be upon both of them, with what is more explicit than what has been mentioned, namely his saying: ﴿And send among them a messenger from themselves who recites to them Your verses﴾, etc. That is why the Prophet ﷺ said: "I am the answer to the supplication of Ibrahim (peace be upon him)."

It has been said: if that is intended, then it is necessary to posit an omitted noun (mudaf) in his speech (peace be upon him), i.e., "make for me one who possesses a tongue of truthfulness among the later ones," or the tongue is a metaphor for the caller by the mention of a part for the whole, since the call is by the tongue; so it is as if he said: "make for me a caller to the truth, truthful among the later ones." It is not hidden that what we have mentioned is sufficient without all of that. In the glosses of our shaykh of shaykhs, the scholar Sibghatullah al-Haydari (may his resting place be fragrant) on the tafsir of al-Baydawi regarding this verse there is a discussion arising from a lack of careful reflection, so do not be deceived by it.

The Imam Malik derived from this verse that there is no harm in a man loving that he be praised for righteousness. The benefit of this after death, as some of the eminent scholars have said, is the turning of aspirations toward that by which he attains nearness to God Most High, and that it may become a cause for the one who praises him, or others, to acquire something like what he was praised for, so that he is rewarded, and the one praised shares in that reward, as is required by: "Whoever establishes a good practice, he will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts by it until the Day of Resurrection." And it is not hidden from you that matters are by their intentions.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 85:

﴿And make me﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿among the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss﴾. The meaning of inheriting the Garden has already passed, so recall it. The supplication of Abraham, peace be upon him, with this, after what preceded of the supplications, has been cited as evidence that righteous deeds do not necessitate entry into Paradise, and likewise that a servant's having a station with God, exalted and majestic is He, [does not necessitate it]. Otherwise, he, peace be upon him, would have been independent of seeking perfection in knowledge and action, and likewise of seeking to be joined with the righteous who are brought near to Him, exalted is He, rather than seeking that. You know that it is good to extend discourse in a place of supplication, and one cannot dispense with a necessary consequence by its premise in speech. Therefore, it is preferable to argue for this from other than what was mentioned, and that is abundant and well known. Furthermore, some of the reports contain what indicates the greater excellence of these supplications.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya related in al-Dhikr, and Ibn Mardawayh, through the route of al-Hasan, from Samura ibn Jundub, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When a servant performs ablution for an obligatory prayer and perfects the ablution, then goes out from the door of his house intending the mosque, and says when he goes out: 'In the name of God, who created me, and it is He who guides me, may God Most High guide him to what is right' - and the wording of Ibn Mardawayh is: 'to the right of deeds' - 'and it is He who feeds me and gives me drink, may God Most High feed him from the food of Paradise and give him drink from the drink of Paradise. And when I am ill, it is He who cures me, may God Most High cure him, and make his illness an expiation for his sins. And it is He who causes me to die then gives me life, may God Most High give him life the life of the blessed and cause him to die the death of the martyrs. And it is He in whom I hope that He will forgive me my sin on the Day of Judgment, may God Most High forgive him all his sins, even if they were like the foam of the sea. My Lord, grant me wisdom and join me with the righteous,' may God Most High grant him wisdom and join him with the righteous of those who passed and the righteous of those who remain. 'And grant me a tongue of truth among the later generations,' it is written on a white page that so-and-so son of so-and-so is among the truthful, then God Most High makes him successful afterward in truthfulness. 'And make me among the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss,' God Most High makes for him palaces and dwellings in Paradise."

Al-Hasan, may God Most High be pleased with him, would add to it: "And forgive my parents as they raised me when I was small." And it seems he took this from His saying:

And forgive my father. Ibn ʿAbbas said, as Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him, that this means: bestow upon him repentance by which he deserves Your forgiveness. Its essence is: guide him to faith, as is hinted at by the causal clause ﴿Indeed, he was among the astray﴾. This is evident if this supplication was made before his death. If it was made after death, then the supplication for forgiveness is on its apparent meaning, and it was permissible to supplicate for forgiveness for a polytheist, although God the Exalted does not forgive that He be associated with, because he, peace be upon him, had not been revealed that at that time, and reason does not judge it impossible. In Nawawi's commentary on Muslim: that His not forgiving shirk (association of partners with God), Mighty and Majestic is He, is specific to this Ummah, and those before them could be forgiven. In this there is a discussion. It was said: he was concealing his faith out of taqiyya (dissimulation under fear of harm) from Namrud (Nimrod), and for this reason he promised him seeking forgiveness. Then, when his enmity to faith became clear, either in this world through revelation or in the Hereafter, he disavowed him.

His saying on this view, ﴿among the astray﴾, is based on what became apparent to others of his condition. Or its meaning is: among the astray in concealing his faith and not confessing it with his tongue, out of taqiyya from Namrud. The discussion on this matter is lengthy, and some of it has preceded, so reflect.

Page 100

ولا تُخْزِنِي ("And do not disgrace me") by punishing my father, or by causing him to be sent among the astray because of his not having been granted success in faith, or by rebuking me for what I neglected, or by lowering my rank below that of some of the heirs, or by punishing me.

Since the outcome is unknown, and punishing one who has committed no sin is rationally permissible, this request was valid from him, peace be upon him. It has also been said that it is possible this was meant as a lesson for others. The word is from al-khizy (khizy), in the sense of humiliation (al-hawan), or from al-khazaya (khazaya), with the kha vowelled with a fatha, in the sense of shame (al-haya'). يَوْمَ يُبْعَثُونَ ("on the Day they are resurrected"), that is, all of mankind. The pronoun is implied, although no antecedent has been mentioned before it, because of the widespread fame of the resurrection, which makes mention of it unnecessary. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the astray, and that the statement is part of the supplication for his father, as if he had said: "Do not disgrace me on the day the astray are resurrected and my father is among them." It is not hidden that, according to the first view, it is also permissible for it to be part of the supplication for his father, and this has been deemed the more apparent, because interposing a supplication for his father between the supplications for himself goes against what is apparent. According to what has been mentioned, he would have supplicated for the one most closely attached to him after finishing his supplication for himself.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 88:

﴿The Day when neither wealth nor children will benefit⁠﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿the Day when they are resurrected﴾. It was brought in as an emphasis on the terror of that Day, and as a preparation for the exception that follows it. And that (what extends) up to His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign⁠﴾ etc., is part of the speech of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. Ibn 'Atiyyah, after parsing the adverbial phrase as a substitute for the first adverbial phrase, said: "In my view these verses are disconnected from the speech of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and they are reports from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, concerning the attributes of that Day, about which Ibrahim asked that Allah not disgrace him." It is not hidden that this is not valid given the substitution (badaliyyah).

By "children" (al-banun) is meant its apparent, understood meaning. It was also said that what is meant by them is all helpers. It was also said that the meaning is: the Day when nothing of the worldly goods and adornments will benefit, and mention was limited to wealth and children because they are the greatest of the worldly goods and adornments.

And His saying, Exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 89:

﴿Except for one who comes to Allah with a sound heart.﴾ This is an exception from the most general of the objects (al-mafa'il, the grammatical objects). "Man" (مَن) is in the accusative position, meaning: on a Day when neither wealth, even if it was spent in this world on the paths of righteousness and good deeds, nor children, even if they are righteous and worthy of intercession, will benefit anyone, except one who comes to Allah with a heart that is sound (salim) from the sickness of disbelief and hypocrisy, since the benefit of each of these two is conditional upon faith. In this there is support for the view that his (peace be upon him) seeking forgiveness for his father was a request for his guidance to faith, because it is impossible to seek forgiveness for him after his death as a disbeliever, given that he (peace be upon him) knew that it would not benefit him, since it falls under the category of intercession.

It has also been said: it is an exception from the subject of "yanfa'u" (benefits), and "man" is in the nominative position as a substitute (badal) for it, and the statement is based on an omitted genitive construction (mudaf) attached to "man", meaning: neither wealth nor children will benefit, except the wealth and children of one who comes to Allah with a sound heart, in that he spent his wealth in the path of righteousness, guided his children to the truth, urged them toward good, and intended by them that they be servants of Allah, obedient to Him, intercessors for him on the Day of Resurrection.

It has also been said: it is an exception from what wealth and children indicate by the indication of the specific over the general (dalalat al-khass 'ala al-'amm), namely, absolute wealth. The statement also requires an omitted genitive construction, as if it were said: on a Day when no wealth benefits, except the wealth of one who comes to Allah with a sound heart, and his wealth is the soundness of his heart; and this is of the religious wealth, and it has been alluded to in some traditions.

Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah narrated from Thawban, who said: "When the verse ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver﴾ was revealed, some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'If we knew which wealth is best, we would acquire it.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'The best of it is a remembering tongue, a grateful heart, and a righteous wife who helps the believer in his faith.'"

It has also been said: it is a discontinuous exception (istithna' munqati') from "wealth," and the statement also requires an omitted genitive construction,
page 101
meaning: neither wealth nor children will benefit, except the state of one who comes to Allah with a sound heart, and by his state is meant the soundness of his heart. Al-Zamakhshari said: there must be an omitted genitive construction; if it were not assumed, the exception would have no meaning. Abu Hayyan rejected this, saying that if one were to assume, for example, "But one who comes to Allah with a sound heart will be safe or will benefit," the meaning would be correct.

Al-Kashshaf answered him by saying that what is intended is that, by way of exception from "wealth," the meaning cannot be achieved without assuming the omitted genitive construction; and what the objector mentioned is a change of the whole clause to another clause, which is not part of the matter at all. Since this did not fit the context, al-Zamakhshari treated it as settled, so he was not criticized for it in any way. It has also been permitted for the exception to be connected by assuming a circumstantial (hal) construction, based on the type of usage in the line:

"Their greeting among them is a painful blow."

An example of this would be to ask: "Does Zayd have wealth and children?" and you reply: "His wealth and children are the soundness of his heart," meaning the negation of wealth and children from him, and the affirmation of soundness of the heart in their place.

Furthermore, that the intended "sound heart" is the heart sound from the sickness of disbelief and hypocrisy is what is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Sirin and others. Al-Imam said: it is the heart free from corrupt beliefs and from inclination toward the desires and pleasures of this world, and righteous deeds follow from this, since a sign of the soundness of the heart is its effect on the limbs.

Sufyan said: it is the heart in which there is nothing other than Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Al-Junayd, may his secret be sanctified, said: it is the one stung by the fear of Allah the Exalted, anxious and disturbed by the dread of separation. The application of "salim" to the one stung (ladigh) is widespread in the Arabic language. It has also been said: it is the one who is safe from shirk and sins, who has submitted himself to the judgment of Allah the Exalted, who is at peace with His friends and wars against His enemies, and who submits wherever he looks, recognizes, surrenders, and yields to Allah the Exalted, humbling himself to His worship, glorified is He. The most suitable meaning for the context is the one transmitted (al-ma'thur), and what has been mentioned of the Sufi interpretations. In al-Kashshaf, regarding what is related from al-Junayd, may his secret be sanctified, and what follows, it says: this is among the innovations of exegeses (bida' al-tafasir). Abu Hayyan agreed with this regarding the first (the view of al-Junayd).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 90:

﴿And the Garden will be brought near to the God-fearing﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon ﴿[it] will not benefit﴾. The past-tense form used here, and in the sentences that follow it and are linked to it in the same chain of conjunction, indicates the certainty and firm establishment of the occurrence, just as the present-tense form in the conjoined element (al-maʿṭūf ʿalayhi) indicates continuity, and it is directed toward benefit. Thus the statement indicates the continuation of the absence of benefit and its continuity, as the context of awe-inspiring terror (tahwil) requires. That is: the Garden will be brought near to the God-fearing, away from disbelief. It has been said: away from it and from all other sins, in such a way that they see it from the place of standing (al-mawqif) and become acquainted with the various kinds of its beauties, so they rejoice that they are gathered toward it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 91:

﴿And Hellfire is brought forth for those who go astray﴾. Those who go astray from the path of truth, which is piety (taqwa) and faith (iman). That is, it is made manifest to them, so that they see it, along with the various terrifying states within it, and they feel regret at being the ones driven toward it. Regarding the difference between the two verbs, as mentioned by some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun), there is a preference for the side of promise, because the expression "brought near" (izlaf), which is the utmost degree of nearness, indicates the nearness of entry into Paradise and its certainty. For this reason it was placed first, since the precedence of His mercy (ta'ala). By contrast, "bringing forth" (ibraz), which is showing, even from a distance, carries a hope of salvation, as it is said: "From one pillar to another there is relief" (min al-'amud ila al-'amud faraj).

Ibn Kamal said: The difference between the two verbs indicates that the place of gathering (arḍ al-hashr) is near to Hellfire. The sum of this is that Paradise is far from the place of gathering by a spatial distance, and Hellfire is near to it by a spatial nearness. Therefore "bringing near" (izlaf), that is, approach (taqrib), was attributed to Paradise and not to Hellfire. It was said: Perhaps this is based on the view that Paradise is in the heaven and Hellfire is beneath the earth, and that the replacement of the earth on the Day of Resurrection by its extension and the removal of its mountains (kariyyatuha) is what makes the matter of distance and nearness become clear. But it is not hidden that Paradise being in the heaven is something the People of the Sunnah believe, and there is no significant disagreement among them about it. As for Hellfire being beneath the earth, there is hesitation about it. Imam al-Jalal al-Suyuti said in Itmam al-Diraya: "We believe that Paradise is in the heaven, and we withhold judgment regarding Hellfire, and we say: its location is where only Allah the Most High knows. No hadith has been established for me that I rely upon in this matter. It has been said: it is beneath the earth." End of quote.

The view that the replacement of the earth is by its extension and the removal of its mountains is an opinion held by some. Imam al-Qurtubi, after quoting many hadiths in al-Tadhkira, preferred that the replacement of the earth means that Allah, glorified is He, creates another earth, white, of silver, upon which no unlawful blood has been shed and in which no injustice has ever occurred. The better way to put the distance of Paradise and the nearness of Hellfire from the place of gathering is: reaching Paradise is by crossing the bridge (sirat), which is set up over the back of Hell (matn jahannam), as the reports have stated. So arrival at Hell comes first and arrival at Paradise last, through crossing, and this is evident in nearness and distance. Furthermore, the apparent meaning of the verse requires that Paradise be moved from its place today, on the Day of Resurrection, since nearing requires moving, and there is nothing in the hadiths, to our knowledge, that indicates this.

Yes, there is something in them that indicates the moving of Hellfire. In al-Tadhkira, Muslim narrated from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Hell will be brought on that Day, having seventy thousand reins, with each rein seventy thousand angels." The apparent meaning of "it will be brought" (yu'ta bi-jahannam) is that it will be brought from the place where Allah created it, and this has been stated explicitly in al-Tadhkira.

Abu Bakr al-Razi said in his Questions: If it is said: Allah the Most High said, "And Paradise is brought near for the God-fearing" (wa-uzlifat al-jannatu lil-muttaqin), meaning it was drawn near, and Paradise does not move from its place nor is it transferred? We say: its meaning is: the God-fearing are brought near to Paradise, and this is like when pilgrims approach Mecca and say: "Mecca has drawn near to us." It was also said: its meaning is that it was hidden from them, and when the veils between it and them were lifted, that was a bringing near. End of quote. It is objected to the latter that the same could be said regarding Hell, and then one would ask about the reason for the difference between the two verbs.

It is objected to the view that Paradise does not move from its place that it contradicts the apparent meaning of the verse, and saying so does not require transmitting a hadith indicating its moving on that day. So there is no barrier to saying it, while entrusting the manner to the knowledge of One whom nothing can overpower and who is All-Knowing of everything. If interpretation is intended, then let it be by taking nearness as nearness in terms of sight. A thing may be seen as near even when in reality it is at the greatest distance, as is observed with the stars. And the distant may be brought near in sight by means of optical lenses and instruments arranged for that purpose. Conversely, the situation may be reversed by them as well, so that the near is seen as distant. Since this occurs through instruments in this world, it may occur in the other world by what none knows except the Subtle, the All-Aware. So reflect. And Allah the Most High knows best.

Al-A'mash read "fabburrizat" with fa'. Malik ibn Dinar read "wa-barazat" with a fatha and light pronunciation (takhfif), and "al-jahimu" in the nominative as the subject (fa'iliyya).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 92–94:

﴿And it will be said to them: "Where is that which you used to worship"﴾ in the world ﴿"instead of Allah"﴾ meaning: where are your gods that you claimed would be your intercessors in this situation? ﴿"Can they help you"﴾ by repelling what you see of the Blazing Fire and its punishment? ﴿"Or can they help themselves"﴾ by repelling that from themselves? This is a question of rebuke to which no answer is expected. For this reason it is said: ﴿"So they will be thrown into it"﴾, meaning they will be cast into the Blazing Fire on their faces, again and again, until they settle at its bottom. So *kabkabah* (repeated overturning, a doubling of the root) is a repetition of *kabb* (overturning), and it is one of the forms in which the letter (fa') is doubled, as al-Zajjaj and the majority of the Basran grammarians said. The Kufans held that the third letter is a substitute for the like of the second: the original form of (kabkaba) according to them is (kabbaba), and a kaf was substituted for the second ba'. The plural pronoun refers to what they used to worship besides Allah, namely the idols, and it is emphasized by the separate pronoun, I mean (hum). Both pronouns are for rational beings, but they are used for the idols as mockery, or on the basis of ascribing to them understanding and speech. That is, the idols and the deviators who worshipped them will be overturned in it.

[Page 103]

The expression of them with this title, rather than "the worshippers," is to record upon them the description of deviation. And in delaying their mention after the mention of their gods there is a hint that they will be brought down into the overturning after them, so that they will see the wretched state of those gods, and their hope will be cut off before they enter the Blazing Fire.

It is narrated from al-Suddi that the pronoun in (they will be thrown) and its emphasis refer to the idolaters of the Arabs, and "the deviators" refers to the rest of the idolaters. It is also said that the pronoun refers to idolaters in general, and by "the followers" are meant the followers, while "the deviators" are the leaders who were followed. And it is said that the pronoun refers to the idolaters of mankind in general. ﴿"And the deviators"﴾ are the devils. All of these, as you see, are far-fetched, and the last is the most remote.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 92–94:

﴿And it will be said to them: "Where is that which you used to worship"﴾ in the world ﴿"instead of Allah"﴾ meaning: where are your gods that you claimed would be your intercessors in this situation? ﴿"Can they help you"﴾ by repelling what you see of the Blazing Fire and its punishment? ﴿"Or can they help themselves"﴾ by repelling that from themselves? This is a question of rebuke to which no answer is expected. For this reason it is said: ﴿"So they will be thrown into it"﴾, meaning they will be cast into the Blazing Fire on their faces, again and again, until they settle at its bottom. So *kabkabah* (repeated overturning, a doubling of the root) is a repetition of *kabb* (overturning), and it is one of the forms in which the letter (fa') is doubled, as al-Zajjaj and the majority of the Basran grammarians said. Both pronouns are for rational beings, but they are used for the idols as mockery, or on the basis of ascribing to them understanding and speech. That is, the idols and the deviators who worshipped them will be overturned in it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 95:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the hosts of Iblis﴾. The apparent meaning is that by it are meant the devils (shayatin), and that it is conjoined (ʿatf) to what precedes it. Conjunction (ʿatf) requires, for the most part, that the two things be distinct in their essence, and there is no need to derive it from the less common usage and make it of the type of:

"To the king, the generous one, and the son of the lofty one (al-humam)"

It has been said: the intended meaning of "the hosts of Iblis" is those who follow him from the disobedient among the two species (jinn and humankind). Some of the eminent scholars preferred the first view and claimed that it is the correct view, because the context (siyaq) and what immediately precedes (sabbaq) concern the explanation of the miserable state of the polytheists in Hellfire, and Ibrahim, peace be upon him, had said this to his polytheist people. Therefore there is no merit in mentioning the state of another group in this situation; rather, they have no existence in the story. The mention of the devils together with the polytheists is because they are the ones who made the worship of idols seem good to them. It is not hidden that generalization (li-l-taʿmim) also has a basis, insofar as it adds greater awe (tahwil) to that Day. As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿all of them﴾, it is an emphasis (taʾkid) on the pronoun and what is conjoined to it.

The words of Allah, glory be to Him, ﴿They will say﴾ and so on, are a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*, a new sentence that begins without grammatical connection to what precedes it), answering a question that arises from what came before. It is as if, when it was said, "they will be thrown headlong into it, they and the deities and the misguided ones, their worshippers and the devils who called to them," it was asked, "So what happened?" and the answer was given: ﴿They will say﴾, that is, the worshippers, the misguided ones, ﴿while they﴾, that is, the misguided ones, ﴿therein dispute﴾, that is, they dispute with those who are with them of the idols and the devils. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*). The meaning is: they will say, acknowledging their error and their immersion in misguidance, regretful, reproaching themselves, while the situation is that they are about to dispute with those who are with them, addressing their deities, since Allah, exalted is He, makes them fit to be addressed: ﴿By Allah, we were surely in manifest error﴾. The particle (*in*) is a lightened form of the heavy (*inna*), and its noun, according to what has been said, is a omitted pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-sha'n*), and the lam is a distinguishing particle between it and the negative particle, as the Basrans held. That is: indeed it (that is, the matter) — we were in manifest error. The Kufans held that (*in*) is a negative particle and the lam has the meaning of (*illa*, except), that is: we were only in an error that is clear, with no concealment in it. Their describing it as clear serves to emphasise the display of their remorse and regret, and to make plain their error in their opinion even though the truth was evident, as their introducing the oath with the letter (*ta'*), which implies wonder, indicates, according to what has been said.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 98–99:

His words, glorified is He: ﴿when we made you equal to the Lord of the worlds﴾ are an adverbial clause (*zarf*) modifying their being in ﴿manifest error﴾. It has also been said that it modifies a deleted element (*mahdhuf*) indicated by the context, meaning "we went astray." It has also been said that it modifies the error mentioned earlier. There is a grammatical weakness in this view (*ḍaʿf ṣināʿī*), since a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) that has been described by an adjective does not govern what follows the adjective. This weakness is eased by the fact that the governed element is an adverbial clause. It has also been said that it is an adverbial clause modifying ﴿manifest﴾. It is also permitted that *idh* ("when") be causal (*taʿlīliyya*), as has been said regarding His words, exalted is He: ﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you did wrong, that you will be sharing in the punishment﴾ [43:39]. The use of the present tense (*ṣīghat al-muḍāriʿ*) serves to bring the past scene vividly before the mind (*istiḥḍār al-ṣūra*). The meaning is: "By God, we were indeed in extreme and gross error at the time we made you equal," or "because we made you equal, O idols, in deserving worship with the Lord of the worlds, who is the lowest of His creatures, the most abject, and the most powerless."

﴿And none led us astray except the criminals.﴾ The apparent meaning, based on what preceded, namely that the dispute is with the idols and the devils, is that "the criminals" refers to the devils, so that this would be part of the dispute with them, even if it is not addressed in the form of direct address, just as the earlier dispute with the idols was. That "the criminals" refers to them has been transmitted from Muqatil. In Irshad al-Aql al-Salim (*Irshad al-Aql al-Salim*) it is stated that this is an explanation of the cause of their error, after their acknowledgment that it proceeded from them. "The criminals" refers to their leaders and their great ones, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, we obeyed our masters and our great ones, and they led us astray from the way﴾ [33:67].

It is narrated from al-Suddi that they are the earlier generations whom they followed. It has also been said that they are whoever called them to worship idols from among the jinn and mankind.

It is narrated from Ibn Jurayj that they are Iblis and the son of Adam who committed murder, because he was the first to establish killing and sins. The restriction (*qaṣr*) has been said to be relative to the idols, and perhaps they intended by denying that the idols led them astray a humiliation of them, by saying they have no power. This contains an emphasis on their being in manifest error. Perhaps the better view is that it is a true restriction (*qaṣr ḥaqīqī*), on the claim that they alone are the sole cause of misguidance, so much so that the causality of others is as if there were no causality. This is clear regarding the devils, because the misguidance of others among the great ones and their like is through their misguidance, since they are the ones who adorn falsehood for both the follower and the one followed. It is possible to consider this regarding others through some kind of interpretation, when "the criminals" is taken to mean others. Furthermore, the polytheists will continue to be in bewilderment on the Day of Resurrection, not knowing what to hold on to, so attributing misguidance to one thing at one time and to another at another time does no harm. Moreover, the attribution to each is considered in this light.

It is also permitted that the dispute be among the worshippers, some with others, and that the address in ﴿we make you equal﴾ be to the idols without committing to the view that they are capable of speech. Rather, it is like the address of one in distress to a stone or a tree, and in it there is exaggeration in expressing regret and remorse. The meaning is that the worshippers, while disputing with one another, each saying to the other, "You are the source of my error, and had it not been for you I would have been a believer," acknowledged their sin, marveled at it, and explained its cause. It is also permitted that it comes from the idols, whom God makes speak so that they dispute with the worshippers. In that case the pronoun in ﴿they﴾ refers to them, and the meaning is: the worshippers said, acknowledging their error, marveling at it, and explaining its cause, "If we were..." etc., while the idols dispute with them, saying, "We are inanimate objects, free of all sins, and you took us as gods and cast us into this calamity." All of this is on the assumption that the clause ﴿they said﴾ is a resumptive new sentence (*mustaʾnafa*), as is the apparent view. It is also permitted that ﴿the hosts of Iblis﴾ be the subject (*mubtadaʾ*) and the clause ﴿they said﴾ etc. its predicate, with the pronoun in ﴿they said﴾ and what follows it referring back to it.

You know that, although this is contrary to the apparent meaning, it is not feasible on the assumption that by "the hosts of Iblis" the devils are meant, because the statement mentioned cannot be said by them. And if by them is meant those who follow him from the disobedient among the two groups (jinn and mankind), including idol-worshippers and others, it would be objected that the statement mentioned is the saying of one group among them, namely the worshippers, so attributing it to all is contrary to the apparent meaning and is very far-fetched. Indeed, even if its invalidity were asserted, it would not be far-fetched that each person, whether one of the idol-worshippers or other than them, disputes with whoever meets him, without the other being fit for dispute, and says what has been mentioned to the idols, out of extreme bewilderment and vexation.

Yes, if by "the hosts of Iblis," on the assumption that it is the subject and the pronouns refer to it, is meant the misguided themselves, and the idafa (construct) is for definiteness (*li-l-ʿahd*), and the expression of them by this title after expressing them by the earlier title is for humiliating them, then it is not very far-fetched.

Some people have permitted the initial (*ibtidāʾiyya*) and predicative (*khabariyya*) readings mentioned above, and they interpreted "the hosts" as the disobedient in general, and made the pronoun in ﴿they said﴾ refer to ﴿the misguided﴾, and the pronoun in ﴿they﴾ and ﴿dispute﴾ refer to the hosts or to the idols. In this view, besides the verse departing from good coherence (*ḥusn al-intiẓām*), there is what is not hidden from people of understanding.

[Page 105]

Allah's words, ﴿So we have no intercessors﴾ ﴿nor any close friend﴾, are consequent upon what they acknowledged of the enormity of their transgression and the manifestness of their misguidance. The intent is regret and lamentation over the loss of an intercessor who would intercede for them regarding what they are in, or a sincere friend who would be concerned about that. Because of the increased lowness of their state, they progressed in lamentation: first they negated that there would be for them anyone who could benefit them by rescuing them from the punishment through his intercession, and then they negated that there would be for them anyone whose concern is their affair, who pities them and feels for them, even if he does not deliver them. The intercessor was mentioned in the context of negation in the plural, although the ruling of this plural in terms of comprehensiveness, because of the superfluous *min* (*min al-za'idah*, the extra "min" that intensifies negation), is the ruling of the singular without disagreement. The disagreement is only concerning cases where the *min* does not come after the negation and precede the plural, in deference to what they used to say in affirmation in the plural.

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: The intercessor is pluralized because of the multitude of intercessors, and the friend is singularized because of their paucity. Do you not see that when a man is afflicted by the oppression of a tyrant, a large group from the people of his town rise up out of mercy for him and for the sake of reward, if he has not preceded most of them in acquaintance? As for the sincere friend in your affection, who is concerned with what concerns you, he is more rare than the eggs of the *anuq* (a bird considered extremely rare). It is also permissible that by "the friend" he intends the plural, i.e., it is applied to him because he is of the form of the verbal noun (*masdar*), unlike the intercessor.

Al-Baydawi mentioned another reason for singularizing "the friend": that a single friend strives more than the intercessors strive. Its summary is that the singular is, by custom, equivalent in meaning to the plural, and therefore it is sufficed with, because of the semantic correspondence (*mutabaqah ma'nawiyyah*, agreement of meaning rather than form) that it contains, as is said:

The people are a thousand, of which one is like a single one,
and a single one is like a thousand, if a matter befalls us.

Some of the scholars said: The mention of the intercessors in the plural form is merely for the sake of the verse-ending (*fasilah*, the rhyming closure of a verse), whereas the mention of the friend in the singular is because the context calls for the singular; the purpose of the verse-ending has already been achieved before it. And this, as you see, is weak.

Sa'd Afandi said: It is not far that the plural of the first and the singular of the second is an indication that there is no difference between the two kinds of comprehensiveness. But in this there is that choosing a form to convey a point of Arabic grammar is not the custom of the Glorious Qur'an. What I incline to is that the singular is the original, and the plural, though it fulfils the same function, is in accordance with the manner in which they used to say and assert in the world the multiplicity of intercessors. And it is not harmful in this that what is negated here is more general than what is affirmed there, in terms of its inclusion of idols, great ones (*kubara'*, leaders), angels, and prophets (peace be upon them), as is what is understood immediately.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Jurayj, that the meaning is: ﴿So we have no intercessors﴾ from the people of heaven, ﴿nor any close friend﴾ from the people of earth.

Some of them claimed that by "the intercessors" here they meant what they meant by "the criminals" among their great ones and masters, and they based the negation on their saying: ﴿And none misled us except the criminals﴾. So it is as though they said: Our masters and great ones who misled us are criminals punished like us, so they were unable to strive for our benefit or to intercede for us.

In *al-Kashshaf* (it is said): ﴿So we have no intercessors﴾, as we see the believers having intercessors from among the angels and the prophets, ﴿nor any close friend﴾, as we see them having friends; for there is no mutual friendship in the Hereafter except among the believers. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Intimate friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the God-fearing﴾. Or (the meaning is): ﴿So we have no intercessors﴾ ﴿nor any close friend﴾ from among those whom we used to count as intercessors and friends, because they used to believe that their idols were their intercessors with Allah the Exalted, and they had friends from among the devils of mankind. Or they meant that they had fallen into a destruction, knowing that intercessors and friends would neither benefit them nor ward off anything from them, so by their negation they intended the negation of whatever benefit is connected to them, because what does not benefit is judged as the nonexistent. End of quotation.

According to this last opinion, the apparent meaning is that the speech is a metonymy (*kinayah*, an indirect expression) for the severity of the matter, such that no one can benefit in it even with the slightest benefit. This is a sound (*wajih*) view. The first view can hardly be made to work according to the school of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school that rejects intercession for the release from the Fire, after entering it or before it). For the apparent meaning of their saying "So we have no intercessors, as we see the believers having intercessors from among the angels and the prophets" is: "So we have no intercessors who would rescue us from the Fire, as we see the believers having intercessors from among the angels and the prophets who rescue them from it." Therefore al-Zamakhshari's preference for this view is strange. Except that it may be said: the intended comparison is in terms of the general category of intercession, and the Mu'tazilah permit some of its types, such as intercession for an increase in ranks in Paradise. But this is not free from remoteness. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

The intercessor was mentioned in the context of negation in the plural, although the ruling of this plural in terms of comprehensiveness, because of the superfluous *min* (*min al-za'idah*, the extra "min" that intensifies negation), is the ruling of the singular without disagreement. The disagreement is only concerning cases where the *min* does not come after the negation and precede the plural, in deference to what they used to say in affirmation in the plural.

Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: The intercessor is pluralized because of the multitude of intercessors, and the friend is singularized because of their paucity. Do you not see that when a man is afflicted by the oppression of a tyrant, a large group from the people of his town rise up out of mercy for him and for the sake of reward, if he has not preceded most of them in acquaintance? As for the sincere friend in your affection, who is concerned with what concerns you, he is more rare than the eggs of the *anuq* (a bird considered extremely rare). It is also permissible that by "the friend" he intends the plural, i.e., it is applied to him because he is of the form of the verbal noun (*masdar*), unlike the intercessor.

Al-Baydawi mentioned another reason for singularizing "the friend": that a single friend strives more than the intercessors strive. Its summary is that the singular is, by custom, equivalent in meaning to the plural, and therefore it is sufficed with, because of the semantic correspondence (*mutabaqah ma'nawiyyah*, agreement of meaning rather than form) that it contains, as is said:

The people are a thousand, of which one is like a single one,
and a single one is like a thousand, if a matter befalls us.

Some of the scholars said: The mention of the intercessors in the plural form is merely for the sake of the verse-ending (*fasilah*, the rhyming closure of a verse), whereas the mention of the friend in the singular is because the context calls for the singular; the purpose of the verse-ending has already been achieved before it. And this, as you see, is weak.

Sa'd Afandi said: It is not far that the plural of the first and the singular of the second is an indication that there is no difference between the two kinds of comprehensiveness. But in this there is that choosing a form to convey a point of Arabic grammar is not the custom of the Glorious Qur'an. What I incline to is that the singular is the original, and the plural, though it fulfils the same function, is in accordance with the manner in which they used to say and assert in the world the multiplicity of intercessors. And it is not harmful in this that what is negated here is more general than what is affirmed there, in terms of its inclusion of idols, great ones (*kubara'*, leaders), angels, and prophets (peace be upon them), as is what is understood immediately.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Jurayj, that the meaning is: ﴿So we have no intercessors﴾ from the people of heaven, ﴿nor any close friend﴾ from the people of earth.

Some of them claimed that by "the intercessors" here they meant what they meant by "the criminals" among their great ones and masters, and they based the negation on their saying: ﴿And none misled us except the criminals﴾. So it is as though they said: Our masters and great ones who misled us are criminals punished like us, so they were unable to strive for our benefit or to intercede for us.

In *al-Kashshaf* (it is said): ﴿So we have no intercessors﴾, as we see the believers having intercessors from among the angels and the prophets, ﴿nor any close friend﴾, as we see them having friends; for there is no mutual friendship in the Hereafter except among the believers. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Intimate friends on that Day will be enemies to one another, except the God-fearing﴾. Or (the meaning is): ﴿So we have no intercessors﴾ ﴿nor any close friend﴾ from among those whom we used to count as intercessors and friends, because they used to believe that their idols were their intercessors with Allah the Exalted, and they had friends from among the devils of mankind. Or they meant that they had fallen into a destruction, knowing that intercessors and friends would neither benefit them nor ward off anything from them, so by their negation they intended the negation of whatever benefit is connected to them, because what does not benefit is judged as the nonexistent. End of quotation.

According to this last opinion, the apparent meaning is that the speech is a metonymy (*kinayah*, an indirect expression) for the severity of the matter, such that no one can benefit in it even with the slightest benefit. This is a sound (*wajih*) view. The first view can hardly be made to work according to the school of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school that rejects intercession for the release from the Fire, after entering it or before it). For the apparent meaning of their saying "So we have no intercessors, as we see the believers having intercessors from among the angels and the prophets" is: "So we have no intercessors who would rescue us from the Fire, as we see the believers having intercessors from among the angels and the prophets who rescue them from it." Therefore al-Zamakhshari's preference for this view is strange. Except that it may be said: the intended comparison is in terms of the general category of intercession, and the Mu'tazilah permit some of its types, such as intercession for an increase in ranks in Paradise. But this is not free from remoteness. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 102:

The "law" (law) in His words, exalted is He, ﴿So if only we had a return (karrah)﴾ is used to express a wish (tamanni), as evidenced by the accusative case of His words, glorified is He, ﴿and we would be among the believers﴾ as the answer to it. Its origin is law of impossibility (al-imtina'iyyah), and since a wish is for what is impossible, it is used for that meaning either as a sent metaphor (majaz mursal) or as a subsequent metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah). Then it became common until it became like a literal meaning in that sense. It was also said that it is literal in what has been mentioned. It was also said that its origin is the verbal noun (masdariyyah), but this is nothing.

The meaning: "So would that we had a return to the world, so that we would be among the believers, and then nothing would befall us if we died and were resurrected like what we are in of the punishment, in which no one can benefit." It was also permitted that law is conditional (shartiyyah), with its answer omitted, and the estimate is: "We would have done such-and-such good deeds," or "we would have been freed from the punishment," or "we would have had intercessors and friends," or: "The criminals did not lead us astray." The first estimate is more eloquent. The omitted element is estimated after ﴿so we would be﴾ etc., because the verbal noun derived from it is conjoined to (karrah), i.e.: "So if only we had a return, so that we would be among the believers, we would have done etc."

Shaykh al-Islam (Abu al-Su'ud) criticised this, saying that it only establishes the realisation of the content of the answer on the assumption that their return and their faith both occur together, without any indication that return necessarily implies faith at all, although that is the definite intended meaning. Regarding his words, "without any indication" etc., there is a discussion, as it is said: it is possible to say that the sense of the verse is: if return and the faith that follows it were made possible for us, we would do from the acts of worship of the people of faith what expression falls short of; and binding oneself to the fruits of faith is a binding to faith first. Their intended meaning is to explain that return necessitates doing all good deeds. As for faith itself after this witnessing, it does not need explanation.

Some people said: their words ﴿so we would be among the believers﴾ mean: "so we would be among those whose faith is accepted," and God's acceptance of their faith is not at all consequent upon their return, rather it may fail to occur. So their intended meaning must be: "If return is made possible for us, and if our faith is accepted, we would do etc." Thus the aim is not to indicate that return necessitates faith, as Shaykh al-Islam claimed. This was objected to on the grounds that the facilitation of return occurs only through God's mercy and pardon, and that entails the acceptance of their faith. The truth is that one should not turn to the possibility that "law" is conditional, nor strain toward it, given the eloquence of the apparent and immediately understood meaning.

The discussion of His words, ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers﴾ and ﴿And indeed your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾, has already been given earlier, so there is no need to repeat it. You know our position on it, so recall it. There is no great distance in time from it. Shaykh al-Islam (a title for a leading jurist) has a discussion of this verse, whose content is not hidden from the careful reader, so reflect on it.

﴿The people of Noah denied the messengers﴾. The word qawm (people), as in al-Misbah (al-Misbah al-Munir, a dictionary of Arabic), may be treated as masculine or feminine, and likewise every collective noun (ism jam', a noun denoting a group that has no singular form from the same root), such as rahT (a group of men) and nafar (a small group). For this reason it is diminutive as quwaymah. It was also said that it is masculine, and the feminine marker was attached to its verb in view of the meaning of community and group. Their denial of the messengers is considered in terms of the consensus of all of them on monotheism and the fundamentals of the law, which do not differ with the difference of times and ages. It is also permitted that by the messengers is meant Noah, peace be upon him, by making the lam (the definite article) generic (lam al-jins, the article indicating the whole class). This is like your saying: "So-and-so rides beasts and wears garments," while he has only one beast and one garment.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 106–108:

"When" in His saying, ﴿When their brother Noah said to them﴾, is an adverbial clause of time governing the verb "denied," on the basis that it refers to a long span of time in which what happened on both sides occurred until the matter was completed. Likewise, their denial refers to what proceeded from them from the beginning of his call, peace be upon him, until its end. Some claimed that "when" (idh) indicates causation, meaning: "they denied because he said to them," ﴿Their brother Noah﴾, that is, their kinsman, as one says: "O brother of the Arabs," and "O brother of Tamim." On this is the poet's saying:

They do not ask their brother when he calls them in calamities for proof of what he says.

The pronoun refers to the people of Noah. It has also been said that it refers to the messengers, and that "brotherhood" means kinship of nature, but this is contrary to the apparent meaning. ﴿Will you not fear God﴾, Mighty and Majestic is He, since you worship other than Him? ﴿Indeed I am to you a messenger﴾ from God, Exalted is He, Who sent me for your benefit. ﴿Trustworthy﴾, well known for trustworthiness among you. It has also been said: trustworthy in conveying His message, glorified is His majesty. ﴿So fear God and obey me﴾ in what I command you of monotheism and obedience to God, Exalted is He. The command to fear God, Exalted is He, is placed before the command to obey, because fear of God, Exalted is He, is the cause of obeying him, peace be upon him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 109–110:

﴿And I ask of you no reward for it﴾: that is, for that to which I am devoted of supplication and advice. ﴿No reward at all﴾: that is, I do not seek from you any reward for that whatsoever, neither wealth nor anything else. ﴿My reward is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾: for it is He, glorified is He, who rewards me for that out of His bounty, not anyone else. The fa' in His words, exalted is He, ﴿So fear Allah and obey me﴾ is for the sequencing of what follows upon what precedes it, namely his - peace be upon him - being free from greed, just as its counterpart earlier is for the sequencing of what follows upon his being a messenger from Allah, exalted is He, with what contains the benefit of both abodes together with his trustworthiness. The repetition is for emphasis and to draw attention to the fact that each of the two is independently sufficient in making piety and obedience obligatory, so how much more so when both are combined. It has been read as «إنْ أجْرِي» with the yā' sukūn, and this and the fatḥah are two well-known dialects in such cases; the grammarians differed over which of the two is the original.
