Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 111–112:

﴿They said: "Shall we believe you, when the lowest (ones) follow you?"﴾ That is: while they have followed you. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial (ḥāl) clause, and the "wāw" with "qad" is obligatory in it when its verb is in the past tense; and many of the great scholars do not make this obligatory.

ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud), Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Aʿmash, Abu Ḥaywa, al-Ḍaḥḥak, Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ, Saʿid ibn Abi Saʿid al-Ansari, Talha, and Yaʿqub read "wa-atbāʿuka" (and your followers), the plural of tābiʿ, like ṣāḥib and aṣḥāb. It was also said: it is the plural of tabīʿ, like sharīf and ashrāf; and it was also said: the plural of tabaʿ, like baṭal and abṭāl. It is in the nominative case as a subject (mubtadaʾ), and "al-arhalūn" (the lowest) is its predicate, and the clause is also in the position of a circumstantial clause. It was also said: it is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon the concealed pronoun in "nu'minu" (we believe), and that is made acceptable by the separation with "laka" (you). "Al-arhalūn" is its attribute. It is not hidden that this is weak in meaning.

From al-Yamani: "wa-atbāʿika" in the genitive, coordinated upon the pronoun in "laka" (you). This is rare, though the Kufans analogized it. "Al-arhalūn" is raised by their being implied (as its subject), and it is the plural of "al-arhal" in its sound form. Al-radhala means baseness and lowliness. The apparent meaning is that they regarded the believers in him, upon him be peace, as lowly only because of the badness of their deeds, which is indicated by his saying in the reply: ﴿He said: "And what is my knowledge of what they used to do?"﴾ That is: my duty is only to take outward appearances into account and base rulings upon them, not to pry and search into inner states. "Ma" is interrogative; al-Ḥawfi and al-Ṭabarsi said it is negative, and on this reading there is an ellipsis in the speech, meaning: "And my knowledge of what they used to do is established."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 113:

﴿Their reckoning is only﴾, that is, their being held to account for what they do is not my concern, ﴿but with my Lord﴾. Scrutinizing the inner states belongs to His affairs, may He be exalted and glorified, for He is the One who has knowledge of them. ﴿If only you perceived﴾, that is, anything at all, or: if you were among those who have awareness, you would know this. But you are not like that, which is why you said what you said. The alif-lam (al-, the definite article) in this sense is for the generic (al-jins, the category as a whole).

A group said: their contempt for them was due to the scantiness of their share of worldly goods. It was also said: it was because they practiced base crafts, and they were, as narrated from Ikrima, weavers and cobblers. It was also said: it was because of the lowliness of their lineage. The root of all of this is the feebleness of their minds and the shortness of their vision, for poverty is not at all a baseness:

*Glory may reach a youth whose cloak is worn out, and the collar of whose shirt is patched.*

Likewise, the lowliness of a craft does not diminish one's nobility in the Hereafter, nor does it bring any deficiency upon the pious person in the sight of Allah, may He be exalted and glorified. Abu al-Atahiya recited:

*No deficiency attaches to a pious servant when his piety is sound, even if he weaves or cups (for a living).*

A similar principle applies to lineage. It has been said:

*My father is Islam; I have no other father, when they boast of Qays or Tamim.*

What the jurists mention in the chapter on kafa'a (social parity in marriage) is based on the custom of the common people, for the regulation of livelihood and the like. Moreover, it has been narrated from Imam Malik that no consideration of any of this is valid at all, and that Muslims, however they may be, are equal to one another. The alif-lam in these views is for the known referent (al-'ahd, the specific, previously identified group).

The response to what they alluded to in their statement, namely that their faith was not based on reflection and insight but on a worldly self-interest, such as gaining strength through collective numbers by which they could be counted among the people of nobility and enrolled in their ranks, is as follows.

Its summary: my duty is only to judge by outward appearances, not to split open hearts or to search out what is in the innermost secrets. So the fact that their faith is not sincere, as you claim, does me no harm. It has also been suggested that when they said: ﴿and the lowest have followed you﴾, and meant those who have no share of worldly goods, or whose lineages are base, or who were of the base crafts, he (peace be upon him) feigned unawareness of their intent, and it appeared to them that they meant by "the lowest" those who lack sincerity in their deeds and who did not believe from reflection and insight. So he answered them with what has been mentioned, as though he knew nothing of "the lowest" except that. If this is taken as a kind of wise approach (al-uslub al-hakim, a rhetorical method of responding to an interlocutor in a way that suits their situation), it does not seem far-fetched to me. It contains much subtle refutation of them and condemnation of what they hold, which is not hidden.

Some have claimed that by "the lowest" they meant his wives, his sons, his daughters, and his grandsons. Their contempt on account of lineage cannot truly apply to all of them, as is not hidden, so there must be consideration of predominance (al-taghlib, giving precedence to the majority or the more prominent) or the like.

Al-A'raj, Abu Zur'a, and Isa ibn Umar al-Hamdani read ﴿yash'urun﴾ with the yā' of the third person (they perceive, rather than "you perceive").

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 114:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And I am not one to drive away the believers﴾, is an answer to what their speech implied of demanding that he drive them away, and of making their faith conditional upon that, since they made following them (ittiba') a barrier to it. They had, in this, placed him in the position of one who claims that he (peace be upon him) is among those who drive away the believers, and that he is among those who share in this practice with them. Thus the predicate was placed first (i.e., the subject was fronted), and the negative particle was given precedence, to convey that this is not his (peace be upon him) characteristic, but rather the characteristic of those addressed.

It has also been permitted that the fronting is for the sake of restriction (al-taqwa, i.e., restricting the negation), and this is the less burdensome reading, as is not hidden. It has been said: they asked him (peace be upon him) to drive them away, and he answered them with this, just as the leaders of Quraysh asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to drive away those among the weak who had believed in him. Then the verse was revealed: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord﴾, and so on.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 115:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿I am only a clear warner﴾, is like the cause (ʿillah) for what precedes it. That is: I am only a messenger sent to warn the responsible (mukallafin) people and to restrain them from what does not please Him, glory be to Him, whether they are of the noble or of the lowly. So how could it be possible for me to drive away those whom you claim to be lowly?!

Its summary is: I am restricted to warning the responsible people and do not go beyond that to driving away the lowly among them. Or: it is incumbent upon me only to warn you with clear proof, and I have done so; and it is not incumbent upon me to win the approval of some of you by driving away the others. Its summary is: I am restricted to warning you and do not go beyond that to seeking your approval.

It has also been said: the two sentences together form the answer, and the placement of the pronoun (innama, "I am only") before the negative particle indicates that they claimed he was described by two attributes: the first, following their desires by driving away the believers so that they would believe, and the second, that he is a clear warner. The ruling is then restricted to the second rather than the first, but this is not free from discussion.

﴿They said, "If you do not desist, O Noah, you will surely be among those stoned."﴾ That is, among those pelted with stones, as narrated from Qatadah. It is a threat of killing, as narrated from al-Hasan. Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi that the meaning is "among those reviled," with stoning used metaphorically for reviling, as in "stabbing" used for insulting. In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim (Abu al-Su'ud's commentary), it is said that they, may Allah destroy them, said this at the end of the matter.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 117:

The meaning of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿My Lord, indeed my people have denied me﴾ is that they persisted in denying me and insisted upon it after I had called them for these lengthy periods of time, and my calling them only increased them in flight. This is not an informing of the continuation of their denial, because he (peace be upon him) knew that the Knower of the unseen and the seen is more knowing. Rather, he intended to make manifest that for which he supplicates against them, namely their denial of the truth, and not their threatening him and belittling him in their saying: ﴿If you do not desist, O Noah, you will surely be among those stoned﴾, as a gentle approach to opening the door of response. It has also been said: to repel the illusion of creation in it of excess, or harshness. It has also been said: it is a statement from which no informing was intended at all, but was presented for the purpose of grief and lamentation, as in his saying:

My people, they killed Umaym, my brother, so if I shoot, my arrow will strike me.

And what makes that unlikely, in general, is the consequence of the supplication against them with His, the Exalted's, saying:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 118–120:

﴿So decide between me and them with a decision﴾, that is: judge between us by what each of us deserves. Al-fataha here means al-hukuma (judgment), and fathan is a verbal noun (masdar). It is also permissible that it be a direct object (maf'ul bihi), in the sense of mafthuhan (an opening, a resolution). This is a summary report of his supplication, peace be upon him, which is detailed in Surah Nuh: ﴿And save me and those of the believers who are with me﴾, that is, from their intent or from the ill consequences of their deeds. In it there is an indication that the punishment is about to descend upon them. ﴿So We saved him and those with him﴾, in accordance with his supplication, peace be upon him, ﴿in the laden ship (al-fulk al-mashhun)﴾, that is, filled with them and with what they needed, whether provisions such as food or property such as livestock.

Al-fulk (ship) is used both as a singular and as a plural. Where it occurs in the Noble Qur'an as a fasila (rhyme-final word at the end of a verse), it is used in the singular; where it does not occur as a fasila, it is used in the plural, as in the verse about the sea. ﴿Then We drowned the rest afterwards﴾, that is, after their rescue. The particle thumma (then) here indicates a gradation in rank. For this reason He, glorified is He, said ba'd (afterwards), ﴿the remaining ones﴾, that is, from among his people.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 124–127:

﴿When their brother Hud said to them: Will you not be mindful of God?﴾ ﴿Indeed I am to you a trustworthy messenger.﴾ ﴿So be mindful of God and obey me.﴾ ﴿And I do not ask you for any reward for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds.﴾

The narration of the command to taqwa (God-consciousness) and obedience, and the denial of asking for a reward, in the five stories, and their being placed at the head of them with this, is to alert that the foundation of the prophetic mission (al-ba'tha) is the call to knowledge of the truth and to obedience in that which brings the one called closer to reward and further from punishment. And that the prophets, upon them be peace, are agreed upon this, even if they differed in some branches of the laws that vary according to the differences of times and eras, and that they, upon them be peace, are entirely free from worldly greed.

Perhaps this course was not followed in the two stories of Musa and Ibrahim, upon them both be peace, for variety, along with mention of what gives this sense. It was also said: what is mentioned there is more important. The dwellings of 'Ad were between Oman and Hadramawt, and they were the most fertile and prosperous of lands, but God Most High turned them into deserts and sand dunes. And he points to...

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 128:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do you build on every high place⁠—﴾ means: on every road (ṭarīq), as has been narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah.

Ibn Jarir and a group [of scholars] related from Mujahid that al-rīʿ is the wide pass between two mountains. And from Abu Ṣakhr that it is a mountain and a high place above the ground. And from ʿAṭaʾ that it is a spring of water. But most [scholars] hold that it is a high place, and this is a narration from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. From the same root is rīʿ al-nabāt (the swelling of plants), which is their rising through growth and increase. Ibn Abi ʿAbla read ﴿rayʿin﴾ with a fatḥah on the rāʾ.

﴿A landmark⁠—﴾ means: a sign (ʿalam), as has been related from the Scholar (al-Ḥabr), may Allah be pleased with him. It has also been said: a lofty, well-built palace, as though it were a landmark. This is the view of al-Naqqash and others, and Ibn al-Munayyir preferred it. The narration from al-Ḥabr can be read in this light. In that case, His saying, ﴿you frivolously⁠—﴾ means you play frivolously by building it, since they had no need for it and built it only for display and boasting.

ʿAbath (frivolity) is that which has no benefit, either in reality or in effect. Raising buildings without a lawful purpose has also been condemned in our own Sharia. It has also been said that their frivolity lay in building them so that they could be guided by them on their journeys, though the stars suffice for this. This was objected to on the ground that there is a need for such [markers] when the sky is completely overcast or in similar circumstances.

The reply is that overcast skies are rare, especially in the lands of the Arabs. Moreover, even if there were a need for them, it would not require that they be built on every high place, so that building them in this way would be frivolous.

The scholar al-Yamani said: their elevated places suffice in place of them, so building them is frivolous. It has also been said that they used to build these in order to overlook passers-by and travellers, so that they might mock them and make sport of them. This is related from al-Kalbi and al-Ḍaḥḥak, and from Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr, that the verse refers to dovecotes: they built towers on every high place to play with doves and amuse themselves with them. It has also been said that it refers to a toll-house, which they built at every road-head so that they could sit in it and levy tolls on the wealth of those passing by them. There is a counterpart to this in our lands today. There is no power and no strength except with Allah, the Most High, the Mighty.

The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl), and on some opinions it is a future circumstantial phrase (ḥāl muqaddarah).

﴿And you take﴾, i.e., you make, ﴿reservoirs﴾, i.e., water channels and underground conduits, as narrated from Qatadah. In another narration from him, they are water pools. From Mujahid, they are lofty palaces. It has also been said that they are strong fortresses. They cited the verse of Labid:

*And mountains remain after us, and reservoirs.*

It is not a clear text for the claim being made.

﴿So that you may abide forever﴾, i.e., hoping to live forever in this world, or acting like one who hopes for eternity therein. Thus, *la'alla* (لَعَلَّ) retains its meaning of hope. It has also been said that it is for causation (*ta'lil*). In the recitation of Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud), it reads *kay takhludun* (كَيْ تَخْلُدُونَ), "in order that you may abide forever."

Ibn Zayd said: it is interrogative, in the manner of reproach and mockery of them, meaning, "Will you abide forever?" That *la'alla* is used interrogatively is the view of the Kufan school of grammar (*madhhab Kufi*).

Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: the meaning is *ka'annakum khalidun* (كَأنَّكم خالِدُونَ), "as if you were to abide forever." This reading was also attributed to Qatadah, as narrated from him. In the codex of Ubayy, it reads *ka'annakum takhludun* (كَأنَّكم تَخْلُدُونَ). The apparent sense of what has been mentioned is that *la'alla* here is for comparison (*lit-tashbih*). al-Waqidi clearly transmitted this from al-Baghawi.

In al-Burhan: this is a rare meaning that the grammarians did not mention. However, it occurs in Sahih al-Bukhari that *la'alla* in the verse is for comparison. End quote.

Qatadah read *tukhladun* (تُخْلَدُونَ), in the passive voice and unstressed, and it is said: *khalada al-shay'* and *akhladahu ghayruh* (the thing became lasting, and another made it lasting). Ubayy and Alqamah read *tukhallidun* (تُخَلَّدُونَ), in the passive voice and with the doubled letter, as the poet said:

*Will anyone be content except one made to last forever,*
*free of worries, who does not spend the night in dread?*

﴿And when you strike﴾, i.e., when you intend to strike with a whip or a sword, ﴿you strike as tyrants﴾, dominant and oppressive, without mercy, without intent to discipline, and without consideration of the consequence. The conditional (al-shart) was interpreted as referring to what was mentioned so that the causal relation (al-tasabbub) would be valid. Restricting the response (al-jaza') by a circumstance does not validate it, because the unrestricted (al-mutlaq) is not a cause of the restricted (al-muqayyad). It has been said that the unity of the two does no harm, for the purpose is emphasis (al-mubalaghah). It has also been said that the response clause is considered in terms of informing and reporting, and that is, as you see, far-fetched. A parallel to the verse is his saying:

*Whenever you send it forth, you send it forth blameworthy*

His (peace be upon him) rebuke of them for what was mentioned indicates that the love of this world and arrogance had taken control over their hearts, to the point that this removed them from the limit of servitude.

[Page 111]

**Fa-ttaqū Allāh** — "So fear God": abandon these deeds, **wa-aṭī‘ūn** — "and obey me" in what I call you to, **fa-innahu anfa‘u lakum** — for it is more beneficial for you. **Wa-ttaqū alladhī amaddakum bimā ta‘lamūn** — "And fear the One who has provided you with what you know," i.e., with the blessings that you recognize. Here *mā* is a relative pronoun (ism mawṣūl), the returning pronoun (al-ʿāʾid) is omitted, and *al-ʿilm* (knowledge) is used in the sense of *al-maʿrifah* (recognition).

As for His saying, exalted is He: **amaddakum bi-anʿāmin wa-banīn** ("He has provided you with livestock and sons"), it is treated as a substitute of part (badal al-baʿḍ) — as stated by more than one of the scholars of meanings (ahl al-maʿānī). Their reasoning is that the purpose is to draw attention to the blessings of God Most High, and the context calls for emphasis on this matter, either because it is sought in itself or as a means (dharīʿah) to other forms of gratitude through taqwā. His statement, glorified is He, **amaddakum bi-anʿām** and so on, is more complete in fulfilling this purpose, since it indicates the blessings in detail without referring them to the knowledge of the obstinate addressees. Its relation is thus like that of (*wajhuhu*) in: "Zayd impressed me, his face" (*aʿjabanī Zaydun wajhuhu*), since the second is included in the first, because *mā taʿlamūn* encompasses the livestock and what follows it of coordinated items. The exaggeration (mubālaghah) produced by detail after generalization is not hidden.

In al-Baḥr (al-Baḥr al-Muḥīt by Abū Ḥayyān): the statement of God Most High, **bi-anʿām**, according to the view of some grammarians (naḥwiyyīn), is a substitute (badal) for His statement, **bimā taʿlamūn**, and the governing element (al-ʿāmil) is repeated, like His saying, Most High: **ittabiʿū al-mursalīn** ("Follow the messengers") and **ittabiʿū man lā yasʾalukum ajran** ("Follow those who ask of you no reward"). Most grammarians do not consider such as substitutes; rather, it is for them a repetition of clauses (takrār al-jumal) even though the meaning is one, and it is called *al-tatbīʿ* (following/appositive restatement). For them, the governing element may be repeated only when it is a preposition (ḥarf jarr) and not what is dependent on it, as in: *marartu bi-Zaydin bi-akhīka* ("I passed by Zayd, by your brother"). End of quotation.

Then he mentioned the sons, because they help them in guarding and tending the livestock. From this the reason for coupling the two is known.

Its relation is thus like that of (*wajhuhu*) in: "Zayd impressed me, his face" (*aʿjabanī Zaydun wajhuhu*), since the second is included in the first, because *mā taʿlamūn* encompasses the livestock and what follows it of coordinated items. The exaggeration (mubālaghah) produced by detail after generalization is not hidden.

In al-Baḥr (al-Baḥr al-Muḥīt by Abū Ḥayyān): the statement of God Most High, **bi-anʿām**, according to the view of some grammarians (naḥwiyyīn), is a substitute (badal) for His statement, **bimā taʿlamūn**, and the governing element (al-ʿāmil) is repeated, like His saying, Most High: **ittabiʿū al-mursalīn** ("Follow the messengers") and **ittabiʿū man lā yasʾalukum ajran** ("Follow those who ask of you no reward"). Most grammarians do not consider such as substitutes; rather, it is for them a repetition of clauses (takrār al-jumal) even though the meaning is one, and it is called *al-tatbīʿ* (following/appositive restatement). For them, the governing element may be repeated only when it is a preposition (ḥarf jarr) and not what is dependent on it, as in: *marartu bi-Zaydin bi-akhīka* ("I passed by Zayd, by your brother"). End of quotation.

A similar view is reported from al-Safāqisī. Abū Ḥayyān said: the clause is an explanation of what precedes it and has no place in i‘rāb. He began with mention of the livestock because by them comes leadership (riyāsah) and strength against the enemy, and the wealth without which the enjoyment of sons and others is, in most cases, not complete; and they are the most beloved of property to the Arabs. Then he mentioned the sons, because they help them in guarding and tending the livestock. From this the reason for coupling the two is known.

The commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 134–135:

The connection of the gardens and springs in His saying, ﴿and gardens and springs﴾, is evident, and likewise the reason for their being mentioned together with the cattle.

As for His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Indeed I fear for you﴾ and so on, it is in the position of giving a reason, meaning: I fear for you, if you do not fear God (taqwa) and do not stand up to give thanks (shukr) for these blessings, ﴿the punishment of a tremendous day﴾, in this world and in the Hereafter. For ingratitude for a blessing entails punishment, just as giving thanks for it necessitates its increase. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿If you are thankful, I will surely increase you; but if you are ungrateful, indeed My punishment is severe﴾. He gave the reason as mentioned, without making taqwa necessitate increase, because the loss of a blessing grieves more than its increase delights, and warding off harms takes precedence over securing benefits.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 136:

﴿They said: "It is all the same to us whether you admonish or are not among those who admonish."﴾ "Indeed, we will not desist from what we are upon." They said this in a manner of belittlement and of indifference to what he (ﷺ)... [see note below] — 

Let me correct that: the passage refers to Prophet Hud (ʿalayhi al-salam), not the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), so the translation should read accordingly.

They said this in a manner of belittlement and of indifference to what he, peace be upon him, had warned them of. They departed from the expression "or you did not admonish" (am lam taʿiz), which the apparent sense requires, in order to give emphasis to the depreciation they attached to his admonition, peace be upon him. In their speech, within the sublime composition, is the equivalence of his admonishing and his not admonishing, and "non-existence" here is absolute non-existence, namely that he is not counted among the admonishers and is not of their kind. It was said that the emphasis is conveyed by the use of kāna (to express continuity) and of "al-wāʿizīn" (to express perfection), and that both are considered after the negation according to the context, meaning: "It is all the same to us whether you admonish or the negation of your being among the company of those who admonish continues, a complete negation such that its opposite is not hoped from you." Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: the contrast with what has been mentioned is for the sake of the fāṣila (verse-ending rhyme), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is all the same to you whether you call them or you are silent﴾. Often what is good with the fawāṣil is not good without them. But this is not a valid point, as is not hidden.

It is related from Abu ʿAmr and al-Kisāʾi that the ẓāʾ is assimilated into the tāʾ in "waʿaẓta" (idghām). Ibn Muhaysin and al-Aʿmash also read with idghām, except that al-Aʿmash added the object pronoun and read "awaʿaẓtanā." It should be that this is ikhfāʾ (partial assimilation), because the ẓāʾ is voiced and emphatic (muṭbaqah) while the tāʾ is voiceless and open (munfatiḥah); thus the ẓāʾ is stronger than it. Idghām is only good between two identical letters, or between two close letters when the first is weaker than the second. As for assimilating the stronger into the weaker, it is not good. However, if any such thing occurs in the Qur'an by the transmission of trustworthy reciters, it must be accepted, even if other readings are more eloquent and more regular.

The statement of Him, exalted is He: ﴿This is nothing but the custom of the former peoples﴾ is a justification for their claim of equality (with the dead). That is: this which you have brought us is nothing but the habit of the former peoples, who fabricated its like and called to it. Or: this which we are upon, of life and death, is nothing but an ancient custom that people have always followed. Or: this religion which we are upon is nothing but the custom of the former peoples who preceded us, from among our fathers and others, and we are their followers.

Abu Qilaba and al-Asma'i related from Nafi' the reading «khuluq» (with a damma on the kha' and a sukun on the lam), and its meaning is as already explained.

Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud), Alqamah, al-Hasan, Abu Ja'far, Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir and al-Kisa'i read «khalq» (with a fatha on the kha' and a sukun on the lam). That is: this is nothing but the fabrication and lies of the former peoples. This meaning is supported by what Alqamah related from Abdullah, that he recited «illa ikhtilaq al-awwalin» (nothing but the fabrication of the former peoples). This is like the saying of the rest of the disbelievers: (the fables of the former peoples). Or: our creating this is nothing but the creation of the former peoples; we live as they lived and we die as they died. Their intent is the denial of resurrection and reckoning, which is implied by their threat of punishment. And perhaps their saying ﴿and we will not be punished﴾, that is, for what we are upon of deeds, is more explicit in this regard.

﴿So they denied him﴾: meaning they persisted in denying him, peace be upon him. ﴿So We destroyed them﴾ on account of him, with a furious wind.

﴿Indeed in that is a sign, yet most of them were not believers﴾. ﴿And indeed your Lord, He is the Mighty, the Merciful﴾. ﴿Thamud denied the messengers﴾. It is said by some that it is a non-Arabic (ʿajamī) name, but most scholars hold that it is Arabic and is not declined (ghayr munṣarif), because it is the name of a tribe. It is on the pattern faʿūl, from al-thamd, which is a small amount of water with no source. From this comes the saying, "So-and-so is mathmūd (wasted/depleted); the women have depleted (thamadat-hu) him," meaning they cut off the source of his semen (māʾah) through his excessive intercourse with them. Also, mathmūd describes a man upon whom requests have multiplied until the source of his wealth is exhausted, or it means what remains in the skin, or what appears in winter and disappears in summer.

In al-Qamus: "Thamud is a tribe. It is declined (yuṣraf) and its thāʾ may be vowelled with a ḍammah, and it has also been read that way."

In Sabāʾik al-Dhahab: "Originally it was the name of the tribe's forefather, then it was transferred and made the name of the tribe." The reason the verb here is feminine (kadhdhabat) is similar to what preceded in His saying, ﴿«ʿĀd denied»﴾, and the same applies to His saying, glorified is He:

The Most High's saying: ﴿Will you be left secure in what is here?﴾ is a denial that they should be left secure, in the blessings they enjoy, from the punishment of a great Day. The interrogative here is like it in His earlier saying ﴿Do you build...﴾ and His later saying ﴿Do you come...﴾. It seems the people believed this, and so he (peace be upon him) denied it to them. It is also permitted that the interrogative is for affirmation (taqrir), a reminder of the blessing in that He left them and the means of their benefit secure from enemies and the like, and an urging to thank Him for that through faith.

In al-Kashf it is stated that this is more fitting in this context, and "ma" is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), and "hahuna" (here) indicates the present, near place. That is: "Will you be left in what is in this place of yours of blessing?"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 147–148:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿In gardens and springs﴾ ﴿and crops and palm trees, whose spathes are delicate﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "what is here" (ma hahuna), with the preposition repeated, as Abu al-Baqa' and others said. In the statement there is both summary (ijmal) and detail (tafsil), similar to what preceded in the story of 'Ad. It has also been permitted that it be an adverbial complement (zarf) for "secure" (amin), which occurs as a circumstantial qualifier (hal), but this is not right. Al-Hadim (hadim, "delicate, soft") is that whose parts are folded into one another, as if it had been crushed (hudima), that is, pressed flat.

Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, about it. He said to him: "It is what is folded one part into another." He said: "Do the Arabs know that?" He said: "Yes. Have you not heard the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

A dwelling of a fair-cheeked, tender maiden, of folded flanks and smooth wrists.

Page 113
Al-Zuhri said: it is the soft one when it first emerges. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the one whose dates are without a pit (nawa), and this was narrated from al-Hasan.

It was also said: it is the one hanging down because of the abundance of its fruit. It was said: it is the ripe one of the dates, narrated from 'Ikrimah. It was said: the dates that are beginning to ripen (al-rutab al-mudhannab), narrated from Yazid ibn Abi Ziyad. So describing the spathe (tal') as "delicate" (hadim) is either literal or metaphorical, and it is literally a description of its fruit.

Some of them, according to some of the opinions, made the spathe a metaphor for the fruit, since it is the beginning of it leading to it. And "palm trees" (nakhl) is a collective noun of genus that is masculine as in His saying: ﴿As if they were trunks of hollow palm trees﴾, and feminine as here. This is not because the intended meaning is the females, for that is known from the context, even if the pronoun is masculine.

Its being singled out for mention, despite its inclusion among the gardens, is either because of its excellence over the other trees among them, or because by "gardens" other trees besides it are intended.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 149:

﴿And you hew out dwellings from the mountains, exultant (fari·hin)﴾. That is: insolent and exulting, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Muhammad ibn al-'Ala'. In another narration from Ibn 'Abbas, its tafsir is given as "eager, attentive" (nashitin muhtammin). Abu Salih said: that is, skilful (hadhiqin). Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) also interpreted it accordingly.

Ibn Zayd said: that is, strong (aqwiya'). You know that this clause falls within the scope of the preceding interrogation, and what best fits it, according to the first view and the second view alike, is each of the remaining opinions; they are all equal in this respect. However, it is understood from the words of some scholars that farahah (the sense of fara-hah) is literally "vigour/eagerness" and metaphorically applies to other things. Accordingly, its interpretation as "eager" is preferred if the intent is admonition.

Abu Haywa, 'Isa and al-Hasan read "tanhitun" with a fatha on the ha'. It is also read "tanhatun" with an alif after the ha' for the sake of prolonging the vowel (ishba'an). From 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Muhammad, from his father, that he read "yanhitun" with the ya' at the beginning of the verb and a kasra on the ha'. Also from Abu Haywa and al-Hasan, both read with the ya' (taḥtiyya) and a fatha on the ha'. 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud), Ibn 'Abbas, Zayd ibn 'Ali, the Kufans, and Ibn 'Amir read "farihin" with an alif after the fa'. The reading of the majority is more eloquent, for the reason they mention in (hadhir and hadhir). Mujahid read "mutafarrihin".

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 150–152:

﴿So fear Allah and obey me﴾ ﴿And do not obey the command of the extravagant﴾. It seems that by the address he meant the majority of his people, and by "the extravagant" their great ones and leaders in disbelief and misguidance. They were nine men (rahṭ).

The attribution of obedience to a command is metaphorical (majaz), whereas it is literally attributed to the one who commands; and in this there is an emphasis (mubalagha) that is not hidden. That this does not suit the context is a matter open to discussion.

It is also permissible that obedience (ṭā'a) be a metaphor (isti'ara) for compliance (imtithal), because of the resemblance between them in leading to the doing of what one has been commanded; or it may be a metonymic figure (majaz mursal) in which the cause is mentioned for its necessary consequence.

It is possible that there is here a veiled metaphor (isti'ara makniyya) and an imaginative metaphor (isti'ara takhyiliyya). It has also been permitted that "the command" (al-amr) means "the affairs" (wahid al-umur), but there is in this what there is of remoteness.

Extravagance (al-isrāf) is transgressing the limit in every action a person performs, though its use in spending is most well known. Here it means increase in corruption. This has been clarified, as it is said, by the words of the Exalted: ﴿who cause corruption in the land﴾. Perhaps the intention is to censure them for being misguided in themselves through disbelief and sins, and for misguiding others by calling them to that; and as an allusion to the fact that the evil of their deeds is not restricted to themselves, as a spur to complying with the prohibition. It is said: "in the land" (fi al-ard), and by it is meant the land of Thamud; and it is said: the whole earth. Since "they cause corruption" (yufsidūna) does not preclude their occasionally doing good, it is followed by the words of the Exalted: ﴿and do not set things right﴾, to show the completeness of their corruption and that no reform whatsoever had mingled with it.

Since "they cause corruption" (yufsidūna) does not preclude their occasionally doing good, it is followed by the words of the Exalted: ﴿and do not set things right﴾, to show the completeness of their corruption and that no reform whatsoever had mingled with it.

They said, "You are only one of those who have been bewitched."

That is, those who have been bewitched so much that their intellects have been overcome. It was also said: it means "one of those who have the sihr," that is, the windpipe (ri'ah), so it is a metaphor for his being one of the human beings. According to this view, the words of the Exalted, ﴿You are nothing but a human being like us﴾, serve as an emphasis for it. According to the first view, it is a resumed sentence giving the reason: "You are bewitched, because you are a human being like us, with no distinction over us. Your claim is only due to a defect in your intellect." ﴿So bring us a sign﴾, that is, a token (ayah) ﴿of the truth of your claim﴾, ﴿if you are among the truthful﴾ in it.

﴿He said: "This is a she-camel."﴾ That is, after God Most High brought her forth in answer to his supplication.

It is related that they proposed to him a pregnant she-camel (ʿusharāʾ, one in the tenth month of pregnancy) that would emerge from a rock, which they specified, and then give birth to a young camel (saqb). Peace be upon him sat down, pondering. Gabriel, peace be upon him, said to him: "Pray two rakʿas and ask your Lord." He did so, and the she-camel came forth and knelt before them, and she gave birth to a young one like her in size. At that point he said to them: ﴿This is a she-camel; she has a share of water﴾, that is, a portion of drinking. Water was drunk in turns (al-shiqy and al-qīt, meaning a share of watering and of sustenance), and this drinking was from a spring that was with them.

In Majmaʿ al-Bayān, it is related from ʿAlī, may God honour his face, that this spring was the first spring to gush forth in the earth, and that God, Mighty and Majestic, caused it to flow for Ṣāliḥ, peace be upon him. ﴿And for you is a share of a known day﴾: so be content with your share of water and do not crowd her out of her drinking.

Ibn Abī ʿAbla read "شُرْبُ" with a ḍammah on the shīn in both places. From the verse it is inferred that the water of wells and the like may be divided in this manner. ﴿And do not touch her with harm﴾, such as striking or hamstringing her, ﴿lest there seize you the punishment of a tremendous day﴾. The day is described as "tremendous" because of the magnitude of what befalls in it, and this is more emphatic than describing the punishment as tremendous; it is the figurative attribution (al-majāz fī al-nisba, metaphor in the attribution of a quality to a thing other than its true subject). As for making ﴿ʿaẓīm﴾ (tremendous) an attribute of ﴿ʿadhāb﴾ (punishment) and putting it in the genitive by virtue of proximity (al-mujāwara, grammatical attraction of case by adjacency), as in the phrase "hādhā juḥru ḍabbin kharibin" (this is the hole of a ruined lizard), this is not sound.

﴿So they hamstrung her﴾. The hamstringing is attributed to all of them, although the one who actually hamstrung her was a single man among them, Qidar ibn Salif. He was a wood-cutter (nassaj, lit. "weaver"), as mentioned by more than one scholar. A report states that Mis'ta' drove her into a narrow place in a mountain pass, shot her in the leg with an arrow, and she fell. Then Qidar struck her. This is because it is related that the one who hamstrung her said: "I will not hamstring her until you all are pleased." So they would enter upon a woman in her tent and say, "Are you pleased?" and she would say, "Yes." The same was done with the children, and they all were pleased.

It has also been said that the hamstringing is attributed to them all because it was done by their command and with the help of all of them, as is made clear by the words of God Most High: ﴿Then they called their companion, and he took the task and hamstrung her﴾. There is a discussion regarding this.

﴿Then they became regretful﴾, out of fear of the descent of the punishment, as a group has said. It has been objected that this is refuted by the words of God Most High: ﴿And they said﴾, that is, after they had hamstrung her, ﴿"O Salih, bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the messengers."﴾ It has been answered that the phrase "after they had hamstrung her" is open to dispute, since the conjunction "wa" (and) does not indicate sequence. So it is possible that they meant: "bring us the miracle that you promise us." Or the "wa" is circumstantial, meaning: "and the situation is that they had requested it from Salih and had promised him that they would believe in it when it appeared." Furthermore, it is possible that some of them regretted and others said that, with the action of some being attributed to all because they did not forbid it, or something similar. Or they all regretted first out of fear, then their hearts hardened and their fear went away, or the reverse. It has also been allowed to say that they regretted hamstringing her with the regret of repentance, but it occurred at the time of witnessing the punishment, and at that time regret does not benefit. It has been said that it did not benefit them because they did not compensate for what they had done with the required faith.

It has also been said that they regretted leaving her young camel (saqab) alone, but its weakness is not hidden. Similar to this is what has been said: that they regretted hamstringing her because of the milk they lost, for it is reported that on her day she would provide them with as much milk as they wished.

﴿Then the punishment seized them, the promised one.﴾ It was a single shout by which their bodies became lifeless and their hearts burst, and they all died to the last one. Stones were also rained down upon them during this.

﴿Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed, your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿The people of Lot denied the messengers.﴾ ﴿When their brother Lot said to them,﴾ and they were among his in-laws, peace be upon him, ﴿"Will you not fear God?"﴾ ﴿"Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.﴾ ﴿So fear God and obey me.﴾ ﴿And I do not ask you for any payment for it; my payment is only from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿Do you approach males among the worlds?"﴾

It is a rebuke and a reproach. "Approaching" (al-ityān) is a metonymy (kināya) for sexual intercourse. "Al-dhukrān" is the plural of "dhakar," the opposite of "unthā." The apparent meaning is that "min al-ʿālamīn" is connected to it, meaning: Do you approach males among the offspring of the children of Adam, despite their great numbers, the variety of their kinds, and the predominance of their females over their males, as if females had become scarce for you? Thus "al-ʿālamīn" here means people, because the ones approached are specifically the males among them. The indication is the act being attributed to them and the plural with the "wāw and nūn" ending, without regard to taghlīb (the figurative privileging of the masculine gender). As for the exclusion of angels and jinn, it is by rational necessity.

It is also permissible for it to be connected to "ta'tūn" (you approach), meaning: Do you approach males from among the worlds other than you, none of whom shares in it with you? In this case "al-ʿālamīn" means everyone from whom approaching can proceed, and "al-ʿālam," according to this, is that by which the Creator, glory be to Him, is known. The plural is for taghlīb, and the exclusion of others is for the reason mentioned. That donkeys and pigs also mount males does not harm this, regarding the matter of exclusivity, either because it is rare or because they are removed from the sphere of consideration. It is also permissible that "al-ʿālamīn," on the second reading, means people as well. And if it is said that they include those among the worlds who came before, then the verse indicates that they were the first to establish this evil practice, as His words, exalted is He, make clear: ﴿No one among the worlds preceded you in it.﴾

The word *min* (مِن) in His saying, ﴿from your spouses﴾ (مِن أزْواجِكُمْ), is for *bayan* (explanation, specification) if *ma* is intended to mean the category of females. In that case, the sentence probably contains two omitted nouns, meaning: "and you leave the coming to the private parts of what has been created for you." Alternatively, it is for *tab'id* (partitive, indicating a part) if *ma* is intended to mean the permissible organ of the spouses. This is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "what your Lord has made right for you from your spouses" (ما أصْلَحَ لَكم رَبُّكم مِن أزْواجِكُمْ). In that case, only one omitted noun needs to be assumed, meaning: "and you leave the coming to what He created." According to what has been said, the sentence contains an allusion (*ta'rid*) that they used to have intercourse with their wives in their rear passages (مُحاشِهِنَّ) as well. It was not explicitly denounced as it was with the denunciation of intercourse with males, because it is lesser in sin.

According to the well-known view of the *Ahl al-Sunnah* (the Sunni scholars), this is forbidden, and indeed a major sin (كَبِيرَةٌ). It has been said that it is permissible. The discussion of this has already been presented in detail under His saying: ﴿Your wives are a tilth for you, so come to your tilth however you wish﴾ (نِساؤُكم حَرْثٌ لَكم فَأْتُوا حَرْثَكم أنّى شِئْتُمْ).

It has also been said: there is no omitted noun in the sentence at all, and the intended meaning is to censure them for leaving what was created for them and for not paying any attention to it in any way, let alone coming to it. You know that the meaning is clear under this interpretation. His saying, ﴿Rather, you are a transgressing people﴾ (بَلْ أنْتُمْ قَوْمٌ عادُونَ), is a transitional *idrab* (a shift to a new point, using "bal"). *Al-'adi* is one who exceeds in his wrongdoing and goes beyond the limit. Its complement is omitted, and it is either general or specific, meaning: "Rather, you are a people who transgress and exceed the limits in all sins, and this is among them," or "who exceed the limit of desire, since you have surpassed the rest of people, and even most animals."

It has been said: "They exceed the limit in wrongdoing, since they wronged by coming to what was not created for coming to, and by leaving what was created for it."

In *al-Bahr* (the book *al-Bahr al-Muhit*), it is stated that the opening of the sentence with the pronoun of address (you) is to magnify their deed, and to draw attention to the fact that they are specifically characterized by this, as if it were said: "Rather, you are a transgressing people, and not others."

[p. 116]

They said: "If you do not desist, O Lut, you will surely be among those expelled." (26:167)

That is, from desisting from rebuking us and disparaging our affair, or from what you are upon of claiming prophethood, calling us to faith, and denying what you have denounced of our affair. "You will surely be among those expelled" — that is, among those banished from our well-known town. It seems they used to expel whoever they were angry with for some reason. It was also said that it was because of his denouncing that abomination among them, with harshness and ill treatment. For this reason they threatened him, peace be upon him, with this, and they turned away from the more concise "We will surely expel you" to what is mentioned, and the emphasis in the speech is not hidden.

He said: "Indeed, I am, of your deed, among those who detest." (26:168) That is, among those who hate in the utmost degree. Al-Raghib said: it is said "qalahu" and "yaqlihi" (he hated him). Whoever takes it from the root with waw, it is from al-qalw, meaning throwing, from the saying of the people: "qalat al-naqatu bi-rakibiha qalwan" (the she-camel threw her rider), and "qalawtu bil-qulla idha ramaytaha" (I threw the pebble when I cast it). So the one who is hated is thrown off by the heart because of its hatred, so it does not accept him. Whoever takes it from the root with ya', it is from "qalaytu al-sawiq ʿala al-miqlah" (I fried the parched meal on the frying pan), so the intensity of hatred fries the heart and liver and scorches them. Thus the statement of Abu Hayyan that "qala" in the sense of "abghada" (hated) is ya'i (from the ya' root), while the one meaning "tabakha wa shawa" (cooked and roasted) is waw-root, arises from lack of familiarity. The change from "qali" to what is in the sublime arrangement is because it is more eloquent: for when it is said "qali" it indicates no more than his being engaged in the act, unlike His saying "min al-qalin" (among those who detest), which indicates that he, along with his engagement, is among a people known and famed for it, so he is firmly rooted and deeply versed in it. Ibn Jinni and others have explicitly stated this. The lam in "li-amalikum" is said to be for explanation, as in "saqyan laka" (watering for you), so it is connected to an omitted element, namely "a'ni" (I mean). It was also said that it is for emphasis, and its connection, according to those who hold that the emphatic particle's connection is omitted, is: "Indeed I am among those who detest, of your deed, among those who detest."

It was said that it is connected to the aforementioned "al-qalin" (those who detest), and adverbials are given latitude that other things are not, so they are placed first where other things cannot be placed. The intended "your deed" is either what he, peace be upon him, denounced of them, namely coming to males and abandoning what their Lord, glorified is He, created for them, or what encompasses that and all else he forbade them from and commanded them the opposite of, of heart-based and bodily deeds,

He (peace be upon him) answered their threat with what has been mentioned, as a signal that he was not concerned by it, and that he desired deliverance from the evil of their neighbourhood, because of his intense hatred for their deeds. For this reason he turned away from debating with them and turned to God Most High, saying: ﴿My Lord, save me and my family from what they do﴾, that is, from the ill consequences of their deeds, or from what they do, and from His worldly punishment.

It has been said: it is possible that this is a supplication for protection from being afflicted with the likes of their deeds. This applies to his family, but not to him (peace be upon him), since there is no fear of his being afflicted with such things because of his ʿismah (infallibility, divine protection from sin). It has been objected that the punishment is likewise, since one is not punished for what he did not commit, and this is a clear objection. How can this be so, when He, Glorified is He, said: ﴿And beware of a trial that will not strike those among you who have done wrong in particular﴾?

It has been said: the infallible may supplicate for preservation from falling into what he has been protected from, as indicated by the words of the Most High, relating about Abraham (peace be upon him): ﴿And keep me and my sons away from worshipping idols﴾. This is accepted. However, the apparent meaning is that what is intended is deliverance from what befalls them because of their deeds of the worldly punishment. This is supported by the apparent meaning of the words of the Most High: ﴿So We saved him and his family, all of them﴾ ﴿except an old woman among those who remained behind﴾.

The apparent meaning is that by "his family" what is meant is the people of his household. It has been permitted that what is meant by them is whoever followed his religion, metaphorically, so that it includes the believing members of his household and all others who believed in him. It has been said: there is no need for this generalisation, since none believed in him (peace be upon him) except the people of his household. The "old woman" here refers to his wife (peace be upon him), who was a disbeliever, inclined towards the people and pleased with their action. Describing her as an "old woman" serves as an indication that the destruction of her does not weigh heavily upon Lot (peace be upon him) and the rest of his family, according to the demands of human nature.

It has been said: it is an indication that she had persisted in disbelief and remained in it until she became an old woman. They departed and the one left behind among them left me behind, so I am as if I were a stranger among those who remain.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 172–173:

﴿Then We destroyed the others.﴾ We annihilated them with the utmost and most dreadful annihilation, and that was the overturning (al-i'tifak). The apparent reading is that it is conjoined to "We saved" (najjayna), and the destruction is separated in time from the deliverance from the punishment in general, so there is no need to say that what is meant is: "We intended to save him," or: "We decreed by it," or the meaning of "so We saved him" is: "We responded to his supplication for his deliverance." All of that is contrary to the apparent meaning. Al-Tibi permitted that "thumma" (then) denotes sequence in rank.

﴿And We rained upon them a rain﴾ That is, a kind of rain that was not customary, for it was stones of sijjil (baked clay), as stated in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when Our command came, We made its highest part its lowest and rained upon it stones of sijjil⁠﴾.

The combining of the two punishments for them is an increase in their humiliation. It has been said that the overturning was for one group and the rain for another of them, and this (according to what is narrated from Muqatil) was for those who were outside the town for some of their needs; and perhaps this is what Qatada meant by "the stragglers" (al-shudhdhadh) in what is narrated from him. ﴿So evil was the rain of those who were warned﴾: the lam in "al-mundharin" is for the genus, and by this it is possible for the mudaf ilayhi (genitive noun) to be the subject (fa'il) of "sa'a" (evil was), based on its being in the sense of "bi'sa" (how evil), and the object of praise or blame is omitted, which is their rain. If "sa'a" is not in that sense, it is permissible for it to be for the specific (al-ahd).

Verses 174–177 of Surah al-Shu'ara' (26):

﴿Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers.﴾ ﴿And indeed, your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿The companions of al-Ayka (the thicket) denied the messengers.﴾ Al-Ayka is the dense thicket that grows lush trees, and it is a thicket along the seashore toward Madyan, inhabited by a group of people. They were among those to whom Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) was sent, and he was a stranger among them, which is why it says: ﴿When Shu'ayb said to them, "Will you not fear Allah?"﴾, and it was not said "their brother." It has also been said that al-Ayka means tangled trees, and their trees were the doum palm, which is the muql. According to both opinions, "the companions of al-Ayka" are other than the people of Madyan. There is a strange report from Ibn 'Abbas that they are the same as the people of Madyan.

The two Haramis (Ibn Kathir and Nafi') and Ibn 'Amir read "Layka" with an open lam followed by a ya', without an alif, and it is not diptote here. In Surah Sad (38) it is also read this way. Abu 'Ubayda said: "We found in some books of tafsir that Layka is the name of a town, and al-Ayka refers to the whole region, like Makka and Bakka. I saw it in the Imam (master copy) of the Qur'an of 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, in al-Hijr and Qaf as 'al-Ayka,' and in al-Shu'ara' and Sad as 'Layka.' After that, the copies of all the cities gathered together and did not differ." In al-Kashshaf it says: whoever reads with the accusative case and claims that "Layka," on the pattern of "Layla," is the name of a place, is mistaken, led to this by the script of the mushaf, since it is written here and in Sad without an alif. In the mushaf there are things written contrary to the standard orthography, and in these two surahs they were written according to the pronunciation of the reciter, just as grammarians now write "Lana" and the preferable "Lawla" to show the pronunciation of the lightened form, whereas elsewhere in the Qur'an they are written according to the original form. The story is one, and "Layka" is an unknown name. End of quotation.

It has been objected that this is a claim without proof, and that sufficient proof against the opponent is the established reading in the seven readings, which is mutawatir. Moreover, there is what you have heard from some books of tafsir, even if you do not rely on it. For al-Bukhari narrated in his Sahih: "al-Ayka" and "Layka" mean the thicket. Furthermore, unusual names are not prohibited. In al-Bahr it says: that the root (l-y-k) is absent from the language of the Arabs, as those who deny this mutawatir reading cling to, even if true, does no harm; the word may be non-Arabic, and the roots of foreign speech often differ from those of Arabic. Thus the word combines being a proper noun, foreignness and feminine gender as reasons for not declining it. In sum, al-Zamakhshari's denial of the correctness of this reading comes close to apostasy, and we seek refuge in Allah the Exalted.

Al-Mubarrad, Ibn Qutayba, al-Zajjaj, al-Farisi and al-Nahhas preceded him in this. It was also read "Layki" with the hamza removed, its vowel placed on the lam, and in the genitive with a kasra. It is written according to the pronunciation without a hamza, and according to the original form with a hamza, and likewise its counterparts.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 178–182:

﴿Indeed, I am to you a trustworthy messenger.﴾ ﴿So fear Allah and obey me.﴾ ﴿And I do not ask you for any reward for it; my reward is only from the Lord of the worlds.﴾ ﴿Give full measure﴾ i.e., complete it. ﴿And do not be among those who cause loss﴾ i.e., by diminishing people's rights through short-measure (tatfif). The emphasis derived from the construction may be directed toward the prohibition, or it may be that the concept (mafhum) is not taken into account for expressions like what was said regarding His words, exalted is He: ﴿Do not consume usury, doubled and redoubled﴾. In any case, in the aforementioned prohibition there is an emphasis on the command preceding it. ﴿And weigh﴾ the things that are weighed ﴿with a true balance﴾, i.e., with a straight scale. It was said: al-qistas is the steelyard (qabban), and this is narrated from al-Hasan. According to some, it is an arabicized word of Roman origin, meaning justice, and this is narrated from Mujahid. According to others, it is Arabic. It was said: it is from al-qist, and its pattern is fi'lā'l with the doubling of the middle radical irregularly, since it is not doubled on its own with the separation by the lam. It was also said: it is from qastas, which is quadriliteral, and its pattern is fi'lāl. The intended meaning is the command to fulfill and complete the weight, and the prohibition of deficiency, not the prohibition of excess. Apparently, it was neither prohibited nor commanded in measuring and weighing, and it seems that this is evidence that whoever does it has done well, and whoever does not do it, there is no blame upon him.

It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the meaning of ﴿And weigh﴾ etc.: Make your affairs all balanced by the balance of justice which Allah, exalted is He, has set for His servants. And the apparent meaning, since He, glory be to Him, equated it with it, is ﴿Give full measure﴾ as previously mentioned.

And most of the Seven read "bil-qusṭās" with a damma on the qaf.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 183:

﴿And do not deprive people of their due⁠﴾ meaning: do not diminish for them anything of their rights, whatever right it may be. The genitive construction of "things" (ashya') is generic (jinsiyya, a generic or class-denoting usage), and it may be inclusive (li-l-istighraq, the sense of encompassing all instances). The intended sense is the correspondence of plural to plural, so the meaning is: do not deprive anyone of anything. It is also permissible that the plural indicates the types, since they used to deprive people of everything, whether great or small. This is a generalisation after specifying part of what is meant by mention, because of the extent of their immersion in it. It has been said that what is meant by "their things" is dirhams and dinars, and depriving them (bakhsuha) is by clipping their edges. Were it not for this, it would not have been put in the plural. Bakhasa is transitive to two objects, so the two accusative nouns are its objects. It has also been said that it is transitive to one object, and so the second is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal).

﴿And do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief⁠﴾ through killing, raiding, highway robbery and the like. Al-'athw is corruption, or its greatest degree. "Causing mischief" (mufsidin) is an emphatic circumstantial clause (hal muakkida). It is also permissible that what is meant is "causing mischief to your hereafter," in which case it is an establishing circumstantial clause (hal mu'assisa).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 184:

﴿And be mindful of Him who created you, and the former generations (al-jibilla al-awwalin).﴾ That is: and those possessing the jibilla (i.e., the created nature and disposition), or: those who were molded (majbulin) according to their conditions upon which they built, and their paths which they were predisposed to follow, those who preceded you among the nations. It has come in a narration from Ibn 'Abbas that the jibilla is a group that numbers ten thousand, as if it was likened, so it is said, to a great piece of a mountain (jabal). It is also said: it is a large group in general, as if it were likened to what has been mentioned as well.

Abu Husayn, al-A'mash, and al-Hasan, in one report from him, read «al-jubulla» (الجُبُلَّةَ) with a damma on the jim and the ba' and a shadda on the lam. As-Sulami read «al-jibla» (الجِبْلَةَ) with a kasra on the jim and a sukun on the ba', like al-khilqa (creation). In one copy from him, it is read with a fatha on the jim and a sukun on the ba'. It is said that the shadda on the lam in both readings is for emphasis (mubalagha).

They said: ﴿You are only one of the bewitched.﴾ ﴿And you are not but a human being like us.﴾ The discussion here is similar to what preceded it in the story of Thamud. However, here he (God) introduced the conjunction *wa* (and) between the two clauses to indicate that each of *al-taskhir* (being bewitched) and *al-bashariyyah* (being human) is incompatible with prophethood, so how much more so when both are combined. They intended by this to exaggerate the denial. In the earlier story it was not introduced, since only one meaning was intended, namely that he was bewitched, and then he was affirmed to be a human like them. This is what al-Kashshaf (the commentary of al-Zamakhshari) states. In al-Kashf (of Ibn al-Munayyir), it is noted that this contains an allusion to the particular placement of each (clause), and that the discussion there concerns his being like them, which is not distinguished by anything that would entail superiority. For this reason they followed it with their words: ﴿So bring us a sign.﴾ This shows that they did not regard being human as incompatible with prophethood; rather, they made the description a preliminary to commonality, and that he was too bold in his claim. Here, however, they presented that in the manner of what is incompatible with prophethood, so each one was made an independent attribute of incompatibility, in order to be more emphatic. They also treated the denial of prophethood as an established matter, and for this reason they followed it with their words: ﴿And indeed we think you are one of the liars﴾, etc. Al-Nisaburi said, regarding the reason for the distinction: Salih (peace be upon him) used few words in his address, so they used few words in their reply; Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) used many words in his address, and for this he was called "the orator of the prophets," so they used many words in their reply. Perhaps he meant that Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) pressed hard in warning them, so they pressed hard in denying him; this was not the case with Salih (peace be upon him) and his people, so reflect.

(*Wa-in*) in His words, glorified is He: ﴿And indeed we think you are one of the liars﴾ is the lightened form of the heavy (*inna*), and the *lam* in (*la-min*) is the *lam* that distinguishes (the two). The Kufans said: (*in*) is negative and the (*lam*) carries the meaning of (*illa*, except), and this is a well-known disagreement. That is: "Indeed the matter is that we think you are one of the liars in the claim," or "We do not think you but one of the liars in it." Their meaning is that he (peace be upon him, and far be it from him) was firmly established in lying in his claim of prophethood, or in it and in the claim of the descent of the punishment which is indicated by the command to piety as a warning. The apparent sense of their situation is that by *al-zann* (thinking/supposing) they meant certain knowledge.

And as for His words, Mighty and Majestic be He: ﴿So cause fragments of the sky to fall upon us, if you are of the truthful﴾. This is among the demands (iqtirāḥ, a proposal or demand put to a prophet) which contain all manner of denial, similar to ﴿If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾. Perhaps they answered with this the implication of the command to fear God (taqwā) that we mentioned. "Kisafan" means pieces, as was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah. It is the plural of kisfah, like qiṭʿah.

Most readers recited "kisfan" with a kasra on the kāf and a sukūn on the sīn. It is also the plural of kisfah, like sidrah and sidr. It was said that al-kisf and al-kisfah are like al-rīʿ and al-rīʿah, meaning a piece. By "the sky" (al-samāʾ) is meant either the canopy, which is the apparent meaning, or the clouds. The apparent view is that the prepositional phrase is connected to an omitted element that functions as an adjective to what precedes it. Its connection to "afsiṭ" (cause to fall) is very far-fetched. It was also permitted that "the sky" means the direction of height. The apodosis (jawāb) of "in" (if) is omitted, indicated by "fa-askiṭ" (so cause to fall). Whoever permits the apodosis to precede it makes "fa-askiṭ" the apodosis.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 188–189:

﴿He said: My Lord knows best what you do.﴾ That is, He, exalted is He, knows best your deeds, including disbelief and acts of disobedience, and what punishment you deserve for them.
Page 120
﴿So He will surely send it down upon you in accordance with what you deserve, at the time appointed for it, without doubt.﴾

﴿But they denied him﴾ — they persisted in denying him, and they denied him with denial after denial. ﴿So the punishment of the Day of the Shade seized them.﴾ This is in accordance with what ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥatim and al-Ḥakim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas: that Allah, exalted is He, sent upon them a intense heat, which seized their breaths, so they entered the inner parts of their houses, but it entered upon them there, so they fled out from them into the wilderness. Then Allah, exalted is He, sent upon them a cloud which shaded them from the sun — and this is the shade (ẓullah). They found in it coolness and pleasure, so they called out to one another, until, when they had gathered beneath it, Allah, exalted is He, dropped upon them fire from it, and it consumed them all.

Many narrations also state that Allah, exalted is He, imposed upon them the heat for seven days and their nights, and then there occurred what occurred of going out into the wilderness and what followed it. This was in accordance with what they had proposed, especially according to the view that by "the sky" they meant the cloud. The attribution of the punishment to "the Day of the Shade" rather than to the shade itself indicates that they had a punishment other than the punishment of the shade, and leaving its description unspecified magnifies its matter.

Ibn Jarir, al-Ḥakim and Ibn Abi Ḥatim transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas — may Allah be pleased with both of them — that he said: "Whoever from the scholars tells you what the punishment of the Day of the Shade is, then deny it." It seems he meant by this the whole of the punishment of the shade mentioned in the previous report together with the other punishment which the attribution to the Day indicates. ﴿Indeed, it was the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾ That is, in its severity and terror, and the dreadfulness of the all-encompassing calamity and overwhelming catastrophe that befell them therein.

﴿Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them are not believers﴾. ﴿And indeed your Lord is the All-Mighty, the Most Merciful﴾. This is the last of the seven narratives that were presented for what you already know. Perhaps the restriction to this number, as has been said, is because it is a complete number. I entrust the knowledge of the secret of that, and likewise the knowledge of the secret of arranging the narratives in this manner, to the presence of the All-Knowing of the Unseen, exalted is His majesty.

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And indeed it is a revelation (تَنْزِيلُ, tanzil) from the Lord of the worlds﴾, etc., returns to what was at the beginning of the noble surah of praising the magnificent Qur'an and refuting what the polytheists said about it. So the pronoun refers to the Qur'an. It was also said that it is an affirmation of the truth of those narratives and an alert to the inimitability (i'jaz) of the Qur'an and the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), for reporting about them from one who did not learn them can only be by revelation from Allah, mighty and majestic. So the pronoun refers to the mentioned noble verses that narrate those related stories. It is also permissible that it refers to the Qur'an, of which they are a part, and the description of that as "tanzil" is for emphasis; the meaning is that it is indeed sent down from Allah, exalted. Describing Him, glorified is He, with the lordship of the worlds indicates that its sending down is among the rulings of His nurturing and His compassion toward all.
