"Revealed with it" — that is, He sent it down. The bā' here is for transitivity (al-ta'diyah). Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is for accompaniment (al-musahabah), and the prepositional phrase is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), as in His saying, ﴿And they entered with disbelief﴾. That is: it descended accompanied by it. ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit﴾ — meaning Jibril, peace be upon him. He is referred to as "the Spirit" because through him the creatures are given life in matters of religion; or because he is wholly spirit, unlike people who have a spirit within their bodies. He, peace be upon him, is described as "the Trustworthy" because he is the trustworthy bearer of His revelation, and the one who conveys it to whomever He wills of His servants — exalted is His majesty — without any alteration or distortion whatsoever.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr, and Ibn 'Amir recited: (nazzala bihi al-ruha al-amina), with the zay doubled and both al-ruh and al-amin in the accusative, meaning: Allah, exalted is He, caused the Trustworthy Spirit to descend with it.

[Page 121]

﴿upon your heart﴾ is related to (descended), not to the Trustworthy (al-Amin). By "the heart" is meant either the spirit (al-ruh), which is one of its usages, as al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said. That the revelation descended upon it, according to what many have said, is because it is the perceiver and the one addressed by the command, not the body.

It may be said: since he ﷺ had two aspects, a angelic aspect through which he receives (yastafidu) and a human aspect through which he overflows (yafidu), the descent was made upon his spirit ﷺ, because it is the one characterized by the angelic attributes through which he receives from the Trustworthy Spirit.

As an allusion to this, it was said: "upon your heart" rather than "upon you," which is shorter. It was also said that this is because the Qur'an did not descend in pages (suhuf) as other scriptures did.

Or the heart means the specific organ, which is the well-known usage. Specifying it for the descent is said to allude to the perfection of his ﷺ understanding and comprehension of that which was sent down, since no intermediary is considered in its arrival at the heart, which is the seat of intellect (al-'aql), as the apparent meaning of many verses and hadiths indicates, and as reason testifies, as is not hidden. (﴿for whoever has a heart, or gives ear while he is a witness﴾). The Imam has extensively argued for this in his tafsir, and refuted those who held that the brain is the seat of intellect.

It was also said: it is an allusion to the soundness of his heart, peace be upon him, and its purity, since it was a dwelling place for the speech of the Exalted. From this one knows the state of all his other limbs (ajza'), ﷺ, for the heart is the chief and king of all the organs, and when the king is sound, the subjects are sound.

And in a hadith: "Verily, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Verily, it is the heart."

It may be said: the specification may be because Allah, exalted is He, made for the heart of His Messenger ﷺ a special hearing by which he hears what is revealed to him of the Qur'an, distinguishing his status above all else he hears and retains, according to what has been said. Al-Nawawi mentioned this in his commentary on Sahih Muslim regarding His saying: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾, that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made for his heart ﷺ a sight, so he saw Him, glorified is He, with it on the night of the Mi'raj.

All of this is according to the view that Jibril, peace be upon him, descends with the Qur'anic words preserved for him, after the Qur'an had descended entirely from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) to the House of Majesty (Bayt al-'Izza), or which he memorizes from the Tablet at the command to descend, or which are inspired to him, or which he hears from Him, glorified is He, according to what some of the eminent early scholars said, in His presence; then he casts them to the Prophet ﷺ exactly as they are, without any alteration whatsoever.

Likewise according to the view that Jibril, peace be upon him, cast upon him the Qur'anic meanings, and that he expressed them in these Arabic words, then descended with them thus and cast them to the Prophet ﷺ.

As for the view that he, peace be upon him, descended only with the meanings to the Prophet, peace be upon him, and that he, peace be upon him, understood those meanings and expressed them in the language of the Arabs, it was said that the heart here means only the specific organ, and its specification is because meanings are perceived only through the faculty deposited in it. It was also said that it may be meant the spirit, and his spirit, peace be upon him, due to its extreme sanctity and perfection in itself, perceives the meanings without the mediation of any instrument. Some people held this view and made the verse a proof for it, but it is an inferior view. Similarly is the view that Jibril, peace be upon him, cast upon him the meanings, so he expressed them in words, and he descended with what he himself expressed. The preponderant view is that the words, like the meanings, are from Him, Mighty and Majestic, and Jibril, peace be upon him, has no part in them whatsoever.

The Prophet ﷺ used to hear them and retain them with divine, holy powers, not like the hearing of humans from him, peace be upon him, and his human faculties would be affected at that time. For this reason there appears on his noble body ﷺ what appears, and this is called the burden (bura'a') of revelation, to the point that it is sometimes supposed that he fainted, peace be upon him, and it is sometimes supposed that he dozed off.

On this is explained what Muslim narrated from Anas, who said: "While the Messenger of Allah, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, was among us, he dozed off briefly, then raised his head smiling. We said: 'What made you laugh, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'A sura has just been revealed to me,' and he recited: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. ﴿Indeed We have given you al-Kawthar﴾ ﴿So pray to your Lord and sacrifice﴾ ﴿Indeed your enemy is the one cut off﴾.'"

Whoever says that the more likely view is that the entire Qur'an descended while awake does not need to interpret this report as meaning that the sura al-Kawthar, which had been revealed earlier while awake, occurred to him during that dozing, or that al-Kawthar, in which the sura was revealed, was presented to him, and he recited it to them. Furthermore, according to what has been said, that some of the Qur'an descended upon him, peace be upon him, while he was asleep, based on this report, what we have said still stands regarding his hearing, peace be upon him, of what descends to him ﷺ, and his retaining it with divine, holy powers; and his sleep, peace be upon him, does not prevent that. How could it, when it is authentically reported from him ﷺ that he said: "My eyes sleep, but my heart does not sleep."

[Page 122]

Some of the leading scholars among the later ones, in the gatherings of wisdom (hikmah), when explaining how speech is conveyed and revelation descends from Allah, Exalted is He, through the angel upon the heart of the Prophet ﷺ, mentioned that the human spirit, when it is stripped of the body and released from the bond of its vessel and the abode of its nature, emigrating to its Lord, glorified is He, to witness His greatest signs, and is purified from the filth of sins, pleasures, desires, habitual whisperings, and attachments, there shines upon it the light of knowledge and faith in Allah, Exalted is He, and His highest dominion (malakut). When this light becomes firm and essentialized, it becomes a holy substance, called in the language of theoretical wisdom the active intellect (al-'aql al-fa'al), and in the language of the prophetic Law the holy spirit (al-ruh al-qudsi). By this intense intellectual light, the secrets of what is in the earth and heaven gleam within it, and the realities of things become visible through it, just as with physical visual light the imaginal forms become visible to the faculty of sight when no veil obstructs it.

The veil here is the traces of nature and the preoccupations of this lower world. When the soul is emptied of the motives of nature and the occupation with what lies beneath it of desire, anger, sense, and imagination, and turns its face toward the Truth and toward the realm of the highest malakut, it connects with ultimate happiness; the secret of the malakut shines upon it, the holiness of the lahut (divinity) is reflected upon it, and it sees the wonders of Allah's greatest signs. Then, if this spirit is holy, of intense powers and strong effects due to its strong connection with what is above it, no matter occupies it from another matter, and no direction above it prevents it from the direction below it. It controls both extremes, and its power encompasses both sides, due to its firm establishment at the common boundary between the realm of dominion (mulk) and the realm of malakut, like weak spirits which, when they incline toward one side, the other side disappears from them, and when they rest upon one faculty, they are distracted from the other.

When this holy spirit—which is not occupied by one matter from another, nor diverted by one mode of existence from another—turns its attention and receives the divine knowledge without human instruction, but from Allah Exalted Himself, its influence extends to its faculties, and the image of what it witnessed with its holy spirit is represented to his human spirit, and its form emerges from it into the outer world, and is represented to the outward senses, especially hearing and sight, since these are the noblest of the outward senses. So he sees with his sight a sensible person in the utmost beauty and splendor, and he hears with his hearing speech arranged in the utmost excellence and eloquence. The person is the angel descending by Allah's permission, bearing the divine revelation; the speech is the speech of Allah, Exalted is He; and in his hand is a tablet in which is a book, the Book of Allah, Exalted is He. This matter represented with what is with him or in him is not merely an imaginary image that has no existence outside the mind and imagination, as says he who has no share of the knowledge of the inner reality and no foothold in the secrets of revelation and the Book, like some followers of the Peripatetics (al-Mashsha'iyyun). Far be it from Allah, Exalted is He, from this belief, which arises from ignorance of the manner of sending down and descent.

Then he said: "An illumination of the heart and an intellectual indication. You must know that the angels have real essences and relative essences, related to what is below them, like the relation of the soul to the body that exists in the next world. As for their real essences, they are only of the order of command, decree, and word. As for their relative essences, they are only of creation and destiny, from which arise the angels of the tablet (al-mala'ikah al-lawhiyyah), the greatest of whom is Israfil, peace be upon him. These angels of the tablet take the divine speech and the sublime knowledge from the angels of the pen (al-mala'ikah al-qalamiyyah), and record them in the pages of their destined tablets of the Book. The first category of angels met the Prophet ﷺ during his ascension (mi'raj), and he witnessed the Spirit of Holiness while awake. When the prophetic spirit connects with their world, the world of divine revelation, it hears the speech of Allah, Exalted is He, which is the communication of realities through true conversation, and this is the overflowing and receiving at the station of (﴿two bow-lengths away or nearer﴾), which is the station of nearness, the seat of truthfulness, and the source of revelation and inspiration.

Likewise, when the Prophet associates with the highest angels, he hears the rustling of their pens and the casting of their speech, which is the speech of Allah, Exalted is He, descending in the place of their knowledge, which is their essences and their intellects, since they are in the station of nearness. Then when he, peace be upon him, descends to the courtyard of the heavenly malakut, there is represented to him the image of what he understood and witnessed on the tablet of his soul, which is in the world of heavenly destined spirits. Then the effect spreads from it to the outward, and at that moment there occurs to the senses a kind of astonishment and sleep, because the holy spirit, by controlling both sides, employs the sensory faculties, but not for animal purposes, rather in the path of journeying to the Lord, glorified is He. So it spreads the spirit in the path of knowing Him, Exalted is He, and obeying Him. Therefore, when Allah, Exalted is He, addresses him with address without an external veil—whether the address is without intermediary or through the intermediary of the angel—and he is made to know the unseen, and there is impressed upon the bezel of his prophetic soul the engraving of the malakut and the image of the jabarut, the power of the outward sense is drawn upward, and there is represented to it an image not separated from its meaning and its true spirit, unlike the images of dreams and imaginations empty of meaning. Thus the reality of the angel is represented to it in its sensible form according to what it can bear, so he sees an angel in a form other than the form he had in the world of command, because when command descends it becomes a created, measured creation. So he sees its created, destined form, and hears speech that is heard, after what had been intelligible revelation, or sees a tablet with writing in its hand. Thus the one to whom revelation is made connects with the angel first through his intellectual spirit, receives from him the divine knowledge, witnesses with his intellectual sight the greatest signs of his Lord, and hears with his intellectual hearing the speech of the Lord of the worlds from the Supreme Spirit.

Then when he descends from this lofty divine station, the angel is represented to him in a sensible form according to his capacity, then it descends into his outward sense, then into the air. And so it is with the speech as well: he hears sounds and letters arranged and heard, which he alone perceives to the exclusion of others. Thus each of the angel, his speech, and his book has come from his unseen to his witnessed, and from the inner core of his secret to his senses."

This transmission is not a matter of the angel who brings the revelation moving or being transported from his station and place, since each one has a known station which he does not exceed or leave. Rather, the matter returns to an inner movement (inbi'ath nafsi) in the Prophet (peace be upon him) from the realm of the unseen (nash'at al-ghayb) to the realm of manifestation (nash'at al-zuhur). For this reason, a kind of dazed faintness (shibh al-dahash wa-al-ghashy) would overtake him, then he would see and hear, and then the informing and reporting would come from him. This is the meaning of the sending down of the Book (tanzil al-kitab) and the causing to descend of the speech (inzal al-kalam) from the Lord of the worlds. End of quotation.

There is in this what the foundations of Islam reject, as is not hidden from you. Several of the scholars of hadith, exegetes and others have explicitly stated that the angel moves, and he is a body in their view, and none of them, as far as we know, has interpreted his descent. Yes, they have interpreted the descent (nuzul) and the causing to descend (inzal) of the Qur'an.

Al-Isfahani said at the beginning of his tafsir: The People of the Sunnah and the Community agreed that the speech of Allah the Exalted is sent down (munazzal), but they differed about the meaning of inzal. Some of them said: it is the manifestation of the recitation. Others said: Allah the Exalted inspired His speech to Jibril (peace be upon him) while he was in the heavens, and taught him its recitation, and then Jibril conveyed it on earth as he descended in the place. In this there are two ways:
The first is that the Prophet (ﷺ) was stripped of the form of humanity and into the form of angelhood, and received it from Jibril (peace be upon him).
The second is that the angel was stripped down into humanity so that the Prophet (peace be upon him) could take it from him. The first is the harder of the two states. End of quotation.

Al-Tibi said: Perhaps the descent of the Qur'an upon the Messenger (peace be upon him) is that the angel receives it in a spiritual manner (talaqquf ruhani), or preserves it from the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), then descends with it to the Messenger and casts it upon him.
Page 124
Al-Qutb said in the marginal notes on the Kashshaf: Inzal in the language means to give shelter, and also means moving a thing from high to low; neither of these two is realized in speech, so it is used in a figurative meaning.

Whoever says: the Qur'an is a meaning subsisting in the Essence of Allah the Exalted, then its inzal is that the words and letters indicating that meaning come into existence and He records them in the Preserved Tablet.
Whoever says: the Qur'an is the expressions indicating the meaning subsisting in His Essence, then its inzal is merely its recording in the Preserved Tablet, and this meaning is suitable as a figurative sense of the first of the two linguistic meanings.
It is possible that the intended sense of its inzal is its recording in the lowest heaven after its recording in the Preserved Tablet, and this is suitable to the second meaning.
The intended sense of the sending down of the books upon the messengers is that the angel receives them from Allah the Exalted in a spiritual manner, or preserves them from the Preserved Tablet and descends with them, then casts them upon them. End of quotation. In this there is a discussion that is not hidden.

In my view, its inzal is its manifestation in the world of witnessing (alam al-shahadah) after it was in the world of the unseen (alam al-ghayb). Furthermore, the apparent sense of the verse requires that the whole Qur'an was brought down by the Trustworthy Spirit upon his noble heart (ﷺ). This contradicts what has been said: that Allah the Exalted spoke the final verses of Surat al-Baqarah to him directly on the night of the Mi'raj, without an intermediary, relying on what Muslim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken on the night journey, he reached the Lote-Tree of the Utmost Boundary..." the hadith, in which: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was given the five prayers, and was given the final verses of Surat al-Baqarah, and whoever of his community does not associate anything with Allah was forgiven the grave sins."

It is answered, after accepting the premise, that what was mentioned as evidence for this may be that Jibril (peace be upon him) also descended with what was mentioned, as confirmation and affirmation or the like. The descent of Jibril (peace be upon him) with a single verse twice has been established for this reason. It is also permitted that the verse is meant in terms of the majority of cases. Some have considered it to be so for another reason: that some of the Qur'an was brought down by Israfil (peace be upon him), which was in the early period of prophethood. In this there is the point that this has not been established at all.

In al-Itqan: Imam Ahmad narrated in his History, through Dawud ibn Abi Hind, from al-Sha'bi, who said: Prophethood was sent down upon the Prophet (ﷺ) when he was forty years old. Israfil (peace be upon him) was joined to his prophethood for three years, teaching him words and things, but the Qur'an was not sent down upon him through his tongue. When three years had passed, Jibril (peace be upon him) was joined to his prophethood, and the Qur'an was sent down upon him through his tongue for ten years. End of quotation.

This is explicit in contradicting that, although it contradicts the sound and well-known report that Jibril (peace be upon him) is the one who brought the revelation to him (peace be upon him) from the very beginning, except that other angels, besides him (peace be upon him), also descended to him with some matters, and they often descend to accompany Jibril in conveying the Qur'anic verses, peace be upon him and them.

Some people considered it to be so in terms of the majority of cases, because the descent of Jibril (peace be upon him) may not be upon the heart, based on what Shaykh Muhyi al-Din (may his secret be sanctified) mentioned in the fourteenth chapter of the Futuhat, from his saying: Know that the angel comes to the Prophet (peace be upon him) with the revelation in two states: sometimes he descends with the revelation upon his heart, and sometimes he comes to him in a bodily form from outside, and casts what he brought upon that Prophet's ear so that he hears it, or casts it upon his sight so that he sees it, and thus he obtains from seeing what he obtains from hearing, equally.

It has been objected that there is no need for what was mentioned, and what has been transmitted from Muhyi al-Din (may his secret be sanctified) does not indicate that the descent of revelation to every prophet occurs in these two states. It is possible that the descent of revelation to our Prophet (ﷺ) was in the first state only. Even if we grant its indication of generality, and that the descent of revelation to our Prophet (peace be upon him) may be by the angel taking a human form, based on some sound reports about that, we do not grant that it indicates that the descent of revelation, when the revealed thing is the Qur'an, occurs in the second state. Even if we grant its indication of that, we do not grant the validity of making it a basis for interpreting the verse. How can the speech of Allah the Exalted be interpreted by a speech
Page 125
that contradicts its apparent meaning, issued from a non-infallible person? It is sufficient for Muhyi al-Din (may his secret be sanctified) among the scholars of the Shari'ah that they interpret his words to accord with the speech of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, so that he is safe from criticism. Perhaps whoever interprets in such a matter thinks well of Muhyi al-Din (may his secret be sanctified) and says: he did not say that except on the basis of a legal proof. He (may his secret be sanctified) said, concerning the permission (al-idhn) in the Futuhat: Know that I have not established, by the praise of Allah the Exalted, in this book of mine or any other, ever a matter that is not legislated, and I have not departed from the Book and the Sunnah in anything in my works. And in the three hundred and sixty-sixth chapter of the said book he said: Everything I speak of in my gatherings and compositions comes only from the presence of the Mighty Qur'an, for I have been given the keys of knowledge in it, so I never seek help in any science of the sciences except from it, all of this so that I do not depart from sitting with the Real, may He be exalted, in His intimate conversation with His speech, or with what His speech contains, and so on. So the one who calls for interpretation, in reality, is that proof, not the very words of his noble, sanctified self, and this is what befits the perfect Muslims.

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿So that you may be among the warners﴾ is connected to "descended" (nazala), meaning: it descended with it so that you might warn them with what it contains of terrible punishments. The choice of what is in the noble arrangement is to indicate his (ﷺ) inclusion in the line of those well-known warners, in the truth of the message and the certainty of the punishment warned of. Likewise the saying of the Exalted:

﴿In a clear Arabic tongue﴾ is related to (nazala, "He sent down") according to a group of the eminent scholars. In that case, as al-Shihab said, it is a *badal* (apposition, بَدَلًا) for (bihi, "with it") with the governing word repeated. The fronting of ﴿that you may be﴾ and what follows is for emphasis on the matter of warning, and so that it is not imagined that his being one of the aforementioned warners (ﷺ) depends on the revelation being in a clear Arabic tongue. It is considered good that the particle (bi, بِ) indicates accompaniment, and the prepositional phrase is in the position of a *hal* (circumstantial clause, حالًا) from the pronoun in (bihi). That is: He sent it down with it accompanied by a clearly Arabic language, whose meaning is plain and whose indication is manifest, so that they would have no excuse. It was also said: "in a tongue that makes clear to them what they need of the affairs of their religion and their worldly life." On this view, (mubin, مُبِينٍ) is from (abana, أبان), the transitive form. The first view is more evident.

It is also permitted that the prepositional phrase be related to (al-munthirin, "the warners"), meaning: that you may be among those who warned in the tongue of the Arabs. They are Hud, Salih, Isma'il, Shu'ayb, and Muhammad (ﷺ). Some added Khalid ibn Sinan and Safwan ibn Handhala, upon them both be peace. This has been criticized on the grounds that it leads to the conclusion that the ultimate purpose of his (ﷺ) being among the warners in the Arabic language alone is that he is among those from Hud, Salih, and Shu'ayb (upon them be peace), and its corruption is not hidden. How could it not be, when the greatest calamity in the matter of warning is what Nuh and Musa (upon them both be peace) warned of, and the most effective deterrent upon the hearts of the polytheists is what Ibrahim (upon him be peace) warned of, due to their affiliation with him and their claim that they follow his creed (upon him be peace)? Some have mentioned that the meaning on this aspect is that you warned them just as their forefathers of old were warned, and that you are not an innovator in this, so how did they deny you? The truth is that the aforementioned aspect is weaker than the previous one. As for its being corrupt in meaning, as the critic's words imply, that is not so.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 196:

﴿And indeed, it is in the scriptures of the former peoples.﴾ That is: the mention of the Qur'an is in the earlier books. This is on the reading that the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, and the sentence contains an elision of a modifier (mudaf), as when one says: "So-and-so is in the register of the amir." It has also been said: the intended meaning is that its meaning ("ma'na-hu") is in the earlier books, and this is according to what is most common; for monotheism and all that relates to the Essence and the Attributes, and much of the admonitions and narratives, are recorded in the earlier scriptures. So it does no harm that some of it is not in that, according to the dominant assumption, such as the story of the slander (al-ifk), what concerned the marriage to the wife of Zayd, what the beginning of Surat al-Tahrim contains, and other things.

It is well known from the Imam Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) that he permitted the recitation of the Qur'an in Persian, Turkish, Hindi and other languages without restriction, citing this verse as evidence.

In another narration, the permission was restricted to Persian, because it is the most noble of languages after Arabic, based on the report: "The language of the people of Paradise is Arabic, and Persian is the sweet (durri) tongue."

In another narration, it is permitted in Persian only when it is praise, like Surat al-Ikhlas; but if it is other than that, it is not permitted.

In another, it is permitted in Persian only in prayer when the worshipper is unable to (recite in) Arabic, and what is recited is remembrance and glorification; but reciting in it outside prayer, or in prayer while the reciter is able to (recite in) Arabic, or in prayer while the reciter is unable (to recite in) Arabic but what is recited is stories, commands and prohibitions, then it is not permitted. It is mentioned that this is the view of his two companions.

He had gone to the opposite view, then returned to this (position). A group of reliable and meticulous scholars have authenticated his retraction from the view of permitting recitation in non-Arabic languages without restriction.

The Allamah Hasan al-Shurunbulali has a treatise investigating this question, which he named (al-Nafhah al-Qudsiyyah fi Ahkam Qira'at al-Qur'an wa Kitabatihi bil-Farisiyyah); whoever wants investigation should refer to it.

The Imam's (may mercy be upon him) retraction from what is well known of him was due to the weakness of the argument from this verse against him, as is not hidden from the one who reflects.

In al-Kashf it is said that the Qur'an is what was sent down for its inimitability, and so on to the end of what is mentioned about its meaning; there is no doubt that translation is not Qur'an, even if its meaning is the one subsisting in its speaker, so there is no doubt that it is not possible to recite it.

If it is said: it is the meaning expressed in whatever language, we say: there is no doubt in the difference of names with the difference of languages, and just as the Qur'an is not named Torah, the Torah is not named Qur'an; names have a role in the specific expressions, not merely in the shared meaning. End quote. In this there is a point of discussion, for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if We had made it a non-Arabic Qur'an﴾ requires that it be named Qur'an as well if it were non-Arabic; so the specific Arabic expression has no role in naming it Qur'an. The truth is that the indefinite "qur'anan" has not been known to be transferred from its lexical meaning, so it covers every recited thing; but "al-Qur'an" with the definite article is understood, in the usage of the Shari'ah, as the Arabic; so the specific expression has a role in the naming with regard to it. This is how it occurs in the verse indicating the obligation of recitation, namely His saying, glorified is He: ﴿So recite what is easy of the Qur'an﴾, and with this the purpose is achieved. Making "min" in it partitive and intending the meaning from this part is not hidden in what it entails. It has been said: the pronoun in "innahu" refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but this is not clear. Al-A'mash read "zubri" with a sukun on the ba'.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 197:

﴿Has it not been a sign for them﴾ The hamza (alif of interrogation) is for confirmation (taqrir) or for denial and negation (inkar wa-nafy), and the waw is for conjunction ('atf) upon an implied clause demanded by the context, as if it were said: "Have they been heedless of this, and has it not been a sign for them indicating that it is the revelation of the Lord of the worlds, and that it is indeed in the scriptures of the former peoples?!" Moreover, (lahum) is connected to the verb of existence (al-kawn), placed before its subject and predicate for emphasis (li-l-ihtimam); or it is connected to an omitted word which is a circumstantial clause (hal) of (ayatan), placed before it because (ayatan) is indefinite (nakira). (Ayatan) is the predicate of the verb of existence (kana), placed before its subject, which is the phrase ﴿that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it﴾, because of what has passed many times concerning giving attention to what is placed first and creating suspense toward what comes later. (Al-'ilm) means knowledge in the sense of recognition (ma'rifa), and the pronoun refers to the Qur'an. That is: "Has it not been a sign for them, making the scholars of the Children of Israel recognize the Qur'an by its described attributes mentioned in their books?!"

It is related from Qatadah that the pronoun refers to the Prophet ﷺ. It was also said: (al-'ilm) is in its well-known meaning, and the pronoun refers to the preceding judgment in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And indeed it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ ﴿the Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down﴾ ﴿upon your heart﴾ etc. However, there is distance in this, as is not hidden. Al-Tha'labi mentioned, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, that the people of Makkah sent to the rabbis of Yathrib asking them about the Prophet. They said: "This is his time," and they described his attributes, and they confused matters concerning Muhammad ﷺ, so the verse was revealed concerning that. This is apparent in indicating that the pronoun refers to him (peace and blessings be upon him). This is supported by the fact that the verse is Meccan; Muqatil said it is Medinan.

The scholars of the Children of Israel: 'Abdullah ibn Salam and the like, as related from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, because a group of them embraced Islam and pointed out places in the Torah and the Gospel in which mention of the Messenger ﷺ occurs. It was also said: their scholars are those among them who embraced Islam and those who did not; and it was said: their prophets, for they drew attention to this. This is contrary to the apparent meaning. Perhaps the most apparent of the opinions is that what is intended is his contemporaries (may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him) from the scholars of the People of the Book, both those who became Muslims and others.

Ibn 'Amir and al-Jahdari read (takun) with the feminine form and (ayatun) in the nominative, making it the subject of (takun), and (an ya'lamahu) its predicate. This was deemed weak, because it involves describing an indefinite noun with a definite one; and the fact that the indefinite noun has a circumstantial description (dhu hal) does not remove this objection, based on one of the two possibilities regarding (lahum).

It is permitted that (ayatun) be the subject, with (lahum) connected to an omitted word that is the predicate, and (an ya'lamahu) being a substitute (badal) for the subject, or the predicate of an omitted subject. It is also permitted that the subject be the pronoun of the matter (damir al-qissa), with (lahum ayatan) as a subject and predicate, the whole clause being the predicate of (takun), and (an ya'lamahu) being a substitute or the predicate of an omitted subject. It is also permitted that the subject be the pronoun of the matter, with (ayatun) the predicate of (an ya'lamahu), and the clause the predicate of (takun). It is also permitted that (takun) be complete (tammah), with (ayatun) as its agent, (an ya'lamahu) a substitute or a predicate of an omitted word, and (lahum) either a circumstantial clause or connected to (takun).

Ibn 'Abbas read (takun) with the feminine form and (ayatan) in the accusative, like the reading of one who read (thumma lam takun) with the feminine form, (fitnatahum) in the accusative, (illa an qalu). It is also like the verse of Labid describing the wild ass and the she-ass:

So he went forward and advanced her, and it was his habit, when she turned back, to advance her.

This is either by making the feminine of the subject follow the feminine of the predicate, or by interpreting (an ya'lamahu) as recognition (ma'rifa), interpreting (an qalu) as a saying (maqala), and interpreting (al-iqdam) as "the one who advanced" (al-mutaqaddimah). The claim that the feminine is acquired from the genitive noun it is attached to is worthless, because its well-known condition is absent.

Al-Jahdari read (ta'lamahu) with the feminine form, on the basis that the intended meaning is the group of scholars of the Children of Israel. In the Mushaf it was written as "'ulamau" with a waw between the mim and the alif, and this was explained by saying that it follows the dialect of those who incline the alif of (ulama') toward a waw, just as they wrote (al-salawata, al-zakawata, al-ribawa) with a waw in that dialect.

﴿And if We had sent it down﴾, i.e., the Qur'an as it is, with its exquisite and inimitable composition, ﴿upon some of the non-Arabs﴾ who are unable to speak Arabic. It is the plural of a'jamiyy (non-Arab), as in al-Tahrir and others, except that the ya' of relation (ya' al-nisbah) has been dropped from it for ease. Similar to it is al-ash'arin, the plural of ash'ariyy, in the verse of al-Kumayt:

"Even if you had furnished an unruly rhyme,
I would indeed have entered the houses of the Ash'aris."

Al-Hasan and Ibn Muqsam recited it with the ya' of relation, in accordance with the original form. Ibn Atiyyah said: "It is the plural of a'jam, who is one who cannot express himself clearly, even if he is of Arab lineage. The a'jamiyy is one whose lineage is among the non-Arabs, as opposed to the Arabs, even if he is the most eloquent of people." End of quotation.

It was objected that the feminine of a'jam is 'ajma', and that af'al on the pattern fa'la' does not take the sound plural (jam' salim). It was answered that a'jam originally meant the dumb animal (al-bahimah al-'ajma'), because it cannot speak, and then the term was transferred, or used figuratively, to what was mentioned. In that sense it has no feminine on the pattern fa'la', and therefore it takes the sound plural. This was challenged: the scholar Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr al-Razi has explicitly stated in his book (Gharaib al-Qur'an) that a'jam is one who cannot express himself clearly, and its feminine is 'ajma'. Even if it is granted that it has no feminine in that sense, the original form should be observed.

In this there is a point: that the removal of an obstacle due to an accidental cause permits such a formation, which the grammarians have explicitly stated. Furthermore, the view that af'al fa'la' does not take the sound plural is the position of the Basrans, whereas al-Farra' and others among the Kufans permit it. Thus perhaps whoever said it is the plural of a'jam said so on the basis of that view.

The apparent sense of the mentioned plural requires that it refer to rational beings. It is reported from some of them that it is the plural of a'jam meaning the non-rational dumb beasts, and it was pluralised as rational beings are pluralised, because it was described with "revealed to" (al-tanzil 'alayhi) and with "recitation" (al-qira'ah) in His, the Exalted's, saying:

[Page 128]

﴿Then he recited it to them﴾. The apparent reading is that the pronoun of the subject refers to some of the non-Arabs (al-a'jamin, "those who do not speak Arabic"), and these are attributes of rational beings. The purpose is to show the extent of their obstinacy and the strength of their stubbornness in denial (al-mukabara). It is as if it were said: "Even if We had sent it down in this exquisite, miraculous arrangement (al-nazm) upon one who cannot speak Arabic, or upon one for whom speech is not at all within his capacity, such as the dumb animals, [and] he recited it to them, reciting it correctly and in a manner that breaks normal custom, they still would not have believed in it." This is together with the miraculousness of the recitation added to the miraculousness of what is recited.

It has also been said: the meaning of al-a'jamin is the plural of a'jam, which is more general, whether the being is rational or otherwise. Al-Tabarsi transmitted this from Abdullah ibn Mut'i', and he mentioned that it was narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he was asked about this verse while he was on a camel, so he gestured toward it and said: "This is one of the a'jamin."

Al-Tabari, according to al-Bahr [i.e., Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit], narrates something similar from Ibn Mut'i', and the purpose is likewise to show the extent of their obstinacy. It has also been said: it is the plural of a'jam, intended to mean that which does not reason. The pronoun of the subject in (qara'ahu) refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the pronoun in (alayhim) refers to some of the a'jamin; likewise the pronoun in (kanu) [refers to them]. The meaning is: if We had sent down this Qur'an upon some of the beasts, and Muhammad (ﷺ) had recited it to those beasts, they (those beasts) would not have believed in it; so likewise these people, for they are like cattle, nay, they are more astray in the way. And what is in this is not hidden.

It has also been said: the meaning is: "If We had sent it down upon some of the a'jamin in the language of the non-Arabs, and he recited it to them, they would not have believed in it, because they did not understand what is in it."

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir transmitted this from Qatada, but it is far from what the context requires, which is to explain their persistence in obstinacy and denial.

Some have used this verse as evidence for preventing the inclusion of the Arabic language in the concept of the Qur'an, since, if it were included in its definition, it would not be conceivable that it be sent down in the language of non-Arabs, for that would entail one and the same thing being both Arabic and non-Arabic, which is impossible.

It has been answered that the pronoun in (nazzalnahu) does not refer to the specific Qur'an whose definition includes Arabic, but to the Qur'an in general, meaning what is recited, more general than being Arabic or otherwise. This is similar to the return of a pronoun to the general within the specific, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿No one is granted a long life, nor is any of his life shortened﴾, and so on, for the pronoun in (umrihi) returns to a person without the description of (mu'ammar, "one granted a long life"), since it is not conceivable that the lifespan of one granted a long life be shortened, as is not hidden.

Some others responded: the speech contains an elided noun (hadhf mudaf), and the meaning is: "If We had sent down its meaning in the language of non-Arabs upon some of the a'jamin, then reflect."

In the wording (ba'd, "some") under all the opinions there is an indication that the one upon whom it is supposed to be sent down is one individual from among that group, whoever he may be. And (bihi, "in it") is connected to (mu'minin, "believers"). Perhaps its being placed before it is for emphasis and for harmony with the ends of the verses (ru'us al-ay).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 200–201:

The pronoun in His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus We have caused it to enter into the hearts of the guilty﴾ — according to what the coherence of the preceding and following pronouns in a single thread requires — refers to the Qur'an, and this is the view of al-Rummani and others. The meaning, as has been said, is: in the like of that wondrous thread mentioned, We have caused it to enter, i.e., We have caused the Qur'an to enter into the hearts of the guilty, so they understood its meanings, recognized its eloquence, and knew that it is beyond human capacities. To this was added the knowledge of the People of the Two Books (ahl al-kitab) concerning its matter, and the good tidings of the revealed Books of its descent. Then His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿They do not believe in it﴾ is a resumptive clause (jumlah mustanifah) brought to explain that they are not affected by such matters that call to belief in it, but rather they persist in what they are upon, ﴿until they see the painful punishment﴾, which compels belief in it, and at that time that will not benefit them.

By "the guilty" is meant the polytheists, to whom the pronouns in (lahum), (alayhim) and (kanu) refer, and the expression was turned away from their pronoun to what has been mentioned, to emphasize their blame. Al-Zamakhshari said regarding this meaning: That is, in the like of this thread We have caused it to enter into their hearts, and thus We have established and fixed it in them, and in the like of this state and this attribute of disbelief in it and denial of it We have placed it in them. So however they are dealt with and treated, and in whatever manner their affair is arranged, there is no way for them to change from their rejection and denial of it, as He, glorified is He, said:
Page 129
﴿And if We had sent down to you a Book on paper, and they had touched it with their hands, those who disbelieved would have said: This is nothing but manifest magic.﴾

The placement of His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿They do not believe in it﴾ etc. relative to what precedes it is the placement of the clarifier and summarizer, because it is brought to confirm it as denied and rejected in their hearts; so there follows what establishes this meaning, namely that they continue in denying it and rejecting it until they witness the threat. It is permissible that it be a circumstantial clause (hal), i.e., We have caused it to enter into them while not believed in. End of quotation.

It has been objected that the first view is more fitting to the context of explaining the extreme of their obstinacy and arrogance, together with the convergence of the evidences of faith, the closeness of the principles of guidance and direction, and the complete cutting off of their excuses. It may be said that this explanation is more in accord with His consoling of the Prophet (ﷺ), which is like the foundation of this noble surah, and with which it opens, where He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they will not become believers﴾. As if He, glory be to Him and exalted is He, after mentioning the extent of their obstinacy and the severity of their stubbornness in arrogance, — and this is an interpretation clear in itself — so it is, in my view, preferable to what was previously mentioned.

In al-Matali' it is stated that the pronoun refers to the denial and disbelief indicated by His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿They were not believers in it﴾, and this is the view of Yahya ibn Salam, and it is related from Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan. The meaning: Thus We caused the denial of the Qur'an and disbelief in it to enter into the hearts of the polytheists of Mecca and established it in them. His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿They do not believe﴾ etc. stands in the position of clarification of that. On this view it does not appear that it is a circumstantial clause. And I do not see that this meaning is far removed from the view of one who said: That is, in the like of this thread We caused the Qur'an to enter, and in the like of this state and this attribute of disbelief in it and denial of it We placed it in their hearts.

The summary of the first: Thus We caused the denial of the Qur'an to enter into their hearts. The summary of this: Thus We caused the Qur'an to enter with the attribute of denial of it into their hearts. So reflect.

It is permitted to make the pronoun refer to the proof indicated by His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿Is it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it?﴾ but this is remote both in wording and meaning.

Furthermore, some have held that the intended "guilty" are other than the earlier disbelievers to whom the pronouns refer, namely the polytheists of Mecca who were contemporaries of them and those who come after them. That is an indication of the thread into the hearts of those polytheists: that is, in the like of that thread into the hearts of the polytheists of Mecca We caused it to enter into the guilty others, because they share the attribute. His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿They do not believe in it﴾ etc. is an explanation of the state of the earlier polytheists who were taken into account on the side of the likened-to, or a clarification of the state of the guilty and an explanation of what the comparison requires; and it is, as you see, [unconvincing].

It is reported in al-Bahr from Ibn Atiyyah that the intended are the guilty of every nation, i.e., God's custom concerning them is that they do not believe until they see the punishment, so faith does not benefit them after the punishment has befallen them. This is by way of example for the Quraysh, i.e., these are likewise, and the unveiling of the unseen by what the verse contains was on the Day of Badr. End of quotation.

It seems that he made the pronoun of (We caused it to enter) refer to disbelief in general and not to disbelief in the Qur'an, and the pronoun of (in it) refer to God Most High, or to what they were commanded to believe in, namely the Qur'an; otherwise that is hardly feasible. In any case, one should not rely upon it.

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿They do not believe in it﴾ etc. is an explanation of the state of the earlier polytheists who were taken into account on the side of the likened-to, or a clarification of the state of the guilty and an explanation of what the comparison requires; and it is, as you see, [unconvincing].

It is reported in al-Bahr from Ibn Atiyyah that the intended are the guilty of every nation, i.e., God's custom concerning them is that they do not believe until they see the punishment, so faith does not benefit them after the punishment has befallen them. This is by way of example for the Quraysh, i.e., these are likewise, and the unveiling of the unseen by what the verse contains was on the Day of Badr. End of quotation.

It seems that he made the pronoun of (We caused it to enter) refer to disbelief in general and not to disbelief in the Qur'an, and the pronoun of (in it) refer to God Most High, or to what they were commanded to believe in, namely the Qur'an; otherwise that is hardly feasible. In any case, one should not rely upon it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 202–203:

﴿So that it comes upon them﴾, i.e., the punishment, ﴿suddenly﴾, i.e., unexpectedly, ﴿while they do not perceive﴾, i.e., its coming. ﴿Then they will say﴾ - i.e., in regret over what was missed of faith, and wishing for a respite to make up for what they neglected -: ﴿Will we be reprieved?﴾, i.e., will we be delayed? The fa' (then) in both places is conjunctive, and it is - as the words of al-Kashshaf indicate - for sequence in rank (al-ta'qib al-rutbi) and not sequence in existence (al-ta'qib al-wujudi). It is as if it were said: until their seeing the painful punishment, and then what is more severe than it, which is its sudden arrival, and then what is more severe than that, which is their asking for a respite. This is similar to what is in your saying: (If you do wrong, the righteous will despise you, and then God Most High will despise you). Thus it is not objected that being struck suddenly without perception cannot validly be followed in existence by seeing.

Sariy al-Din al-Misri - may God have mercy on him - said, in explaining what the fa' (then) indicates of sequence: the seeing of the punishment sometimes occurs after its signs have preceded it, the appearance of its preliminaries and the witnessing of its indications, and at other times suddenly, with nothing preceding it of that kind. Thus their seeing of the punishment required explanation, so the explanatory fa' (al-fa' al-tafsiriyyah) was used to join to it the words of God Most High: ﴿so that it comes upon them suddenly﴾. Sequence between them is valid in meaning, because the rank of the explanation in mention is that it comes after what is explained, as is done in detail relative to summary, as is derived from the investigations of al-Sharif in his commentary on al-Miftah.

It is possible that the verse is of the type of inversion (al-qalb), as is one of the aspects in the words of God Most High: ﴿And how many a town We destroyed, and Our might came upon it﴾, for the sake of emphasizing the suddenness of their seeing the punishment, until it is as if they saw it before the suddenness. The meaning is: until the painful punishment comes upon them suddenly, and they see it. End of quotation.

Some of them made it for detail (al-tafsil). It was objected - against what the author of al-Kashshaf said - that the painful punishment includes intensity of suddenness, so sequence in rank is not valid. This is an illusion, as is not hidden.

The apparent view is that the clause ﴿while they do not perceive﴾ is a confirming circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkidah) for what "suddenly" conveys, for it is - as al-Raghib said - the sudden arrival of a thing from where one does not expect it.

Then, this seeing and what follows it, if it is in this world - as has been said - then the coming of the painful punishment in it suddenly is not obscure, for it may overtake them in it unexpectedly, what did not pass through their minds, in a moment of heedlessness. If it is in the Hereafter, then the manner of its coming suddenly in it - according to what some of them claimed - is that it is meant that it comes to them without preparation for it and without expectation. So understand. Some of them chose that this is more general, whether it is in this world or in the Hereafter.

Al-Hasan and 'Isa read ﴿ta'tiyahum﴾ with the feminine ta' (ta' al-ta'nith). Al-Zamakhshari interpreted this on the basis that the pronoun refers to the Hour, and Abu Hayyan on the basis that it refers to the punishment, with the interpretation of "the retribution." Abu al-Fadl al-Razi said: it refers to the punishment, and it was made feminine because it includes the Hour, so it took the feminine from it; this is because they used to ask for the punishment of the Resurrection, denying it. End of quotation.

This is in the utmost strangeness. It seems he considered the idafah (annexation) of the punishment to the Hour as meaningful, based on the claim that what is meant is: until they see the painful punishment of the Hour. He said: by its taking the feminine from it because of its annexation to it, since annexation to a feminine noun may give the masculine annexed noun the feminine form, as in his saying:

As the spear-head's chest was reddened with blood.

I have not seen anyone precede him in this.

Al-Hasan read ﴿baghtatan﴾ with a vowel on the ghayn (bagħtatan). In the reading of Ubayy - may God be pleased with him - (wa yarawhu baghtatan).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 204–207:

﴿Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ That is, they seek it before its appointed time. This is their saying: "Rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment" and their saying: "Bring us what you threaten us with," and the like.

﴿Have you considered?﴾ That is: then inform (me). ﴿If We let them enjoy for years﴾ That is: a period of time, through long-lasting actions and pleasant living, or the lifespan of the world, as is related from Ikrimah. This was expressed in this way to indicate its brevity. ﴿Then there comes to them what they were promised﴾ That is: the punishment they were being promised. ﴿Will not avail them﴾ That is: what (or) what kind of benefit will avail them. ﴿What they were enjoying﴾ That is: their being given that lengthy enjoyment, with "mā" being a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah), as is the preferred reading, or "that which they were being given enjoyment of from the comforts of the worldly life," with "mā" being a relative pronoun whose returning pronoun has been omitted. In either case, the interrogative is for negation and denial.

It has been said: "mā" is negative, meaning: that did not avail them in repelling the punishment or lessening it. The first is preferable, as it better fits the form of the question and is more indicative of the negation of benefit in the most eloquent and emphatic manner.

Regarding the connection of the noble composition, there are three aspects, as in al-Kashshaf:

The first: His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Have you considered?﴾ etc., is connected to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Shall we be given respite?﴾, and His saying, "Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?" is a parenthetical rebuke and denial that one who is exposed to a punishment, in which he asks for respite and reprieve even for the blink of an eye and is not granted it, should seek to hasten the punishment. The meaning according to this, as in al-Kashf, is: when it was mentioned that they would not believe without witnessing the punishment, He, glorified is He, said: indeed this promised punishment, even if delayed for a few days, will surely overtake them, and then what they were in of delusion, which resulted in non-belief, will not benefit them. The original composition is: "They will not believe until they see the punishment, and such and such. If We let them enjoy for years, then there comes to them this promised punishment, then what thing or what benefit will their enjoyment of those few days avail them?" So the verb of seeing and the interrogative were brought to be in the sense of "inform (me)," conveying the meaning of wonder and denial, and that this story is one which everyone should be informed of so that they may wonder.

"Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?" was placed in the middle for rebuke, the hamzah in it being for denial, and the fa' was brought to indicate its sequence after what preceded it, as if, when the punishment was described, it was said: "Would any rational person seek to hasten this punishment?"

In al-Irshad, the preferred view is that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Have you considered?﴾ is connected to His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Shall we be given respite?﴾, and that the fa' is for the sequence of the interrogation according to that view, while it precedes the hamzah in meaning and is placed after it in form, because the hamzah requires initial position. And that ﴿Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ is a parenthetical rebuke and reproach, and the fa' in it is for conjunction with an implied element required by the context, that is: Will their state be as mentioned, of asking for respite when the painful punishment descends, so that they seek to hasten Our punishment? There is between the two such incompatibility as is not hidden from anyone. Or: Will they be heedless of that despite its certainty and establishment, so that they seek to hasten, etc.? The author of al-Kashf, after establishing what we mentioned, said: the conjunction with an implied element in this aspect has no basis. Perhaps the fair-minded would say: each has its direction.

The second: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ is a statement with which they will be rebuked on the Day of Resurrection when they say, ﴿Shall we be given respite?﴾. It is related to us subtly (and "yasta'jilūn" here) in the sense of "you hastened," since they will be told that on that day. The matter of the sequence or the conjunction with an implied element, and the connection of ﴿Have you considered?﴾ etc. with their saying ﴿Shall we be given respite?﴾, is like what preceded in the previous aspect.

The third: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ is connected to what follows and is not sequential to what precedes. This is because their seeking to hasten the punishment was only due to their belief that it would not occur or overtake them, and that they were enjoying long lifespans in safety and security. So He, mighty and majestic is He, said: ﴿Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾, out of insolence, arrogance, mockery, and reliance on long hope. Then He, glorified is He, said: Suppose the matter is as they believe, of their being given enjoyment and long life; when the threat overtakes them after that, what will benefit them then of the length of their lives and the pleasantness of their livelihood that passed?

According to this, ﴿Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ etc. is a conjunction with an implied element without disagreement, like ﴿Do they mock?﴾ and ﴿Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Have you considered?﴾ etc. expresses wonder at their state, sequenced upon the mockery and hastening, and the speech is like what you say to your addressee: "Will you be deceived by the multitude of tribes and wealth? Suppose they have reached beyond what you hope; is not death after them, and their leaving them in regret?!"

This aspect is more apparent than the one before it. In any case, His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Our punishment﴾ is connected to ﴿they seek to hasten﴾, and was placed before it to announce that the focus of denial and rebuke is that the thing sought to be hastened is His punishment, glorified is His majesty, together with what there is in it, according to some, of observing the rhyme endings.

It was recited "yumta'ūn" (they are given enjoyment), from the causative form. In the verse there is a great admonition for one who has a heart.

It is related from Maymun ibn Mihran that he met al-Hasan during the circumambulation (ṭawāf), and he had been wishing to meet him. He said to him: "Admonish me." Al-Hasan did not add to him beyond reciting this verse. Maymun said: "You have admonished, and have made it eloquent."
