Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 204–207:

﴿Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ That is, they seek it before its appointed time. This is their saying: "Rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment" and their saying: "Bring us what you threaten us with," and the like.

﴿Have you considered?﴾ That is: then inform (me). ﴿If We let them enjoy for years﴾ That is: a period of time, through long-lasting actions and pleasant living, or the lifespan of the world, as is related from Ikrimah. This was expressed in this way to indicate its brevity. ﴿Then there comes to them what they were promised﴾ That is: the punishment they were being promised. ﴿Will not avail them﴾ That is: what (or) what kind of benefit will avail them. ﴿What they were enjoying﴾ That is: their being given that lengthy enjoyment, with "mā" being a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah), as is the preferred reading, or "that which they were being given enjoyment of from the comforts of the worldly life," with "mā" being a relative pronoun whose returning pronoun has been omitted. In either case, the interrogative is for negation and denial.

It has been said: "mā" is negative, meaning: that did not avail them in repelling the punishment or lessening it. The first is preferable, as it better fits the form of the question and is more indicative of the negation of benefit in the most eloquent and emphatic manner.

Regarding the connection of the noble composition, there are three aspects, as in al-Kashshaf:

The first: His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Have you considered?﴾ etc., is connected to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Shall we be given respite?﴾, and His saying, "Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?" is a parenthetical rebuke and denial that one who is exposed to a punishment, in which he asks for respite and reprieve even for the blink of an eye and is not granted it, should seek to hasten the punishment. The meaning according to this, as in al-Kashf, is: when it was mentioned that they would not believe without witnessing the punishment, He, glorified is He, said: indeed this promised punishment, even if delayed for a few days, will surely overtake them, and then what they were in of delusion, which resulted in non-belief, will not benefit them. The original composition is: "They will not believe until they see the punishment, and such and such. If We let them enjoy for years, then there comes to them this promised punishment, then what thing or what benefit will their enjoyment of those few days avail them?" So the verb of seeing and the interrogative were brought to be in the sense of "inform (me)," conveying the meaning of wonder and denial, and that this story is one which everyone should be informed of so that they may wonder.

"Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?" was placed in the middle for rebuke, the hamzah in it being for denial, and the fa' was brought to indicate its sequence after what preceded it, as if, when the punishment was described, it was said: "Would any rational person seek to hasten this punishment?"

In al-Irshad, the preferred view is that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Have you considered?﴾ is connected to His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Shall we be given respite?﴾, and that the fa' is for the sequence of the interrogation according to that view, while it precedes the hamzah in meaning and is placed after it in form, because the hamzah requires initial position. And that ﴿Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ is a parenthetical rebuke and reproach, and the fa' in it is for conjunction with an implied element required by the context, that is: Will their state be as mentioned, of asking for respite when the painful punishment descends, so that they seek to hasten Our punishment? There is between the two such incompatibility as is not hidden from anyone. Or: Will they be heedless of that despite its certainty and establishment, so that they seek to hasten, etc.? The author of al-Kashf, after establishing what we mentioned, said: the conjunction with an implied element in this aspect has no basis. Perhaps the fair-minded would say: each has its direction.

The second: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ is a statement with which they will be rebuked on the Day of Resurrection when they say, ﴿Shall we be given respite?﴾. It is related to us subtly (and "yasta'jilūn" here) in the sense of "you hastened," since they will be told that on that day. The matter of the sequence or the conjunction with an implied element, and the connection of ﴿Have you considered?﴾ etc. with their saying ﴿Shall we be given respite?﴾, is like what preceded in the previous aspect.

The third: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ is connected to what follows and is not sequential to what precedes. This is because their seeking to hasten the punishment was only due to their belief that it would not occur or overtake them, and that they were enjoying long lifespans in safety and security. So He, mighty and majestic is He, said: ﴿Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾, out of insolence, arrogance, mockery, and reliance on long hope. Then He, glorified is He, said: Suppose the matter is as they believe, of their being given enjoyment and long life; when the threat overtakes them after that, what will benefit them then of the length of their lives and the pleasantness of their livelihood that passed?

According to this, ﴿Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ etc. is a conjunction with an implied element without disagreement, like ﴿Do they mock?﴾ and ﴿Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Have you considered?﴾ etc. expresses wonder at their state, sequenced upon the mockery and hastening, and the speech is like what you say to your addressee: "Will you be deceived by the multitude of tribes and wealth? Suppose they have reached beyond what you hope; is not death after them, and their leaving them in regret?!"

This aspect is more apparent than the one before it. In any case, His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Our punishment﴾ is connected to ﴿they seek to hasten﴾, and was placed before it to announce that the focus of denial and rebuke is that the thing sought to be hastened is His punishment, glorified is His majesty, together with what there is in it, according to some, of observing the rhyme endings.

It was recited "yumta'ūn" (they are given enjoyment), from the causative form. In the verse there is a great admonition for one who has a heart.

It is related from Maymun ibn Mihran that he met al-Hasan during the circumambulation (ṭawāf), and he had been wishing to meet him. He said to him: "Admonish me." Al-Hasan did not add to him beyond reciting this verse. Maymun said: "You have admonished, and have made it eloquent."

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 208:**

﴿We did not destroy any town﴾ from the towns that were destroyed, ﴿except that it had warners﴾, who had warned its people, as a way of establishing the proof against them. The prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa'l-majrur, "the prepositional phrase") is linked to an omitted element that functions as a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), and ﴿warners﴾ is the subject (mubtada'). The sentence is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal, "a state-describing complement") of ﴿town﴾. This is what Abu Hayyan said. Then he said: "The i'rab (grammatical analysis) is that ﴿la-ha﴾ ("for it") is in the position of a hal, and ﴿warners﴾ is raised by the prepositional phrase, meaning: 'except being for it warners,' so the hal here comes as a single word rather than a sentence. The coming of a hal after a negated element is like your saying: 'I did not pass by anyone except standing, eloquently.'" End of quote. In both cases, the hal comes from an indefinite noun.

It is said that this is justified by its generality (ʿumūmuhā), because it falls within the scope of negation, with the addition of ﴿min﴾ ("any") before it. It seems that this speaker treated generality as what permits the hal, by analogy with how the grammarians treated it as what permits beginning a sentence with an indefinite noun, since the underlying reason is the same.

Al-Zamakhshari held that ﴿la-ha warners﴾ is a sentence in the position of a descriptive qualifier (sifah) of ﴿town﴾. Abu Hayyan did not allow a sentence that follows ﴿illa﴾ ("except") to be a qualifier. He then said: "The position of the majority of grammarians is that a qualifier does not come after ﴿illa﴾ when it depends on the exception particle, as in: 'No one came to me except a rider.' When such a construction is heard, it is analyzed as a substitute (badal), meaning: 'except a man who is riding.'" He said: "What supports the soundness of this view is that the Arabs say: 'I did not pass by anyone except standing,' and it is not transmitted from them: 'I did not pass by anyone except standing (in the nominative).' So if the sentence were a qualifier of the indefinite noun, the singular form would have come after ﴿illa﴾ as its qualifier. If the qualifier does not depend on the particle, it comes after ﴿illa﴾, as in: 'No one came to me except Zayd is better than ʿAmr,' for the underlying sense is: 'No one came to me who is better than ʿAmr except Zayd.'" End of quote. So take note of this.

Whatever the case, the pronoun in ﴿la-ha﴾ refers to ﴿town﴾, which, as you have heard, carries the sense of a plural. It is as if it were said: "We did not destroy the towns except that for all of them there were warners," in the sense that every one of them had warners, whether each town had one warner or more.

Page 132

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 209:

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Reminder﴾ (dhikra) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿warners﴾ according to al-Kisa'i, and as an absolute object (maṣdar) according to al-Zajjaj. As a circumstantial qualifier, one may either supply (possessors of a reminder) or supply (reminding ones), or leave it on its apparent sense for the sake of emphasis (mubalagha). As an absolute object, the governing word is ﴿warners﴾, because it carries the meaning of "reminders," so it is as if it were said: "reminders a reminder," i.e., a reminding.

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that it be an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), in the sense that they warn for the sake of admonition and reminding; and that it be in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject with the meaning (this is a reminder), and the sentence is then parenthetical (i'tiradiyya); or that it be a qualifier with the meaning (warners who are possessors of a reminder, or reminding ones); or that they are made the reminder itself, as an intensification of their diligence in reminding and their prolixity therein.

It is also permitted that it be linked to (we destroyed), as an object of purpose, and the meaning is: We did not destroy any town of wrongdoers except after We had established the proof against them by sending warners to them, so that their destruction would be a reminder and a lesson to others, so that they would not disobey as they disobeyed. Then he said:

This is the reliable view, and this was clarified in al-Kashshaf by his saying: Because it is a threat to the mockers, and because they deserve to be made a deterrent and a lesson for others, like the earlier nations, since they did the same as their deeds of mockery and denial, so they were requited with what they were requited with; and then the speech fits together, end of quote.

It has been objected that the view of the majority is that what precedes (illa) does not govern what follows it, except when it is the exception, the excepted-from, or a follower of it not dependent on the particle. The object of purpose is not one of these three, so it cannot be linked to (we destroyed).

The permissibility of this may be derived according to the view of al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash, though neither of them put it in the accusative as an object of purpose here, and that was because of the strain involved in parsing it that way; and the matter of coherence is easy, as is not hidden.

﴿And We were not wrongdoers﴾: that is, it is not Our way that there should proceed from Us, in accordance with wisdom, what would be in the form of injustice if it proceeded from anyone else, such as destroying anyone before warning him, or punishing one who has not done wrong. And to indicate the negation of such a thing being part of His affairs, Exalted is His affair, He said: "and We were not" instead of "and We do not wrong."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 210:

﴿Nor have the devils brought it down.﴾ This is connected to His words, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾, etc. It is a refutation of the claim of the polytheists of Quraysh that Muhammad (ﷺ) had a companion from among the jinn who informed him, just as soothsayers are informed, and that the Qur'an is something the jinn cast to him, upon him be prayers and peace.

The expression is in the form of tanazzala (the intensive form, "were brought down" with repetition), because if the descent had occurred, it would have been by gradual eavesdropping (istiraq). Al-Hasan and Ibn al-Sameeqa recited "al-shayatun" (الشَّياطُونَ). Abu Hatim said: "This is an error on the part of al-Hasan, or against him." Al-Nahhas said: "It is an error according to all the grammarians." Al-Mahdawi said: "It is not permissible in Arabic." Al-Farra' said: "The shaykh erred; he thought that it was the nun found in hija'in." Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: "If it is permissible to cite the verse of al-Ajjaj and Ru'ba as evidence, then why is it not permissible to cite the recitation of al-Hasan and his companion, given that we know they did not recite it except that they had heard it?" Yunus ibn Habib said: "I heard a Bedouin say: 'I entered gardens, behind which were bastun,' so I said: 'How this resembles the recitation of al-Hasan!'" End of quote.

This recitation has been justified on the basis that since its final part is like the final part of Yabrin and Filastin, and it has been said of these two, Yabrun and Filastun, a similar treatment was applied to it, so it was said: al-Shayatun.

Its proper derivation, according to that, as in al-Kashshaf, is from al-shaytutah, which means destruction. In al-Bahr, citing some scholars, it says: if its derivation is from shat, meaning "it burned," yashitu shawtah, then there is a basis for both recitations. It has been said that its basis is that the intensive form of it is shayyat, and its plural is al-shayyatun; they lightened the yā', and it has been narrated from them both with shaddah (doubling), and others recited with it.

Some said: it is the plural of shiyat, the verbal noun of shat (like khat, khiyatan), as if they both referred the description to the verbal noun with its meaning, for intensity, then pluralized it; all of this, as you see. The author of al-Kashf said: there is no basis at all for correcting this recitation.

Ibn Jinni elaborated greatly in correcting it, then said: "In any case, al-shayatun is an error." Abu Hayyan does not accept that it is an error and says: it was recited by al-Hasan, Ibn al-Sameeqa, and al-A'mash, and it cannot be said that they erred, because they hold a place in knowledge and the transmission of the Qur'an. And God, exalted is He, knows best.

What I think is that whenever the attribution of this recitation to these eminent figures is sound, it is necessary to find a justification for it, for they do not recite except on the basis of transmission, like the other reciters in all that they recite according to us. The Mu'tazila claimed that some recitations are based on opinion (ra'y).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 211–212:

﴿And it is not befitting for them﴾, i.e., it is not proper or suitable for them. ﴿Nor can they﴾, i.e., they are not at all able to do that. ﴿Indeed, they﴾, i.e., the devils (shayatin), ﴿from hearing﴾ what the angels (peace be upon them) speak in the heaven, ﴿are removed﴾, i.e., they are prevented by meteors (shuhub, sing. shihab), after they had been able to do so, as is indicated by the words of God Most High: ﴿And we touched the heaven, and found it filled with a strong guard and meteors. And we used to sit there in positions to listen. But whoever listens now will find a watching meteor lying in wait for him﴾. The purpose is to give the reason for what was mentioned before in the most emphatic manner, for if they are prevented from hearing what the angels say in the heaven, they are prevented all the more from taking the Glorious Qur'an from the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), or from the House of Glory (Bayt al-'Izzah), or from hearing it when God, Mighty and Majestic, reveals it to whomever He wills in His heaven.

It has been said: the meaning is that they are removed from hearing the speech of the angels (peace be upon them), because that hearing is conditioned upon sharing in the essential attributes, accepting the outpouring of the Truth, and being impressed by the angelic forms, whereas their souls are wicked, dark, and evil by nature, and do not accept that. The Noble Qur'an contains realities and unseen matters that can be received only from the angels (peace be upon them).

This has been objected to: if he means that hearing the speech of the angels (peace be upon them) in general is conditioned by qualities whose opposites they possess, then this is not accepted. How so, when it is established that the devils used to steal hearing? The apparent meaning of the verses is that they continue to steal it to this day, snatching a snatch, and a piercing meteor follows them. Also, if what was mentioned were a condition for hearing, and it is absent in them, then what is the benefit of the guard and of preventing them from hearing with the meteors?

Also, if what was mentioned were correct, it would not be possible for them to hear the Glorious Qur'an from the angels (peace be upon them), whether or not it contains realities and unseen matters. So what is the point of his saying "and the Qur'an contains..." etc.?

And if he means that hearing the speech of the angels (peace be upon them), when it is revelation sent down upon the prophets (peace be upon them), is conditioned by what was mentioned, then this, apart from being contrary to the apparent sense of the speech, is also not accepted. How so, when it is established that when Gabriel (peace be upon him) descends with the Qur'an, a guard descends with him to protect the revelation from the devil? God, Mighty and Majestic, has said: ﴿He does not disclose His unseen to anyone, except to a messenger whom He has chosen; then indeed He sends before him and behind him a guard﴾, ﴿so that He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord﴾. Also, the apparent sense of removal from hearing requires that they were enabled to hear before and then were prevented from it. It would then follow, on what was mentioned, that they used to hear revelation before, although their souls are wicked, dark, and evil by nature. So the claim that the said sharing is a condition for hearing is refuted. If it is claimed that the condition was present at that time, then it was lost, and it is maintained that the essential nature may change, this is something for which no proof has been established. And analogizing all the devils to Iblis (may God's curse be upon him) is something whose unsoundness is not hidden. So reflect.

In sum, what I incline to regarding the meaning of the verse is what I mentioned first. What relates to this will come shortly, God willing. It has also been permitted that the pronoun in ﴿Indeed, they﴾ refers to the polytheists, and the meaning would be that they do not lend an ear to the truth because of their obstinacy. There is in the verse a trace of the words of God Most High: ﴿And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the taghut (false deities), who bring them out of the light into the darkness﴾, but this is very far-fetched.

﴿So do not invoke any other god along with Allah, lest you be among those who are punished.﴾ It is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), even though it is impossible that the forbidden act (shirk, associating partners with God) could proceed from him, peace and blessings be upon him. The purpose is to stir him up and urge him to increase in ikhlas (sincerity, sincere devotion). It is therefore a kinaya (an indirect expression) meaning: "Be sincere in tawhid (monotheism) until you see no one alongside Him, mighty and majestic is He, other than Him." It also contains a lutf (kindness, gracious guidance) toward all accountable people (mukallafun), by clarifying that shirk is so ugly and evil that it is forbidden even to one from whom it could not possibly proceed. So how much more must it be forbidden to anyone else?!

It seems that the fa' here is fasiha (an elocutionary fa', one that signals an implied condition), meaning: "If you have come to know what has been mentioned, then do not invoke any other god along with Allah."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 214:

﴿Warn﴾ (of the punishment that shirk and sins entail) ﴿your closest kinsfolk﴾, that is, those of near kinship, or those who are closer to you than others.

The ʿashīrah (clan, the close kin of a man), according to al-Jawhari, is the man's nearest relatives. Al-Raghib said: they are the people of a man by whom he gains numerical strength, that is, they become for him like a complete number, which is ten.

It is well known that the levels of lineage are six:

The first is the shaʿb (the people, the broadest group) (with a fatḥah on the shīn), which is the most remote lineage, such as ʿAdnān.

The second is the qabīlah (tribe), which is what the shaʿb divides into, such as Rabīʿah and Muḍar.

The third is the ʿimārah (the sub-tribe) (with a kasrah on the ʿayn), which is what the lineages of the qabīlah divide into, such as Quraysh and Kinānah.

The fourth is the baṭn (the clan), which is what the lineages of the ʿimārah divide into, such as Banū ʿAbd Manāf and Banū Makhzūm.

The fifth is the fakhdh (the subclan), which is what the lineages of the baṭn divide into, such as Banū Hāshim and Banū Umayyah.

The sixth is the faṣīlah (the immediate family), which is what the lineages of the fakhdh divide into, such as Banū al-ʿAbbās and Banū ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib. Below the faṣīlah there is nothing but the man and his offspring.

Abu ʿUbayd related, from Ibn al-Kalbi, from his father, an order that puts the shaʿb first, then the qabīlah, then the faṣīlah, then the ʿimārah, then the fakhdh. Thus he placed the faṣīlah in the position of the ʿimārah in mentioning it after the qabīlah, and the ʿimārah in the position of the faṣīlah in mentioning it before the fakhdh. No report contrary to this has been transmitted. The ʿashīrah is not mentioned in either of these two orders. In al-Baḥr it is stated that it lies below the fakhdh and above the faṣīlah, and the apparent meaning is that this is according to the first order.

Some scholars, after citing the above order from al-Nawawi (may Allah have mercy on him), reported that he said in Taḥrīr al-Tanbīh: "Some have added the ʿashīrah before the faṣīlah." It may be understood from the words of some that when the ʿashīrah is described as "closest," it becomes one with the faṣīlah, which is the sixth of the levels. You know that if nearness is included in its concept, as may be understood from the words of al-Jawhari, then the claim of identity makes the mention of that description unnecessary.

In the Kulliyyāt of Abu al-Baqāʾ: "Every large group of people who trace their descent to a famous father by some additional matter is a shaʿb, such as ʿAdnān. Below it is the qabīlah, which is what the lineages of the shaʿb divide into, such as Rabīʿah and Muḍar. Then the ʿimārah, which is what the lineages of the qabīlah divide into, such as Quraysh and Kinānah. Then the baṭn, which is what the lineages of the ʿimārah divide into, such as Banū ʿAbd Manāf and Banū Makhzūm. Then the fakhdh, which is what the lineages of the baṭn divide into, such as Banū Hāshim and Banū Umayyah. Then the ʿashīrah, which is what the lineages of the fakhdh divide into, such as Banū al-ʿAbbās and Banū Abi Ṭālib. The ḥayy (tribe, living group) applies to all of these, since it refers to the group of people who dwell together in one quarter of them." End of quotation.

He did not mention the faṣīlah in this, and it seems he holds that it is identical with the ʿashīrah.

The reason the Prophet (ﷺ) specified his closest kinsfolk for mention, despite the universality of his mission, is to remove the suspicion of favouritism, and to show that concern for them is more important, and that one begins with those who are nearest, then those after them, as He (Exalted) said: ﴿Fight those of the disbelievers who are near to you﴾.

Regarding the manner of the warning, there are many reports:

Among them is what al-Bukhari related from Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with both of them), who said: "When ﴿And warn your closest kinsfolk﴾ was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) climbed al-Ṣafā and began calling out: 'O Banū Fihr! O Banū ʿAdiyy!' – for the clans of Quraysh – until they gathered. Whoever could not come out sent a messenger to see what it was. Abu Lahab and Quraysh came, and he said: 'Tell me, if I informed you that a cavalry in the valley intended to attack you, would you believe me?' They said: 'Yes, we have never known you to tell anything but the truth.' He said: 'Then I am a warner to you before a severe punishment.' Abu Lahab said: 'May you perish all day! Did you gather us only for this?' Then this was revealed: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish he. His wealth did not avail him, nor what he earned.﴾"

Among them is what Aḥmad and a group related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When ﴿And warn your closest kinsfolk﴾ was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) summoned Quraysh, both general and specific, and said: 'O assembly of Quraysh, save yourselves from the Fire, for I cannot benefit you or harm you in any way. O assembly of Banū Kaʿb ibn Lu'ayy, save yourselves from the Fire, for I cannot benefit you or harm you in any way. O assembly of Banū Quṣayy, save yourselves from the Fire, for I cannot benefit you or harm you in any way. O assembly of Banū ʿAbd Manāf, save yourselves from the Fire, for I cannot benefit you or harm you in any way. O assembly of Banū ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, save yourselves from the Fire, for I cannot benefit you or harm you in any way. O Fāṭimah, daughter of Muḥammad, save yourself from the Fire, for I cannot benefit you or harm you in any way. But you have a bond of kinship, and I shall keep it moist with its moisture.'"

In some reports it is stated that when the verse was revealed, he (ﷺ) gathered the Banū Hāshim and seated them at the door, and gathered his wives and family and seated them in the house, then he looked down on them and warned them.

In another of them it is stated that he (ﷺ) commanded ʿAlī (may Allah honour his face) to prepare food and gather the Banū ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib for him. He did so and gathered them, and they were forty men on that day. After they had eaten, when he wished to speak to them, Abu Lahab forestalled him with speech and said: "Your companion has bewitched you." So they dispersed. Then he invited them again the next day to the same, and then forestalled them with speech, saying: "O Banū ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, I am the warner to you from Allah (Exalted), and the bringer of good news. I have come to you with what no one has come with: I have brought you this world and the next. So submit, and you will be safe; obey, and you will be guided."

Beyond these there are other reports and narrations. If all of them are sound, the way to reconcile them is to say that the warning was repeated.

Among the narrations are some which the Shīʿah cling to regarding what they claim concerning the matter of the caliphate. These are either interpreted figuratively, or weak, or fabricated. ﴿And warn your closest kinsfolk﴾, and your household of the sincere ones.

[Page 135]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 215:

﴿And lower your wing to those among the believers who follow you.﴾ This is a command to him (ﷺ) to show humility, by way of a dependent metaphor (isti'ara tab'iyya), or an allegorical metaphor (isti'ara tamthiliyya), or a free metaphor (majaz mursal), whose relation (*'alaqa*) is necessity (*luzum*). The raising of the wing is used to mean arrogance, and on this the poet's verse runs:

*You are renowned for lowering the wing, so do not be among those who raise it as a falcon raises its wings.*

It has been said that *min* (in *min al-mu'minin*) is explicative (*bayaniyya*), because *man* in *man ittaba'a* is, in its basic meaning, more general than those who follow for religion or for other reasons, so there is a vagueness in it. Mentioning *al-mu'minin*, meaning those who follow the religion, removes this vagueness. It has also been said that *min* is partitive (*tab'idiyya*), based on the commonness of *man ittaba'a* applying to those who follow the religion, and on taking *al-mu'minin* to mean those who affirm with the tongue, even if hypocritically. There is no doubt that those who follow the religion are some of the believers in this sense. It is also permitted to take it to mean those who were close to faith, even though they had not believed. There is also no doubt that the followers mentioned are some of them. In the verse, on both views, there is a command to humility toward those who follow the religion.

[p. 136]

Some have said, on the assumption that *min* is explicative: the believers here refers to those who had not yet believed but were close to believing, like those whose hearts are to be won over (*al-mu'allafa*). This is a metaphor on the basis of the first meaning. The phrase *man ittaba'aka* was commonly used of those who truly believed and of those who believed only figuratively, so it was clarified by the words of God Most High, ﴿among the believers﴾, that the intended people are those who were close to belief. That is, be humble toward those who were close, in order to win them over and bring them together. On the assumption that *min* is partitive, *al-mu'minin* refers to those who said "We believe," and they are of two kinds: a kind who affirmed and followed, and a kind from whom nothing was found but affirmation. Thus it is said "among the believers," and some of those who affirmed and followed are meant. That is, be humble toward some of the believers, namely those who followed you out of love and affection.

On this view, those to whom he (ﷺ) is commanded to show humility, on the assumption that *min* is explicative, are not the same as those to whom he, peace and blessings be upon him, is commanded to show humility on the assumption that *min* is partitive.

Some eminent scholars have said: following and faith are twins, since what is understood from following him, peace and blessings be upon him, is religious following, and likewise what is understood from faith is true faith. The mention of *min al-mu'minin* serves to convey generality, like the mention of ﴿flies with its two wings﴾ after "bird" in God's words: ﴿nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾. The verse conveys the command to humility toward everyone among his kin (ﷺ) and others who believed.

Al-Tibi said: Following the arts of eloquence means interpreting the speech as using the device of placing the apparent noun in place of the pronoun. The original would be: "Warn your nearest kin, and lower your wing to whoever among them follows you." Instead it says "the believers," so that it is general and indicates that the quality of faith is what makes its bearer deserving of honor, and that one who has it should be humble for its sake, whether he is of your kin or not. This is not far-fetched. However, I prefer that *min* be explicative, and that the generality of *man ittaba'aka* is taken according to its basic meaning.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj, who said: «When the verse ﴿And warn your nearest kin﴾ was revealed, he (ﷺ) began with the people of his household and his clan, and that was hard on the Muslims, so God Most High revealed: ﴿And lower your wing to those among the believers who follow you.﴾»

﴿Then if they disobey you, say: "Indeed, I am innocent of what you do."﴾ The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿disobey you﴾ refers to the one warned (ﷺ) and those he warned, who were his kinsfolk. That is: if they disobey you and do not follow you after you have warned them, then say: "Indeed, I am innocent of your deeds," or of what you do of calling upon another god alongside Allah, the Exalted. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to the disbelievers, as implied by the context. It has also been said that it refers to those among the believers who followed him. That is: if they disobey you, O Muhammad, in the rulings and the branches of Islam after they have affirmed you, believed in you, and humbled themselves before you, then say: "Indeed, I am innocent of what you do of sins." That is: make clear your lack of approval of that and your denunciation of it to them. On this view, it is mentioned that if he (ﷺ) had been commanded to disavow them, he would not have remained an intercessor (shafi') for the sinners on the Day of Resurrection. And the verse, on any view other than this one, is abrogated (mansukhah).

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Zayd that he said: "Allah, glorified is He, commanded him with this, then abrogated it, and commanded him to fight them." In al-Bahr (Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit): "This is a truce (muwada'ah) which the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf) abrogated."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 217:

﴿And rely upon the Mighty, the Merciful﴾. So He, glorified is He, subdues those among them and among others who disobey you by His might, and He helps you by His mercy. The mention of the attribute of might first has been said to be because it is more fitting to the situation of consoling (the Prophet) for the hardships that befall him from the people. It has also been allowed that this is because might is like the cause that makes reliance (tawakkul) valid, and mercy is like the cause that calls one to it. Many have explained it as a man entrusting his affair to One who owns his affair and is able to benefit him and harm him.

They have said: the one who relies (mutawakkil) is one who, when a matter overtakes him, does not seek to repel it from himself by means that are disobedience to God, the Exalted. Some have mentioned that this is among the lowest and least of the levels of tawakkul. It has been related from some of the knowers (ʿarifin) that among people there are three degrees:

The first: tawakkul together with seeking and engaging in the means, with the intention of occupying the self, benefiting creation, and abandoning claims.

The second: tawakkul together with dropping the seeking and lowering the gaze from the means, striving to correct tawakkul and to suppress the self's aspiration to honour, devoting oneself to preserving the obligations.

The third: tawakkul together with knowledge of the reason for tawakkul, which tends toward release from the cause of tawakkul. This is that one knows that God, the Exalted, has not left any matter neglected, but has finished with all things and decreed them, and His glorified concern is to drive decrees to their appointed times. So the mutawakkil is one who has relieved his self of the toil of looking at and attending to the means, being at rest with what has preceded in the allotment, while the two states are equal. This is that he knows that seeking does not benefit and that tawakkul does not prevent. Whenever he sees a return (ʿiwad) through his tawakkul, his tawakkul is tainted and his intention is flawed. When he is freed from the bondage of means and in his tawakkul regards nothing but the pure right of God, the Exalted, God, the Exalted, suffices him in every important matter.

The Allama al-Tibi explained that in the words of the Exalted, ﴿And rely﴾ etc., there is an allusion to the three degrees, though with some obscurity in it.

In the codices of the people of Madina and Syria it is written ﴿fa-tawakkal﴾ with the fa, and Nafi', Ibn ʿAmir, Abu Jaʿfar and Shayba recited it so. It has been construed as a substitution (ibdal) from the response of the conditional clause.

In al-Kashshaf, the fa was made a conjunction (lil-ʿatf), with what follows it coordinated to ﴿fa-qul﴾ or ﴿fa-la tadʿu﴾. What was mentioned first is more apparent.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 218–219:

﴿The One who sees you when you stand﴾, that is, for prayer; ﴿and your movements among those who prostrate﴾, that is, He, glory be to Him, sees your change from one state, such as sitting and prostration, to another, such as standing; ﴿among those who prostrate﴾, that is, among those praying behind you when you lead them. They were described as "those who prostrate" because prostration is the state in which the servant is nearest to his Lord, mighty and majestic, and it is the most excellent of the pillars (arkan) of prayer, as stated by a group of the imams. This interpretation of the sentence as mentioned is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and a group of exegetes. However, some of them said: the meaning is: when you stand for prayer with the people in congregation. It was also said: the meaning is: He sees you when you stand for tahajjud (night prayer) and sees your movements, that is, your going and coming among those who perform tahajjud, so that you may observe their conditions and look upon them from where they do not perceive, and penetrate their inner selves and how they work for their hereafter, as it is narrated that when the obligation of the night prayer was abrogated (naskh), the Prophet (ﷺ) went around the houses of his Companions on that night to see what they were doing, out of eagerness for the abundance of their acts of obedience. He found them like beehives, because of the hum of their remembrance of Allah the Exalted and their recitation that he heard.

And from Mujahid: that the meaning of His words, glory be to Him, ﴿and your movements among those who prostrate﴾ is the movement of his (peace be upon him) gaze over those who pray behind him, for he (ﷺ) used to see from behind him. In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from Anas, who said: "The prayer was called to be established, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned to us with his face and said: Straighten your rows and close the gaps, for I see you from behind my back."

And in the narration of Abu Dawud, from Abu Hurayrah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "Straighten, straighten, straighten, and by Him in whose hand is my soul, I see you from behind me as I see you from in front of me." The remoteness of applying what is in the verse to this meaning is not hidden.

It was also said: the meaning of "those who prostrate" is the believers, and the meaning is: He sees you when you stand to perform the message, and sees your movement and your going back and forth among the believers, or with them, in what involves proclaiming the command of Allah the Exalted and exalting His word, glory be to Him.

The interpretation of "those who prostrate" as "the believers" is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah, but that the meaning is what has been mentioned is not free from obscurity.

And from Ibn Jubayr that by them are meant the Prophets (peace be upon them), and the meaning is: and He sees your movement as other Prophets move in conveying what they were commanded to convey. This is as you see it. The interpretation of "those who prostrate" as the Prophets was related by a group including al-Tabarani, al-Bazzar and Abu Nu'aym, also from Ibn 'Abbas, except that he (may Allah be pleased with him) interpreted the movement among them as the transfer through their loins until his mother gave birth to him (peace be upon him). It is permissible, on taking the movement to mean transfer through the loins, that by "those who prostrate" is meant the believers. The verse has been used as evidence for the faith of the Prophet's (ﷺ) parents, as many of the eminent Sunni scholars held, and I fear disbelief upon whoever says otherwise about them, may Allah be pleased with them both, despite the displeasure of the reader and his like. However, I do not hold the verse to be a proof for this claim.

The seeing of Allah the Exalted is an unveiling fitting to His majesty, mighty is His dignity, which differs from scientific knowledge (inkishaf 'ilmi), and it relates to the existent and to the non-existent external object according to the knowers of Allah (al-'arifin). They said: Allah's seeing of the non-existent is like a person's seeing the Resurrection and similar things in a dream. Many of the theologians (mutakallimun) denied its relation to the non-existent, and some of them traced it back to the attribute of knowledge; the verification of this is in its proper place. In describing Him, exalted is He, as seeing his (ﷺ) state by which he deserves His guardianship (wilaya), after describing him with what was mentioned earlier, is a confirmation of trust in Him (tawakkul) and a settling of His noble heart (peace be upon him) upon it.

Jannah ibn Hubaysh read (wa-yuqallibuka), the present tense of (qallaba) with shaddah, and Abu Hayyan construed it as coordinated with (yarak), and coordination with (taqum) was also permitted. In this reading there is an indication that his (ﷺ) movement among those who prostrate occurs in its fullest form, and the perfection of movement in prayer is that it be with humility (khushu') by which one is heedless of all besides Allah the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 220:

﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing﴾ with respect to everything to which hearing can validly relate, and included in this is what he (ﷺ) says. ﴿The All-Knowing﴾ with respect to everything to which knowledge can validly relate, and included in this is what he (ﷺ) does or intends, upon him be prayers and peace. The nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya) indicates that He, glorified is He, is characterized by what has been mentioned eternally, without beginning and without end, and that this does not depend on the existence of the things heard and known in the external world. The restriction (al-hasr) in it is real, meaning: He, exalted is He, is such, and no other than He, glorified and exalted is He.

It seems that the sentence is connected to the two sentences that occur in the scope of the jaza' (the apodosis of the conditional). It was brought for the purpose of urging the previous statement and reliance on Him. It is also permissible that it be connected to what is within the scope of the silah (the relative clause), and its purpose is to urge the performance of the words and actions that occur in prayer in the most perfect manner. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 221:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?﴾ etc. is cited to demonstrate the impossibility of the devils descending upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), after demonstrating that they are prevented from descending with the Qur'an. This verse, His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ etc., and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Nor have the devils brought it down﴾ etc., are sisters (akhawat, i.e., closely related passages). They have been separated by verses that are not in their meaning, so that the mention of their subject is returned to and the matter of what they contain is repeated again and again. This indicates that the meaning in which they were revealed is among the meanings to which Allah, exalted is He, has given intense attention. An example of this is a man who speaks about a matter while having concern for some part of it and special care for it, so you see him repeating its mention and not ceasing to return to it. The interrogative here is for confirmation (taqrir). ʿAlā man (upon whom) is connected to (tanazzalu, descend) and has been placed before it because the prepositional phrase requires initial position (sadarat al-majrur). Fronting the prepositional phrase does no harm, as has been explained in grammar (al-nahw).

Al-Zamakhshari said regarding this: "Man" (من) implies the meaning of interrogation. The meaning of "implication" (tadammun) is not that the noun indicates two meanings together, the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a particle. Rather, its meaning is that the original form was "amana," and the interrogative particle was dropped, and usage continued with its deletion, just as it was deleted from "hal," whose original form is "ahal," as the poet said:

"Ask the horsemen of Yarbu' about our strength: did they see us at the slope of the plain, the one with the hills?"

When you introduce the prepositional particle upon "man," then in your mind estimate the hamza before the prepositional particle, as if you were saying: a-ʿalā man tanazzalu al-shayatin (is it upon whom the devils descend?), like your saying: a-ʿalā Zayd marrta (is it upon Zayd that you passed?). End of quote.

The author of al-Fara'id (Sahib al-Fara'id) criticized him with his saying: What was mentioned is problematic in light of their saying: min ayna anta (from where are you) and min ayna ji'ta (from where have you come), and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿From what thing did He create him﴾, and their saying: fima (for what), bima (with what), mimma (from what), hatta-ma (until when), and similar. The author of al-Kashf answered that there is no problem with examples like "min ayna anta?" because the estimate is: "amin al-Basrah am min al-Kufah" (is it from Basrah or from Kufah), for example. It is not hidden that it
صفحة 139
is not needed, according to what the grammarians have verified, to all of that.

The clause ﴿upon whom descend﴾ etc. is in a position of accusative (nasb) governed by (unabbi'ukum, I inform you), because it is suspended (mu'allaq) by the interrogative. It is either serving in place of the second object if you consider the verb transitive to two, or serving in place of two objects if you consider it transitive to three. The intended meaning: "Shall I inform you of the answer to this question—I mean, upon whom do the devils descend?" The original form of (tanazzalu) is (tatanazzalu), and one of the two tā's has been deleted.

According to Abu Hayyan, the discourse is on the sense of speech (qawl), as if it were said: "Say, O Muhammad: Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend?"

[Page 139]

﴿Upon every lying sinner they descend﴾. That is, one who is abundant in *ifk*, which is lying, and abundant in sin (*ithm*). The word *kull* ("every") here denotes abundance, though it is also permissible to take it as denoting totality. There is no improbability in their descending upon every person who is perfect in lying and sin, such as the soothsayers (*kahana*, sing. *kahin*), for example Shiqq ibn Ruhm ibn Nadhir and Satih ibn Rabi'a ibn 'Adiy. The meaning of restriction (*takhsis*) through the means of clarification in context, or the context, or the implicit contrary meaning (*mafhum al-mukhalafa*), according to those who hold it, is to limit their descent to every person who possesses the qualities mentioned, and to restrict it to them without going beyond them to others. Since the sanctuary of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is too pure for any trace of those qualities to approach it, the impossibility of their descent upon him, peace and blessings be upon him, is made clear.

﴿They cast the hearing﴾, that is, the lying sinners cast their hearing, meaning they direct their hearing to the devils. The casting of hearing is a metaphor for intense listening in order to receive. It is as if it were said: they listen with the utmost attentiveness to the devils, and thus receive from them what they receive. ﴿And most of them﴾, that is, of the lying sinners, ﴿are liars﴾ in what they say of the sayings. The majority here is in regard to their statements, in the sense that these people rarely speak the truth in their statements, and in most of them they are liars. Its meaning is: most of their statements are false, not in regard to their persons, such that the attribution of lying to most of them would imply that the least of them are truthful absolutely. This would require that "most" be understood as "all".

It is not the meaning of "lying sinner" that one speaks nothing but falsehood, such that truth is impossible from him. Rather, it is one who abounds in lying. Thus it does not contradict this if he rarely speaks the truth on some occasions. It is also permissible that "hearing" means "what is heard", and that its casting is a metaphor for mentioning it: that the lying sinners convey to people what is heard from the devils. And most of them are liars in what they relate about the devils. Some of them did not approve of this, either because it is remote or because its benefit is small, as has been said.

There has been disagreement regarding the cause of most of their statements being false. It has been said: after the mission (*ba'tha*), the cause is that they receive from the devils conjectures and signs, since they have no share of the knowledge of the unseen, and they are veiled from the news of heaven. Because their souls are not pure, their conjectures rarely come true. Along with that, the lying sinners add to them, because they do not fulfil their purpose according to their imaginings, things most of which do not correspond to reality.

Before the mission, when they were not veiled from the news of heaven, and used to hear from the angels, peace be upon them, what they heard of the unseen reports, it is possible that the cause is the great number of errors of the lying sinners in understanding, due to the deficiency of their understanding of those reports. It is also possible that the cause is their adding to what they understand of the truth things from their own selves, most of which do not correspond to reality. It is also possible that the cause is the great number of errors of the devils who inspire them in understanding from the angels, peace be upon them, due to the deficiency of their understanding of them. It is also possible that the cause is the devils adding to what they understand of the truth from the angels, peace be upon them, things from their own selves, most of which do not correspond to reality. It is also possible that it is all of what has been mentioned.

It has been said: before the mission, it is possible that the cause is one of these matters. As for after the mission, the cause is the great amount of lying they mix in with what the devils snatch when they eavesdrop on the angels, and then cast to them.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "Some people asked the Prophet ﷺ about the soothsayers (*kuhhan*). He said: 'They are nothing.' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, they sometimes tell us things that turn out to be true.' He said: 'That word of truth is something the jinn snatches away and throws into the ear of his friend, and they mix into it more than a hundred lies.'"

[Page 140]

It has been said: both before and after the mission, the cause is the great mixing of falsehood by the lying sinners with what they receive from the devils. As for its being great before the mission, it is due to the apparent meaning of the report mentioned. As for its being great after the mission, it is due to what 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatada, that he said regarding this verse: "The devils used to ascend to the heaven and listen, then descend to the soothsayers and inform them. The soothsayers would relate what the devils had brought of the hearing, and mix with it much falsehood, then they would relate it to the people. As for what was from the hearing of heaven, it would be true, and as for what they mixed with it of falsehood, it would be false."

It is not hidden that the claim that after the mission the devils cast what they snatch from the hearing to the soothsayers is not agreed upon (*ghayr mujma' 'alayhi*, i.e., not subject to consensus). Among those who hold it is one who permits that the pronoun in "they cast" (*yulqunna*) refers to the devils, and the meaning is: the devils cast what they heard from the Highest Assembly (*al-mala' al-a'la*) before they are pelted, of some unseen matters, to their allies, and most of them are liars in what they inspire to them, since they do not make them hear in the manner in which the angels, peace be upon them, spoke, due to their wickedness, or due to the deficiency of their understanding, or their retention, or their conveying.

It has been said: the meaning according to this is that the devils listen attentively and hearken to the Highest Assembly before being pelted, and most of them are liars in what they inspire to their allies afterwards, due to their wickedness, or because they do not hear in themselves, or they do not make their allies hear, after that hearing, the speech of the angels, peace be upon them, in its proper form.

The clause "they cast" (*yulqun*), if the pronoun refers to the lying sinners, is a descriptive clause (*sifa*) for "every lying sinner", because it has the sense of the plural, whether what is meant by casting the hearing is listening to the devils or casting what is heard to the people.

It is also permissible that it be a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*), informing of their state on both interpretations, because each of their receiving from the devils and their casting to the people occurs after the descent. The supposition of an implied subject (*taqdir al-mubtada'*) is preferred on this view. It is also permissible that it be a resumptive clause built upon a question, as if it were said: what do they do at the descent of the devils, or what do they do after their descent? So it is said: "They cast to them their hearing, so that they may memorize what is inspired to them, or they cast what they hear from them to the people." It is also permissible that it be an anticipated circumstantial clause (*hal muntazara*) on both interpretations as well.

And if the pronoun refers to the devils, and the meaning is "what you heard first", it has been said: it may be a resumptive clause explaining the purpose of the descent, built upon a question about it, as if it were said: why do they descend upon them? So it is said: "they cast to them what they have heard." It may also be an anticipated circumstantial clause from the pronoun of the devils, meaning: they descend upon every lying sinner, casting to them what they hear from the Highest Assembly. On this interpretation, and the meaning being "what you heard second", it has been said: it cannot be a resumptive clause like what was mentioned just before, nor a circumstantial clause either, because the casting of hearing in the sense of listening attentively precedes the mentioned descent. How then could it be its purpose, or a concomitant (*hal muqarina*) or anticipated circumstantial clause? It is thus necessary that it be a resumptive clause informing of their state.

It has been objected that this is not sound, because mentioning their prior state before their mentioned descent, which precedes it, is not befitting the eloquence of the revelation. From here it has been said that making the pronoun refer to the devils and understanding the casting of hearing as their attentive listening and eavesdropping on the Highest Assembly is something with no way to it. But there is consideration in this.

The clause "most of them are liars" is either a resumptive clause, or it admits both the resumptive and the circumstantial.

Now, know that there is a problem raised against some of the possibilities in the verse, because according to it, it indicates that the devils hear from the angels, peace be upon them, what they hear and cast to the lying sinners. Already preceding is what indicates their being prevented from hearing, namely His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Indeed they are removed from the hearing﴾.

It has been answered that what is meant by hearing in what precedes is the hearing that counts, and what is meant here is hearing in general, and what is meant by it is the snatching mentioned in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿except one who snatches a snatch, and a piercing flame pursues him﴾, and the word mentioned in the report of the two Sahihs and Ibn Mardawayh cited just above. It has been objected that one who snatches does not remain alive until he conveys what he snatched to his ally, due to the apparent meaning of His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿except one who snatches a snatch, and a piercing flame pursues him﴾, for its apparent meaning is that he is destroyed by the flame that reaches him.

It has been answered that the denial of his remaining alive is not granted, nor do we concede that the verse is apparent in what has been mentioned, since there is nothing in it beyond the piercing flame pursuing him, and this may signify repelling as it may signify destruction. Thus the pursuit may be for repelling while he remains alive, for the report mentioned requires that he remain so.

It has come from Ibn 'Abbas that the devils were not veiled from the heavens, and they used to enter them and bring news of them, and cast it to the soothsayers. Then when 'Isa, peace be upon him, was born, they were prevented from three heavens. When Muhammad ﷺ was born, they were prevented from all the heavens. There is not one of them who wishes to snatch the hearing except that he is pelted with a flame, which is a spark of fire, and it never misses. So some of them it kills, some of them it burns their faces, and some of them it renders insane, so that he becomes a ghoul who misleads people in the deserts.

It has been said: what is meant by hearing in what precedes is the hearing of the revelation, and here is the hearing of the unseen other than it. They are not prevented from it before the mission or after it. This is taken from the words of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Khaldun in the introduction to his history, which was not woven on its pattern, although there is room for criticism in it. He said: the verses only indicate the prevention of the devils from one kind of news of the heaven, namely what relates to the news of the mission, and they were not prevented from anything other than that. Indeed, it may be said that in his words afterwards there is some indication that the prevention was only before the prophethood, not before that nor after it.

It is not hidden that the apparent indications attest to their being prevented absolutely until the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, it may be claimed that in the verses there is what indicates that the guarding of the heaven by the stars did not occur newly, and that its creation was for that purpose. This is apparent that they were also prevented before his birth, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, from the news of heaven. This is problematic for the apparent meaning of the isolation (*'azl*), unless it is claimed that the prevention before was not like the prevention after, so the isolation from what was previously made the prevention severe in relation to him.

In *al-Yawaqit wa'l-Jawahir fi 'Aqa'id al-Akabir* by our master 'Abd al-Wahhab al-Sha'rani, may Allah have mercy on him: "The correct view is that the devils have been prevented from hearing since the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent, until the Day of Resurrection, and even if they eavesdrop, they do not reach mankind to inform them of what they have stolen, rather the shooting stars burn them and destroy them." End of quotation.

It has been said: those who hold this are bound to interpret what is in the report of the two Sahihs as referring to soothsayers who existed before the mission, whom the questioners encountered. This is what the words of al-Qadi also imply. Al-Nawawi transmitted from him in his commentary on Sahih Muslim that he said: "Soothsaying among the Arabs was of three kinds. One is that a person has a jinn friend who informs him of what he steals by listening from the heaven. This kind ceased from the time our Prophet ﷺ was sent, until the end of what he said." This is also the apparent meaning of al-Busiri's words, where he says:

"When He sent at His mission the shooting stars as guards, and the expanse was too narrow for them,
They drive the jinn away from their seats for hearing, as the shepherds drive away the wolf.
So the sign of soothsaying was erased by signs from the revelation, of which there is no effacement for them."

It has been said in answer to the objection something like this: that the descent of the devils and their casting of what they hear from the heaven to their allies, according to what the mentioned verse indicates in one of its possible meanings, was only before the mission, since there was then no prevention, or there was prevention but it was not severe.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 222–223 (part 2 of 3):

The prevention from hearing that is indicated by His words, ﴿Indeed they are removed from hearing﴾, occurred after the mission (al-bi'thah), and it was in its most complete form. This is problematic in my view with regard to Ibn al-Sayyad and what came from him. The scholars counted him among the soothsayers (kuhhan, sing. kahin), and it is authentically reported that when the Prophet ﷺ asked him about his matter, he said: "A truthful one and a liar come to me." The Prophet ﷺ tested him by concealing for him the verse of the smoke, which is His words: ﴿So watch for the day when the sky brings forth a manifest smoke﴾. The Prophet ﷺ said: "I have hidden something for you." Ibn al-Sayyad said: "It is al-Dukh," meaning al-Dukhan (smoke), which is a dialectal form of it, as the majority of scholars have held. The Prophet ﷺ said to him: "Begone! You will never surpass your measure."

Al-Qadi said, as al-Nawawi also reported from him: The soundest of the opinions is that he did not discover from the verse that the Prophet ﷺ had concealed anything except this incomplete wording, in the manner of the soothsayers, when Satan casts to them just enough that he snatches it before the shooting star reaches him. What points to this is the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Begone! You will never surpass your measure," meaning: the measure that the soothsayers attain of being guided to part of a thing, without its reality becoming clear to them, and without it leading them to clarifying and verifying the matters of the unseen.

It may be said in resolving this difficulty: Ibn al-Sayyad was of the second category of soothsayers, those whom the devils inform of what occurs or happens in the regions of the earth, and of what is hidden from them, whether near or far.

The correct view is the permissibility of their existence after the mission, contrary to the Mu'tazilah and some of the theologians, who held that the existence of this category, and likewise the category mentioned just above, is impossible. It is also possible that the Prophet ﷺ had secretly told some of his companions who were with him what he had concealed, or that the chapter of Smoke was written on his hand ﷺ, or that he wrote the verse alone on his hand, ﷺ. Both of the last two opinions were related by al-Dawudi from some scholars, as in the commentary on Sahih Muslim.

Whatever the case, Ibn al-Sayyad informed of an event that had just occurred, which the devils become aware of without eavesdropping from the sky. This is in no way a knowledge of what is in the heart. Nevertheless, he did not give a complete account of it, but reported it in the manner of the earlier soothsayers, who preceded the time of the mission and belong to the first category, in terms of deficiency.

Perhaps al-Qadi's meaning in his saying "he did not discover from the verse that he ﷺ had concealed except this incomplete wording, in the manner of the soothsayers when Satan casts to them just enough that he snatches it, etc." is to liken his state, although he belongs to the second category, to the state of those soothsayers before him who belonged to the first category. Otherwise his statement would be problematic together with what we quoted from him earlier, as is not hidden. It seems that he holds that the stoning of those who eavesdrop on hearing also occurred before the mission, but it was not on the same scale as what happened after the mission. A group of the traditionists (muhaddithun) went this way.

Some people said: When Satan snatches a snatch and a piercing shooting star follows him, he casts what he has snatched to whoever is below him before the shooting star reaches him. Then whoever is below him conveys it to the soothsayer. This hardly holds true.

It was also said: What the devils cast to the soothsayers after the mission is what they hear from the angels in the clouds (al-'anan), and this is what is meant by His words: ﴿they cast [their] hearing﴾. What they are prevented from is hearing from the angels in the sky, and this is what is meant by His words: ﴿Indeed they are removed from hearing﴾. This was argued from what al-Bukhari and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The angels speak about the matter on earth in the clouds (al-'anan, which is the cloud), and the devil overhears the word and pours it into the ear of the soothsayer as one pours into a bottle, and they add to it a hundred lies."

It is not hidden that the report contains no reference to hearing from the angels in the sky in its well-known sense, neither by negation nor by affirmation. It may be chosen to hold that the devils were only prevented after the mission from hearing what is of significance in the knowledge of the unseen from the angels of the sky or the clouds. Whoever snatched a snatch of significance was followed by the shooting star, which destroyed him and did not allow him to convey it in any way to the soothsayers. As for hearing what is not of significance, this may still occur for them, and they convey it to the soothsayers, mixing into it from falsehood what they mix. Thus where they are judged to be removed from hearing, the intended hearing is complete, significant hearing; and where they are judged to be casting hearing, the intended hearing is hearing in general, the least of what truly counts as hearing. The apparent view is that what Ibn al-Sayyad obtained was of this kind of hearing, and one hardly turns away from this. It may be said that he was of the second category of soothsaying, unless one of the three possibilities is established, and there is discussion about establishing that.

Yes, the Prophet's ﷺ saying "I have hidden" is apparent in indicating that there is something hidden in a palm or a sleeve or the like, and the verse, unless it was written, cannot be like that. For this reason those who hold that he ﷺ concealed the verse only in his heart needed to interpret "I have hidden" as "I have concealed." It may be said, though far-fetched, that the devils were prevented after the mission from hearing altogether by burning meteors that strike them.

Taking the pronoun of "they cast" as referring to the devils is weak, because the context is explaining to whom they are sent down, not describing their condition or the casting of their hearing, meaning their attentive listening, to the exalted assembly. ﴿And most of them﴾ means all of them, and the expression is used to indicate that the majority mentioned is sufficient for the purpose.

The meaning is: they listen attentively in order to hear, but they do not hear, except that ﴿and most of them are liars﴾ has been placed in the position of ﴿they do not hear﴾. Or: the casting of hearing means casting to them what the people hear from the liars. It does not follow from this that they heard it from the angels, since it is possible that they invented it from themselves by guess and conjecture and cast it to their associates, and it is not far-fetched that they are truthful in some of it.

The matter of calling it "heard" is trivial. What is transmitted in the hadith of the two Sahihs and in Ibn Mardawayh is to be understood as referring to what happened before the mission. It is said that they used to hear in general, and what is in the verse may be understood in this way, and some have gone this way. But understanding the snatching of the word in it as their guessing it through some celestial configurations and the like, so that it may be considered as occurring after the mission, is something I do not think anyone would accept. There is nothing in the story of Ibn al-Sayyad that is explicit that what he said was from hearing from the angels that the devil cast to him.

You may be inclined to find it unlikely that the angels in the sky would speak about what the Prophet ﷺ had concealed, and that the devils would ascend at the moment of the question, without delay, and eavesdrop and descend in the swiftest time with what Ibn al-Sayyad answered. That is only a kind of soothsaying.

As for the reality of the matter, according to what the eminent scholar Abd al-Rahman ibn Khaldun stated: the human soul has a readiness to strip away from humanity toward the spirituality that is above it. From this there arises a glimpse for humans of the category of the pious, through what they have been created with. They do not need in this any acquisition, nor any aid from any of the faculties, nor from any imaginings, nor from bodily actions, whether speech or movement, nor from any matter at all.

Rational division indicates that there is here another category of humans, falling short of the rank of this category by the shortfall of an opposite from its complete opposite. It is a category of humans created so that their rational faculty moves in its thinking movement by will, when the inclination toward that follows it, while it is deficient in this. So it clings, for the work of stratagem, to particular sensible or imagined things, such as transparent bodies, animal bones, rhymed prose, and whatever birds or animals appear on the left or the right. It sustains this perception and imagining, seeking aid through it in that stripping away it intends, and it acts as an escort for it. This faculty, which is the source in this category for that perception, is soothsaying. Because these souls are created with deficiency and shortcoming from perfection, their perception of particulars is greater than their perception of universals, and they are occupied with particulars, heedless of universals. For this reason the imagination in them is often at its strongest, and particulars are present and ready to them, and it is to them like a mirror in which they constantly look. The soothsayer cannot attain perfection in perceiving intelligibles, because his deficiency is innate and his revelation is satanic. The highest state of this category is that it seeks aid through speech containing rhymed prose and balance, in order to occupy itself with it away from the senses, and to some extent it becomes able to achieve that deficient stripping away. Thus there comes into its heart, from that movement, and from what escorts it of that foreign element, something that it casts upon its tongue. Sometimes it is truthful and agrees with the truth, and sometimes it lies, because it completes the matter of its deficiency with something foreign to the faculties themselves, alien to them and not suited to them. So truth and falsehood both befall it, and it is not reliable. Sometimes it resorts to conjectures and guesses, out of eagerness to attain perception, in its own claim, and to deceive the questioners.

Since the stripping away of the Prophet ﷺ from humanity and his connection with the exalted assembly occurred without any escort and without any aid from a foreign element, he was truthful in everything he brought. Truthfulness is among the distinctive qualities of prophethood. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said to Ibn al-Sayyad, when he asked him, uncovering his condition, with his words, "How does this matter come to you?" He said: "A truthful one and a liar come to me." The Prophet ﷺ said: "The matter has been mixed up for you." By this he, ﷺ, intended to deny prophethood from him, by indicating that it is something in which falsehood is in no way admissible.

It was said: "The highest state of this category is rhymed prose" because the source of rhymed prose is lighter than all other sources, whether of visible or audible things. The lightness of the source indicates the nearness of that stripping away and connection, and the distance in it from weakness in general. The sciences of the soothsayers are not confined to what comes from the devils; rather, just as some come from the devils, some come from themselves through their partial stripping away and their connection in general, by means of some causes, with a world in which future events and others are not hidden. Thus the cutting off of news of the sky from the devils after the mission, through stoning, if it is granted, does not indicate the cutting off of soothsaying.

Then, if these soothsayers lived in the era of prophethood, they would recognize the truthfulness of the Prophet and the evidentiary force of his miracle, because they have some measure of awareness (wijdan) of the matter of prophethood. What prevents them from faith and drives them to obstinacy is only the whisperings of greed for attaining prophethood themselves. This is what happened to Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt, for he used to hope to become a prophet. The same happened to Ibn al-Sayyad, Musaylima, and others. Sometimes those hopes are cut off and they believe in the best manner of faith, as happened to Tulayha al-Asadi and Qarib ibn al-Aswad, and they had in the Islamic conquests (al-futuhat al-islamiyya) effects that bear witness to the goodness of their faith.

It has been mentioned, in explaining the readiness of certain individuals, whether they are soothsayers or others, to report unseen matters before they occur, a lengthy discussion whose summary is that the human soul has a spiritual nature (ruhaniyya), and it possesses perception in its own essence without any intermediary. However, it is veiled from this by immersion in the body and the senses and their preoccupations, because the senses always draw it toward the outward by the bodily perception with which it was created. Sometimes it plunges from the outward to the inward, so the veil of the body is lifted for a moment, either by the property that belongs to humans absolutely, such as sleep, or by a property found in some individuals, such as the soothsayers who speak in rhymed prose (ahl al-saj'), the practitioners of casting pebbles and date stones (ahl al-turuq bil-hasa wal-nawa), those who gaze into transparent bodies such as mirrors, waters, the hearts, livers and bones of animals, and the insane may be added to them, or by religious discipline, like the people of unveiling (ahl al-kashf) among the Sufis, or by magical practice, like the people of unveiling among the Jogis. Then the soul turns at that time toward the essences above it from the higher assembly (al-mala' al-a'la), because of the connection in existence between its horizon and their horizon. Those essences are pure perception and intellects in actuality, and in them are the forms of existing things and their realities, as established in its proper place. So some of those forms become manifest to them and they acquire knowledge from them. Sometimes those perceived forms fall into the imagination, which shapes them into diverse molds, and then they return to the sense with what they have perceived, either in bare form or within its molds, and so they report it. End of quotation.

It is not hidden that this contains a line of thought akin to what the philosophers say about the higher assembly, which they often call the world of the immaterial (alam al-mujarradat), and sometimes call the world of intellects (alam al-uqul). These are commonly restricted by them to ten, but they have no proof for this restriction. Hence some of their later scholars said they are almost countless. The theologians (mutakallimun) and the verifying scholars of the earlier generations have statements on this matter that this place is too narrow to mention. I say, and none denies it except the ignorant: for Allah, glory be to Him,

[page 145]

there are special things in times, places and persons. It is not far-fetched, after the cutting off of news from heaven from the devils by meteors, that He may grant to some human souls the special property of speaking what is true, entirely or in part, together with an awareness and unveiling that gives knowledge of what they report or without that, by causing Him, glorified be He, to make them utter something, so they speak it without knowing what they report, and it agrees with reality.

This has happened to me, when I was about five years old. I came back from the kuttab to the house and began to play in it, as children do. My mother, may Allah have mercy on her, forbade me from that and ordered me to sleep so that I would wake in the morning and go to the kuttab. I said to her: "Tomorrow the vizier will be killed, and I will not go to the kuttab," which is something that hardly passes through the mind. She paid no attention to that and put me to sleep. When I woke in the morning I prepared to go, but a son of her sister came and whispered something to her that I did not hear, and her state changed, and she forbade me from going. I do not know why. I wanted to go out to the street to play with my peers, but she forbade me again. She sat, anxious of heart, seeking someone to inform her about the condition of my father, may he have mercy, since he had gone out shortly before sunrise to the school. I went out to the street when she was heedless, and I found people running and hurrying, saying that the vizier had been killed by some of his servants while he was at the dawn prayer. I returned to her hastily, delighted at the truth of my words. I had forgotten it and it had not come to my mind until I heard people talking about it.

In al-Yawaqit wal-Jawahir of al-Sha'rani, may Allah have mercy on him, in the section distinguishing miracle from soothsaying, it is stated that soothsaying consists of utterances that flow on the tongue of the soothsayer, which sometimes agree and sometimes disagree. There is in this a trace of what we have mentioned. This is what I have, and Allah knows best.

It appears, as has been said, that His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Shall I inform you﴾ and so on, is a statement brought by Him, exalted be He, to clarify the purification of the Prophet ﷺ from being one upon whom the devils descend, far be it from him, and to nullify their claim that the Qur'an is of the kind that is cast to soothsayers. In al-Bahr there is what is clear that it is in the sense of speech, i.e., "Say, O Muhammad: Shall I inform you..." and it is brought for the purification and nullification mentioned.

[Page 139]

﴿Upon every lying sinner they descend﴾. That is, one who is abundant in *ifk*, which is lying, and abundant in sin (*ithm*).
