The word *kull* ("every") here denotes abundance, though it is also permissible to take it as denoting totality. There is no improbability in their descending upon every person who is perfect in lying and sin, such as the soothsayers (*kahana*, sing. *kahin*), for example Shiqq ibn Ruhm ibn Nadhir and Satih ibn Rabi'a ibn 'Adiy. The meaning of restriction (*takhsis*) through the means of clarification in context, or the context, or the implicit contrary meaning (*mafhum al-mukhalafa*), according to those who hold it, is to limit their descent to every person who possesses the qualities mentioned, and to restrict it to them without going beyond them to others. Since the sanctuary of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is too pure for any trace of those qualities to approach it, the impossibility of their descent upon him, peace and blessings be upon him, is made clear.

﴿They cast the hearing﴾, that is, the lying sinners cast their hearing, meaning they direct their hearing to the devils. The casting of hearing is a metaphor for intense listening in order to receive. It is as if it were said: they listen with the utmost attentiveness to the devils, and thus receive from them what they receive. ﴿And most of them﴾, that is, of the lying sinners, ﴿are liars﴾ in what they say of the sayings. The majority here is in regard to their statements, in the sense that these people rarely speak the truth in their statements, and in most of them they are liars. Its meaning is: most of their statements are false, not in regard to their persons, such that the attribution of lying to most of them would imply that the least of them are truthful absolutely. This would require that "most" be understood as "all".

It is not the meaning of "lying sinner" that one speaks nothing but falsehood, such that truth is impossible from him. Rather, it is one who abounds in lying. Thus it does not contradict this if he rarely speaks the truth on some occasions. It is also permissible that "hearing" means "what is heard", and that its casting is a metaphor for mentioning it: that the lying sinners convey to people what is heard from the devils. And most of them are liars in what they relate about the devils. Some of them did not approve of this, either because it is remote or because its benefit is small, as has been said.

There has been disagreement regarding the cause of most of their statements being false. It has been said: after the mission (*ba'tha*), the cause is that they receive from the devils conjectures and signs, since they have no share of the knowledge of the unseen, and they are veiled from the news of heaven. Because their souls are not pure, their conjectures rarely come true. Along with that, the lying sinners add to them, because they do not fulfil their purpose according to their imaginings, things most of which do not correspond to reality.

Before the mission, when they were not veiled from the news of heaven, and used to hear from the angels, peace be upon them, what they heard of the unseen reports, it is possible that the cause is the great number of errors of the lying sinners in understanding, due to the deficiency of their understanding of those reports. It is also possible that the cause is their adding to what they understand of the truth things from their own selves, most of which do not correspond to reality. It is also possible that the cause is the great number of errors of the devils who inspire them in understanding from the angels, peace be upon them, due to the deficiency of their understanding of them. It is also possible that the cause is the devils adding to what they understand of the truth from the angels, peace be upon them, things from their own selves, most of which do not correspond to reality. It is also possible that it is all of what has been mentioned.

It has been said: before the mission, it is possible that the cause is one of these matters. As for after the mission, the cause is the great amount of lying they mix in with what the devils snatch when they eavesdrop on the angels, and then cast to them.

Al-Bukhari, Muslim, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "Some people asked the Prophet ﷺ about the soothsayers (*kuhhan*). He said: 'They are nothing.' They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, they sometimes tell us things that turn out to be true.' He said: 'That word of truth is something the jinn snatches away and throws into the ear of his friend, and they mix into it more than a hundred lies.'"

[Page 140]

It has been said: both before and after the mission, the cause is the great mixing of falsehood by the lying sinners with what they receive from the devils. As for its being great before the mission, it is due to the apparent meaning of the report mentioned. As for its being great after the mission, it is due to what 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatada, that he said regarding this verse: "The devils used to ascend to the heaven and listen, then descend to the soothsayers and inform them. The soothsayers would relate what the devils had brought of the hearing, and mix with it much falsehood, then they would relate it to the people. As for what was from the hearing of heaven, it would be true, and as for what they mixed with it of falsehood, it would be false."

It is not hidden that the claim that after the mission the devils cast what they snatch from the hearing to the soothsayers is not agreed upon (*ghayr mujma' 'alayhi*, i.e., not subject to consensus). Among those who hold it is one who permits that the pronoun in "they cast" (*yulqunna*) refers to the devils, and the meaning is: the devils cast what they heard from the Highest Assembly (*al-mala' al-a'la*) before they are pelted, of some unseen matters, to their allies, and most of them are liars in what they inspire to them, since they do not make them hear in the manner in which the angels, peace be upon them, spoke, due to their wickedness, or due to the deficiency of their understanding, or their retention, or their conveying.

It has been said: the meaning according to this is that the devils listen attentively and hearken to the Highest Assembly before being pelted, and most of them are liars in what they inspire to their allies afterwards, due to their wickedness, or because they do not hear in themselves, or they do not make their allies hear, after that hearing, the speech of the angels, peace be upon them, in its proper form.

The clause "they cast" (*yulqun*), if the pronoun refers to the lying sinners, is a descriptive clause (*sifa*) for "every lying sinner", because it has the sense of the plural, whether what is meant by casting the hearing is listening to the devils or casting what is heard to the people.

It is also permissible that it be a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*), informing of their state on both interpretations, because each of their receiving from the devils and their casting to the people occurs after the descent. The supposition of an implied subject (*taqdir al-mubtada'*) is preferred on this view. It is also permissible that it be a resumptive clause built upon a question, as if it were said: what do they do at the descent of the devils, or what do they do after their descent? So it is said: "They cast to them their hearing, so that they may memorize what is inspired to them, or they cast what they hear from them to the people." It is also permissible that it be an anticipated circumstantial clause (*hal muntazara*) on both interpretations as well.

And if the pronoun refers to the devils, and the meaning is "what you heard first", it has been said: it may be a resumptive clause explaining the purpose of the descent, built upon a question about it, as if it were said: why do they descend upon them? So it is said: "they cast to them what they have heard." It may also be an anticipated circumstantial clause from the pronoun of the devils, meaning: they descend upon every lying sinner, casting to them what they hear from the Highest Assembly. On this interpretation, and the meaning being "what you heard second", it has been said: it cannot be a resumptive clause like what was mentioned just before, nor a circumstantial clause either, because the casting of hearing in the sense of listening attentively precedes the mentioned descent. How then could it be its purpose, or a concomitant (*hal muqarina*) or anticipated circumstantial clause? It is thus necessary that it be a resumptive clause informing of their state.

It has been objected that this is not sound, because mentioning their prior state before their mentioned descent, which precedes it, is not befitting the eloquence of the revelation. From here it has been said that making the pronoun refer to the devils and understanding the casting of hearing as their attentive listening and eavesdropping on the Highest Assembly is something with no way to it. But there is consideration in this.

The clause "most of them are liars" is either a resumptive clause, or it admits both the resumptive and the circumstantial.

Now, know that there is a problem raised against some of the possibilities in the verse, because according to it, it indicates that the devils hear from the angels, peace be upon them, what they hear and cast to the lying sinners. Already preceding is what indicates their being prevented from hearing, namely His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Indeed they are removed from the hearing﴾.

It has been answered that what is meant by hearing in what precedes is the hearing that counts, and what is meant here is hearing in general, and what is meant by it is the snatching mentioned in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿except one who snatches a snatch, and a piercing flame pursues him﴾, and the word mentioned in the report of the two Sahihs and Ibn Mardawayh cited just above. It has been objected that one who snatches does not remain alive until he conveys what he snatched to his ally, due to the apparent meaning of His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿except one who snatches a snatch, and a piercing flame pursues him﴾, for its apparent meaning is that he is destroyed by the flame that reaches him.

It has been answered that the denial of his remaining alive is not granted, nor do we concede that the verse is apparent in what has been mentioned, since there is nothing in it beyond the piercing flame pursuing him, and this may signify repelling as it may signify destruction. Thus the pursuit may be for repelling while he remains alive, for the report mentioned requires that he remain so.

It has come from Ibn 'Abbas that the devils were not veiled from the heavens, and they used to enter them and bring news of them, and cast it to the soothsayers. Then when 'Isa, peace be upon him, was born, they were prevented from three heavens. When Muhammad ﷺ was born, they were prevented from all the heavens. There is not one of them who wishes to snatch the hearing except that he is pelted with a flame, which is a spark of fire, and it never misses. So some of them it kills, some of them it burns their faces, and some of them it renders insane, so that he becomes a ghoul who misleads people in the deserts.

It has been said: what is meant by hearing in what precedes is the hearing of the revelation, and here is the hearing of the unseen other than it. They are not prevented from it before the mission or after it. This is taken from the words of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Khaldun in the introduction to his history, which was not woven on its pattern, although there is room for criticism in it. He said: the verses only indicate the prevention of the devils from one kind of news of the heaven, namely what relates to the news of the mission, and they were not prevented from anything other than that. Indeed, it may be said that in his words afterwards there is some indication that the prevention was only before the prophethood, not before that nor after it.

It is not hidden that the apparent indications attest to their being prevented absolutely until the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, it may be claimed that in the verses there is what indicates that the guarding of the heaven by the stars did not occur newly, and that its creation was for that purpose. This is apparent that they were also prevented before his birth, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, from the news of heaven. This is problematic for the apparent meaning of the isolation (*'azl*), unless it is claimed that the prevention before was not like the prevention after, so the isolation from what was previously made the prevention severe in relation to him.

In *al-Yawaqit wa'l-Jawahir fi 'Aqa'id al-Akabir* by our master 'Abd al-Wahhab al-Sha'rani, may Allah have mercy on him: "The correct view is that the devils have been prevented from hearing since the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent, until the Day of Resurrection, and even if they eavesdrop, they do not reach mankind to inform them of what they have stolen, rather the shooting stars burn them and destroy them." End of quotation.

It has been said: those who hold this are bound to interpret what is in the report of the two Sahihs as referring to soothsayers who existed before the mission, whom the questioners encountered. This is what the words of al-Qadi also imply. Al-Nawawi transmitted from him in his commentary on Sahih Muslim that he said: "Soothsaying among the Arabs was of three kinds. One is that a person has a jinn friend who informs him of what he steals by listening from the heaven. This kind ceased from the time our Prophet ﷺ was sent, until the end of what he said." This is also the apparent meaning of al-Busiri's words, where he says:

"When He sent at His mission the shooting stars as guards, and the expanse was too narrow for them,
They drive the jinn away from their seats for hearing, as the shepherds drive away the wolf.
So the sign of soothsaying was erased by signs from the revelation, of which there is no effacement for them."

It has been said in answer to the objection something like this: that the descent of the devils and their casting of what they hear from the heaven to their allies, according to what the mentioned verse indicates in one of its possible meanings, was only before the mission, since there was then no prevention, or there was prevention but it was not severe.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verses 222–223 (part 2 of 3):

The prevention from hearing that is indicated by His words, ﴿Indeed they are removed from hearing﴾, occurred after the mission (al-bi'thah), and it was in its most complete form. This is problematic in my view with regard to Ibn al-Sayyad and what came from him. The scholars counted him among the soothsayers (kuhhan, sing. kahin), and it is authentically reported that when the Prophet ﷺ asked him about his matter, he said: "A truthful one and a liar come to me." The Prophet ﷺ tested him by concealing for him the verse of the smoke, which is His words: ﴿So watch for the day when the sky brings forth a manifest smoke﴾. The Prophet ﷺ said: "I have hidden something for you." Ibn al-Sayyad said: "It is al-Dukh," meaning al-Dukhan (smoke), which is a dialectal form of it, as the majority of scholars have held. The Prophet ﷺ said to him: "Begone! You will never surpass your measure."

Al-Qadi said, as al-Nawawi also reported from him: The soundest of the opinions is that he did not discover from the verse that the Prophet ﷺ had concealed anything except this incomplete wording, in the manner of the soothsayers, when Satan casts to them just enough that he snatches it before the shooting star reaches him. What points to this is the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Begone! You will never surpass your measure," meaning: the measure that the soothsayers attain of being guided to part of a thing, without its reality becoming clear to them, and without it leading them to clarifying and verifying the matters of the unseen.

It may be said in resolving this difficulty: Ibn al-Sayyad was of the second category of soothsayers, those whom the devils inform of what occurs or happens in the regions of the earth, and of what is hidden from them, whether near or far.

The correct view is the permissibility of their existence after the mission, contrary to the Mu'tazilah and some of the theologians, who held that the existence of this category, and likewise the category mentioned just above, is impossible. It is also possible that the Prophet ﷺ had secretly told some of his companions who were with him what he had concealed, or that the chapter of Smoke was written on his hand ﷺ, or that he wrote the verse alone on his hand, ﷺ. Both of the last two opinions were related by al-Dawudi from some scholars, as in the commentary on Sahih Muslim.

Whatever the case, Ibn al-Sayyad informed of an event that had just occurred, which the devils become aware of without eavesdropping from the sky. This is in no way a knowledge of what is in the heart. Nevertheless, he did not give a complete account of it, but reported it in the manner of the earlier soothsayers, who preceded the time of the mission and belong to the first category, in terms of deficiency.

Perhaps al-Qadi's meaning in his saying "he did not discover from the verse that he ﷺ had concealed except this incomplete wording, in the manner of the soothsayers when Satan casts to them just enough that he snatches it, etc." is to liken his state, although he belongs to the second category, to the state of those soothsayers before him who belonged to the first category. Otherwise his statement would be problematic together with what we quoted from him earlier, as is not hidden. It seems that he holds that the stoning of those who eavesdrop on hearing also occurred before the mission, but it was not on the same scale as what happened after the mission. A group of the traditionists (muhaddithun) went this way.

Some people said: When Satan snatches a snatch and a piercing shooting star follows him, he casts what he has snatched to whoever is below him before the shooting star reaches him. Then whoever is below him conveys it to the soothsayer. This hardly holds true.

It was also said: What the devils cast to the soothsayers after the mission is what they hear from the angels in the clouds (al-'anan), and this is what is meant by His words: ﴿they cast [their] hearing﴾. What they are prevented from is hearing from the angels in the sky, and this is what is meant by His words: ﴿Indeed they are removed from hearing﴾. This was argued from what al-Bukhari and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The angels speak about the matter on earth in the clouds (al-'anan, which is the cloud), and the devil overhears the word and pours it into the ear of the soothsayer as one pours into a bottle, and they add to it a hundred lies."

It is not hidden that the report contains no reference to hearing from the angels in the sky in its well-known sense, neither by negation nor by affirmation. It may be chosen to hold that the devils were only prevented after the mission from hearing what is of significance in the knowledge of the unseen from the angels of the sky or the clouds. Whoever snatched a snatch of significance was followed by the shooting star, which destroyed him and did not allow him to convey it in any way to the soothsayers. As for hearing what is not of significance, this may still occur for them, and they convey it to the soothsayers, mixing into it from falsehood what they mix. Thus where they are judged to be removed from hearing, the intended hearing is complete, significant hearing; and where they are judged to be casting hearing, the intended hearing is hearing in general, the least of what truly counts as hearing. The apparent view is that what Ibn al-Sayyad obtained was of this kind of hearing, and one hardly turns away from this. It may be said that he was of the second category of soothsaying, unless one of the three possibilities is established, and there is discussion about establishing that.

Yes, the Prophet's ﷺ saying "I have hidden" is apparent in indicating that there is something hidden in a palm or a sleeve or the like, and the verse, unless it was written, cannot be like that. For this reason those who hold that he ﷺ concealed the verse only in his heart needed to interpret "I have hidden" as "I have concealed." It may be said, though far-fetched, that the devils were prevented after the mission from hearing altogether by burning meteors that strike them.

Taking the pronoun of "they cast" as referring to the devils is weak, because the context is explaining to whom they are sent down, not describing their condition or the casting of their hearing, meaning their attentive listening, to the exalted assembly. ﴿And most of them﴾ means all of them, and the expression is used to indicate that the majority mentioned is sufficient for the purpose.

The meaning is: they listen attentively in order to hear, but they do not hear, except that ﴿and most of them are liars﴾ has been placed in the position of ﴿they do not hear﴾. Or: the casting of hearing means casting to them what the people hear from the liars. It does not follow from this that they heard it from the angels, since it is possible that they invented it from themselves by guess and conjecture and cast it to their associates, and it is not far-fetched that they are truthful in some of it.

The matter of calling it "heard" is trivial. What is transmitted in the hadith of the two Sahihs and in Ibn Mardawayh is to be understood as referring to what happened before the mission. It is said that they used to hear in general, and what is in the verse may be understood in this way, and some have gone this way. But understanding the snatching of the word in it as their guessing it through some celestial configurations and the like, so that it may be considered as occurring after the mission, is something I do not think anyone would accept. There is nothing in the story of Ibn al-Sayyad that is explicit that what he said was from hearing from the angels that the devil cast to him.

You may be inclined to find it unlikely that the angels in the sky would speak about what the Prophet ﷺ had concealed, and that the devils would ascend at the moment of the question, without delay, and eavesdrop and descend in the swiftest time with what Ibn al-Sayyad answered. That is only a kind of soothsaying.

As for the reality of the matter, according to what the eminent scholar Abd al-Rahman ibn Khaldun stated: the human soul has a readiness to strip away from humanity toward the spirituality that is above it. From this there arises a glimpse for humans of the category of the pious, through what they have been created with. They do not need in this any acquisition, nor any aid from any of the faculties, nor from any imaginings, nor from bodily actions, whether speech or movement, nor from any matter at all.

Rational division indicates that there is here another category of humans, falling short of the rank of this category by the shortfall of an opposite from its complete opposite. It is a category of humans created so that their rational faculty moves in its thinking movement by will, when the inclination toward that follows it, while it is deficient in this. So it clings, for the work of stratagem, to particular sensible or imagined things, such as transparent bodies, animal bones, rhymed prose, and whatever birds or animals appear on the left or the right. It sustains this perception and imagining, seeking aid through it in that stripping away it intends, and it acts as an escort for it. This faculty, which is the source in this category for that perception, is soothsaying. Because these souls are created with deficiency and shortcoming from perfection, their perception of particulars is greater than their perception of universals, and they are occupied with particulars, heedless of universals. For this reason the imagination in them is often at its strongest, and particulars are present and ready to them, and it is to them like a mirror in which they constantly look. The soothsayer cannot attain perfection in perceiving intelligibles, because his deficiency is innate and his revelation is satanic. The highest state of this category is that it seeks aid through speech containing rhymed prose and balance, in order to occupy itself with it away from the senses, and to some extent it becomes able to achieve that deficient stripping away. Thus there comes into its heart, from that movement, and from what escorts it of that foreign element, something that it casts upon its tongue. Sometimes it is truthful and agrees with the truth, and sometimes it lies, because it completes the matter of its deficiency with something foreign to the faculties themselves, alien to them and not suited to them. So truth and falsehood both befall it, and it is not reliable. Sometimes it resorts to conjectures and guesses, out of eagerness to attain perception, in its own claim, and to deceive the questioners.

Since the stripping away of the Prophet ﷺ from humanity and his connection with the exalted assembly occurred without any escort and without any aid from a foreign element, he was truthful in everything he brought. Truthfulness is among the distinctive qualities of prophethood. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said to Ibn al-Sayyad, when he asked him, uncovering his condition, with his words, "How does this matter come to you?" He said: "A truthful one and a liar come to me." The Prophet ﷺ said: "The matter has been mixed up for you." By this he, ﷺ, intended to deny prophethood from him, by indicating that it is something in which falsehood is in no way admissible.

It was said: "The highest state of this category is rhymed prose" because the source of rhymed prose is lighter than all other sources, whether of visible or audible things. The lightness of the source indicates the nearness of that stripping away and connection, and the distance in it from weakness in general. The sciences of the soothsayers are not confined to what comes from the devils; rather, just as some come from the devils, some come from themselves through their partial stripping away and their connection in general, by means of some causes, with a world in which future events and others are not hidden. Thus the cutting off of news of the sky from the devils after the mission, through stoning, if it is granted, does not indicate the cutting off of soothsaying.

Then, if these soothsayers lived in the era of prophethood, they would recognize the truthfulness of the Prophet and the evidentiary force of his miracle, because they have some measure of awareness (wijdan) of the matter of prophethood. What prevents them from faith and drives them to obstinacy is only the whisperings of greed for attaining prophethood themselves. This is what happened to Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt, for he used to hope to become a prophet. The same happened to Ibn al-Sayyad, Musaylima, and others. Sometimes those hopes are cut off and they believe in the best manner of faith, as happened to Tulayha al-Asadi and Qarib ibn al-Aswad, and they had in the Islamic conquests (al-futuhat al-islamiyya) effects that bear witness to the goodness of their faith.

It has been mentioned, in explaining the readiness of certain individuals, whether they are soothsayers or others, to report unseen matters before they occur, a lengthy discussion whose summary is that the human soul has a spiritual nature (ruhaniyya), and it possesses perception in its own essence without any intermediary. However, it is veiled from this by immersion in the body and the senses and their preoccupations, because the senses always draw it toward the outward by the bodily perception with which it was created. Sometimes it plunges from the outward to the inward, so the veil of the body is lifted for a moment, either by the property that belongs to humans absolutely, such as sleep, or by a property found in some individuals, such as the soothsayers who speak in rhymed prose (ahl al-saj'), the practitioners of casting pebbles and date stones (ahl al-turuq bil-hasa wal-nawa), those who gaze into transparent bodies such as mirrors, waters, the hearts, livers and bones of animals, and the insane may be added to them, or by religious discipline, like the people of unveiling (ahl al-kashf) among the Sufis, or by magical practice, like the people of unveiling among the Jogis. Then the soul turns at that time toward the essences above it from the higher assembly (al-mala' al-a'la), because of the connection in existence between its horizon and their horizon. Those essences are pure perception and intellects in actuality, and in them are the forms of existing things and their realities, as established in its proper place. So some of those forms become manifest to them and they acquire knowledge from them. Sometimes those perceived forms fall into the imagination, which shapes them into diverse molds, and then they return to the sense with what they have perceived, either in bare form or within its molds, and so they report it. End of quotation.

It is not hidden that this contains a line of thought akin to what the philosophers say about the higher assembly, which they often call the world of the immaterial (alam al-mujarradat), and sometimes call the world of intellects (alam al-uqul). These are commonly restricted by them to ten, but they have no proof for this restriction. Hence some of their later scholars said they are almost countless. The theologians (mutakallimun) and the verifying scholars of the earlier generations have statements on this matter that this place is too narrow to mention. I say, and none denies it except the ignorant: for Allah, glory be to Him,

[page 145]

there are special things in times, places and persons. It is not far-fetched, after the cutting off of news from heaven from the devils by meteors, that He may grant to some human souls the special property of speaking what is true, entirely or in part, together with an awareness and unveiling that gives knowledge of what they report or without that, by causing Him, glorified be He, to make them utter something, so they speak it without knowing what they report, and it agrees with reality.

This has happened to me, when I was about five years old. I came back from the kuttab to the house and began to play in it, as children do. My mother, may Allah have mercy on her, forbade me from that and ordered me to sleep so that I would wake in the morning and go to the kuttab. I said to her: "Tomorrow the vizier will be killed, and I will not go to the kuttab," which is something that hardly passes through the mind. She paid no attention to that and put me to sleep. When I woke in the morning I prepared to go, but a son of her sister came and whispered something to her that I did not hear, and her state changed, and she forbade me from going. I do not know why. I wanted to go out to the street to play with my peers, but she forbade me again. She sat, anxious of heart, seeking someone to inform her about the condition of my father, may he have mercy, since he had gone out shortly before sunrise to the school. I went out to the street when she was heedless, and I found people running and hurrying, saying that the vizier had been killed by some of his servants while he was at the dawn prayer. I returned to her hastily, delighted at the truth of my words. I had forgotten it and it had not come to my mind until I heard people talking about it.

In al-Yawaqit wal-Jawahir of al-Sha'rani, may Allah have mercy on him, in the section distinguishing miracle from soothsaying, it is stated that soothsaying consists of utterances that flow on the tongue of the soothsayer, which sometimes agree and sometimes disagree. There is in this a trace of what we have mentioned. This is what I have, and Allah knows best.

It appears, as has been said, that His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Shall I inform you﴾ and so on, is a statement brought by Him, exalted be He, to clarify the purification of the Prophet ﷺ from being one upon whom the devils descend, far be it from him, and to nullify their claim that the Qur'an is of the kind that is cast to soothsayers. In al-Bahr there is what is clear that it is in the sense of speech, i.e., "Say, O Muhammad: Shall I inform you..." and it is brought for the purification and nullification mentioned.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 224:

The words of the Most High, ﴿And the poets—the deviators follow them﴾, are brought in order to declare the Prophet (ﷺ) free of being one of the poets, may peace and blessings be upon him, and God forbid that he should be, and to refute the claim of the disbelievers that the Qur'an belongs to the category of poetry.

What is understood from "poetry" (shi'r) here is ordered, rhymed speech. For this reason many exegetes (mufassirun, sing. mufassir, one who does tafsir, i.e. Qur'anic exegesis) said: they accused him, peace and blessings be upon him, of bringing rhymed, metrical verse, to the point that they interpreted what came in the Qur'an as being metrical with minimal alteration, such as the words of the Most High, ﴿And do not kill the soul which God has forbidden﴾, which by this reckoning would be a hemistich of al-Tawil (a metre), and His words, glorified is He, ﴿Indeed, Qarun was among the people of Musa﴾, which would be of al-Madid (a metre), and His words, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿So they became such that nothing could be seen but their dwellings﴾, which would be of al-Basit (a metre), and the words of the Blessed and Exalted, ﴿Away with Ad, the people of Hud﴾, which would be of al-Wafir (a metre), and the words of the Majestic and Exalted, ﴿Send blessings upon him and greet him with peace﴾, which would be of al-Kamil (a metre), and so on through other metres that they extracted from it, from all the other bahr (metres) as well. They have also extracted from it what resembles a complete line of verse, such as the words of the Most High, ﴿And He will disgrace them, give you victory over them, and heal the breasts of a believing people﴾.

This has been criticized: they did not intend this aim in what they charged him with, peace and blessings be upon him, since it is not hidden from the dullest of non-Arabs, let alone the eloquent Arabs, that the Qur'an which he brought is not in the styles of poetry, and they only called him a poet when he brought them the Qur'an. The extraction of what has been mentioned, and the like, from it is only for the sake of its great eloquence and smoothness, and it was not revealed for the purpose of versification.

Had the possibility of extracting ordered speech from a text been taken as a criterion for speech being poetry, many children would have been poets, for much of their speech can be made to fit this. The apparent meaning is that they only intended to accuse him, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, of bringing imaginative speech that has no reality, and, since this was usually the case with poets who produce ordered speech, they described him, peace and blessings be upon him, as a poet, and what he brought as poetry. The meaning of the verse is: the poets are followed by, and imitate, and take the same path as, the deviators who stray from the sunnah (the way), who are confused about what they do and what they leave undone, and who do not keep to one course in deeds, words and states. Not so the others among the people of right guidance, who are rightly guided to the path of truth and firm upon it.

The restriction (hasr) is derived, according to al-Zamakhshari, from the construction of ﴿yattabi'uhum﴾ and so on upon "the poets", as he established in his commentary on the words of the Most High, ﴿God mocks them﴾, and His words, glorified is He, ﴿And God determines the night and the day﴾. Whoever does not see restriction in such a construction takes it from the appropriate descriptive attribute (al-wasf al-munasib), namely that deviation (al-ghawayah) has been made the cause of following, so when the cause is absent, the following is absent too.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen that they wander distraught in every valley?﴾ This is cited as evidence (istishhad) that only the misguided follow the poets, and it affirms (taqrir) that claim. The address is to everyone who is able to see, to indicate that their condition is so clear and manifest that seeing it is not restricted to one observer rather than another. The plural pronoun refers to the poets. That is: Have you not seen that the poets, in every valley of the valleys of idle talk and gossip, in every ravine of the ravines of fancy and imagination, and on every path of the paths of error and misguidance, wander aimlessly on their faces, not guided to any specific road among the roads, but bewildered in the deserts of deviation and foolishness, and lost in the wilderness of arrogance and shamelessness? Their habit is tearing apart protected honour, defaming pure and noble lineages, amorous verse concerning forbidden women, erotic poetry, flagrant indecency, and oscillating between the two extremes of excess and deficiency in praise and satire.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 226:

﴿And that they say what they do not do﴾ — of deeds — being indifferent to the blame that follows from it. How, then, could it be imagined that one would follow them in that path, join them, and be counted in their line, when his sacred precinct is far removed from the approach of any trace of being characterised by any of the matters mentioned, and who is characterised by the noble qualities of excellence, adorned with the beautiful morals of nobility, possessor of all sacred perfections, and attained the whole of the lofty human attributes; firmly established upon the most upright method, steadfastly upon the straight path, such that the sound intellect sees in him no flaw; speaking every right matter, calling to the path of God, the Mighty, the Praiseworthy; supported by overwhelming miracles and manifest signs, filled with the various kinds of brilliant wisdom and the sorts of brilliant knowledge, standing by itself in a fine arrangement and an excellent style, which has rendered incapable every skilled orator and rebuked every consummate enchanter.

Now, it has been said concerning his exemption — may God's blessings and peace be upon him — from being one of the poets: "Indeed, the followers of the poets are the deviators, and his followers, upon them be blessings and peace, are not like that."

This has been objected to: there is no doubt that to explain his not being among them by the fact that his followers are not deviators is something not befitting his lofty station. It was also said: the plural pronoun refers to the deviators. This has been objected to on the ground that the ones spoken of are the poets. And it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, that the deviators are the transmitters who memorize the poetry of the poets and narrate it from them, delighting in it.

In another report from him, they are those who admire their poetry, even if they have not memorized it. And from Mujahid and Qatadah: they are the devils.

It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the verse was revealed concerning the poets of the polytheists: 'Abdullah ibn al-Zib'ari, Hubayrah ibn Wahb al-Makhzumi, Musafi' ibn 'Abd Manaf, Abu 'Izzah al-Jumahi, and Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt. They said: "We say the same as Muhammad says." They used to satirise him, and the Bedouins of their people would gather around them to listen to their poetry and their lampoons. They are the deviators whom those (Bedouins) follow.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh also related from him that he said: Two men engaged in mutual lampooning during the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ, one of them from the Ansar and the other from another people, and each of them had with him deviants of his people — who were the foolish — so God Most High revealed ﴿And the poets﴾ and the verses that follow. There is some doubt about the soundness of this report. The apparent meaning from the context is that the verses were revealed in response to the disbelievers who said what they said about the Qur'an.

ʿIsa ibn ʿAmr read "al-shuʿarāʾa" (الشُّعَرَاءَ) in the accusative, on the basis of the construction of the verb with a pronoun (ishtighal). As-Sulami and al-Hasan, in one of the reports from him, read "yatbaʿuhum" (يَتْبَعُهُمْ) with a light (unshaddated) form.

Al-Hasan and ʿAbd al-Warith, from Abu ʿAmr, read "yattabiʿhum" (يَتَّبِعْهُمُ) with shaddah and with the ʿayn sukun for lightening. They have said "ʿaḍd" (عَضْدٌ) with a sukun on the ḍad, so they changed the ḍammah that comes after a fathah; therefore changing it when it comes after a kasrah is more fitting. Harun reported a fathah on the ʿayn from some of them, and Abu Hayyan found this problematic. It was also said that it too is for lightening, and its preference over the sukun is because the purpose is achieved by it, together with the fact that it observes the original in general, since between the two vowels there is a homogeneous kinship, which is not the case between a ḍammah and a sukun. This is strange, as is not hidden.

﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds, remember Allah often, and defend themselves after being wronged.﴾ This is an exception for the righteous believing poets, who remember Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, often, and whose poetry is mostly about tawhid (affirming the oneness of God), praising Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, urging obedience, wisdom and admonition, renouncing the world, warning against inclining towards it, being deceived by its adornments or captivated by its perishable pleasures, encouraging what is with Allah the Exalted, and spreading the excellence of His Messenger ﷺ, praising him and mentioning his miracles, so that his love penetrates the hearts of the listeners and their desire to follow him increases. It also includes spreading praise of his family, his Companions and the righteous of his community for the same purpose. If at some times they did produce satire, it was by way of defending themselves against those who had satirized them, without transgression or excess, as indicated by the reading of some of them: "and defended themselves with the like of what they were wronged with."

It has also been said that the intended ones excepted are the believing poets who used to defend the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and confront the satirists of the polytheists. This is supported by what Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah, that this verse was revealed concerning a group of the Ansar who satirized the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, among them Ka'b ibn Malik, Abdullah ibn Rawahah and Hassan ibn Thabit. Al-Suddi related something similar.

It is also supported by what a group related from Abu Hasan Salim al-Barrad, who said: When the verse "And the poets..." was revealed, Abdullah ibn Rawahah, Hassan ibn Thabit and Ka'b ibn Malik came weeping and said: "O Messenger of Allah, Allah the Exalted has revealed this verse, and He knows that we are poets; we are ruined." Then Allah the Exalted revealed: "Except those who believe..." etc. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ called them and recited it to them. You know that the lesson is drawn from the generality of the wording, not from the particularity of the occasion of revelation.

Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn Asakir related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he recited the words of Allah the Exalted "Except those who believe" to the end of the attributes, and said: They are Abu Bakr, Umar, Ali and Abdullah ibn Rawahah. Perhaps this is from restricting it to some of what the wording indicates, for something has come from him in some narrations that indicates generality.

Furthermore, the verse has been used as evidence for the blameworthiness of poetry, of exaggeration in praise and satire and its other arts, and for its permissibility in asceticism, good manners and noble character, and for the permissibility of satire for one who has been wronged, as a form of defence. So it is said.

Know that poetry is a branch of speech: its good is good and its bad is bad. In a hadith: "Indeed, there is wisdom in some poetry."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ heard poetry and approved of it. "He ﷺ said to Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him: 'Satirize them — meaning the polytheists — for the Spirit of Holiness (Ruh al-Quds) will help you.'" In another narration: "Satirize them, and Jibril is with you."

[Page 148]

Ibn Sa'd related from Ibn Buraydah that Jibril, peace be upon him, helped Hassan with seventy verses in his eulogy of the Prophet ﷺ.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari in al-Tarikh, Abu Ya'la and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ka'b ibn Malik that he said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Allah the Exalted has revealed what He has revealed concerning the poets, so how do you view it?" He ﷺ said: "The believer struggles with his sword and his tongue. By Him in whose hand my soul is, what you pelt them with is like the spraying of arrows."

Ibn Sa'd related from Muhammad ibn Sirin: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said one night while they were on a journey: 'Where is Hassan ibn Thabit?' He said: 'At your service, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'Recite.' So he began reciting to him, and he listened until he finished his recitation. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'This is more painful to them than the impact of arrows.'"

It is narrated from Hisham ibn Urwah, from his father, from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that "the Prophet ﷺ built a pulpit for Hassan ibn Thabit in the mosque, on which he recited poetry."

Al-Daylami related from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, in a marfu' report: "The poets who die in Islam, Allah the Exalted will command them to compose poetry with which the wide-eyed houris will sing to their husbands in Paradise; and those who died in polytheism will call for woe and perdition in the Fire."

Each of the Rightly-Guided Caliphs, may Allah be pleased with them all, recited poetry, and so did many of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. From the poetry of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him:

Did the phantom of Salma in the valleys of al-Batha' keep you awake, and a matter in the tribe that has happened?
You see from Luayy a faction that neither admonition nor the sending of a caller can turn from disbelief.
A truthful Messenger came to them, but they denied him and said: "You will not remain among us."
And when we invited them to the truth, they turned their backs and snarled like the snarling of the panting dogs that dwell in holes.
How often have we struck among them with a kinsman's blood, and abandoning piety is a thing that for them is no mere loss.
So if they return from their disbelief and their disobedience, the lawful good things are not like the foul ones.
And if they ride their insolence and their error, the punishment of Allah will not be far from them.
We are men from the stock of Ghalib, to whom belongs the honour in its noble branches.
So may the Lord of the dancing women at evening be more fitting for the lean, swift camels that are driven over the rough ground.
Like the dark-eyed gazelles around Makkah, kneeling, coming down to the water of the well with its many barriers.
If they do not soon return from their error — and I am not one who breaks an oath sworn one day.
A raid will surely fall upon them, one that brings true punishment, that makes the pure women, the menstruating ones, unlawful.
It leaves corpses around which birds gather, and the disbelievers show no more mercy than the son of Harith.
So convey to the Banu Sahm a message from you, and to every ingrate who seeks evil, a searcher.
If you tarnish my honour by your bad opinion, I am not disgraced in your honour.

From the poetry of Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, who was the most discerning of his time in poetry and the most penetrating in knowledge of it:

Ka'b threatened me three times, and the one who counts them is counting; and there is no doubt that the word is what Ka'b said.
It is not the fear of death that troubles me, for I am mortal; but the fear of sin is what follows sin.

And his saying, which is also attributed to al-A'war al-Thaqafi:

Take it easy, for affairs are in the hand of God and their decrees are His.
So what is forbidden will not reach you, and what is commanded will not fall short of you.

And from him, when he wore a new cloak and people looked at him; it is also attributed to Waraqah ibn Nawfal, from some verses:

Nothing of what you see whose freshness remains: God remains, while wealth and children perish.
The treasures of Hurmuz did not avail him one day, nor did 'Ad, who sought eternity, live forever.
Nor Sulayman, when the winds ran for him, and mankind and jinn came and went among them.
There is a pool there, reached without falsehood; it must be reached one day, as they reached it.

From the poetry of Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him:

The self-sufficiency of the soul suffices it until it restrains it; and though poverty bites it, it does not harm it.

From the poetry of Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, who was excellent in it, to the point that it was said he was the most poetic of the Caliphs, may Allah be pleased with them all. He mentions Hamdan and their support for him at Siffin:

When I saw the horses crowded with spears, their forelocks and reddened necks bleeding.
And dust rose into the sky as if it were the haze of a cloudy day clothed in darkness.
The son of Hind called out to Kulla' and Himyar, and Kindah to Lakhm and the tribe of Judham.
I turned to Hamdan, those who are the true men, when fate befalls me, my shield and my arrows.
So a band of Hamdan's horsemen answered me, knights of Hamdan, not base men.
They plunged into its flame and scattered its sparks, and in battle they were like drinkers of wine.
So if I were a gatekeeper at the gate of Paradise, I would say to Hamdan: "Enter in peace."

They gathered what was attributed to him, may Allah be pleased with him, of poetry in a large diwan, but only a little of it is authentic.

From the poetry of his son al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with them both, when he went out to his companions dyed with henna:

We blacken its tops, but its roots refuse; I wish that what blackens of it were the root.

From the poetry of al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with him, when his brother al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, rebuked him about his wife:

By your life, I truly love a home in which Sakinah and al-Rabab dwell.
I love them both and spend most of my wealth, and for the blamer there is no reproach in my sight.

From the poetry of Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with her, which she said on the day of the death of her father, peace be upon him:

What would it matter to one who smells the dust of Ahmad, if he never smells precious perfumes for the rest of time?
Calamities have poured upon me, which if they had been poured upon the days, they would have turned into nights.

From the poetry of al-Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, on the day of Hunayn, boasting of his steadfastness with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ:

Has my wedding feast, my deceit and my position in the valley of Hunayn reached you, while the spears were being lowered?
And my saying when the soul surged with fear, and heads rolled and forearms were cut off.
And how I turned back the horses when they were charging at Zawra', giving with both hands and withholding.
Seven of us helped the Messenger of Allah in war, while those who had fled fled from him, and they were put to flight.

From the poetry of his son Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with them both:

When the troubles of worry visit a young man and he occupies his thoughts with the night, and the night is oppressive.
And he came to me early in the morning seeking a need, which no one but me could fulfil, and no one could help him from the misfortune of time.
I relieved his worry with my wealth from his situation, and a nocturnal worry that conversed with him departed from him.
And he had a favour upon me by his opinion that I am good, and I am grateful to the one who thought well of me.

And so on, as far as you wish.

It is not the case, as some have said, that any man or woman of the Banu Abd al-Muttalib did not compose poetry — far be it, the Prophet ﷺ, so that this would be more effective in his mission, peace be upon him.

There is also much poetry from the great Successors and those after them, among the leading imams of religion and jurists of the Muslims. Among it is the saying of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him:

One who exhausts the camels, yet rests in a land towards which death is seeking him in that very land.
And one who laughs while death hangs over his head; if he knew the unseen, he would die of grief.
Whoever has not been given knowledge of the continuation of tomorrow, does not think about provision for the day after tomorrow.

Thorough investigation of this subject requires a separate book, and what has been mentioned suffices.

Many other great figures have also praised it. It is reported from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he wrote to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari: "Order those under you to learn poetry, for it indicates noble character, sound judgement, and knowledge of lineages." And from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face: "Poetry is the scale of the intellects."

Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, used to say: "If you read something of the Book of Allah the Exalted and do not understand it, seek it in the poetry of the Arabs, for poetry is the register of the Arabs."

And what Ahmad and Ibn Abi Shaybah related from Abu Sa'id, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "While we were travelling with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, a poet appeared reciting, and the Prophet ﷺ said: 'For one of you to have his belly filled with pus is better than for it to be filled with poetry.'" Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, interpreted this as referring to poetry containing obscenity. A similar report is narrated from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 26, verse 227 (part 2 of 3):

Al-Kalbi narrated from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas, from Aisha, that it reached her that Abu Hurayrah was narrating from the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and grant him peace): "It is better for one of you to have his belly filled with pus than to have it filled with poetry," meaning poetry in which he (the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace) was satirized. Al-Murshidi mentioned this in his fatawa, citing the book *Bustan al-Zahidin*. It is clear that the stated meaning is far-fetched given the wording "filled," since a little or a lot of what contains obscenity or satire against the Master of Creation (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) is equal.

How well al-Mawardi said: "Poetry in the speech of the Arabs is recommended, permissible, or forbidden. What is recommended is that which warns against this world and encourages the Hereafter and urges noble character. What is permissible is that which is free of obscenity or falsehood. What is forbidden is of two kinds: falsehood and obscenity, and both are a defect in the one who composes it. As for the one who recites it, if he recites it under compulsion, it is not a defect; if he recites it by choice, he is defective."

Al-Ruyani followed him in this and made poetry containing satire of a Muslim, whether truthful or false, forbidden as well. A group agreed with him, except that the sin of the truthful is lighter than the sin of the liar, as al-Qamuli said, and the sin of the one who relates it (is lighter), according to al-Rafi'i, than the sin of the one who recites it.

Page 151

Al-Adhra'i said: "This is not absolute. Rather, it applies when the one who relates and the one who recites are equal. But if he recited it and did not spread it, and the one who relates it spread it, then his sin is greater without doubt." By the qualifier "Muslim" he excluded satire of a disbeliever, for that has its own details.

Some scholars also distinguished satire of a Muslim. This is because many scholars allowed satire of the disbeliever in general, citing the Prophet's (ﷺ) command to Hassan and others to satirize the polytheists. Some of them said: this applies to disbelievers in general, and likewise a hostile combatant (harbi), whether dead or alive, provided he has no protected relative who would be harmed by it. As for a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under protection), a mu'ahad (one under treaty), or a harbi who has a dhimmi or Muslim relative who would be harmed by it, satirizing him is not permitted, as al-Adhra'i, Ibn al-Imad and others stated. They said: the satire of Hassan, even though it targeted a specific person, was directed at a harbi; and even if we concede otherwise, it was a defense of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and so it is among the acts of devotion, let alone the permissible.

Al-Ghazali added the innovator (mubtadi') to the category of the harbi, and a group followed him. So satirizing the innovator for his innovation is permitted, but only for a legitimate purpose, such as warning others against him. Ibn al-Imad permitted satirizing the apostate, but not one who abandons prayer or the married adulterer. What he said about the apostate is clear, for he is like the harbi, and even worse. As for the latter two, this applies where they do not openly flaunt their sin. But one who openly flaunts his sinfulness may be satirized only for that which he openly flaunts, because backbiting him about that alone is permitted.

Al-Balqini said: "The more correct view is that it is forbidden to satirize the open sinner mentioned, even for the purpose of deterring him, because he may repent while the stigma of the circulating poetry remains upon him. This is not the case with the disbeliever when he accepts Islam."

It is answered that his open defiance of sin and his indifference to people and their talk about him has made him one whose honor is not respected or observed. He has effectively forfeited the sanctity of his own person with respect to what he openly flaunts, so he is not concerned with the stigma remaining upon him.

Yes, if it were said that reciting it is forbidden after repentance, when it would harm him or his Muslim or dhimmi relative, or after his death if it would harm any of those mentioned, that would not be far-fetched.

A group also mentioned that among the forbidden is poetry containing tashbib (amatory verse) about a youth, even an unspecified one, with mention that he is the lover of the speaker; or about a specific non-related woman, even if he does not describe her obscenely; or about an unnamed woman while describing her obscenely. They did not distinguish between composing such verse and reciting it. Some of them considered specification in the case of a youth as in the case of a woman, so tashbib about an unspecified person is not forbidden.

Al-Adhra'i said: "This is the closer view, and the first is very weak." He also said: "It is certain that if he composes amatory verse about his own wife and mentions nothing but love and longing, or mentions only some of the obvious comparisons, it is not harmful. Likewise if he mentions an unknown woman and mentions nothing evil."

In al-Ihya', there is a question about the prohibition of tashbib with descriptions such as the cheeks, the side-locks, and other attributes of women. The sound view is that composing it and reciting it, aloud or not, is not forbidden. The listener should understand it as referring to a specific woman; if he applies it to his own wife, it is permitted, but if he applies it to another, he is sinning by that application. One who has this description should avoid listening to it. Some virtuous scholars mentioned that what is forbidden to compose is not always forbidden to transmit. For in the accounts of the military campaigns (maghazi), the poems of the disbelievers who satirized the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) have been transmitted, and no one has objected to this.

It has been narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) permitted the poetry that the poets exchanged on the days of Badr, Uhud and others, except the qasida of Ibn Abi al-Salt that rhymed in ha'. End of quote.

Al-Adhra'i said: "There is no doubt about this when it contains no obscenity and no harm to any living or dead Muslim, and when no need calls for it. The scholars have censured Jarir and al-Farazdaq for their mutual satire, but they did not censure one who cited such verse as evidence in grammar (i'rab) or other branches of the science of language. The statements of the imams must be understood to refer to something other than this, namely what is customary among the people of play and idleness, and to the recitation of the poetry of contemporary poets when composing it is forbidden, for it contains nothing but harm, or slander against the living, or the disparagement of the living regarding their dead, or the mention of the faults of the dead, and the like. It is not something cited as evidence in language or anything else. Thus nothing remains except playing with people's honor." Some added that poetry containing indirect allusion (ta'ridh) is also forbidden, and they treated indirect satire as equivalent to explicit satire. This has a sound basis.

Another said: "Poetry that contains boasting is blameworthy, and a little of it is like a lot of it. The truth is that if it includes a legitimate purpose, there is no harm in it. The early generations (al-salaf) had much poetry of this kind, and some of it has already been mentioned to you." Most scholars interpreted the previous report as applying to a case where poetry dominated a person and possessed him, to the point that he was occupied with it instead of the Qur'an, jurisprudence and the like. This is why the word "filling" is used. The conclusion is that what is blameworthy is the heart being filled with poetry so that it has no room for anything else and does not turn to anything else.

The report does not condemn composing or reciting poetry for a legitimate religious need. Otherwise there would be a contradiction between it and the sound reports that indicate the permissibility of this, and those are too numerous to count and too far from accepting interpretation, as is not hidden.

As for what is narrated from Imam al-Shafi'i, his saying:

*If not for poetry, which disgraces scholars,*
*I would today be the greatest poet after Labid.*

This is to be understood in the same way the majority understood the report, otherwise what he said is itself poetry. Similar to this is the statement of our shaykh, Ala' al-Din Ali Effendi (may Allah shelter him with His mercy), addressing the foremost of the viziers in Constantinople, Dawud Pasha, in some verses:

*Even if its caller were to accept poetry as a virtue,*
*I would stand between its composer and its reciter.*

That said, there will come, if Allah the Exalted wills, further discussion related to this topic when we reach His saying: ﴿And We did not teach him poetry, nor is it fitting for him﴾.

Among the subtle points: Sulayman ibn Abd al-Malik heard the saying of al-Farazdaq:

*So they spent the night beside me, prostrate,*
*and I spent the night unlocking the seals of the seal.*

He said to him: "The prescribed punishment (hadd) has become obligatory upon you." He replied: "O Commander of the Faithful, Allah the Exalted has averted the punishment from me by His saying: ﴿And that they say what they do not do﴾."

﴿And those who have done wrong will know what overturning they will be overturned to﴾. This is a severe threat and an emphatic warning, because of what the word "will know" (sa-ya'lamu) carries of the awfulness of its object, and because of the generality and universality in "those who have done wrong." The righteous predecessors used to admonish one another with it. Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) concluded his will with it when he appointed Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) as successor. He ordered Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) to write, during his final illness at that time:

*In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.*

*This is what Abu Bakr ibn Abi Quhafa has bequeathed at the last of his time in this world and the first of his time in the Hereafter, at the moment when the disbeliever comes to believe, the wicked is guarded against, and the liar is believed: I have appointed Umar ibn al-Khattab as your successor. If he acts justly, that is my assumption of him and my hope in him. If he deviates and changes, I have no knowledge of the unseen. I intended only good, and for every person is what he has earned. ﴿And those who have done wrong will know what overturning they will be overturned to﴾.*

Interpreting "wrong-doing" (zulm) as disbelief, though it is common in several places in the noble Qur'an, is, as has been said, not the most suitable here, because of His saying: ﴿after they were wronged﴾. Al-Tibi said: the context of the verse, after mention of the polytheists who harmed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the hardships he suffered from them, as passed at the beginning of the surah, supports interpreting wrong-doing as disbelief.

Muhyi al-Sunnah (al-Baghawi) transmitted: "Those who have done wrong" means those who associated partners with Allah and satirized the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Ibn Abbas and Ibn Arqam, from al-Hasan, read: "what overturning (munfalat) they will be turned to" (yanfalitun), with the letter fa and the letter ta with two dots above, from infilat meaning escape. The meaning is that the wrongdoers hope to escape from the punishment of Allah the Exalted, but they will come to know that they have no way of escaping. Here "sa-ya'lamu" is suspended (mu'allaqah), and "ayya" is an interrogative modifying "munqalab," and its governing element is "yanqalibuna," and the clause fills the place of the two objects. So says al-Bahr.

Abu al-Baqa said: "Ayya munqalabin" is a modifying accusative of an elided verbal noun, and the governing word is "yanqalibuna," meaning "they will turn over a turning," and "sa-ya'lamu" does not govern it, because the interrogative is not governed by what precedes it. This was objected to, saying it is confused, because when "ayya" is used as a qualifier it is not interrogative, and they have stated explicitly that the qualifier is the counterpart of the interrogative. The detailed analysis of the categories of "ayy" is to be sought in the books of grammar. And Allah knows best.

* * *

Among what has been said about some verses by way of allusion (isharah):

(Ta Sin Mim): Al-Junayd said: "The ta is the joy of the repentant in the field of mercy, the sin is the delight of the knowers in the field of union, and the mim is the station of the lovers in the field of nearness."

It has also been said: "The ta is the purity of the foot from the defilements of occurrence, the sin is the splendor of His Exalted attributes which are unveiled in the mirrors of proof, and the mim is His glory, glorified is He, which appeared with the quality of radiance in the hearts of the people of recognition."

It has also been said: "The ta is the purity of the heart of His Prophet (ﷺ) from attachments to the two worlds, the sin is his (ﷺ) lordship over the prophets and messengers (peace be upon them), and the mim is his (ﷺ) witnessing of the beauty of the Lord of the worlds."

It has been said: "The ta is the Tree of Tuba, the sin is the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary, and the mim is Muhammad (ﷺ)." And other things have been said.

﴿Perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief that they do not become believers﴾ etc. In this there is an allusion to the perfection of his (ﷺ) compassion for his community, and that eagerness for the faith of the disbeliever does not prevent the preceding wisdoms.

﴿And when your Lord called out to Musa: "Go to the wrongdoing people, the people of Pharaoh. Will they not fear Allah?"﴾ up to the end of the story. In this there is an allusion to the goodness of mutual support in religious interests, to dealing gently with the astray in binding him by decisive proofs, and that it is not fitting to neglect honoring one whom you raised as a child and then saw Allah the Exalted grant him, out of His grace, what He granted him as an adult.

**Page 154**

Some of them said: Indeed, in it (the story of Moses) there is an allusion to what is within the souls. Moses is taken as an allusion to the Moses of the heart, Pharaoh to the Pharaoh of the self (nafs), his people to the soul-based qualities (al-sifat al-nafsaniyya), and the Children of Israel to the spiritual qualities (al-sifat al-ruhaniyya). The deed (al-fi'la) is taken as an allusion to killing the Copt of desire, and the staff as an allusion to the staff of remembrance, meaning "There is no god but God." The hand is taken as an allusion to the hand of power, and its being white as an allusion to its being supported by divine support. The onlookers (al-nazirin) are taken as an allusion to the people of unveiling (arbab al-kashf), who see by the light of God, Exalted. The magicians are taken as an allusion to human attributes and blameworthy characters. The people are taken as an allusion to the human-nature attributes (al-sifat al-nasutiyya), the reward as an allusion to animal portions (al-huzuz al-hayawaniyya), the ropes as an allusion to the ropes of stratagems, and the staves as an allusion to the staves of deceptions and imaginings. The cities are taken as an allusion to the stages of the self (atwar al-nafs), and so on.

They followed this same method of allusion throughout the other stories. They took Abraham as an allusion to the heart, his father and his people as an allusion to the spirit (al-ruh) and what is generated from it, and the idols as an allusion to whatever suits the natures among the higher and lower things, and so on, of what is not hidden from one who has a heart or who gives ear while being a witness.

The Greatest Shaykh (Ibn 'Arabi), may his secret be sanctified, has a wondrous discourse on these stories, and whoever wishes it should seek it in his books. He, may his secret be sanctified, is among those who held that the sin of Abraham, peace be upon him, which he meant by his saying ﴿And the One from Whom I hope He will forgive my sin on the Day of Recompense﴾, was his attributing illness to himself in his saying ﴿and when I am ill, it is He who heals me﴾. He, may his secret be sanctified, also mentioned that he met Abraham, peace be upon him, and asked him about his intent in it, and he answered him with what he mentioned.

He said, in the chapter on the secrets of zakat in the Futuhat (al-Futuhat al-Makkiyya): Indeed, the saying of the Messenger (ﷺ), ﴿My reward is only from the Lord of the worlds﴾, does not detract from the perfection of his servitude. For that saying is so that it may be known that every sincere deed seeks a reward by its very nature, and this does not take the servant out of the attributes of servitude. The servant is in the form of a hired worker, but he is not truly a hired worker, since the master does not hire his own servant but hires a stranger. Rather, the deed itself necessitates the wage, and it does not take it; it is the doer, who is the servant, who takes it. So he is the one who receives the wage from God, Exalted. Thus he resembles the hired worker in receiving the wage, but differs from him in being hired. End quote.

He also verified this in the three hundred and sixteenth chapter of the Futuhat, and he mentioned in the four hundred and seventeenth chapter that the reward of every prophet is according to the measure of the hardship he suffered from those who opposed him.

﴿The devils did not bring it down﴾ ﴿and it is not fitting for them, nor are they able﴾ ﴿indeed they are removed from hearing it﴾. In this there is an allusion that the devil has no capacity to bear the Qur'an, because he was created from fire, and fire has no capacity to bear light. Do you not see how the fire of Hellfire cries out for help when the believer passes by it, saying: "Pass on, O believer, for your light has extinguished my flame"? Likewise, it has no power to hear it.

This applies to the first level of its manifestation, so it is not objected that, according to what has been mentioned, it would follow that the devils cannot hear the verses of the Qur'an when we recite them, nor memorize them, and this is not so. Yes, it has been mentioned that they cannot hear the Verse of the Throne (ayat al-kursi) and the end of Surat al-Baqara; this is due to a special property in those two.

﴿And warn your nearest kindred﴾. In this there is an allusion that lineage, if faith is not joined to it, benefits nothing. And since the veil of kinship is thick, the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to warn his nearest kindred. ﴿And lower your wing to those among the believers who follow you﴾: they are the people of the spiritual kinship (al-nasab al-ma'nawi), which is closer than the physical kinship (al-nasab al-suwari), as Ibn al-Farid, may his secret be sanctified, indicated with his saying:

A kinship closer in the law of passion between us
than a kinship from my two parents.

And I praise God, Exalted, as is due to Him, that He has made me among those who are successful in both kinships, in that He has granted me faith and made me among the descendants of the Master of the Two Worlds (ﷺ). So I am, through my father's mother, a descendant of al-Hasan, and through my father, a descendant of al-Husayn, may God be pleased with them both:

A lineage as if upon it is light
from the sunlight of forenoon, and from the cleft of dawn a pillar.

And God, Mighty and Majestic, is the Lord of Kindness, the Bestower of favors of every kind upon mankind. May blessings and peace be upon the Master of the worlds, and upon his family and all his companions.
